Core must know Important asked often Tough where senior interviews are decided ★★★★★ interview frequency

1️⃣ JVM & Memory

Everything else in Java sits on top of the JVM. Interviewers use this section to separate "writes Java" from "understands Java": class loading, where objects live, and how garbage collection actually works.

Class Loading & Parent Delegation

Why interviewers ask: it explains ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError, why two copies of the same class can be "different", and how app servers and Spring Boot isolate classes.

Loading a class happens in three phases: Loading (read bytes → Class object), Linking (verify bytecode, prepare static fields with defaults, resolve symbolic refs) and Initialization (run static initializers, in order). Classes are loaded lazily: on first active use.

Three built-in loaders form a hierarchy: Bootstrap (core java.base, native), Platform (JDK modules like java.sql), Application (your classpath). Analogy: a junior engineer who receives a request first asks their manager, who asks their director; only if nobody above can handle it does the junior do it themselves. That is parent delegation: every loader asks its parent first, so core classes can never be shadowed by a malicious java.lang.String on the classpath.

Interview angle: "Can you override java.lang.String by putting your own on the classpath?" No: Bootstrap answers first and the app loader never gets to define it. "Why does Tomcat break delegation?" Web-app loaders look locally first so each WAR can ship its own library versions.
ErrorWhenTypical cause
ClassNotFoundExceptionChecked; thrown by Class.forName/loadClassClass simply isn't on the classpath (missing jar)
NoClassDefFoundErrorError; class was present at compile timeStatic initializer failed earlier, or the jar was removed after compiling

Pitfalls

  • Static initializers run once per loader; a failure is remembered and later uses throw NoClassDefFoundError.
  • Class loader leaks: redeploying a web app while a thread (or ThreadLocal) still references its classes keeps the whole loader alive → Metaspace OOM.

Likely follow-ups

  • What triggers initialization? (new, static method call, static field write, reflection, subclass init, main class.)
  • How does Spring Boot's fat jar load nested jars? (Custom LaunchedURLClassLoader.)
  • Where does class metadata live? (Metaspace since Java 8; PermGen before.)

Java 8 vs 17

Java 9 renamed the Extension loader to Platform loader and stopped using URLClassLoader for the app loader, so casting ClassLoader.getSystemClassLoader() to URLClassLoader now fails.

Runtime Data Areas: Stack vs Heap vs Metaspace

Why interviewers ask: it underpins "is Java pass-by-value?", StackOverflowError vs OutOfMemoryError, and why local variables are thread-safe.

Each thread gets its own PC register and JVM stack of frames (one per method call: local variables, operand stack, return address). All threads share the heap (every object and array) and Metaspace (class metadata, static fields' home). References live on the stack; the objects they point to live on the heap.

public class Demo {
    static int counter = 0;                 // Metaspace (static)

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int x = 10;                         // primitive → stack frame of main
        Order o = new Order("A1");          // ref on stack, object on heap
        update(o, x);
        System.out.println(o.id + " " + x); // prints "A1-upd 10"
    }

    static void update(Order ord, int n) {
        ord.id = ord.id + "-upd";           // mutates the shared heap object
        n = 99;                             // only this frame's copy changes
        ord = new Order("B2");              // rebinding local ref: caller unaffected
    }
}
  1. Entering main: the frame holds x directly.
  2. new Order allocates on the heap; o is just a reference stored in the frame.
  3. Calling update pushes a new frame. The reference value and the int value are copied: pass-by-value.
  4. Through the copied reference we mutate the one shared object, so main will see it.
  5. n = 99 changes only this frame's slot; x in main is untouched.
  6. Rebinding ord points this frame's slot at a new object. o in main still points at @1.
  7. Frame popped. Output: A1-upd 10. @2 is unreachable and will be collected.
AreaScopeHoldsError when fullTune with
JVM stackPer threadFrames: locals, operand stackStackOverflowError-Xss
HeapSharedAll objects, arrays, String poolOutOfMemoryError: Java heap space-Xms -Xmx
MetaspaceShared, native memoryClass metadata, method bytecode, statics' homeOutOfMemoryError: Metaspace-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize
Code cacheSharedJIT-compiled native codeJIT stops compiling (slow)-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize

Pitfalls

  • "Java is pass-by-reference" — wrong. It copies the reference value. Rebinding a parameter never affects the caller.
  • Deep recursion (e.g. naive tree DFS on a 1M-node linked chain) overflows the thread stack: switch to an explicit stack.

Likely follow-ups

  • Where do static fields live? (Metaspace holds the class; static object instances are on the heap.)
  • Are string literals on the heap? (Yes, in the heap-resident string pool since Java 7.)
  • What is escape analysis? (JIT can scalar-replace objects that never escape a method, effectively allocating on the stack.)

Compilation Pipeline & Bytecode

Why interviewers ask: "Is Java compiled or interpreted?" is a warm-up that reveals whether you know the JVM runs bytecode, not your source, and that the machine code is produced at runtime.

javac turns .java into .class files containing platform-neutral bytecode: a stack-machine instruction set (aload_0, invokevirtual, getfield…). At runtime the JVM first interprets that bytecode, counts how often each method and loop runs, and hands hot code to the JIT, which emits native machine code. Analogy: a script is translated once into a universal stage language; every theatre (OS/CPU) then performs it in its own accent, rehearsing the popular scenes until they are fast.

Every class file carries a constant pool: a table of strings, numbers, class names and method signatures that instructions reference by index. That is why "abc" literals are shared, why invokevirtual #12 needs resolution at link time, and where lambdas' invokedynamic bootstrap entries live. Generics are erased here: List<String> is just List in the descriptor, with a Signature attribute kept for reflection.

$ javap -c -p Order.class          # -c disassembles, -p includes private members
int total(int qty) {
   0: iload_1                       // push parameter qty
   1: aload_0                       // push this
   2: getfield  #7  // Field price:I
   5: imul
   6: ireturn
}
$ javap -v Order.class | grep -A3 "Constant pool"   # view the pool and its indexes
Interview angle: "Why can Kotlin and Scala call Java freely?" They compile to the same class-file format and share the constant-pool/descriptor conventions. "Why does string concatenation in a loop look different in Java 9+ bytecode?" javac emits invokedynamic to StringConcatFactory instead of a StringBuilder chain, so the JVM picks the strategy at runtime.
StageInput → outputWhenInspect with
javac.java → .class (bytecode + constant pool)Build timejavap -c -v
Interpreterbytecode → executed directly, profiling countersFirst calls of every method-XX:+PrintCompilation shows what leaves it
JIT (C1/C2)hot bytecode → native code in the code cacheAfter invocation/back-edge thresholds-XX:+PrintCompilation, JITWatch

Pitfalls

  • Bytecode is not "half compiled to machine code"; -Xint runs pure interpreted and is 10–50× slower, proving where the speed really comes from.
  • Constant-pool limits are real: a class can hold at most 65,535 pool entries and a method at most 64 KB of bytecode ("code too large" from huge generated classes).

Likely follow-ups

  • Is the bytecode verified? (Yes, during linking; skipping it with -Xverify:none is deprecated.)
  • What is the "magic number"? (Every class file starts with 0xCAFEBABE, then the major version: 61 for Java 17.)
  • Where does a lambda's body go? (A private synthetic method in the same class, bound at first call via invokedynamic + LambdaMetafactory.)

Object Layout & Allocation: Header, Compressed Oops, TLAB, Escape Analysis

Why interviewers ask: "How big is new Object()?" and "is allocation expensive?" test whether you know allocation is a pointer bump, not a malloc, and why a 33 GB heap can be slower than a 31 GB one.

Every object starts with a header: the mark word (8 bytes: identity hash, GC age bits, lock state) and a klass pointer to its class metadata (4 bytes when compressed). Fields follow, reordered by the JVM for alignment, and the whole object is padded to a multiple of 8 bytes. So new Object() is 16 bytes and new Integer(1) is 16 bytes too (12 header + 4 int); an int[0] is 16 bytes because arrays also store a length.

Compressed oops (-XX:+UseCompressedOops, on by default for heaps under ~32 GB) store references as 32-bit offsets shifted by 3, which halves reference size and improves cache hit rate. Cross the 32 GB line and references silently double, so a 34 GB heap often holds fewer objects than a 30 GB one.

Allocation is fast because each thread owns a TLAB (Thread-Local Allocation Buffer) carved out of Eden: new is a bump-the-pointer increment with no lock. Analogy: instead of queuing at the bakery counter for every slice, each thread takes a whole tray and cuts its own slices. When the JIT proves via escape analysis that an object never leaves the method (not stored in a field, not returned, not passed to an unknown call), it can skip the heap entirely and scalar-replace the object with its fields in registers.

ObjectHeaderPayloadPadded size (compressed oops)
new Object()12016 B
Integer12416 B (vs 4 B for int)
String "ab"12ref + hash + coder ≈ 1224 B + 16 B for the byte[] (Compact Strings, Java 9+)
Long[1000]161000 × 4 refs~4 KB + 1000 × 16 B boxes ≈ 20 KB (vs 8 KB for long[])
Real world: a Map<Long, Long> with 10 M entries costs roughly 10 M × (32 B node + 16 + 16 B boxes) ≈ 640 MB; a primitive-specialised map (Eclipse Collections, fastutil) holds it in ~160 MB. Measure with JOL (jol-core, ClassLayout.parseInstance(o).toPrintable()).

Pitfalls

  • Setting -Xmx33g "for headroom" disables compressed oops (check with -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal) and can shrink usable capacity.
  • Calling System.identityHashCode or synchronizing on an object writes into the mark word; biased locking that relied on it was removed in Java 15.
  • Escape analysis is defeated by anything the JIT cannot see through: storing into a collection, logging the object, or a virtual call it could not inline.

Likely follow-ups

  • How do you measure object size? (JOL; Instrumentation.getObjectSize; never Runtime.freeMemory deltas.)
  • Why are TLABs per thread and not per core? (A thread can migrate cores; the invariant that matters is "only one writer".)
  • Can Java allocate on the stack? (Not by language rule; only as a JIT optimisation via scalar replacement.)

GC Fundamentals: Reachability, Generations, Minor vs Full GC

Why interviewers ask: the single most common JVM question. They probe whether you know what gets collected (unreachable, not "unused"), why young collections are cheap, and what "stop-the-world" costs your p99 latency.

The collector starts from GC roots (each thread's stack locals, static fields, JNI handles, the classes held by live loaders) and marks everything transitively reachable. Everything else is garbage, including cycles: two objects pointing only at each other are collected, which is why Java never needed reference counting. Marking needs a consistent snapshot, so classic collectors stop the world: all Java threads are parked at a safepoint while GC threads work.

The weak generational hypothesis says most objects die young (request DTOs, iterators, boxed temporaries). So the heap is split into a Young generation (Eden plus two Survivor spaces S0/S1) and an Old generation. A minor GC only walks the young gen, copying the few live objects into the empty survivor space and bumping their age in the mark word; after MaxTenuringThreshold copies (default 15, often lowered adaptively) they are promoted to Old. Analogy: a restaurant clears every table after each seating (cheap, frequent); it only deep-cleans the whole building (expensive, rare) when the storeroom is full. A major/full GC collects Old too (and Metaspace); it is the one that produces multi-second pauses.

Minor GCs are fast because cost is proportional to live objects, not to Eden size, and because old-to-young pointers are tracked by a card table so the collector never scans the whole Old gen.

Minor (young) GCMajor / Full GC
ScopeEden + SurvivorsOld (+ young, + Metaspace for full)
TriggerEden fullOld full, promotion failure, System.gc(), Metaspace threshold
AlgorithmCopying (cost ∝ live objects)Mark-sweep-compact (cost ∝ whole heap)
Typical pausems to tens of mshundreds of ms to seconds
Log signature (Java 9+)Pause Young (Normal)Pause Full (Allocation Failure)
Interview angle: "Can you force GC?" System.gc() is a hint that most collectors honour with a full GC — disastrous in production, hence -XX:+DisableExplicitGC. "Why do long pauses appear after weeks of uptime?" Slow leaks or oversized caches fill Old until a full GC has to compact gigabytes.

Pitfalls

  • Setting a survivor space too small promotes short-lived request objects to Old, which then needs frequent full GCs — the classic "tune -Xmn, not -Xmx" fix.
  • A safepoint pause is not only GC: a thread in a long counted loop without a safepoint poll can delay everyone ("time-to-safepoint"), visible via -Xlog:safepoint.
  • Objects are freed when unreachable, not when out of scope — a local still on the stack in a long method keeps its whole graph alive.

Likely follow-ups

  • What are GC roots exactly? (Thread stacks, static fields via live loaders, JNI globals, synchronization monitors, JVM-internal structures.)
  • Why two survivor spaces? (Copying needs an empty destination; two halves let you alternate without compaction.)
  • What is a card table? (A byte per 512-byte chunk of Old, marked dirty on writes via a write barrier so minor GC scans only dirty cards for old→young refs.)

G1: Region-Based, Pause-Goal-Driven Collection

Why interviewers ask: G1 is the default since Java 9, so "what does your service run on and how do you tune it?" is really "explain G1". Regions, remembered sets, and mixed collections are the vocabulary they expect.

G1 (Garbage-First) abandons contiguous generations: the heap is a grid of equal regions (1–32 MB, ~2048 of them, -XX:G1HeapRegionSize), each dynamically labelled Eden, Survivor, Old or Humongous (an object ≥ half a region gets its own contiguous regions, allocated straight into Old). The generations still exist logically, but as sets of regions that grow and shrink.

Young collections are still stop-the-world copying, evacuating live objects from Eden/Survivor regions into fresh ones. When Old occupancy crosses -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent (default 45), G1 runs concurrent marking (SATB snapshot-at-the-beginning) alongside your threads to learn how much live data each Old region holds. Then a series of mixed collections evacuate young regions plus the Old regions with the most garbage first (hence the name), stopping when the pause budget is spent. Analogy: a hotel cleaning crew given 30 minutes per round cleans the messiest rooms first and leaves nearly-clean rooms for later.

To evacuate one region without scanning the whole heap, each region keeps a remembered set (RSet): which other regions hold pointers into it, maintained by a post-write barrier. The pause-time goal -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis (default 200 ms) is a target, not a guarantee: G1 sizes the young gen and picks how many Old regions to include per pause to hit it.

# Typical Java 17 service flags (G1 is already the default)
java -Xms4g -Xmx4g \
     -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 \
     -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=35 \
     -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=8m \
     -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/app/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=50m \
     -jar app.jar
# sample log line:
# [2.345s][info][gc] GC(12) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 512M->96M(4096M) 14.2ms
Reading that line in an interview: GC number 12, young pause, triggered by Eden exhaustion; heap went from 512 MB used to 96 MB used out of 4 GB, in 14 ms. Mixed pauses read Pause Young (Mixed); Pause Full means G1 lost its budget entirely and you should look for humongous churn or an undersized heap.

Pitfalls

  • Setting MaxGCPauseMillis=10 does not make pauses 10 ms; G1 shrinks Eden to try, causing constant young GCs and lower throughput. Keep it realistic (50–200 ms).
  • Humongous allocations (large byte buffers, huge ArrayList growth) bypass the young gen; watch -Xlog:gc+humongous, or raise region size so they are no longer humongous.
  • to-space exhausted in the log means evacuation failed and a Full GC follows: increase heap or G1ReservePercent.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is SATB? (Snapshot-at-the-beginning: a pre-write barrier records overwritten references so anything live when marking started stays marked, at the cost of some floating garbage.)
  • Is G1 fully concurrent? (No — marking is concurrent, evacuation/compaction is always stop-the-world.)
  • When would you leave G1? (Heaps of 100s of GB or sub-10 ms pause needs → ZGC; batch throughput with no latency SLA → Parallel.)

Java 8 vs 17

Java 8 defaulted to Parallel GC and G1 was still maturing; Java 9 made G1 the default (JEP 248). Java 10 parallelised the G1 Full GC fallback, Java 12 added prompt uncommit of unused regions back to the OS, and Java 17's G1 abandons "biased locking" concerns entirely. Unified logging (-Xlog) replaced -XX:+PrintGCDetails in Java 9.

ZGC & Shenandoah, and Choosing a Collector

Why interviewers ask: "Which GC would you choose and why?" checks whether you can trade throughput for latency deliberately rather than cargo-culting flags.

ZGC (production since Java 15) and Shenandoah (Red Hat, production since 15 in OpenJDK builds) do what G1 cannot: they compact concurrently, relocating live objects while application threads run. Pauses no longer scale with heap or live-set size and stay well under a millisecond on multi-terabyte heaps.

The trick is a load barrier: every reference read passes through a few instructions that check whether the object has been moved and, if so, fix up the reference on the spot. ZGC encodes that state in unused bits of the 64-bit pointer itself (colored pointers: marked0/marked1/remapped/finalizable), so no header space is needed; Shenandoah originally used a forwarding pointer in the object and now also uses a barrier-based scheme. Analogy: mail forwarding — instead of stopping the city to move everyone at once, each letter is redirected the moment someone tries to deliver it to the old address.

The cost is throughput: barriers add a few percent of CPU, and concurrent GC threads compete with your threads, so an allocation-heavy service needs headroom (ZGC in Java 17 is non-generational, so it must also mark the whole heap every cycle; generational ZGC arrived in Java 21).

CollectorFlagStrategyPauseThroughputSweet spot
Serial-XX:+UseSerialGCSingle thread, STW copy + mark-compactLong, ∝ heapBest per core1-CPU containers, CLI tools, <1 GB heaps; auto-chosen when JVM sees <2 CPUs or <1792 MB
Parallel-XX:+UseParallelGCMulti-threaded STW, generationalLong but less frequentHighestBatch/ETL, Spark executors, anything measured in total time
G1 (default)-XX:+UseG1GCRegions, concurrent mark, STW incremental evacuationTarget-driven, ~10–200 msHigh (−5–10% vs Parallel)General-purpose services, 2–64 GB heaps
ZGC-XX:+UseZGCColored pointers, fully concurrent mark + compact<1 ms regardless of heapMedium (−10–15%)Latency SLOs, huge heaps (8 MB–16 TB), trading/ads/gateways
Shenandoah-XX:+UseShenandoahGCLoad barriers, concurrent compact<10 ms typicalMediumSame as ZGC; available in Red Hat/Temurin builds, not Oracle JDK
Decision rule to say out loud: "Default to G1. If p99 latency is dominated by GC and CPU headroom exists, try ZGC and give it ~20% more heap. If it is an overnight job, use Parallel. Never hand-pick Serial unless the container has one CPU — and know that the JVM already does that for you."

Pitfalls

  • ZGC needs allocation headroom: if your threads allocate faster than it can concurrently reclaim, you get allocation stalls (logged), which look like pauses. The fix is more heap or fewer allocations, not more GC threads.
  • In Java 17 ZGC is not generational, so a young-object-heavy workload pays full-heap marking each cycle; benchmark rather than assume.
  • Colored pointers require 64-bit and disable compressed oops — a ZGC heap of the same size holds fewer objects than a G1 heap.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why does ZGC need a load barrier but G1 does not? (G1 moves objects only while the world is stopped, so no thread can observe a stale reference.)
  • What is a "floating garbage"? (Objects that die during a concurrent cycle but are collected only in the next one.)
  • Which GC does Java 17 pick in a 1-CPU Kubernetes pod? (Serial, unless you set one explicitly — a common surprise in resource-limited deployments.)

Java 21 preview

Generational ZGC (-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational) collects young objects separately, cutting CPU overhead substantially; it becomes the ZGC default in Java 23.

JIT: Tiered Compilation, Inlining, OSR, Deoptimization

Why interviewers ask: to see whether you know why the first 10,000 requests after a deploy are slow, why micro-benchmarks written with System.nanoTime lie, and why "small methods are faster" is literally true on the JVM.

HotSpot ships two JIT compilers. C1 (client) compiles quickly with light optimisations and inserts profiling counters; C2 (server) compiles slowly but aggressively using that profile. Tiered compilation (default since Java 8) walks each method up the levels: 0 interpreted → 1–3 C1 variants → 4 C2. A method becomes "hot" after roughly 10,000 invocations, or a loop after enough back-edges (-XX:CompileThreshold is the legacy knob; tiered uses Tier3InvocationThreshold etc.). Compilation happens on background threads; until it finishes, the interpreter keeps running.

The most valuable optimisation is inlining: copying a callee's body into the caller so other optimisations (escape analysis, constant folding, dead-code elimination) can see across the call. Limits apply — by default (check your JDK) callees over 35 bytecodes are inlined only when hot, and over 325 never — which is why keeping methods small genuinely helps. Virtual calls are inlined speculatively when profiling shows one or two receiver types (monomorphic/bimorphic); three or more (megamorphic) fall back to a slower vtable/itable dispatch.

On-stack replacement (OSR) lets a long-running loop switch from interpreted to compiled code mid-iteration, so main's tight loop still gets fast. Deoptimization is the reverse: when a speculation breaks (a new subclass appears, an uncommon branch is taken, a class is unloaded), the compiled frame is thrown away and execution drops back to the interpreter, later recompiling with new knowledge. Analogy: a chef memorises the regular's order to skip the menu; when a new customer sits down, they go back to asking.

@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)
@Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Fork(2)
@State(Scope.Thread)
public class TotalBench {
    Order order; int qty;

    @Setup public void setup() { order = new Order(19); qty = 3; }

    @Benchmark
    public int total() {
        return order.total(qty);        // returned → not dead-code eliminated
    }

    @Benchmark
    public void sinkExample(Blackhole bh) {
        bh.consume(order.total(qty));   // Blackhole defeats DCE/constant folding
    }
}
Interview angle: "Your hand-rolled loop measures 0 ns per call — why?" C2 proved the result unused and deleted the call, or constant-folded it because the inputs were compile-time constants. JMH's warm-up iterations, forks, and Blackhole exist precisely to reach and then honestly measure tier-4 code. In production the same effect appears as "the first minutes after deploy are slow": mitigate with traffic warm-up, CDS/AppCDS, or (Java 24+) AOT cache; do not benchmark cold JVMs.

Pitfalls

  • Interfaces with many implementations at one call site (e.g. a generic Handler.handle() dispatcher) go megamorphic and lose inlining; hot paths sometimes justify a switch on type.
  • Huge methods (generated code, giant switch) exceed HugeMethodLimit (8000 bytecodes) and are never compiled: split them.
  • A full code cache (CodeCache is full. Compiler has been disabled) silently drops you to the interpreter; watch -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize on big apps.

Likely follow-ups

  • How do you see what got compiled? (-XX:+PrintCompilation; -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining; JFR "Compilation" events.)
  • Does final help the JIT? (Barely — C2 already speculates on class hierarchy; final mostly helps readers and static final constants.)
  • What is GraalVM native-image then? (Ahead-of-time compilation to a closed-world binary: instant start, no JIT warm-up, but no runtime speculation and limited reflection.)

Strong, Soft, Weak & Phantom References; Cleaner

Why interviewers ask: "how would you build a memory-sensitive cache" and "why is finalize deprecated" both land here; it also exposes the classic listener/cache leak in code review.

A normal field or local is a strong reference: as long as any GC root can reach an object strongly, it stays. java.lang.ref adds three weaker kinds. A SoftReference is cleared only when the JVM is under memory pressure (before throwing OOM; HotSpot uses an LRU-ish policy via -XX:SoftRefLRUPolicyMSPerMB), a WeakReference is cleared at the very next GC that finds the object otherwise unreachable, and a PhantomReference never lets you get() the object at all — it exists only to be enqueued on a ReferenceQueue after the object is finalized, so you can run cleanup for native resources.

WeakHashMap holds keys weakly: when nobody else references the key object, the entry vanishes (on the next map operation, which polls the queue). Use it to attach metadata to objects you do not own (class → generated proxy, Thread → context). Analogy: a coat check that throws away a coat as soon as the customer leaves the building, rather than keeping every coat forever.

Object.finalize() is deprecated for removal (Java 9, JEP 421 in 18): it runs on a single finalizer thread at unpredictable times, resurrects objects (they need two GC cycles), and can be delayed indefinitely. The replacement is java.lang.ref.Cleaner: register a static-nested cleanup action that holds no reference to the owner; it runs when the owner becomes phantom-reachable, and you can also invoke it deterministically from close().

public final class NativeBuffer implements AutoCloseable {
    private static final Cleaner CLEANER = Cleaner.create();

    // Must NOT be an inner class or lambda capturing 'this' → would keep owner alive
    private record State(long address) implements Runnable {
        public void run() { Native.free(address); }
    }

    private final State state;
    private final Cleaner.Cleanable cleanable;

    public NativeBuffer(long size) {
        this.state = new State(Native.malloc(size));
        this.cleanable = CLEANER.register(this, state);
    }

    @Override public void close() { cleanable.clean(); }   // explicit, idempotent
}
ReferenceCleared whenget() can returnUse for
StrongNever while reachableAlways the objectEverything normal
SoftReferenceMemory pressure, before OOMObject or nullMemory-sensitive caches of recomputable data (images, parsed templates)
WeakReferenceNext GC once only weakly reachableObject or nullCanonicalizing maps, WeakHashMap, listeners, ThreadLocal keys
PhantomReferenceEnqueued after finalizationAlways nullPost-mortem cleanup; the mechanism under Cleaner
Real world: Guava/Caffeine weakKeys()/softValues(); ThreadLocal stores its key weakly in the thread's map (values strongly — hence the leak in thread pools); JDBC drivers and DirectByteBuffer use Cleaner to free off-heap memory.

Pitfalls

  • Soft references make GC pauses worse and OOM diagnosis harder ("the heap looks full but it is all soft"); a bounded LRU (Caffeine with maximumSize) is usually the better cache.
  • WeakHashMap with String or Integer keys rarely works as intended: interned literals and the Integer cache are strongly held forever, and equal-but-distinct keys are looked up by equals while only the stored key instance matters for clearing.
  • A Cleaner action that is a lambda referencing this captures the owner and the object is never phantom-reachable — the leak you wrote to prevent a leak.

Likely follow-ups

  • Is WeakHashMap thread-safe? (No; wrap with Collections.synchronizedMap or use Caffeine.)
  • Why is System.runFinalization() useless? (It only hints; Java 18 deprecates the whole finalization mechanism for removal.)
  • Does a weak reference stop the object being cached in a strong map somewhere else? (No — one strong path anywhere keeps it alive; weak only expresses your intent.)

Java 8 vs 17

Cleaner arrived in Java 9. Java 17's DirectByteBuffer and many JDK internals already run on it; finalize is marked @Deprecated(forRemoval = true) and can be disabled with --finalization=disabled from Java 18.

Java 8 → 17 Memory & Runtime Changes You Must Know

Why interviewers ask: most shops migrated from 8 to 11/17 recently; "what changed under the hood?" is a standard senior question, and container awareness explains a whole class of OOM-killed pods.

The headline: PermGen is gone (Java 8) in favour of Metaspace in native memory that grows on demand; G1 became the default (Java 9); the JVM became container-aware (10, backported to 8u191); and start-up got Class Data Sharing for application classes (10/13). Analogy: the same engine, but the fuel gauge finally reads the tank it is actually in (the container) instead of the whole garage (the host).

ChangeVersionWhat it means in practice
PermGen → Metaspace8Class metadata moved off-heap; -XX:PermSize/MaxPermSize ignored. "OOM: PermGen space" became "OOM: Metaspace", now caused by class-loader leaks or runaway proxy generation, and unbounded unless -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize is set.
Default GC Parallel → G19 (JEP 248)Throughput drops a few percent, pauses become bounded. Batch jobs may want -XX:+UseParallelGC back explicitly.
Unified logging9 (JEP 158)-XX:+PrintGCDetails -Xloggc: replaced by -Xlog:gc*; old flags print warnings or are removed.
Compact Strings9 (JEP 254)String stores Latin-1 in 1 byte/char (byte[] + coder) — typical heaps shrink 10–20%.
Container support10 (JEP-less, 8u191 backport)-XX:+UseContainerSupport (on by default): heap defaults and availableProcessors() read cgroup limits, not the host. Java 8 < u191 saw 64 host cores and 1/4 of host RAM, then got OOM-killed.
Percentage heap sizing10-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 (default 25) and InitialRAMPercentage replace hard-coded -Xmx in images that run with different memory limits.
CDS / AppCDS by default10, 12, 13Pre-parsed class archive mapped at start-up: 20–40% faster boot. -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa then -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa.
Epsilon, ZGC, Shenandoah11, 15, 15No-op GC for tests; two concurrent-compaction collectors for latency.
Biased locking removed, JEP 356 PRNG, records/sealed15–17Uncontended synchronized on old JDKs relied on biasing; Java 17 uses thin locks + CAS everywhere; language features are covered in later sections.
# Dockerfile CMD for a Java 17 service in a 2 GB / 2 CPU pod
java -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 -XX:InitialRAMPercentage=50.0 \
     -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError \
     -XX:SharedArchiveFile=/app/app.jsa -Xshare:auto \
     -Xlog:gc*,safepoint:stdout:time,uptime,level,tags \
     -jar /app/app.jar
# check what the JVM actually saw:
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E "MaxHeapSize|UseContainerSupport|Use.*GC "
Interview angle: "Your pod has a 2 GB limit, no -Xmx, and gets OOM-killed by Kubernetes — why?" Heap defaulted to 25% (512 MB) and stayed within bounds, but heap + Metaspace + thread stacks + code cache + direct buffers + GC bookkeeping exceeded 2 GB, or a Java 8 image ignored the cgroup entirely. Fix: size the heap as a percentage, budget ~25–30% for non-heap, and set MaxDirectMemorySize when using Netty.

Pitfalls

  • -Xmx beats MaxRAMPercentage if both are set; leftover -Xmx in a base image silently caps you.
  • cgroup v2 awareness landed in Java 15 (backported to 11.0.16 / 8u372); older JDKs on modern Kubernetes nodes fall back to host values again.
  • Metaspace "grows on demand" means a class-loader leak now eats native memory until the OS kills the process, later and more confusingly than the old PermGen OOM.

Likely follow-ups

  • Where do interned strings live? (Heap since Java 7; PermGen before that.)
  • How does the JVM count CPUs in a container? (cgroup CPU quota ÷ period, rounded up; overridable with -XX:ActiveProcessorCount.)
  • Why does Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() differ from -Xmx? (It subtracts one survivor space for copying collectors; with G1 it is close to -Xmx.)

A class is on the classpath but you get NoClassDefFoundError at runtime. Most likely cause?

c. If initialization fails once (an ExceptionInInitializerError), every later use throws NoClassDefFoundError. a would be a ClassFormatError, b is not an error, and the JIT (d) never rejects classes.

Which statement about method parameters is correct?

b. The walkthrough above shows it: mutating through the copied reference is visible to the caller, but rebinding the parameter (c) is not. Immutability (d) is unrelated to passing semantics.

Two objects reference each other and nothing else references them. What happens at the next GC?

d. HotSpot uses tracing from GC roots, so cycles are irrelevant; a describes reference counting, which Java does not use. Whether a minor or full GC collects them (b) depends only on which generation they are in.

Why is a minor GC usually fast even when Eden is 2 GB?

b. Copying collection visits only survivors; a 2 GB Eden with 50 MB live costs about the same as a 200 MB Eden with 50 MB live. Parallelism (a) helps but is not the reason; c confuses scope with reachability.

In the animation, an object bounces between S0 and S1 and is eventually promoted. What controls when the promotion happens?

c. Each copy increments the age bits; at MaxTenuringThreshold (max 15) or when the survivor space cannot hold everything, objects are promoted early. Size alone (a) matters only for G1 humongous objects, which skip young entirely.

A G1 log shows repeated Pause Young (Concurrent Start) (G1 Humongous Allocation) lines and occasional Pause Full. What is the most likely fix?

a. Objects ≥ half a region bypass Eden, land in Old as contiguous regions, fragment the heap, and trigger early marking cycles; when no contiguous run is free a Full GC follows. Lowering the pause goal (b) makes Eden smaller and things worse; d guarantees full GCs.

What does a G1 remembered set allow the collector to do?

c. Each region's RSet records the other regions that point into it, maintained by a write barrier. That is what makes incremental, region-at-a-time collection possible at all. Marking state (d) is in the bitmap, not the RSet.

A trading gateway on a 64 GB heap has p99 latency dominated by 300 ms G1 pauses, with CPU at 40%. Best production move in Java 17?

b. Spare CPU and a latency SLO are exactly ZGC's case: concurrent compaction removes pause-∝-heap behaviour. Parallel (a) makes pauses longer; a 5 ms goal (c) is a target G1 cannot meet on 64 GB; doubling the heap (d) makes each pause bigger.

A hand-written micro-benchmark loop reports order.total(qty) takes 0.3 ns per call. Most likely explanation?

d. After OSR/C2 compilation an unused pure computation is removed entirely; this is why JMH requires returning the value or using Blackhole. Inlining (a) reduces cost but does not delete the multiplication; the constant pool (b) is a class-file structure, not a runtime cache.

What does this print (assume a GC actually runs when requested)?

Object key = new Object();
Map<Object, String> m = new WeakHashMap<>();
m.put(key, "v");
key = null;
System.gc();
Thread.sleep(100);
System.out.println(m.size());
a. The map holds the key weakly; once the only strong reference is nulled and a GC runs, the entry is cleared and size() (which expunges stale entries) reports 0. It would print 1 if the key were a String literal, because interned literals stay strongly reachable from the class's constant pool.

Practice

Predict the output: static vs instance initialization order

class Parent {
    static { System.out.print("PS "); }
    { System.out.print("PI "); }
    Parent() { System.out.print("PC "); }
}
class Child extends Parent {
    static { System.out.print("CS "); }
    { System.out.print("CI "); }
    Child() { System.out.print("CC "); }
}
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] a) { new Child(); new Child(); }
}
Tests: class initialization vs object construction
Hint 1
Static blocks run once per class, parent first, before any constructor.
Hint 2
Instance initializer blocks run right after the implicit super() call, before the constructor body.
Reveal solution

Output: PS CS PI PC CI CC PI PC CI CC

First new Child(): initialize Parent (PS) then Child (CS) — once only. Then construct: Child() implicitly calls super(), so Parent's instance block (PI) and constructor (PC) run, then Child's instance block (CI) and constructor (CC). The second new Child() skips the static blocks entirely.

Which objects are eligible for GC after each line?

Assume no JIT scalar replacement and that Node is a plain class with a next field. For lines 8, 9, 10 and 12, list the objects that are eligible for collection immediately after that line completes.

class Node { Node next; final String name; Node(String n) { name = n; } }

public class Main {
    static Node registry;
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Node a = new Node("A");                     // line 6
        Node b = new Node("B"); a.next = b;         // line 7
        Node c = new Node("C"); b.next = c; c.next = a;  // line 8
        a = null;                                   // line 9
        b = null;                                   // line 10
        registry = c;                               // line 11
        c = null;                                   // line 12
        System.gc();
    }
}
Tests: reachability from roots, cycles, statics as roots
Hint 1
Draw the graph: A→B→C→A is a cycle. Which local variables (roots in main's frame) point into it after each line?
Hint 2
Static fields are GC roots for as long as the class is loaded — and Main is loaded for the life of the program.
Reveal solution
  • After line 8: nothing. a, b, c each directly reference their node and all three nodes are reachable from all three roots via the cycle.
  • After line 9: nothing. a is null, but A is still reachable: b→B→C→A.
  • After line 10: nothing. c→C→A→B still reaches every node. A cycle is not a leak as long as one root points into it.
  • After line 12: still nothing — line 11 stored C in the static field registry, a GC root. All three nodes survive System.gc(). Had line 11 been omitted, all three would have been eligible after line 12 (the cycle by itself keeps nothing alive), and they would die in the very first minor GC without ever being copied.

Interview follow-up worth anticipating: "would a going out of scope have been enough?" No — eligibility depends on reachability, not lexical scope, though in practice the JIT's liveness analysis lets a compiled frame drop a dead local before scope ends.

Scenario: read the GC log and choose the flags

A Java 17 Spring Boot API runs in a Kubernetes pod with a 4 GB memory limit and 2 CPUs. Ops reports p99 latency spikes every few minutes and occasional restarts. The JVM is launched with java -Xmx3500m -jar app.jar. The GC log (-Xlog:gc*) shows, repeatedly:

[412.021s][info][gc] GC(301) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 1850M->1790M(3500M) 38.1ms
[412.612s][info][gc] GC(302) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 1932M->1875M(3500M) 41.7ms
[413.190s][info][gc] GC(303) Pause Young (Concurrent Start) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 2010M->1960M(3500M) 44.0ms
[413.191s][info][gc] GC(304) Concurrent Cycle
[414.870s][info][gc] GC(304) Concurrent Cycle 1679.2ms
[415.402s][info][gc] GC(305) Pause Young (Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 2100M->2090M(3500M) 210.4ms
[415.990s][info][gc] GC(306) Pause Young (Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 2180M->2175M(3500M) 232.8ms
[421.113s][info][gc] GC(310) Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 3410M->3390M(3500M) 3104.5ms

(1) What do the numbers tell you about the live set and the young gen? (2) What is the root cause of the restarts? (3) Which JVM flags would you change, and which would you not change?

Tests: log literacy, distinguishing tuning problems from leaks, container sizing
Hint 1
Look at the "after" value of each pause over time. Is the heap ever going back down?
Hint 2
A full GC that reclaims 20 MB out of 3.4 GB is telling you something no flag can fix. Also compare 3500 MB heap + non-heap against a 4 GB limit.
Reveal solution

1. Reading the numbers. Each young pause frees only ~60 MB (e.g. 1850→1790) although Eden was hundreds of MB: nearly everything allocated is surviving, so these are not short-lived request objects — they are being retained. The post-GC floor climbs monotonically (1790 → 1875 → 1960 → 2090 → 2175 …). Mixed collections reclaim almost nothing (2100→2090). The Full GC compacts 3410 MB down to 3390 MB: the live set really is ~3.4 GB.

2. Root cause. A memory leak (or an unbounded cache), not GC tuning. The steady climb with no reclaim after a full compaction is the signature. The restarts come from two directions: the JVM hits OutOfMemoryError (or spends all its time in 3-second full GCs and fails liveness probes), and separately the pod is over-committed — 3500 MB heap plus ~500–800 MB of Metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, GC data structures and direct buffers exceeds the 4 GB cgroup limit, so the kernel OOM-kills it even before Java's OOM.

3. Flags. Do not reach for MaxGCPauseMillis, a different collector, or a larger heap: none of them make a leaked object collectable, they only move the cliff. Do change:

  • -Xmx3500m → -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 (≈2.8 GB) so heap + non-heap fits the limit; or raise the pod limit to ~5 GB if 3.5 GB of heap is actually needed.
  • Add -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps and -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError so the next failure produces evidence and a clean restart rather than a zombie.
  • Keep -Xlog:gc*, and add -Xlog:gc+heap=debug or JFR (-XX:StartFlightRecording) to capture allocation stacks.

Then find the leak with the dump (Eclipse MAT "Leak suspects" / dominator tree): typical culprits are a static HashMap cache with no eviction, a ThreadLocal in a pool, or an ever-growing listener list — exactly the next problem.

Fix the bug: why does this cache leak?

This "memoization" utility is used to cache rendered templates per request-scoped Session. After a day in production the heap dump shows millions of Session objects retained via TemplateCache.CACHE. Explain the leak and rewrite the class so sessions can be collected once the application drops them, while still caching effectively.

public final class TemplateCache {
    private static final Map<Session, Rendered> CACHE = new HashMap<>();

    public static synchronized Rendered render(Session s, Template t) {
        Rendered r = CACHE.get(s);
        if (r == null) {
            r = t.renderFor(s);
            CACHE.put(s, r);
        }
        return r;
    }
}
// elsewhere: Rendered holds a reference to the Session it was rendered for
record Rendered(Session owner, String html) {}
Tests: strong references from statics, WeakHashMap semantics, bounded caches
Hint 1
A static field is a GC root. What does it (transitively) keep alive, and does anything ever remove entries?
Hint 2
Switching to WeakHashMap is the obvious move — but look at what the value references. Does the key become weakly reachable at all?
Reveal solution

The leak. CACHE is static, so it is reachable for the life of the class loader; it holds every Session ever seen strongly as a key, and nothing evicts. Sessions cannot be collected even after the web layer forgets them. This is the canonical "strong references in a static map" leak.

The trap. Replacing HashMap with WeakHashMap alone does not fix it: the value Rendered strongly references its owner Session, and the map holds values strongly, so the key is always strongly reachable through its own value and is never cleared. WeakHashMap only helps when values do not refer back to keys.

Fix A — weak keys done right (values must not point at the key):

public final class TemplateCache {
    // key weak; value must not reference the Session
    private static final Map<Session, String> CACHE =
        Collections.synchronizedMap(new WeakHashMap<>());

    public static String render(Session s, Template t) {
        return CACHE.computeIfAbsent(s, k -> t.renderFor(k).html());
    }
}

Note that Session must not override equals/hashCode based on mutable state, and identity semantics are usually what you want for per-object metadata.

Fix B — a bounded, eviction-based cache (preferred in production, because weak references make GC behaviour and capacity unpredictable):

private static final Cache<Session, Rendered> CACHE = Caffeine.newBuilder()
        .maximumSize(10_000)
        .expireAfterAccess(Duration.ofMinutes(30))
        .weakKeys()                      // optional: identity keys, cleared on GC
        .build();

public static Rendered render(Session s, Template t) {
    return CACHE.get(s, k -> t.renderFor(k));
}

Either way, also ask whether the Session should be the key at all: caching by session id + template id (both immutable values) removes the object-lifetime coupling entirely, and an explicit evict(sessionId) on logout makes memory behaviour deterministic instead of GC-dependent.

2️⃣ OOP & Language Semantics

Interviewers rarely ask "what is polymorphism"; they ask "what does this print" and watch whether you know which method is chosen, when, and by whom. This section goes from the four pillars to the compiler's tie-break rules (overloading), the runtime's dispatch rules (overriding), object identity (equals/hashCode), the modern modelling tools (records, sealed types, pattern matching), and the generics machinery that makes half of the library's signatures look scary.

The Four Pillars — as Interviewers Mean Them

Why interviewers ask: the textbook definitions are a warm-up; the real probe is whether you can say when each is the wrong tool (inheritance for code reuse, getters that leak mutable state, abstract classes where an interface would do).

Encapsulation is not "make fields private and add getters". It is hiding representation so invariants can only change through methods you control. Analogy: an ATM exposes withdraw/deposit, never "set balance". A getter that returns an internal List breaks encapsulation just as badly as a public field.

Inheritance models is-a and gives you substitutability (Liskov). Use it for polymorphic hierarchies, not for code reuse; composition (has-a) is the default because it hides the delegate's API, can be swapped at runtime, and does not break when the parent changes (the "fragile base class" problem: HashSet.addAll calling add is the classic example from Effective Java).

Polymorphism comes in two flavours: overloading is resolved by the compiler from static types (compile-time), overriding is resolved by the JVM from the runtime class (dynamic dispatch via the vtable). Abstraction is exposing the contract without the mechanism; in Java that means an interface (a capability, multiple allowed, no state) or an abstract class (a partial implementation with fields, constructors, and a template method).

ChooseWhenWatch out
interfaceCapability shared by unrelated types (Comparable, Runnable); you want multiple inheritance of type; API you publishNo instance state; default methods are for evolution, not design
abstract classShared state and a constructor; template method with protected hooks; closely related typesSingle inheritance slot spent; subclass coupling
CompositionReuse behaviour without exposing it; swap implementations; wrap third-party classesMore delegation boilerplate (records/Lombok help)
InheritanceTrue is-a and you own both classes; framework hooks (HttpServlet)Fragile base class; equals becomes hard to get right
Interview angle: "Why favour composition over inheritance?" Answer with a concrete failure: a CountingSet extends HashSet that overrides add and addAll double-counts because HashSet.addAll internally calls add. A forwarding wrapper (ForwardingSet) does not have this problem.

Pitfalls

  • Saying "abstract classes can have constructors and interfaces cannot" and stopping there; the design question is about state and multiple inheritance.
  • Calling an overridable method from a constructor: the subclass override runs before the subclass fields are initialised.
  • Treating "protected" as encapsulation: it is package-visible plus subclasses, i.e. wider than most people think.

Likely follow-ups

  • Can an interface have state? (Only public static final constants; no instance fields.)
  • Is Java "pure" OOP? (No: primitives and static members exist outside objects.)
  • What is the Liskov Substitution Principle in one sentence? (A subtype must be usable anywhere its supertype is, without surprising the caller: Square extends Rectangle with independent setters violates it.)

Overload Resolution Traps: null, Widening vs Boxing vs Varargs

Why interviewers ask: it is the cheapest "what does this print" question that separates people who know the compiler's three-phase algorithm from people who guess.

Overloads are picked at compile time from the static types of the arguments. JLS 15.12.2 runs three phases and stops at the first that finds any applicable method: Phase 1 identity and primitive widening (int→long→float→double, and subtype for references) with no boxing and no varargs; Phase 2 allows boxing/unboxing; Phase 3 allows varargs. Within a phase, the most specific method wins; if two are incomparable (String vs Integer) the call is ambiguous and does not compile.

Analogy: hiring. First look for someone who fits the role exactly or with a small stretch (widening); only if nobody fits do you consider retraining (boxing); only if still nobody, a contractor pool (varargs). So m(int) called with an int prefers m(long) over m(Integer) and over m(int...). A null argument is a reference of every reference type, so the most specific reference parameter wins (String beats Object), but two unrelated ones tie and fail.

public class Overload {
    static void m(Object o)  { System.out.println("Object"); }
    static void m(String s)  { System.out.println("String"); }
    static void m(long l)    { System.out.println("long"); }
    static void m(Integer i) { System.out.println("Integer"); }
    static void m(int... v)  { System.out.println("varargs"); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int x = 5;
        m(x);                    // long
        m(Integer.valueOf(7));   // Integer
        byte b = 1;
        m(b);                    // long
        m();                     // varargs
        m(x, x);                 // varargs
        m((Object) "hi");        // Object
        m((String) null);        // String
        // m(null);              // compile error: String vs Integer ambiguous
    }
}
  1. Argument static type is int. Phase 1 already finds m(long), so boxing to Integer is never tried. Prints long.
  2. Static type Integer. Both m(Integer) and m(Object) are applicable by subtyping; the more specific wins. Prints Integer.
  3. byte widens to long in phase 1. Note that byte boxes to Byte, which would not match m(Integer) even in phase 2. Prints long.
  4. No fixed-arity overload takes zero arguments, so phases 1 and 2 find nothing and phase 3 picks the varargs method. Prints varargs.
  5. Two ints: no two-arg fixed overload exists, so varargs again. Remember that each varargs call allocates an array. Prints varargs.
  6. The cast makes the static type Object. Overloading never looks at the runtime type. Prints Object.
  7. A typed null picks String. A bare null matches every reference overload (including int[] for the varargs method); String and Integer tie, so the call is ambiguous and does not compile. Remove m(Integer) and it would print String.
Interview angle: "void f(Object o) and void f(String s); what does f(null) print?" String, because it is more specific. "Now add f(Integer i)?" Compile error. "How do you fix a call site?" Cast the null: f((String) null).
ArgumentOverloads availablePickedPhase / rule
intm(long), m(Integer)m(long)1: widening beats boxing
intm(Integer), m(Object)m(Integer)2: box then most specific
intm(Integer), m(int...)m(Integer)2 before 3
charm(int), m(Character)m(int)1: char→int is widening
nullm(Object), m(String)m(String)most specific reference
nullm(String), m(Integer)compile errorambiguous

Pitfalls

  • list.remove(1) on a List<Integer> calls remove(int index), not remove(Object): phase 1 exact match wins. Use list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)).
  • Overloads on long vs Integer silently pick long for an int argument; a refactor that adds m(long) can change behaviour with no compile error.
  • Overloading with lambdas: submit(Runnable) vs submit(Callable) is resolved by whether the lambda body returns a value; a block body that throws only is compatible with both and can be ambiguous.

Likely follow-ups

  • Is overloading resolved at compile time or run time? (Compile time, on static types; the JVM then dispatches the chosen signature virtually.)
  • Can you overload on return type alone? (No; the erased signature is name + parameter types.)
  • Why is StringBuilder.append(char[]) vs append(Object) a trap? (Passing a char[] prints its contents, not a reference; println(char[]) behaves the same way.)

Overriding Rules & Dynamic Dispatch

Why interviewers ask: "static methods are hidden, not overridden" and "fields are never dispatched dynamically" are the two facts most candidates get wrong in a predict-the-output question.

An instance method overrides a superclass method with the same name and parameter types. The rules are all about substitutability: the override may return a covariant (narrower) type, may not narrow access (public cannot become protected), may not throw broader or new checked exceptions (unchecked are fine), and must not be final in the parent. private methods are invisible to subclasses, so a same-named method in the child is simply a new method. static methods are resolved on the static type: a same-signature static in the child hides the parent's, it does not override.

At run time, obj.method() uses invokevirtual (or invokeinterface): the JVM looks up the method in the runtime class's vtable. Fields have no vtable; obj.field is resolved on the static type of obj. Analogy: methods are looked up in the employee's actual job description; fields are read off the badge you happened to be shown. super.m() compiles to invokespecial, a non-virtual call into the direct superclass.

class Animal {
    String name = "animal";
    static String kind() { return "Animal.kind"; }
    Animal self() { return this; }
    String speak() throws java.io.IOException { return "..."; }
}
class Dog extends Animal {
    String name = "dog";                        // hides, does not override
    static String kind() { return "Dog.kind"; } // hides, does not override
    @Override Dog self() { return this; }       // covariant return: OK
    @Override public String speak() { return "woof"; } // wider access, fewer exceptions: OK
}
Animal a = new Dog();
System.out.println(a.name);      // animal  (field: static type)
System.out.println(a.kind());    // Animal.kind (static: static type)
System.out.println(a.speak());   // woof (virtual dispatch)
System.out.println(((Animal) new Dog()).speak()); // still woof: casts never change the runtime class
AspectAllowed in overrideNot allowed
Return typeSame or subtype (covariant), since Java 5Wider type; different primitive
AccessSame or wider (protected → public)Narrower
Checked exceptionsSame, fewer, or narrower subclassesNew or broader checked exceptions
Unchecked exceptionsAnything—
static/private/finalStatic hides; private is unrelatedCannot override final; instance cannot override static or vice versa (compile error)
Interview angle: "Why does calling an overridden method from the superclass constructor print null?" super() runs before the subclass field initialisers, and dispatch is already dynamic, so the child's override runs on a half-built object. Effective Java: constructors must not call overridable methods.

Pitfalls

  • Forgetting @Override: a typo like equals(Point p) silently overloads instead of overriding equals(Object).
  • Overriding equals but narrowing visibility or changing the parameter type; the compiler will flag narrowing but not overloading.
  • Interface default vs superclass method: the class (superclass) always wins over an interface default ("class wins" rule).

Likely follow-ups

  • Can a constructor be overridden? (No, it is not inherited; it can be invoked with super(...).)
  • Which bytecode instructions are involved? (invokevirtual, invokeinterface, invokespecial for super/private/constructors, invokestatic, invokedynamic for lambdas and string concat.)
  • Can the JIT devirtualise? (Yes: class-hierarchy analysis and inline caches inline monomorphic call sites; that is why final rarely helps performance.)

equals / hashCode Contract

Why interviewers ask: it is the single most common Java question at every level, and the follow-up "what breaks in a HashSet if you only override equals" is where candidates fall over.

equals must be reflexive (x.equals(x)), symmetric (x.equals(y) == y.equals(x)), transitive, consistent (same answer while the objects are unchanged) and x.equals(null) must be false. hashCode must be consistent across calls and, crucially, equal objects must have equal hash codes. Unequal objects may share a hash (a collision) but should not, for performance.

HashMap/HashSet use hashCode first to choose a bucket ((n - 1) & hash after spreading), and only then call equals on the entries in that bucket. Analogy: a library that files books by the first letter of the title and only then compares titles; if two copies of the same book get different first letters, the second one is filed elsewhere and the lookup never finds it. Override one without the other and the collection silently misbehaves.

instanceof vs getClass(): instanceof lets subclasses compare equal to parents but makes symmetry impossible once the subclass adds a field (the classic Point/ColorPoint example). getClass() == o.getClass() is strictly symmetric but breaks Liskov for harmless subclasses (and for Hibernate proxies). Records, final classes, and "favour composition" sidestep the question.

public final class Point {
    private final int x, y;
    public Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }

    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;                     // fast path, also reflexive
        if (!(o instanceof Point p)) return false;      // null-safe; pattern variable (Java 16)
        return x == p.x && y == p.y;
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(x, y); } // same fields as equals
    @Override public String toString() { return "Point[" + x + "," + y + "]"; }
}
// or simply:  public record Point(int x, int y) {}
Interview angle: "Two objects have the same hashCode; are they equal?" Not necessarily (collision). "They are equal; same hashCode?" Must be. "You override hashCode to return 42 always; is the contract satisfied?" Yes, but every entry lands in one bucket and HashMap degrades to a treeified bucket: O(log n) for Comparable keys, O(n) otherwise.

Pitfalls

  • Mutating a field used in hashCode after inserting into a HashSet: the object is now in the wrong bucket and can never be found or removed. Keys should be immutable.
  • Using instanceof and adding a field in a subclass: ColorPoint.equals(Point) vs Point.equals(ColorPoint) breaks symmetry.
  • Implementing compareTo inconsistent with equals: TreeSet and HashSet will disagree about duplicates (BigDecimal 1.0 vs 1.00 is the standard example).
  • Float fields: compare with Float.compare/Double.compare, not == (NaN, -0.0).

Likely follow-ups

  • How does HashMap pick the bucket? (h ^ (h >>> 16) then & (n-1); see the Collections section.)
  • What does the default hashCode return? (An identity hash stored in the object header on first call; not the memory address.)
  • What is a good multiplier in a hand-rolled hashCode? (31: odd prime, and 31*i == (i<<5) - i.)

Immutability & Defensive Copies

Why interviewers ask: "make this class immutable" is a standard whiteboard task, and the trap is a final field holding a mutable List or Date.

An immutable object's observable state never changes after construction. Recipe (Effective Java item 17): make the class final (or give it only private constructors + static factories) so no subclass can add mutable state; make every field private final; no setters; and, for any mutable component, copy on the way in and on the way out. final only freezes the reference, not the object it points to.

Analogy: a printed receipt. You can hand copies around; nobody can edit the original, so there is nothing to lock. Benefits: inherently thread-safe (safe publication via final fields is guaranteed by the JMM), safe as map keys and set elements, hash can be cached (String does this), and instances can be freely shared and reused (Integer.valueOf, List.of).

public final class Order {
    private final String id;
    private final List<String> lines;   // final reference, mutable object!
    private final Instant created;      // Instant is immutable: no copy needed

    public Order(String id, List<String> lines, Instant created) {
        this.id = Objects.requireNonNull(id);
        this.lines = List.copyOf(lines);   // defensive copy IN (null-hostile, unmodifiable)
        this.created = created;
    }
    public List<String> lines() { return lines; }  // already unmodifiable; no copy OUT needed
    public Order withLine(String line) {            // "mutation" returns a new instance
        var copy = new ArrayList<>(lines); copy.add(line);
        return new Order(id, copy, created);
    }
}
TechniqueWhat it doesGotcha
Collections.unmodifiableList(l)Read-only view of the same listCaller who kept l can still mutate it through the view
List.copyOf(l) (Java 10)Independent unmodifiable copy; returns the same instance if already an immutable listRejects null elements
new ArrayList<>(l)Independent mutable copyMust also not expose it via a getter
clone() on arraysShallow array copyElements themselves are shared
Interview angle: "Is a class with only final fields immutable?" Only if every field's type is itself immutable or is defensively copied. "Why does String cache its hash?" Because immutability guarantees the value never changes, and String is the most common map key.

Pitfalls

  • Returning the internal array or collection from a getter; Arrays.asList and unmodifiableList are views, not copies.
  • Copying in the constructor after validation (TOCTOU): validate the copy, not the parameter.
  • Using java.util.Date/Calendar fields: mutable; prefer java.time.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why must the class be final? (A subclass could add mutable state or override methods to lie about state; a static factory + private constructor is the alternative.)
  • Does immutability hurt performance? (Allocation churn for "modified" copies; mitigated by escape analysis, persistent data structures, or a mutable builder.)
  • How does the JMM treat final fields? (Freeze semantics: correctly constructed objects publish final fields safely even without synchronisation.)

Records (Java 16): Canonical & Compact Constructors

Why interviewers ask: records are the modern answer to "write a value class", and the follow-up "why not use records for JPA entities" checks that you know what records give up.

A record is a transparent, shallowly immutable data carrier: record Point(int x, int y) {} generates private final fields, a public canonical constructor, accessors named x() and y() (no get prefix), and equals/hashCode/toString based on all components. The class is implicitly final, cannot extend anything (it extends java.lang.Record), cannot declare instance fields beyond the components, but can implement interfaces, have static members and extra constructors, and be generic or nested.

The compact constructor (record Range(int lo, int hi) { Range { if (lo > hi) throw ...; } }) has no parameter list, runs before the fields are assigned, and may reassign the parameters (normalisation) but not the fields. Analogy: a passport form; the fields are fixed, and the compact constructor is the clerk checking the form before stamping it.

public record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) implements Comparable<Money> {
    public Money {                                   // compact canonical constructor
        Objects.requireNonNull(amount); Objects.requireNonNull(currency);
        amount = amount.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);   // normalise the parameter
    }
    public static Money zero(Currency c) { return new Money(BigDecimal.ZERO, c); }
    public Money plus(Money o) {
        if (!currency.equals(o.currency)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch");
        return new Money(amount.add(o.amount), currency);
    }
    @Override public int compareTo(Money o) { return amount.compareTo(o.amount); }
}
// usage with pattern matching (Java 16 instanceof; record patterns are Java 21)
Object o = new Money(new BigDecimal("9.99"), Currency.getInstance("USD"));
if (o instanceof Money m && m.amount().signum() > 0) System.out.println(m); // Money[amount=9.99, currency=USD]
Use a recordDo not use a record
DTOs, API request/response bodies, map keys, tuples from streams, config values, event payloadsJPA entities: JPA needs a no-arg constructor, non-final fields for lazy proxies/dirty checking, and identity-based equality
Immutable domain values (Money, Range, Coordinates)Types that need mutable state, inheritance, or hidden fields (caches) beyond the components
Nested "local records" inside a method to group intermediate resultsBeans that frameworks populate via setters (older Spring @ConfigurationProperties without constructor binding)
Interview angle: "Is a record deeply immutable?" No: record Bag(List<String> items) exposes the same mutable list; copy it in the compact constructor with items = List.copyOf(items). "Can I override the accessor?" Yes, e.g. to return a defensive copy of an array component.

Pitfalls

  • Array components: generated equals uses reference equality on arrays, and toString prints [I@1b6d3586. Wrap in a List instead.
  • Jackson needs jackson-databind 2.12+ for records; Spring Boot 2.5+/3.x is fine.
  • A record's hashCode algorithm is unspecified across JDK versions; never persist it.

Likely follow-ups

  • Can a record have a mutable field? (No instance fields except components; static fields are allowed.)
  • What about serialization? (Records deserialise via the canonical constructor, so validation always runs; no readObject tricks.)
  • Local records? (Declared inside a method; implicitly static, cannot capture locals.)

Java 8 vs 17

Java 8 has no records; teams used Lombok @Value or AutoValue. Records arrived as preview in 14/15 and are standard in 16, so they are fully available in 17 without flags.

Sealed Classes & Pattern Matching (instanceof, switch)

Why interviewers ask: it shows you know what changed after Java 8, and the "exhaustive switch" question checks whether you understand why sealing matters rather than just the keyword.

A sealed class or interface lists the only types allowed to extend it: sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square, Rect {}. Each permitted subtype must be final, sealed (continue the closed tree) or non-sealed (reopen it). Together with records this gives Java algebraic data types: a sum type (Shape is one of exactly three) of product types (a record is a tuple of fields). Analogy: an enum whose constants can carry different fields.

Pattern matching for instanceof (standard in Java 16) binds a variable in one step: if (o instanceof Circle c) use(c.radius()). Pattern matching for switch lets you switch on types with guards, and when the selector is sealed the compiler checks exhaustiveness: forgetting a case is a compile error, and no default is needed, so adding a fourth shape later fails the build instead of silently falling into default. Version honesty: pattern switch is preview in Java 17 (--enable-preview, JEP 406) and standard in Java 21 (JEP 441), together with record deconstruction patterns (JEP 440).

public sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square, Rect {}
public record Circle(double r) implements Shape {}
public record Square(double side) implements Shape {}
public record Rect(double w, double h) implements Shape {}

// Java 16+: pattern matching for instanceof (standard)
static double areaOld(Shape s) {
    if (s instanceof Circle c) return Math.PI * c.r() * c.r();
    if (s instanceof Square q) return q.side() * q.side();
    if (s instanceof Rect r) return r.w() * r.h();
    throw new IllegalStateException();       // compiler cannot prove exhaustiveness here
}
// Java 17 with --enable-preview, standard in Java 21: pattern matching for switch
static double area(Shape s) {
    return switch (s) {                         // exhaustive: no default
        case Circle c -> Math.PI * c.r() * c.r();
        case Square q -> q.side() * q.side();
        case Rect r   -> r.w() * r.h();
    };
}
Interview angle: "How would you model a payment result that is either Success(txId) or Failure(code, reason) without exceptions?" A sealed interface with two records; callers must handle both in a switch. This replaces the visitor pattern for most cases.

Pitfalls

  • Adding a default branch "just in case" silently disables the exhaustiveness check you sealed the type for.
  • Permitted subclasses must live in the same module, or the same package if in the unnamed module; a permits clause can be omitted only when all subtypes are in the same compilation unit.
  • Switching on a sealed type with a null selector throws NullPointerException unless you add case null (Java 21).

Likely follow-ups

  • Difference between sealed and final? (Final: no subclasses. Sealed: a known, finite set.)
  • What does non-sealed do? (Reopens that branch to arbitrary subclasses; the switch then needs a default or a case for that branch only.)
  • Enum vs sealed? (Enum constants are singletons with the same fields; sealed records allow different shapes and many instances.)

Java 21 preview

Record patterns: case Rect(double w, double h) when w == h -> "square-ish". Guards use when. Also case null, default ->. In Java 17 these need --enable-preview and the syntax differed (&& guards), so say "17 preview, 21 standard" in interviews.

Enums: Singletons, Strategy per Constant, EnumMap/EnumSet

Why interviewers ask: enums are the JVM-guaranteed singleton (Effective Java's preferred one), and "enum with behaviour" tests whether you reach for a switch or for polymorphism.

An enum is a final class extending java.lang.Enum whose instances are created once during class initialisation, so == is safe and serialization/reflection cannot create duplicates: that makes a one-constant enum the bullet-proof singleton. The compiler adds values() (a fresh array each call, so cache it) and valueOf(String) (throws IllegalArgumentException on unknown names). ordinal() is the declaration index; never persist it, since reordering constants silently corrupts stored data. Persist name() or an explicit code field.

Enums can have fields, constructors (implicitly private), and constant-specific method bodies: declare an abstract method and implement it per constant, which is the Strategy pattern without extra classes. Analogy: each button on a vending machine knows its own price and action; you do not switch on the button label. EnumMap and EnumSet are array/bit-vector backed, faster and more compact than HashMap/HashSet for enum keys.

public enum Op {
    ADD("+") { double apply(double a, double b) { return a + b; } },
    MUL("*") { double apply(double a, double b) { return a * b; } };

    private final String symbol;
    Op(String symbol) { this.symbol = symbol; }
    abstract double apply(double a, double b);       // strategy per constant
    public String symbol() { return symbol; }

    private static final Map<String, Op> BY_SYMBOL =
        Arrays.stream(values()).collect(Collectors.toMap(Op::symbol, o -> o));
    public static Op fromSymbol(String s) { return BY_SYMBOL.get(s); }
}
EnumSet<Op> all = EnumSet.allOf(Op.class);           // bit vector
Map<Op, Integer> counts = new EnumMap<>(Op.class); // array indexed by ordinal
Interview angle: "Why is an enum singleton better than double-checked locking?" No lazy-init race, serialization-safe, reflection-safe (the JVM rejects Constructor.newInstance on enums). The only cost is that it cannot extend a class.

Pitfalls

  • JPA @Enumerated defaults to ORDINAL; use EnumType.STRING or an AttributeConverter.
  • Switching on an enum without a default hides new constants: with a switch expression the compiler forces exhaustiveness.
  • Constant-specific bodies create anonymous subclasses, so getClass() is not the enum class; use getDeclaringClass().

Likely follow-ups

  • Can an enum implement an interface? (Yes; it cannot extend a class.)
  • Are enums thread-safe? (Their constants are immutable unless you add mutable fields, which you should not.)
  • What does Enum.compareTo use? (Ordinal; so TreeSet of enums is in declaration order.)

Generics: Bounds, Wildcards & PECS

Why interviewers ask: "why can't I pass a List<Dog> where a List<Animal> is expected" and "explain ? super T" are quick tests of whether you read library signatures or copy-paste them.

Generic types are invariant: List<Dog> is not a subtype of List<Animal>, because if it were, you could add a Cat through the List<Animal> view and later read it as a Dog. Arrays are covariant (Dog[] is an Animal[]), which is why the JVM must check every array store at run time and throw ArrayStoreException. Generics moved that check to compile time by refusing the conversion.

Wildcards restore flexibility with a rule per direction. List<? extends Animal> is some list of an unknown Animal subtype: you can safely read elements as Animal but cannot add anything (except null), since you do not know whether it is a list of Dogs or Cats. List<? super Dog> is a list of Dog or some supertype: you can safely add a Dog, but reads only give you Object. PECS (Effective Java): Producer Extends, Consumer Super. Analogy: ? extends is a one-way funnel out of the collection; ? super is a funnel into it. Bounded type parameters (<T extends Comparable<? super T>>) let you call methods on T while still returning the exact type.

Animal[] pets = new Dog[2];
pets[0] = new Cat();                  // compiles; ArrayStoreException at run time

List<Dog> dogs = new ArrayList<>();
// List<Animal> animals = dogs;      // does not compile: invariance
List<? extends Animal> readOnly = dogs;   // OK: can read Animal, cannot add
List<? super Dog> sink = new ArrayList<Animal>(); sink.add(new Dog());  // OK

static double sum(Collection<? extends Number> nums) {           // producer
    double s = 0; for (Number n : nums) s += n.doubleValue(); return s;
}
static void fill(List<? super Integer> out, int n) {              // consumer
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) out.add(i);
}
static <T extends Comparable<? super T>> T max(List<? extends T> xs) { ... }
// the ? super T lets Timestamp (Comparable<Date>) participate
Interview angle: "What is the signature of Collections.sort and why?" <T extends Comparable<? super T>> void sort(List<T>): the list is both read and written so it is invariant List<T>, and the ? super T allows a superclass to provide the compareTo. "List<?> vs List<Object>?" List<?> accepts any list and allows no adds; List<Object> accepts only exactly that type.

Pitfalls

  • Using wildcards in return types (List<? extends Foo> get()): forces every caller to deal with the wildcard. Wildcards belong in parameters.
  • List<? extends Number> looks like it should accept add(1); it does not, and the error message ("capture of ?") confuses people.
  • Raw types (List list) switch off generic checking entirely, not just for that variable; the unchecked warning is a real bug report.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why are arrays covariant at all? (Historical: to write generic algorithms like Arrays.sort(Object[]) before generics existed.)
  • What is wildcard capture? (The compiler names the unknown type as a fresh type variable; a helper method <T> void swapHelper(List<T>) lets you work with it.)
  • Can a type parameter have multiple bounds? (<T extends Number & Comparable<T>>; class bound first, erasure uses the first bound.)

Type Erasure, Bridge Methods & Runtime Type Recovery

Why interviewers ask: it explains every "weird" generics limitation (new T(), List<String>.class, instanceof List<String>) and how Jackson's TypeReference and Spring's ParameterizedTypeReference work.

Generics are a compile-time feature: after type checking, the compiler erases every type variable to its first bound (T → Object, T extends Number → Number) and inserts casts at use sites. At run time there is one ArrayList class and new ArrayList<String>().getClass() == new ArrayList<Integer>().getClass(). This was chosen for binary compatibility with pre-Java-5 code. Consequences: no new T(), no T[] creation, no List<String>.class, no instanceof List<String> (only List<?>), no static fields of type T, and no overloading on List<String> vs List<Integer> (same erasure).

Because an override like set(Integer) has a different erased signature from the parent's set(Object), the compiler emits a synthetic bridge method set(Object) that casts and delegates, so virtual dispatch still works. Heap pollution is a variable of parameterised type pointing at an object of the wrong element type, usually via raw types or generic varargs; the ClassCastException then appears far from the cause. Reifiable types are those fully available at run time: raw types, primitives, non-generic classes, and unbounded wildcards like List<?>. To recover a generic type at run time you exploit the one place the compiler keeps it: class signatures (the Signature attribute), read via getGenericSuperclass() as a ParameterizedType, which is the super type token trick.

import java.util.*;
class Node<T> {
    T value;
    void set(T v) { value = v; }
}
class IntNode extends Node<Integer> {
    @Override void set(Integer v) { value = v; }
}
public class Erasure {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        IntNode n = new IntNode();
        Node raw = n;                       // raw type: unchecked warning
