        raw.set("oops");                    // compiles!
        Integer i = n.value;                // ClassCastException here? no: earlier
        List<String> a = new ArrayList<>();
        List<Integer> b = new ArrayList<>();
        System.out.println(a.getClass() == b.getClass());   // true
    }
}
  1. The compiler erases T to Object. Node's bytecode has a field Object value and a method set(Object).
  2. set(Integer) has a different erased signature from set(Object), so the compiler generates a synthetic bridge set(Object) that casts to Integer and calls the real method. javap -p shows it flagged synthetic bridge.
  3. Assigning to a raw Node compiles with an unchecked warning. Nothing happened at run time yet.
  4. raw.set("oops") is a call to set(Object); dispatch lands on the bridge in IntNode, which does (Integer) v. ClassCastException thrown here, in a method you never wrote.
  5. Contrast: with a plain Node<Integer> and no override, the String would be stored happily (heap pollution) and blow up only at Integer i = n.value, where the compiler inserted a checkcast.
  6. There is one ArrayList class at run time. That is why List<String>.class and instanceof List<String> are illegal, and why Map<Class<?>, Object> type-safe heterogeneous containers cannot key on List<String>.
// Super type token: the generic argument survives in the class's Signature attribute
public abstract class TypeRef<T> {
    private final Type type;
    protected TypeRef() {
        ParameterizedType pt = (ParameterizedType) getClass().getGenericSuperclass();
        this.type = pt.getActualTypeArguments()[0];   // e.g. List<String>
    }
    public Type type() { return type; }
}
Type t = new TypeRef<List<String>>() {}.type();     // anonymous subclass carries the signature
// Jackson: new TypeReference<List<User>>() {}; Spring: new ParameterizedTypeReference<List<User>>() {}

// Generic varargs: T... becomes Object[] → possible heap pollution
@SafeVarargs   // promise: the method does not store into or expose the array
static <T> List<T> listOf(T... items) { return List.of(items); }

// Creating T[] the honest way: pass the class token
static <T> T[] newArray(Class<T> type, int n) { return (T[]) java.lang.reflect.Array.newInstance(type, n); }
Not possibleWhyWorkaround
new T(), new T[n]T is Object at run timePass Class<T> or Supplier<T>; Array.newInstance
List<String>.class, x instanceof List<String>Not reifiableList.class plus a super type token
catch (T e), class X extends Throwable<T>Exception matching is by runtime classCatch the bound and rethrow
static T fieldStatics are shared across all parameterisationsPer-instance field
Overload f(List<A>) / f(List<B>)Same erasureDifferent method names
Interview angle: "Why does Jackson need new TypeReference<List<User>>(){} but User.class is enough for a single object?" User.class is reifiable; List<User> is erased, so the only way to smuggle the argument to run time is via a subclass whose signature records it.

Pitfalls

  • @SafeVarargs on a method that stores into or returns the varargs array is a lie; Arrays.asList(T...) returning a List backed by the array is the borderline case (it is safe because the list is not itself generic-varargs-escaping).
  • Kotlin's reified makes people assume Java has an equivalent; it does not (Kotlin inlines the function).
  • Lambdas do not create a subclass, so getGenericSuperclass on a lambda does not give you its type arguments; only an anonymous class works for the token trick.

Likely follow-ups

  • Does erasure affect performance? (Casts are cheap; boxing of primitives in List<Integer> is the real cost. Project Valhalla aims at specialised generics.)
  • What does getGenericSuperclass return for a raw subclass? (A plain Class, so the cast to ParameterizedType throws.)
  • Where else does the compiler keep generic info? (Field and method Signature attributes; that is how frameworks inject List<Handler> beans.)

Nested Classes & the Hidden this$0 Reference

Why interviewers ask: "why did our listener/cache leak the whole service" often traces back to a non-static inner class, and lambda capture rules are the modern follow-up.

Four kinds. A static nested class is just a namespaced top-level class with access to the outer's private statics. An inner (non-static) class carries a hidden this$0 field pointing at the enclosing instance; you create it with outer.new Inner() and it can touch outer instance fields. Local classes are declared inside a method and anonymous classes are unnamed one-off subclasses; both capture effectively-final locals (copied into synthetic fields) and, if the enclosing method is an instance method, also capture the outer this.

That hidden reference is the leak: register an anonymous Runnable or listener from a request-scoped service into a long-lived registry or ScheduledExecutorService and the whole service (and everything it references) stays reachable. Analogy: a sticky note that also has the entire filing cabinet stapled to it. Lambdas are different: they compile to a private method plus invokedynamic, capture only what they use, and capture this only if the body references an instance member. A lambda's this is the enclosing instance; an anonymous class's this is itself.

class Outer {
    private int x = 1;
    static class SN { }                       // no outer reference
    class Inner { int get() { return x; } }   // holds Outer.this ("this$0")

    Runnable anon() {
        return new Runnable() { public void run() { System.out.println("anon"); } };
        // captures Outer.this even though it never uses x  (javac 18+ dropped unused this$0)
    }
    Runnable lambda() { return () -> System.out.println("lambda"); }   // no this captured
    Runnable lambdaUsingX() { return () -> System.out.println(x); }   // captures this
}
Outer o = new Outer();
Outer.Inner in = o.new Inner();               // inner needs an outer instance
Outer.SN sn = new Outer.SN();
KindOuter instance refCan have static membersTypical use
Static nestedNoYesBuilders, Map.Entry-style helpers, node classes
InnerYes (this$0)Only constants (Java 16 allows statics)Iterators over the outer's private state
LocalIf in instance methodJava 16+One-method helpers; local records
AnonymousIf in instance methodJava 16+Super type tokens; legacy listeners
LambdaOnly if body uses itn/aFunctional interfaces
Interview angle: "Why does Effective Java say favour static member classes?" Default to static: no hidden reference, no leak, and serialization does not drag in the outer object. Make it inner only when it genuinely needs the outer instance (e.g. ArrayList.Itr).

Pitfalls

  • Captured locals must be effectively final; mutate through a holder (AtomicInteger, array) or restructure as a stream reduction.
  • Serialising an inner class serialises the outer instance too, often with a NotSerializableException.
  • Inner classes cannot be instantiated from a static context without an outer instance; a common compile error in unit tests.

Likely follow-ups

  • How do lambdas get created at run time? (invokedynamic + LambdaMetafactory spins a hidden class on first call; non-capturing lambdas are singletons.)
  • What is a "synthetic accessor"? (Pre-Java 11, inner classes accessing private outer members needed access$000 methods; nest-based access control (JEP 181) removed them.)
  • Anonymous class vs lambda for a functional interface? (Lambda unless you need state, multiple methods, or a super type token.)

Interfaces in Java 8+: default, static, private Methods & the Diamond Rule

Why interviewers ask: "Java has multiple inheritance now?" is bait; the answer is about how conflicts are resolved and why default methods exist.

Since Java 8 an interface can carry default methods (instance methods with a body, so Collection.stream() could be added without breaking every implementation), static methods (utility factories like Comparator.comparing, not inherited by implementors), and since Java 9 private methods to share code between defaults. Interfaces still have no instance state.

Diamond resolution: (1) a class method always beats an interface default ("class wins"); (2) a more specific interface (sub-interface) beats a less specific one; (3) if two unrelated interfaces both provide a default for the same signature, the class must override and may pick with A.super.m(). Analogy: two managers give conflicting instructions; you must write your own decision and may quote either of them. A functional interface has exactly one abstract method (defaults and Object methods do not count); @FunctionalInterface makes the compiler enforce it. Marker interfaces (Serializable, Cloneable, RandomAccess) carry no methods and are tested with instanceof; annotations replaced most new uses.

interface Flyer   { default String move() { return "fly"; } }
interface Swimmer { default String move() { return "swim"; } }
class Duck implements Flyer, Swimmer {
    @Override public String move() { return Flyer.super.move() + "+" + Swimmer.super.move(); }
}
interface Base { default String id() { return "base"; } }
interface Sub extends Base { @Override default String id() { return "sub"; } }
class Impl implements Base, Sub { }         // id() → "sub": more specific interface wins
class Parent { public String id() { return "parent"; } }
class Child extends Parent implements Sub { } // id() → "parent": class wins over interface

@FunctionalInterface
interface Validator<T> {
    boolean test(T t);
    default Validator<T> and(Validator<? super T> o) { return t -> test(t) && o.test(t); }
    static <T> Validator<T> notNull() { return Objects::nonNull; }
}
Interview angle: "Why not put everything in abstract classes now?" Interfaces still cannot hold state or constructors, and a class can implement many. Default methods are for API evolution and small conveniences, not for building hierarchies of behaviour.

Pitfalls

  • A default method cannot override equals/hashCode/toString; the compiler rejects it.
  • Interface fields are implicitly public static final: using an interface as a "constants holder" pollutes every implementor's namespace.
  • Static interface methods are called via the interface name only (Comparator.naturalOrder()), never through an instance or implementing class.

Likely follow-ups

  • Can an interface be sealed? (Yes, Java 17.)
  • What happens if a lambda targets an interface with two abstract methods? (Compile error; it is not functional.)
  • Is Comparator functional despite having many methods? (Yes: one abstract method compare; equals is from Object, the rest are default/static.)

Object Methods: toString, clone, finalize

Why interviewers ask: "shallow vs deep copy" is a favourite, and "is clone a good idea" checks whether you have read Effective Java.

Every class inherits toString (ClassName@hexIdentityHash by default; override it, logs and debuggers depend on it), equals/hashCode (previous card), getClass, the monitor methods wait/notify/notifyAll (concurrency section), clone and finalize.

Object.clone() is protected and native: it makes a shallow field-by-field copy and throws CloneNotSupportedException unless the class implements the marker Cloneable. Shallow means nested mutable objects are shared between original and copy; a deep copy must clone them too. The API is widely considered broken: no constructor runs, final fields cannot be reassigned, the checked exception is pointless, and subclasses inherit a shallow clone silently. Analogy: photocopying a folder copies the index card but not the documents it points to. Prefer a copy constructor (new ArrayList<>(other)) or static factory, or immutability. finalize is deprecated since Java 9 and scheduled for removal (JEP 421): it runs on an unspecified thread at an unspecified time, resurrects objects and slows GC; use try-with-resources for deterministic cleanup and java.lang.ref.Cleaner as a safety net.

class Team implements Cloneable {
    String name; List<String> members = new ArrayList<>();
    @Override public Team clone() {                       // covariant return, public
        try {
            Team t = (Team) super.clone();                 // shallow: t.members == this.members
            t.members = new ArrayList<>(members);           // make it deep for the mutable part
            return t;
        } catch (CloneNotSupportedException e) { throw new AssertionError(e); }
    }
    Team(Team other) { this.name = other.name; this.members = new ArrayList<>(other.members); } // preferred
}
Copy strategyDepthPros / cons
clone()Shallow by defaultFast for arrays; awkward API, no constructor, breaks with final fields
Copy constructor / factoryAs deep as you write itExplicit, works with final fields, no Cloneable; Effective Java's recommendation
Serialization round-tripDeepSlow; needs Serializable everywhere
Records / immutables + with methodsn/aNo copying needed at all

Pitfalls

  • array.clone() is fine and idiomatic for primitive arrays; for object arrays it is still shallow.
  • Overriding toString to include a lazy-loaded JPA collection triggers queries (or LazyInitializationException) in log statements.
  • Relying on finalize to close files: file descriptors run out long before GC bothers to finalize.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why is Cloneable a marker interface with no clone method? (Historical design flaw; it changes the behaviour of the protected native method.)
  • What is Cleaner? (Java 9 replacement: registers a cleanup action run by a daemon thread when the object becomes phantom-reachable.)
  • Does String.toString() allocate? (No, returns this.)

Integer Cache & Autoboxing Traps

Why interviewers ask: Integer a = 127, b = 127; a == b vs 128 is the most famous Java trick question, and the real point is "never compare boxed values with ==".

Autoboxing compiles Integer a = 127 to Integer.valueOf(127), and valueOf returns a cached instance for -128..127 (the upper bound is tunable with -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax, the lower is fixed). Outside that range every boxing allocates a new object, so == compares two different references. The same caching applies to Byte, Short, Long, Character (0..127) and Boolean; Float/Double are never cached. new Integer(x) always allocates (and is deprecated since 9).

Unboxing a null (int x = map.get(missingKey)) throws NullPointerException, a classic production bug with Map<String, Integer> counters. Mixed comparisons (Integer == int) unbox and compare values, so a == 128 is true while a == b is false. In hot loops, boxing (Long sum = 0L; sum += i) allocates on every iteration; use primitives or IntStream/LongAdder.

ExpressionResultWhy
Integer a=127, b=127; a==btrueBoth from IntegerCache
Integer a=128, b=128; a==bfalseTwo allocations (unless -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax=128+)
Integer a=128; a==128trueUnboxed, numeric compare
Long l=127L; l.equals(127)false127 boxes to Integer; Long.equals checks the class
Integer n=null; int x=n;NPEUnboxing calls n.intValue()
Double a=0.0, b=0.0; a==bfalseNo cache for Double

Pitfalls

  • Objects.equals(a, b) is the null-safe way to compare boxed values; a.equals(b) NPEs when a is null.
  • Ternary mixing Integer and int (flag ? integerObj : 0) unboxes the object and can NPE.
  • Sorting with (a, b) -> a - b on boxed values: unboxing overflow; use Integer.compare.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why does the cache exist? (Small values dominate real programs; the JLS requires -128..127 to be cached so == is at least predictable there.)
  • Does String have a similar cache? (The string pool for literals and intern(); same lesson: use equals.)
  • How does Valhalla change this? (Value classes would remove identity from Integer-like types, making == compare content.)

Access Modifiers, final/static Semantics, Init Order & var

Why interviewers ask: quick sanity checks: "what does protected actually allow", "can a static method use this", "in what order do initialisers run", "where can I use var".

Four access levels: private (class), package-private (no keyword: same package), protected (same package plus subclasses anywhere, but a subclass can only touch it through a reference of its own type), public. Top-level classes can only be public or package-private. Since Java 9, modules add a coarser boundary: public is only reachable if the package is exports-ed.

final on a variable means assign-once (blank finals must be set in every constructor); on a method, no overriding; on a class, no subclassing. static members belong to the class, are initialised once per class loader, cannot reference this, and are not polymorphic. Initialisation order for new Child(): parent statics, child statics (once), then per object: parent field initialisers and instance blocks in textual order, parent constructor body, then the same for the child. Full predict-the-output in the JVM section problem. var (Java 10) infers the type of a local variable with an initialiser; not for fields, parameters, return types, or null/lambda initialisers. It is not dynamic typing: the type is fixed at compile time.

var list = new ArrayList<String>();      // ArrayList<String>, not List<String>
var map = Map.of("a", 1);                 // Map<String,Integer>
// var x;            var y = null;         var f = () -> 1;    // all compile errors
for (var e : map.entrySet()) { }          // fine in for-each and try-with-resources
final var cfg = load();                   // final + var allowed

class Base {
    static final int MAX;                  // blank static final
    static { MAX = Integer.getInteger("app.max", 10); }
    private final int id;
    { System.out.println("instance block"); }
    Base(int id) { this.id = id; }         // must assign blank final exactly once
}
ModifierSame classSame packageSubclass (other pkg)World
privateYesNoNoNo
(package-private)YesYesNoNo
protectedYesYesYesNo
publicYesYesYesYes (if package exported)

Pitfalls

  • static final primitives and Strings are compile-time constants inlined into callers; changing the value without recompiling clients leaves them with the old value.
  • A static method "overridden" in a subclass hides it; calling through a parent-typed reference runs the parent's.
  • var with a diamond (var l = new ArrayList<>()) infers ArrayList<Object>.

Likely follow-ups

  • Can a top-level class be private or protected? (No; only nested classes.)
  • Can an abstract method be static, final, or private? (None: all three prevent overriding.)
  • Does var hurt readability? (Use when the right-hand side names the type or the variable name makes it obvious; avoid var result = service.process().)

Java 8 → 17 Language Changes Cheat-Sheet

Why interviewers ask: most teams are migrating 8 → 17 or 17 → 21; being able to name which release introduced what shows you have actually used the newer versions.

VersionLanguage featureOne-line why it matters
9Private interface methods; modules (JPMS); List.of/Map.of factoriesShare code between default methods; strong encapsulation of sun.*
10var for locals; List.copyOfLess ceremony; cheap immutable copies
11 (LTS)var in lambda parameters; String.isBlank/lines/strip/repeat; single-file java Foo.java; new HttpClientAnnotations on lambda params; scripting
14Switch expressions with -> and yield (standard); helpful NullPointerException messagesNo fall-through, exhaustiveness for enums
15Text blocks """Readable SQL/JSON literals
16Records; pattern matching for instanceof; static members in inner classesValue types without Lombok
17 (LTS)Sealed classes standard; pattern matching for switch (preview); strong encapsulation of JDK internals finalADTs; --add-opens needed for reflective hacks
21 (LTS)Pattern matching for switch + record patterns standard; virtual threads; sequenced collectionsSay "preview in 17, standard in 21"
String sql = """
    SELECT id, total
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'PAID'
    """;                                        // text block (15): closing delimiter sets indentation
int days = switch (month) {                     // switch expression (14)
    case FEB -> leap ? 29 : 28;
    case APR, JUN, SEP, NOV -> 30;
    default -> { var d = 31; yield d; }
};

Pitfalls

  • Java 17 removed --illegal-access: reflection into java.base internals (old Lombok, some serializers) needs explicit --add-opens or an upgrade.
  • Text blocks strip common indentation relative to the closing """; trailing spaces are removed unless escaped with \s.
  • Switch expressions must be exhaustive; old-style switch statements are not checked.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is removed between 8 and 17? (Java EE modules like JAXB/JAX-WS (11), Nashorn (15), CMS GC (14), Applets deprecated.)
  • Which GC is default? (G1 since 9; Parallel in 8.)
  • What is the LTS cadence? (8, 11, 17, 21, then every two years: 25.)

Given static void m(long l), static void m(Integer i) and static void m(int... v), what does m(5) print (each prints its parameter type)?

b. Phase 1 (widening, no boxing) already finds m(long), so m(Integer) (phase 2, boxing) and m(int...) (phase 3) are never considered. It is only ambiguous when two candidates in the same phase are incomparable.

With void f(String s) and void f(Integer i) in scope, what happens for f(null)?

d. null is applicable to both and neither type is more specific than the other. Declaration order (a) never matters in overload resolution. With f(Object) and f(String) instead, String would win.

class A { String n = "A"; static String s() { return "A"; } String i() { return "A"; } } and class B extends A { String n = "B"; static String s() { return "B"; } String i() { return "B"; } }. For A a = new B();, what is a.n + a.s() + a.i()?

c. Fields (a.n) and static methods (a.s()) are resolved on the static type A; only the instance method i() is dispatched on the runtime class B. Option a assumes everything is virtual.

A class overrides equals correctly but not hashCode. Two equal instances are added to a HashSet. What is the most likely size()?

b. HashSet locates the bucket via hashCode first. Default identity hashes differ (almost always), so the second object goes to another bucket and equals is never consulted. There is no fallback (d) and no exception (c). Occasionally the hashes collide and you get 1, which is why the bug is intermittent.

Which hashCode implementation is legal but harmful?

c. A constant satisfies the contract (equal objects have equal hashes) but puts every entry in one bucket, turning HashMap into a linked list or red-black tree. b is also legal and merely weaker. d violates consistency and is illegal. a is the correct implementation.

Which parameter type lets a method both read Numbers from a list and accept a List<Integer> or a List<Double>?

a. Producer, so extends. List<Number> (b) rejects List<Integer> because generics are invariant. ? super Number (c) accepts List<Number> and List<Object> but not List<Integer>, and reads yield only Object.

Why does Animal[] a = new Dog[1]; a[0] = new Cat(); compile but fail at run time, while the List equivalent does not compile?

d. The JVM knows the array is really a Dog[] and throws ArrayStoreException. Generics chose invariance precisely to move this error to compile time. a has the terms reversed; b is backwards: erasure is why the check must be at compile time, not why it is impossible.

Why does Jackson require new TypeReference<List<User>>() {} (with the braces) rather than List<User>.class?

b. This is the super type token. List.class exists (a is wrong) but carries no element type. A lambda would not work here because it does not create a subclass with a Signature attribute.

In Java 17, which statement about a sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square is correct?

c. Sealed classes themselves are final in 17, but pattern matching for switch (JEP 406) is preview there and became standard in 21 (JEP 441), so a is wrong. Permitted subclasses must declare how they continue the hierarchy (b). Records are implicitly final and are the idiomatic leaves (d).

What does this print? Integer a = 127, b = 127, c = 128, d = 128; System.out.println((a == b) + " " + (c == d) + " " + c.equals(d));

a. 127 is served from the IntegerCache (same reference); 128 is allocated twice so == is false; equals compares values. b would need -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax=128 or higher.

Practice

Predict the output: overloading vs overriding in one class

class Shape {
    String name() { return "shape"; }
    static String describe(Shape s)  { return "static:" + s.name(); }
    String show(Shape s)  { return "Shape.show(Shape)"; }
    String show(Circle c) { return "Shape.show(Circle)"; }
}
class Circle extends Shape {
    @Override String name() { return "circle"; }
    static String describe(Shape s)  { return "circle-static"; }
    @Override String show(Shape s) { return "Circle.show(Shape)"; }
}
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Shape s = new Circle();
        Circle c = new Circle();
        System.out.println(s.show(s));
        System.out.println(s.show(c));
        System.out.println(c.show((Shape) c));
        System.out.println(Shape.describe(s) + " / " + s.describe(c));
    }
}
Tests: static-type overload selection, runtime-type override dispatch, static method hiding
Hint 1
For each call, first pick the overload using the declared types of the receiver and argument. Only then ask whether the chosen method is overridden in the runtime class.
Hint 2
s.describe(c) is a static call through an instance reference: it is resolved on the static type Shape, and hiding is not overriding.
Reveal solution
Circle.show(Shape)
Shape.show(Circle)
Circle.show(Shape)
static:circle / static:circle

Line 1: s.show(s): static types are Shape/Shape, so the compiler picks show(Shape). At run time the receiver is a Circle, which overrides show(Shape).

Line 2: s.show(c): argument static type Circle, so show(Circle) is chosen. Circle does not override that overload, so Shape's version runs even though the receiver is a Circle.

Line 3: the cast changes the argument's static type to Shape, selecting show(Shape), which Circle overrides.

Line 4: both calls resolve to Shape.describe (static, resolved on the static type; s.describe(c) is just Shape.describe with a misleading syntax). Inside it, s.name() is a virtual call, so it prints circle. Circle.describe is never called. Note the compiler warning about calling a static method through an instance.

Predict the output: mutable key in a HashSet

import java.util.*;
class Key {
    int v;
    Key(int v) { this.v = v; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof Key k && k.v == v; }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return v; }
}
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Set<Key> set = new HashSet<>();
        Key k = new Key(1);
        set.add(k);
        set.add(new Key(1));
        System.out.print(set.size() + " ");
        k.v = 2;
        System.out.print(set.contains(k) + " ");
        System.out.print(set.contains(new Key(1)) + " ");
        System.out.print(set.remove(k) + " ");
        set.add(k);
        System.out.println(set.size());
    }
}
Tests: bucket lookup by hashCode, consequences of mutating a key after insertion
Hint 1
The set stores k in the bucket for hash 1 and never moves it. After k.v = 2, every lookup of k starts in the bucket for hash 2.
Hint 2
contains(new Key(1)) goes to bucket 1, finds the stored k, and calls k.equals(new Key(1)), comparing 2 with 1.
Reveal solution

Output: 1 false false false 2

set.add(new Key(1)) is rejected because it hashes to the same bucket and equals is true, so size is 1. After k.v = 2, contains(k) looks in bucket 2 (empty) → false. contains(new Key(1)) looks in bucket 1, finds k, but k.equals now compares 2 vs 1 → false. remove(k) also searches bucket 2 → false; the original entry is now unreachable through the API (a leak). set.add(k) stores it again in bucket 2, giving size 2 with the "same" object in the set twice.

Lesson: keys must be immutable, or at least their hash-relevant fields must not change while inside a hash collection. Records or a final field fix this at the type level.

Fix the bug: make this class actually immutable

A reviewer says this "immutable" class can be mutated by callers in three different ways. Find all three and fix them with Java 17 idioms.

public class Itinerary {
    private final String traveller;
    private final List<String> stops;
    private final Date departure;

    public Itinerary(String traveller, List<String> stops, Date departure) {
        this.traveller = traveller;
        this.stops = Collections.unmodifiableList(stops);
        this.departure = departure;
    }
    public String traveller() { return traveller; }
    public List<String> stops() { return stops; }
    public Date departure() { return departure; }
}
Tests: defensive copies, views vs copies, mutable JDK types, subclassing
Hint 1
unmodifiableList is a view over the caller's list. What happens if the caller keeps a reference and calls add?
Hint 2
java.util.Date has setTime. And can someone write class EvilItinerary extends Itinerary?
Reveal solution

The three holes: (1) stops is a view: the caller's original list can still be mutated and the change shows through; (2) departure is a mutable Date shared both on the way in and out; (3) the class is not final, so a subclass can override the accessors or add mutable state.

public final class Itinerary {                              // (3) no subclassing
    private final String traveller;
    private final List<String> stops;
    private final Instant departure;                          // (2) immutable type

    public Itinerary(String traveller, List<String> stops, Instant departure) {
        this.traveller = Objects.requireNonNull(traveller);
        this.stops = List.copyOf(stops);                      // (1) independent, unmodifiable copy
        this.departure = Objects.requireNonNull(departure);
    }
    public String traveller() { return traveller; }
    public List<String> stops() { return stops; }             // safe: already unmodifiable
    public Instant departure() { return departure; }
}
// or, in one line, if no extra invariants are needed:
public record Itinerary(String traveller, List<String> stops, Instant departure) {
    public Itinerary { stops = List.copyOf(stops); Objects.requireNonNull(departure); }
}

If Date must stay in the API, copy it both ways: this.departure = new Date(departure.getTime()) and return new Date(departure.getTime()). Note the record version still needs the compact-constructor copy: records are only shallowly immutable.

Implement: model a payment outcome as an algebraic data type

A payment attempt ends in exactly one of: Approved (transaction id, captured amount), Declined (reason code), or Pending (a retry-after duration). Model this with Java 17 language features so that (a) callers cannot construct any other outcome, (b) a handler that forgets a case fails at compile time, and (c) the types are immutable value objects with sensible equals. Then write a String summarize(PaymentResult r).

Tests: sealed interfaces, records, exhaustive switch, version awareness (17 vs 21)
Hint 1
Sum type = sealed interface; product types = records that implement it.
Hint 2
In Java 17 exact exhaustiveness for a switch with type patterns needs --enable-preview. Offer a 17-without-preview alternative and state its weakness.
Reveal solution
public sealed interface PaymentResult permits Approved, Declined, Pending {}
public record Approved(String txId, BigDecimal amount) implements PaymentResult {
    public Approved { Objects.requireNonNull(txId); if (amount.signum() <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); }
}
public record Declined(String reasonCode) implements PaymentResult {}
public record Pending(Duration retryAfter) implements PaymentResult {}

// Java 21 (or Java 17 with --enable-preview; 17 syntax uses && instead of when for guards)
static String summarize(PaymentResult r) {
    return switch (r) {                                   // exhaustive: no default
        case Approved a -> "approved " + a.txId() + " for " + a.amount();
        case Declined d -> "declined: " + d.reasonCode();
        case Pending p  -> "retry in " + p.retryAfter().toSeconds() + "s";
    };
}

// Java 17 without preview: instanceof patterns; the compiler cannot prove exhaustiveness,
// so the final throw is your (runtime) safety net and a new subtype is NOT caught at compile time.
static String summarize17(PaymentResult r) {
    if (r instanceof Approved a) return "approved " + a.txId();
    if (r instanceof Declined d) return "declined: " + d.reasonCode();
    if (r instanceof Pending p)  return "retry in " + p.retryAfter().toSeconds() + "s";
    throw new IllegalStateException("unreachable: " + r);
}

Why this satisfies the requirements: (a) the permits clause closes the hierarchy and records are implicitly final; (b) the switch expression over a sealed type must cover every permitted subtype, so adding Refunded breaks the build at every switch; (c) records give component-wise equals/hashCode/toString and the compact constructors enforce invariants.

Interview extension: compare with an enum plus nullable fields (loses type safety), a class hierarchy with a visitor (more boilerplate, same exhaustiveness), and exceptions for Declined (control flow via exceptions is slower and hides the outcome from the type system).

3️⃣ Strings

Strings are the most-used class in any Java codebase, and the one interviewers use to test whether you understand references, memory and the compiler. The path here goes from why String is immutable, to where string objects live (pool vs heap), to comparison and hashing, then to the performance topics (StringBuilder, compact strings) and finally the API and regex questions that show up in coding rounds.

Why String is Immutable

Why interviewers ask: it is the gateway question. A weak answer ("because it is final") signals you have memorised a fact; a strong answer connects immutability to the pool, hashing, security and threads.

A String can never change after construction. Every "modifying" method (toUpperCase, replace, concat, trim) returns a new object and leaves the original untouched. Analogy: a printed receipt. You can print a corrected copy, but you cannot edit the one already in someone's hand.

How it is enforced: the class is final (no subclass can add mutating behaviour), the backing array is private final byte[] value (since Java 9; char[] before), no method exposes that array, and constructors defensively copy any array passed in.

Why it was designed this way: (1) Pool sharing: many variables can safely point to one "hello" only if nobody can change it. (2) Security: file paths, class names, JDBC URLs and network hosts are Strings; a mutable String could be altered after a security check and before use. (3) Hash caching: the hash is computed once and stored, which is what makes String a fast, safe HashMap key. (4) Thread safety: immutable objects need no synchronisation.

What immutable does NOT mean: the variable is not fixed. s = s + "x" is legal; it rebinds s to a new object. Immutability is a property of the object, not of the reference.

String s = "java";
s.toUpperCase();              // returns "JAVA" ... and throws it away
System.out.println(s);        // java   (original untouched)

s = s.toUpperCase();          // rebind the reference to the new object
System.out.println(s);        // JAVA

final String t = "fixed";     // final freezes the REFERENCE, immutability freezes the OBJECT
Interview angle: "Can you break String immutability?" With reflection you can set the private value field on older JDKs, but since Java 12 the fields of java.lang.String are filtered from reflection and Java 17's strong module encapsulation blocks setAccessible on java.base internals without --add-opens. The honest answer is "not in practice, and anything that does is undefined behaviour because the JVM intrinsics assume immutability".

Pitfalls

  • Calling s.replace(...) or s.trim() and ignoring the return value: the classic "why did nothing change" bug.
  • Passwords in String stay in the heap until GC and may appear in heap dumps; use char[] and zero it out (that is why Console.readPassword() returns char[]).
  • Immutability makes repeated concatenation O(n2): every += copies the whole string.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why is String a good HashMap key? (Immutable, so its cached hash can never go stale; equals/hashCode are consistent.)
  • Which other JDK classes are immutable? (Wrappers like Integer, BigDecimal, LocalDate, List.of(...) collections, records with immutable components.)
  • How would you write your own immutable class? (final class, private final fields, no setters, defensive copies in and out, no this escape from the constructor.)

String Pool, intern() and Compile-Time Constant Folding

Why interviewers ask: every "predict the output of ==" puzzle lives here. You need to know exactly which expressions produce a pooled object and which allocate a fresh one.

The string pool (String Constant Table) is a JVM-managed hash set of String objects. Every literal in a class's constant pool is resolved to one shared instance, so "hi" written anywhere in the program is the same object. Analogy: a library's single reference copy of a book; everyone reads the same copy instead of buying their own.

new String("hi") always allocates a new heap object (its content copied from the pooled literal), so you end up with two objects. s.intern() asks the pool: "do you have an equal string? if yes give me that one, if not add me and return me". Since Java 7 the pool lives in the main heap (it was in PermGen before), so interned strings are garbage-collected like anything else and the pool can grow (-XX:StringTableSize, default 65536 buckets on recent JDKs, check your JDK).

Constant folding: javac evaluates expressions made only of compile-time constants. "a" + "b" is compiled to the single literal "ab". A final String variable initialised with a constant is itself a constant, so it folds too. A non-final variable, a method call, or anything computed at runtime does not fold: the concatenation runs at runtime and produces a brand-new, un-pooled object.

String a = "hel" + "lo";            // folded by javac to the literal "hello"
final String f = "hel";
String b = f + "lo";                // f is a compile-time constant → folded too
String h = "hel";                   // NOT final
String c = h + "lo";                // runtime concat → new heap object
String d = "hel".concat("lo");      // method call → runtime → new heap object

System.out.println(a == "hello");   // true
System.out.println(b == "hello");   // true
System.out.println(c == "hello");   // false
System.out.println(d == "hello");   // false
System.out.println(c.intern() == "hello"); // true
ExpressionObjects createdPooled?
"hi"0 (reuses the pool entry; created once per literal)Yes
new String("hi")1 heap object (plus the pooled literal if first use)No
"h" + "i"0 at runtime (folded to "hi")Yes
x + "i" (x non-final)1 heap object at runtimeNo
s.intern()0 or adds s itself to the poolReturns pooled instance
Interview angle: "How many objects does String s = new String("abc"); create?" Two if "abc" was not yet in the pool (the pooled literal and the heap copy), one otherwise. "When would you call intern() in production?" Rarely: for millions of duplicate strings read from a file or DB (e.g. country codes, enum-like values) it can cut heap dramatically, but G1's -XX:+UseStringDeduplication does most of that for you by sharing the backing arrays, without pool lookups on the hot path.

Pitfalls

  • Relying on == for strings works "by accident" with literals and breaks the moment a value comes from user input, a file, substring or a database driver.
  • final is what makes a local String a constant; the same code without final gives different == results, which is a favourite trick question.
  • Interning everything: the pool is a hash table with a fixed bucket count; millions of entries lengthen its chains and interning costs a lookup each time.

Likely follow-ups

  • Where is the pool? (Heap since Java 7; PermGen in Java 6 and earlier, where it could cause OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space.)
  • Are pooled strings ever garbage collected? (Yes, when no class constant pool or live reference refers to them.)
  • Does String.valueOf(1) == "1"? (No: runtime conversion creates a heap object.)
  • Does the pool apply to Integer too? (Different mechanism: Integer.valueOf caches -128..127, so == on boxed ints is a similar trap.)

Java 8 vs 17

In Java 8 the pool was already on the heap (moved in 7). Java 8u20 added -XX:+UseStringDeduplication for G1; Java 17 keeps it for G1 and Shenandoah; Java 18 extended it to all collectors. The default string table size grew from 1009 buckets (Java 7) to 60013 (Java 8) to 65536 (Java 11+, check your JDK).

== vs equals vs compareTo, and the hashCode Formula

Why interviewers ask: the follow-up to the pool question. They want to hear "reference vs content", and the hashCode formula is a favourite for probing whether you understand why String works so well in hash-based collections.

== compares references (same object?). equals compares content: same length and same bytes, with a fast reference check first. equalsIgnoreCase compares case-insensitively per character (it does not use locale rules; for Turkish-style problems use toLowerCase(Locale) carefully or a Collator). compareTo gives lexicographic order using UTF-16 code unit values: it returns the difference of the first mismatching chars, or the length difference if one is a prefix; note that uppercase sorts before lowercase ("Z" < "a"). String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER is the ready-made comparator.

hashCode: h = s[0]*31^(n-1) + s[1]*31^(n-2) + ... + s[n-1], evaluated as a Horner loop h = 31*h + c with int overflow. Why 31? It is an odd prime (even multipliers lose the low bits on overflow), small enough to give a good spread for short ASCII strings, and the JIT can compute 31*h as (h << 5) - h. Joshua Bloch picked it empirically over a dictionary of words for fewest collisions.

Hash caching: the result is stored in a private int hash field (plus a hashIsZero boolean since Java 13 so that a genuine zero hash is not recomputed forever). Only immutability makes this cache safe.

String a = "Apple", b = "apple";
a.equals(b);                 // false
a.equalsIgnoreCase(b);       // true
a.compareTo(b);              // negative: 'A'(65) - 'a'(97) = -32
"ab".compareTo("abc");       // -1: length difference when one is a prefix
"".hashCode();               // 0
"a".hashCode();              // 97
"ab".hashCode();             // 31*97 + 98 = 3105
"Aa".hashCode() == "BB".hashCode();  // true: a classic collision (2112)

Objects.equals(a, null);     // false, no NPE; a.equals(null) is also false
"literal".equals(userInput); // NPE-safe idiom when userInput may be null
OperationComparesReturnsNull-safe?
a == bReference identitybooleanYes
a.equals(b)Content, case-sensitivebooleanOnly for b
a.equalsIgnoreCase(b)Content, case-folded per charbooleanOnly for b
a.compareTo(b)Lexicographic (UTF-16 units)int (<0, 0, >0)No (NPE)
a.contentEquals(cs)Content vs any CharSequencebooleanNo
Interview angle: "Two strings have the same hashCode; are they equal?" Not necessarily ("Aa"/"BB"). The contract is only one way: equal objects must have equal hashes. "Why does Java not use a cryptographic hash?" Cost: HashMap.get must be nanoseconds, and collisions are handled by equals anyway (and treeified since Java 8).

Pitfalls

  • compareTo returning e.g. -32 is a contract detail, not a promise: only the sign is guaranteed (Comparator users must not test for -1/1).
  • Sorting user-facing text with compareTo puts "Zebra" before "apple"; use Collator.getInstance(locale) for human ordering.
  • Predictable String hashes enabled hash-flooding DoS on web servers; Java 8's treeified buckets are the mitigation (O(log n) worst case) rather than randomised hashing.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why is hashCode 32-bit when the pool can hold more strings? (Collisions are expected and resolved with equals; hash only narrows the bucket.)
  • Can hashCode be negative? (Yes, on int overflow; HashMap masks with (n-1) & hash after spreading high bits.)
  • What does String.equals do first? (Identity check, then instanceof, then coder and length, then byte comparison via an intrinsic.)

StringBuilder vs StringBuffer vs +

Why interviewers ask: to see whether you know the cost model of concatenation in loops, and whether your knowledge of "the compiler turns + into StringBuilder" is current (it is not, since Java 9).

StringBuilder is a mutable, growable buffer of chars; StringBuffer is the same API with every method synchronized (a 1995 design; almost never what you want, since you rarely share a builder between threads). Both start with capacity 16 (or 16 + str.length() when seeded) and grow with newCapacity = oldCapacity * 2 + 2 when an append does not fit, copying the array each time. Amortised, a build of n chars costs O(n); with += in a loop each iteration allocates a full new String, giving O(n2) copying. Analogy: a whiteboard you keep writing on versus re-printing the whole poster every time you add a word.

What javac generates for +: up to Java 8, a chain of new StringBuilder().append(a).append(b).toString(). Since Java 9 (JEP 280) it emits a single invokedynamic call to StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants. At first execution the JVM builds an optimised MethodHandle that computes the exact final length, allocates one byte array and writes every piece into it: no intermediate builder, no resizing. The recipe is a template string with \u0001 placeholders, so the bytecode is tiny and the strategy can improve in future JDKs without recompiling.

When the compiler helps and when it does not: a single expression a + b + c + d is one indy call (optimal). Inside a loop, each iteration is a separate concat that produces a new String, and the previous result becomes the input of the next: the JVM cannot merge iterations, so it is still quadratic. That is the case where you write the StringBuilder yourself. String.join, Collectors.joining and String.repeat already use a builder or precomputed sizes internally.

// Java 9+: one invokedynamic call, one allocation, optimal.
String line = id + "," + name + "," + price;

// Loop: each iteration allocates a new String of growing size → O(n²) copying.
String csv = "";
for (var row : rows) csv += row + "\n";      // avoid

// Correct: builder sized up front, single toString at the end.
var sb = new StringBuilder(rows.size() * 32);
for (var row : rows) sb.append(row).append('\n');
String csv2 = sb.toString();

// Often even simpler:
String csv3 = rows.stream().collect(Collectors.joining("\n", "", "\n"));
String csv4 = String.join("\n", rows);       // rows must be Iterable<? extends CharSequence>
+ (Java 9+)StringBuilderStringBuffer
Thread-safen/a (immutable result)NoYes (synchronized methods)
Best forSingle expression, few operandsLoops, building in stepsLegacy code only
Bytecodeinvokedynamic to StringConcatFactoryExplicit append callsSame, plus monitor enter/exit
Extra API-insert, reverse, deleteCharAt, setLength, setCharAtSame
Interview angle: "Is + in a loop still bad in Java 17?" Yes, for a different reason: not because of temporary builders but because each iteration creates a complete String that is immediately thrown away. "Why is StringBuffer slow if lock elision exists?" The JIT can elide uncontended locks via escape analysis only when the buffer provably does not escape; in real code it usually does, so the monitor cost remains.

Pitfalls

  • sb.append(a + b) inside a loop still does a concat per iteration; append each piece separately.
  • StringBuilder does not override equals: sb1.equals(sb2) is identity; compare with sb1.compareTo(sb2) (Java 11+) or toString().
  • Reusing one builder across calls with setLength(0) keeps the largest array ever grown alive; fine for a hot loop, a leak if the builder is a long-lived field.
  • -XDstringConcat=inline on javac reverts to the old StringBuilder strategy; useful only for tooling that cannot handle indy.

Likely follow-ups

  • What does StringBuilder.toString() cost? (One array copy of exactly length bytes; the builder keeps its array so it stays usable.)
  • Why did JEP 280 use invokedynamic? (Decouples the concat strategy from the bytecode, like lambdas: the JDK can improve it without recompiling your code.)
  • Which strategy does the JDK use by default? (MH_INLINE_SIZED_EXACT: a method-handle tree that computes exact length, then fills one array.)

Java 8 vs 17

Java 8: + compiles to StringBuilder chains. Java 9+: invokedynamic with StringConcatFactory (JEP 280), faster and allocation-light. StringBuilder.compareTo and isEmpty() on CharSequence arrived in Java 11/15.

Compact Strings, char vs Code Points and Surrogate Pairs

Why interviewers ask: the memory question ("how big is a String?") and the correctness question ("does length() return the number of characters?") both have answers that changed or surprise people.

Compact Strings (JEP 254, Java 9): the backing store changed from char[] (2 bytes per char) to byte[] plus a byte coder field. If every char fits in Latin-1 (U+0000 to U+00FF) the string is stored with 1 byte per char (coder = LATIN1); otherwise it uses UTF-16 (coder = UTF16, 2 bytes per char). Since most strings in server apps are ASCII (JSON keys, URLs, SQL), this roughly halves string memory, which for typical heaps is 20-30% of all live data. It is transparent to your code and can be disabled with -XX:-CompactStrings. Object size for a 10-char ASCII string on a 64-bit JVM with compressed oops: 24-byte String header+fields plus a 32-byte array (16 header + 10 data, aligned to 8), about 56 bytes; before Java 9 it was 24 + 40 = 64 bytes.

char is not a character: a Java char is one UTF-16 code unit. Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (emoji, many CJK ideographs, musical symbols; code points above U+FFFF) need two units, a surrogate pair (high surrogate D800-DBFF followed by low surrogate DC00-DFFF). So "😀".length() is 2, charAt(0) is half a character, substring in the middle produces a broken string, and reverse() on a StringBuilder handles pairs but a hand-written char-swap does not. Analogy: char counts bytes on a wire; a code point is the actual letter that was sent.

Use code point APIs when text can be non-ASCII: codePointCount, codePointAt, codePoints() stream, Character.isSurrogate, Character.toChars(cp), StringBuilder.appendCodePoint. Even code points are not what users perceive as "characters": grapheme clusters (e.g. flags, family emoji with zero-width joiners, "e" + combining accent) need java.text.BreakIterator.getCharacterInstance().

String s = "a😀b";
s.length();                       // 4  (a, high surrogate, low surrogate, b)
s.codePointCount(0, s.length());  // 3
s.charAt(1);                      // '\uD83D' — half a character, not printable alone
s.codePointAt(1);                 // 0x1F600 (128512)
s.substring(0, 2);                // "a\uD83D" — broken: dangling high surrogate
s.codePoints().count();           // 3

// Correct reverse that keeps surrogate pairs intact
String reversed = new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString();   // "b😀a"

// Iterate by code point instead of char
s.codePoints().forEach(cp -> System.out.print(Character.toChars(cp)));

// Coder check (no public API): "abc" → LATIN1 (3 bytes), "aβc" → UTF16 (6 bytes)
Questionchar-based answerCode-point answer
How many characters?length() (UTF-16 units)codePointCount(0, len)
Character at position icharAt(i)codePointAt(offsetByCodePoints(0, i))
IteratetoCharArray(), chars()codePoints()
Buildappend(char)appendCodePoint(int)
User-perceived character-BreakIterator.getCharacterInstance()
Interview angle: "How would you truncate a user's display name to 20 characters?" Not substring(0, 20): use offsetByCodePoints or a BreakIterator, otherwise a name ending in an emoji becomes invalid UTF-16 and can fail JSON serialisation. "Why does the DB column show a different length?" MySQL utf8mb4 counts code points; Java counts UTF-16 units.

Pitfalls

  • Validation like name.length() <= 50 passes for 50 code units, then a DB with a 50-character limit rejects a string containing emoji or accepts more than intended: decide which unit you mean.
  • String.getBytes() without a charset uses the platform default; since Java 18 that is UTF-8 everywhere (JEP 400), in Java 17 it still depends on the OS. Always pass StandardCharsets.UTF_8.
  • Mixing one non-Latin-1 char into a large string (e.g. a smart quote in a big JSON) flips the whole string to UTF-16, doubling its size.

Likely follow-ups

  • Is UTF-16 storage removed? (No: still used when any char is above U+00FF; Latin-1 is the compact fast path.)
  • Does compact strings affect StringBuilder? (Yes, it has the same coder and inflates from Latin-1 to UTF-16 on the first wide char.)
  • What is a BOM and why does it break equals? (U+FEFF at the start of a file read as text; invisible but counted, so "id".equals(header) fails.)

Java 8 vs 17

Java 8: char[], always 2 bytes per char. Java 9+: byte[] + coder (JEP 254). Java 11 added strip, isBlank, lines, repeat; Java 12 indent, transform; Java 15 text blocks and formatted. Java 18 (after 17) made UTF-8 the default charset.

String API Questions That Keep Coming Up

Why interviewers ask: small API details reveal whether you have actually shipped Java code: the old substring leak, the split regex traps, and whether you know the Java 11-17 additions.

substring history: until Java 7u6, substring returned a String that shared the parent's char[] with an offset and count: O(1), but a 5-char substring of a 10 MB string kept the 10 MB alive (a real leak when parsing large files and storing keys). Since 7u6 it copies the range: O(k) but no leak, and the String object shrank (no offset/count fields). Interviewers still ask about it because the old behaviour was famous.

split takes a regex. "a.b.c".split(".") returns an empty array because . matches everything; escape ("\\.") or use Pattern.quote. "a|b".split("|") splits every character. Trailing empty strings are removed ("a,b,,".split(",") gives 2 elements) unless you pass a negative limit; leading empties are kept. For single-char, non-metacharacter delimiters the JDK has a fast path that skips the regex engine entirely.

Whitespace and blanks: trim() strips chars <= U+0020 (ASCII control and space only); strip() (Java 11) uses Character.isWhitespace, so it also removes Unicode spaces such as U+2003 but, notably, neither removes the non-breaking space U+00A0. isBlank() is "empty or only whitespace" by the same Unicode definition; isEmpty() is length() == 0.

APISinceWhat to know
substring(b, e)1.0Copies since 7u6; end exclusive; substring(len) is legal and returns "".
split(regex[, limit])1.4Regex! Trailing empties dropped when limit is 0. Compile a Pattern for hot loops.
String.format(fmt, args) / formatted(args)5 / 15Same engine (Formatter), slow-ish (parses the pattern each call, locale-aware); fine for logs, avoid in hot loops.
String.join(delim, elems)8Delegates to StringJoiner; accepts varargs or Iterable<CharSequence>.
repeat(n)11Doubling copy, O(n); repeat(0) is "", negative throws.
strip / stripLeading / stripTrailing11Unicode-aware; prefer over trim.
isBlank()11True for "" and " "; use instead of trim().isEmpty().
lines()11Stream split on \n, \r, \r\n; lazy.
chars() / codePoints()8IntStream, not Stream<Character>; map with mapToObj(c -> (char) c).
transform(fn)12s.transform(Parser::parse) for fluent pipelines.
Text blocks """15Incidental indentation stripped relative to the closing delimiter; \ at end of line joins lines; \s keeps a trailing space.
indent(n) / stripIndent()12 / 15Helpers built for text blocks.
"a.b.c".split(".").length;            // 0   ('.' matches everything)
"a.b.c".split("\\.").length;          // 3
"a,b,,".split(",").length;            // 2   (trailing empties removed)
"a,b,,".split(",", -1).length;        // 4
",a".split(",").length;               // 2   (leading empty kept: "", "a")

" \u00A0x ".trim();                   // "\u00A0x"  NBSP not removed by trim
" \u00A0x ".strip();                  // "\u00A0x"  ...nor by strip (NBSP is not isWhitespace)
"\u2003x".strip();                    // "x"        em-space removed by strip only

String json = """
    {"id": %d, "name": "%s"}
    """.formatted(42, "Ada");        // text block + formatted (Java 15)

"abc".chars().filter(Character::isLetter).count();     // IntStream, 3
Map<Character, Long> freq = "banana".chars()
    .mapToObj(c -> (char) c)
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(c -> c, LinkedHashMap::new, Collectors.counting()));
// {b=1, a=3, n=2}
Interview angle: "Parse a 2 GB CSV and keep only the first column": with pre-7u6 substring semantics this retained every full line in memory; today it is safe. A follow-up is often "how would you avoid allocating a String per line at all?" (read into a reusable CharBuffer, or use lines() and let each String die young).

Pitfalls

  • String.format("%d", 1_000_000) is locale-sensitive only with the , flag, but %s of a double and %f use the default locale's decimal separator: pass Locale.ROOT for machine-readable output.
  • split("\\s+") on a string with leading whitespace produces a leading "" element; strip() first.
  • chars() yields ints; .boxed() gives Stream<Integer>, not characters, so collect(toList()) prints numbers.
  • replaceAll takes a regex and a replacement with $ group syntax; replace(CharSequence, CharSequence) is the literal, faster one.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is StringJoiner? (Builder with delimiter, prefix, suffix and setEmptyValue; used by String.join and Collectors.joining.)
  • How do text blocks handle indentation? (The closing """ position sets the left margin; whitespace common to all lines is removed.)
  • Difference between String.valueOf(obj) and obj.toString()? (The former returns "null" for null instead of throwing.)

Regex Basics for Interviews: Pattern, Greedy vs Lazy, Backtracking

Why interviewers ask: regex shows up in validation and parsing tasks; they check that you compile once, know matches vs find, and can spot a pattern that will hang production on adversarial input.

String.matches, replaceAll and split compile the regex on every call. In any loop or hot path, compile once into a static final Pattern (it is immutable and thread-safe) and create a Matcher per use (a Matcher is stateful and not thread-safe). Analogy: Pattern is the compiled program, Matcher is one running process over one input.

matches() vs find() vs lookingAt(): matches requires the whole input to match (implicit ^...$); find scans for the next substring that matches and can be called repeatedly; lookingAt anchors only at the start. Groups are read with group(n) or named groups (?<name>...) via group("name").

Greedy vs lazy: .* grabs as much as possible then backtracks; .*? takes as little as possible and extends. <.*> on "<a><b>" matches the whole thing; <.*?> matches <a>. Possessive quantifiers (.*+) and atomic groups (?>...) never give back what they consumed, which makes them both faster and a defence against backtracking explosions.

Catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS): nested or overlapping quantifiers like (a+)+$, (\w+\s?)*$, (.*a){20} have exponentially many ways to partition the input; when the match fails at the end the engine tries all of them. Twenty-five characters of "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!" against ^(a+)+$ takes seconds; thirty takes minutes. Java's engine is a backtracking NFA with no timeout, so an email or URL validator with this shape is a denial-of-service vector. Fixes: remove the nesting, use possessive/atomic constructs, restrict character classes ([^@]+ instead of .+), cap input length before matching.

private static final Pattern LOG = Pattern.compile(
    "(?<level>INFO|WARN|ERROR)\\s+\\[(?<thread>[^\\]]+)\\]\\s+(?<msg>.*)");

record LogLine(String level, String thread, String msg) {}

static Optional<LogLine> parse(String line) {
    Matcher m = LOG.matcher(line);                 // new Matcher per call
    if (!m.matches()) return Optional.empty();     // whole line must match
    return Optional.of(new LogLine(m.group("level"), m.group("thread"), m.group("msg")));
}

// find() iterates over every occurrence
static List<String> hashtags(String text) {
    Matcher m = Pattern.compile("#(\\w+)").matcher(text);
    List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
    while (m.find()) out.add(m.group(1));
    return out;
}

"<a><b>".replaceAll("<.*>", "X");     // "X"      greedy
"<a><b>".replaceAll("<.*?>", "X");    // "XX"     lazy
"aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!".matches("(a+)+");   // hangs: catastrophic backtracking
"aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!".matches("a++");     // false, instantly (possessive)
MethodAnchoringTypical use
matcher.matches() / String.matchesEntire inputValidation ("is this a valid ID?")
matcher.find()Anywhere, repeatableExtraction, tokenising
matcher.lookingAt()Start onlyPrefix parsing
Pattern.asPredicate() / asMatchPredicate()find / matchesstream.filter(P.asPredicate())
Pattern.splitAsStream-Lazy split for large inputs
Interview angle: "Validate an email." The right answer is a simple, linear pattern such as ^[^@\\s]+@[^@\\s]+\\.[^@\\s]+$ plus a length cap, and a note that RFC 5322 is not regex-friendly so you confirm by sending mail. Reciting a 200-char RFC regex is the wrong answer: it is unmaintainable and often backtracks badly.

Pitfalls

  • Forgetting that String.matches is whole-string: "abc".matches("b") is false.
  • Double escaping: the regex \d is the Java literal "\\d"; Java 15 text blocks do not help, but Pattern.quote and Matcher.quoteReplacement do for literal text.
  • Sharing a Matcher across threads (e.g. as a static field) gives corrupted groups; only Pattern is shareable.
  • $ in a replacement string means a group reference; a literal dollar in replaceAll must be \\$ or go through Matcher.quoteReplacement.

Likely follow-ups

  • Does Java support lookahead/lookbehind? (Yes: (?=...), (?!...), (?<=...), (?<!...); lookbehind must have a bounded length.)
  • How would you protect a service from ReDoS? (Length limits, linear patterns, run untrusted matching with a timeout on a separate thread, or use RE2-style libraries.)
  • What does Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE | Pattern.UNICODE_CASE do? (Case folding beyond ASCII; slower, off by default.)

What does this print?
String a = "ja" + "va"; String b = "java"; String x = "ja"; String c = x + "va";
System.out.println((a == b) + " " + (c == b));

c. "ja" + "va" is folded by javac into the literal "java", the same pooled object as b. x is not final, so x + "va" is evaluated at runtime and produces a new heap object; c == b is false. Option a would be right only if x were declared final String x = "ja".

String s = new String("hi"); String t = s.intern(); Which is true?

b. The literal "hi" in the constructor call is already in the pool, so intern() returns that canonical object; s still refers to the separate heap copy created by new. Option a is wrong because intern() returns a reference and never rebinds variables.

Why is 31 used as the multiplier in String.hashCode()?

d. An even multiplier would lose information on overflow; a prime spreads bits well; the shift-and-subtract form was cheap on 1990s hardware. Option c is impossible: "Aa" and "BB" both hash to 2112, so equal hashes never imply equal strings.

In Java 17, what does javac emit for String s = a + "-" + b;?

c. Since Java 9 (JEP 280) concatenation is an invokedynamic call whose bootstrap builds a method handle that sizes the result exactly and allocates once. Option a is the Java 8 strategy, still obtainable with -XDstringConcat=inline.

A StringBuilder created with default capacity currently holds 16 chars. You append 5 more. What is its new capacity?

b. Growth is old * 2 + 2 = 34, taken because it is larger than the 21 needed. Option a would mean growing to exactly the required size on every append, which would make building O(n2); c is pure doubling, which is ArrayList-style thinking (ArrayList actually uses 1.5x).

What does "a😀".length() + " " + "a😀".codePointCount(0, 3) evaluate to?

c. The emoji is outside the BMP and occupies two UTF-16 code units (a surrogate pair), so length() is 3 while there are only 2 code points. Option a is the answer people give when they assume char equals character.

Which is the best production choice for building a large report string in a loop over 100k rows?

a. Pre-sizing avoids every grow-and-copy. Option b is still O(n2): the indy optimisation helps a single expression, but each loop iteration still materialises a full new String. c adds uncontended lock overhead for no benefit, and d parses the format string 100k times.

"1.2.3".split(".") returns an array of length:

d. The argument is a regex; . matches every character, so the result is six empty strings, and trailing empty strings are removed, leaving nothing. Use split("\\.") or Pattern.quote(".") for a.

Practice

Predict the output: pool, final and intern

public class Main {
    static final String K = "ab";
    static String v = "ab";

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String s1 = "abc";
        String s2 = "ab" + "c";
        String s3 = K + "c";
        String s4 = v + "c";
        String s5 = new String("abc");
        String s6 = s4.intern();
        final String local = "ab";
        String s7 = local + "c";

        System.out.println((s1 == s2) + " " + (s1 == s3) + " " + (s1 == s4));
        System.out.println((s1 == s5) + " " + (s1 == s6) + " " + (s1 == s7));
        System.out.println(s5.equals(s6) + " " + (s5.intern() == s6));
    }
}
Tests: constant folding rules, final constant variables, new String, intern()
Hint 1
Ask of every expression: can javac compute the value at compile time? Only literals and final variables initialised with constants qualify.
Hint 2
intern() returns the pooled object but never changes the variable you called it on.
Reveal solution

Output:

true true false
false true true
true true
  • s2: "ab" + "c" is folded to the literal "abc": same pool object as s1. true
  • s3: K is static final with a constant initialiser, so it is a compile-time constant; folded. true
  • s4: v is not final; runtime concatenation creates a new heap object. false
  • s5: new always allocates. false
  • s6: s4.intern() finds the equal pooled "abc" (already there because of the literal) and returns it. true
  • s7: a final local initialised with a literal is also a constant variable (JLS 4.12.4), so local + "c" folds. true
  • Last line: content equality is always true; s5.intern() and s6 both resolve to the single pooled instance. true true

What the interviewer is probing: that you distinguish compile-time constant expression (JLS 15.29) from runtime evaluation, and that intern() is a lookup, not a mutation.

Predict the output: immutability, builders and method calls

public class Main {
    static void change(String s, StringBuilder sb) {
        s = s.concat(" world");
        sb.append(" world");
        sb = new StringBuilder("gone");
        sb.append("!");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String s = "hello";
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("hello");
        change(s, sb);
        s.toUpperCase();
        System.out.println(s + " | " + sb);

        String t = "x";
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) t += i;
        System.out.println(t + " " + (t == "x012") + " " + t.equals("x012"));
    }
}
Tests: pass-by-value of references, immutability vs mutability, ignored return values, runtime concat identity
Hint 1
Java copies the reference. Mutating the object it points to is visible to the caller; reassigning the parameter is not.
Reveal solution

Output:

hello | hello world
x012 false true
  • s.concat(" world") creates a new String and stores it in the local parameter only; main's s still points at "hello".
  • sb.append(" world") mutates the one shared builder, so the caller sees "hello world".
  • sb = new StringBuilder("gone") rebinds the local parameter; the "!" goes to an object the caller never sees.
  • s.toUpperCase() with the result discarded does nothing observable.
  • The loop builds "x012" through runtime concatenation, so it is a heap object, not the pooled literal: == is false, equals is true.

Implement: first non-repeating character, and group anagrams

Part A: given a string, return the index of the first character that appears exactly once, or -1. Part B: given a list of words, group the ones that are anagrams of each other. Both must be O(n) in the total input size (treat the alphabet as constant). State what changes if the input may contain emoji.

static int firstUniqueIndex(String s)                 // "leetcode" → 0, "aabb" → -1
static List<List<String>> groupAnagrams(List<String> words)
// ["eat","tea","tan","ate","nat","bat"] → [[eat,tea,ate],[tan,nat],[bat]]
Tests: counting with arrays vs maps, choosing a canonical key without sorting, insertion order, code points
Hint 1
Two passes for Part A: count, then scan for the first count of 1. A LinkedHashMap is the alternative if you want one structure that remembers order.
Hint 2
For Part B, sorting each word costs O(k log k). A 26-slot count array turned into a string key is O(k) and still canonical.
Reveal solution
static int firstUniqueIndex(String s) {
    int[] count = new int[128];                       // ASCII; use a Map for full Unicode
    for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) count[s.charAt(i)]++;
    for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) if (count[s.charAt(i)] == 1) return i;
    return -1;
}

static List<List<String>> groupAnagrams(List<String> words) {
    Map<String, List<String>> groups = new LinkedHashMap<>();   // keeps first-seen order
    for (String w : words) {
        int[] freq = new int[26];
        for (int i = 0; i < w.length(); i++) freq[w.charAt(i) - 'a']++;
        var key = new StringBuilder(26 * 3);
        for (int f : freq) key.append(f).append('#');            // "#" separator avoids 1,11 vs 11,1 ambiguity
        groups.computeIfAbsent(key.toString(), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(w);
    }
    return new ArrayList<>(groups.values());
}

Complexity. Part A: O(n) time, O(1) space (fixed 128-slot array). Part B: O(N · k) time where k is the average word length, O(N · k) space for the groups; the sort-based version is O(N · k log k).

Unicode variant. charAt splits surrogate pairs, so an emoji would be counted as two half-characters. Iterate with s.codePoints() and count in a HashMap<Integer,Integer> (or an int[] sized to the code point range you accept); the index you return should then be a code point index or a char offset, and you must say which. Also decide whether case matters (toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT) first) and whether to ignore whitespace and punctuation for anagrams.

What the interviewer is probing. Whether you reach for a count array before a HashMap, whether your anagram key is canonical and collision-free (the separator matters), whether you know computeIfAbsent, and whether you flag the char-vs-code-point issue without being prompted.

4️⃣ Collections Internals

Every Java interview touches collections, and senior rounds go straight to internals: how HashMap buckets, resizes and treeifies, why LinkedList is almost never the answer, and what ConcurrentHashMap actually locks. This section walks the framework map first, then each implementation from array-backed lists to concurrent maps, and finishes with iterators, ordering and immutability — the places where "predict the output" questions live.

The Framework Map & Big-O Cheat Sheet

Why interviewers ask: "which collection would you use?" is a filter question; the follow-up "what is the cost of contains?" is where candidates fall over.

Iterable (just iterator(), enables for-each) → Collection (size, add, remove, contains) → three families: List (ordered, indexed, duplicates), Set (no duplicates), Queue/Deque (head/tail access). Map is not a Collection: it is a separate root because a key→value pair is not "an element"; you iterate its views (keySet(), values(), entrySet()).

Analogy: List is a numbered shelf, Set is a guest list, Queue is a ticket line, Map is a phone book. Choose by the operation you do most, not the one you do first.
