Interview angle: "containsValue on a HashMap?" O(n) — it scans every bin. "Why is ArrayList.remove(Object) O(n)?" Linear search plus System.arraycopy shift. Say "average" for hash structures and name the worst case (treeified bin → O(log n), pre-Java-8 → O(n)).

Pitfalls

  • Calling list.get(i) inside a loop over a LinkedList turns O(n) into O(n²). Use the iterator.
  • Set.contains is only O(1) if hashCode is well distributed; a constant hashCode degrades to a single treeified bin.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why does Map not extend Collection? (Different contract: keyed lookup, no notion of a single element; views bridge the gap.)
  • What does Collection.toArray(T[]) do with an array that is too small? (Allocates a new one of the right runtime type.)

ArrayList Internals: Growth, Views and Traps

Why interviewers ask: "amortized O(1)" is the phrase they want; the traps (Arrays.asList, subList) show whether you have been bitten in production.

An ArrayList is a plain Object[] elementData plus an int size. When the array is full, grow() allocates a new array of 1.5× the old capacity — literally oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1) — and Arrays.copyOfs the elements. Default capacity is 10 (allocated lazily on first add). Because copies happen at geometrically spaced sizes, the total copy work over n adds is O(n), so each append is amortized O(1). Insert or remove in the middle is O(n) because System.arraycopy shifts the tail.

Analogy: a parking lot that, when full, builds a lot 50% bigger and moves every car over once. If you know the final size, new ArrayList<>(n) or ensureCapacity(n) avoids the moves entirely.

List<String> fixed = Arrays.asList("a", "b");   // view over the array
fixed.set(0, "z");            // OK, writes through to the array
fixed.add("c");               // UnsupportedOperationException (fixed-size)

List<String> imm = List.of("a", "b");            // Java 9: truly immutable
imm.contains(null);           // NullPointerException! null-hostile
List.of("a", null);           // NPE at construction

List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5));
List<Integer> mid = nums.subList(1, 4);   // VIEW [2,3,4], not a copy
mid.clear();                  // nums is now [1, 5]
nums.add(6);                  // structural change to parent...
mid.size();                   // ...→ ConcurrentModificationException
Interview angle: "How do I remove a range from a list in one line?" list.subList(from, to).clear() — the canonical use of the view. "Why does Arrays.asList(intArray) give a List<int[]> of size 1?" Varargs generics do not autobox primitive arrays; use Arrays.stream(arr).boxed().toList().

Pitfalls

  • remove(int) vs remove(Object): list.remove(1) on a List<Integer> removes index 1, not the value 1. Use remove(Integer.valueOf(1)).
  • Arrays.asList is backed by the array: modifying the array changes the list and vice versa.
  • trimToSize() exists for the rare "built huge list, now read-only forever" case; the JVM does not shrink automatically.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why 1.5× and not 2×? (Less wasted memory; freed old arrays can be reused for a later grow because 1 + 1.5 > 1.5²… roughly, plus allocator friendliness. StringBuilder uses 2×+2.)
  • Maximum size? (Integer.MAX_VALUE - 8, the SOFT_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH; beyond that OutOfMemoryError.)

LinkedList vs ArrayList vs ArrayDeque

Why interviewers ask: the textbook answer ("LinkedList for frequent inserts") is wrong on modern hardware, and they want to hear you say why.

LinkedList stores each element in a Node object with prev/next references: 3 references + object header per element (roughly 24–40 bytes of overhead each), scattered across the heap. Iteration chases pointers, which defeats the CPU cache. ArrayList stores references contiguously, so a scan streams through memory and the prefetcher wins. In practice ArrayList beats LinkedList for almost every workload, including "insert in the middle", because finding the middle is O(n) pointer hops anyway.

The one thing LinkedList does well — O(1) add/remove at both ends — ArrayDeque does better with a circular array and no per-element allocation. ArrayDeque is the standard stack (push/pop/peek) and queue (offer/poll). The legacy Stack class extends Vector (synchronized, exposes get(i)), and its own Javadoc recommends Deque instead. Analogy: a linked list is a scavenger hunt where each clue points to the next house; an array is one street with numbered doors.

ArrayListLinkedListArrayDeque
Random accessO(1)O(n)Not a List
Add/remove at headO(n)O(1)O(1)
Add/remove at tailO(1) amortizedO(1)O(1) amortized
Memory per element1 ref (+ slack)Node: 3 refs + header1 ref (+ slack)
Allows nullYesYesNo (NullPointerException)
Use forDefault listRarely: ListIterator-driven in-place removal while walkingStack, queue, sliding window
Interview angle: "Implement a stack." Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>(). Mention that ArrayDeque iterates head→tail, so push then for-each gives LIFO order — a common surprise when candidates print a "stack".

Pitfalls

  • ArrayDeque rejects null because poll() returns null to mean "empty". LinkedList as a queue does allow nulls, which then become ambiguous.
  • LinkedList implements both List and Deque; using it as a Queue "because it has offer" allocates a node per element for no benefit.

Likely follow-ups

  • When is LinkedList justified? (Removing many elements while iterating with a ListIterator, or when you need a List and a Deque in one object; still rare.)
  • How does ArrayDeque grow? (Doubles the circular array and unwraps the head/tail into the new one.)

HashMap Internals: Hash Spreading, Buckets, Treeify, Resize

Why interviewers ask: this is the Java internals question. They probe hash spreading, index calculation, collision handling and the resize split; strong candidates can draw all four.

A HashMap is an array Node<K,V>[] table whose length is always a power of two. Each slot ("bin" or "bucket") holds a singly-linked chain of Node(hash, key, value, next). put computes hash = h ^ (h >>> 16) where h = key.hashCode(): XOR-ing the high 16 bits into the low bits so keys whose hash codes differ only in high bits (common for Float, aligned pointers, small tables) still spread. The index is (n - 1) & hash — a bit mask, not a modulo, which is why n must be a power of two.

Collisions chain onto the bin. When a chain reaches 8 nodes (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD) and the table has at least 64 bins (MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY), the bin becomes a red-black tree of TreeNodes (O(log n) lookups). If the table is smaller than 64, the map resizes instead, on the theory that a tiny table is the real problem. A tree bin shrinks back to a list when it drops to 6 (UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD) during resize; the gap between 8 and 6 avoids flapping.

Resize happens when size > capacity × loadFactor (0.75 by default): the table doubles and every node is re-homed. Because the new mask exposes exactly one more bit, each node goes to either its old index (lo list, bit = 0) or old + oldCapacity (hi list, bit = 1). Java 8 splits each bin into these two lists in one pass, preserving relative order and rehashing nothing. Analogy: a post office with 8 sorting slots adds 8 more; every letter either stays in its slot or moves to slot+8, decided by one digit of its ZIP code.

// Simplified from java.util.HashMap (Java 8+)
static final int hash(Object key) {
    int h;
    return (key == null) ? 0 : (h = key.hashCode()) ^ (h >>> 16);
}
// putVal: index = (n - 1) & hash
//   bin empty          → table[i] = newNode(hash, key, value, null)
//   bin is TreeNode    → putTreeVal(...)
//   else walk chain    → if key found: replace value
//                        else append; if binCount >= TREEIFY_THRESHOLD - 1 → treeifyBin
// treeifyBin: if tab.length < MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY (64) → resize() instead
// if (++size > threshold) resize();
Interview angle: "Why does HashMap use & instead of %?" Bitwise AND is a single cycle and needs no sign handling; it requires power-of-two capacity, which tableSizeFor guarantees (you ask for 100, you get 128). "Why the tree needs 64 bins?" Trees cost roughly twice the memory per node; below 64 a resize is cheaper and usually fixes the clustering. Tree bins also fall back to Comparable ordering (or identity hash tiebreak) when keys are not comparable, which is why a class with a constant hashCode still works, just slowly.

Pitfalls

  • null key is allowed (exactly one; hash 0, bin 0) and null values are allowed — so get(k) == null does not mean absent; use containsKey or getOrDefault.
  • Iteration order is unspecified and changes after a resize; tests that depend on it break on a JDK upgrade.
  • Treeification requires keys with a sane compareTo or the map falls back to System.identityHashCode ordering — still correct, just slower.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is the time complexity of get? (O(1) average; O(log n) worst case since Java 8, O(n) before.)
  • Why XOR the high bits in? (Small tables use only the low bits of the hash; spreading defends against hash codes that vary only in the high bits.)
  • What is stored per Node? (hash, key, value, next — the cached hash makes resize and chain walks cheap.)

HashMap Java 7 vs 8, Load Factor and Sizing

Why interviewers ask: "why does HashMap hang under concurrent access?" is a classic war story; they check whether you know it is a Java 7 artefact and that Java 8 is still unsafe, just differently.

In Java 7, put inserted at the head of the chain, and resize (transfer()) walked each old chain and head-inserted into the new table — reversing the chain. If two threads resized concurrently, thread A could be pre-empted holding e and next pointers while thread B completed the (reversed) move; when A resumed it re-linked the nodes in the opposite direction, creating a cycle. The next get on that bin walked the cycle forever at 100% CPU.

Java 8 switched to tail insertion and the lo/hi split, which preserves order, so the cycle cannot form. But HashMap is still not thread-safe: two concurrent puts to the same empty bin can each see null, and one write is lost; size can drift; a reader may see a half-built tree. The fix is the same as always: ConcurrentHashMap.

Load factor 0.75 is a time/space trade-off: with a good hash, chain lengths follow a Poisson distribution, and at 0.75 the probability of a bin holding 8 nodes is about 6 in 10 million — which is where TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8 comes from. To store expected entries without a resize, size the map as (int)(expected / 0.75f) + 1; Java 19 added HashMap.newHashMap(expected) to do exactly that.

Java 7Java 8+
Chain insertionHeadTail
Long chainsStay linked lists: O(n) worstTreeify at 8 (table ≥ 64): O(log n) worst
ResizeRehash every node into new tablelo/hi split on one bit, order preserved
Concurrent resizeCan build a cycle → infinite loopNo cycle, but lost updates, wrong size, corrupted tree
Hash spreadingMulti-shift hash()h ^ (h >>> 16)
Interview angle: "We saw a thread stuck in HashMap.get at 100% CPU. What happened?" Java 7 concurrent resize cycle; the fix is ConcurrentHashMap, not synchronized around get only. "What does new HashMap<>(1000) give you?" Capacity 1024, threshold 768 — you still resize once if you store 1000; ask for 1000/0.75 + 1 = 1334 → capacity 2048.

Pitfalls

  • Java 8 did not make HashMap safe for concurrent writes; it only removed the hang. Two puts can still lose one.
  • A load factor of 1.0 saves memory but roughly doubles average chain length; 0.5 halves it at the cost of a mostly empty table. Almost never change it.

Likely follow-ups

  • What happens when capacity reaches 2³⁰? (MAXIMUM_CAPACITY; threshold becomes Integer.MAX_VALUE and the map stops resizing.)
  • Does HashMap ever shrink? (No. clear() keeps the table; build a new map if memory matters.)

Java 8 vs 17

The bin structure has not changed since 8. Java 19 added HashMap.newHashMap(int expected) (plus HashSet.newHashSet, LinkedHashMap.newLinkedHashMap) so callers stop hand-computing expected / 0.75 + 1; on 17 you still compute it yourself.

Mutable Keys and the hashCode/equals Contract

Why interviewers ask: it links OOP fundamentals to data-structure behaviour and produces a satisfying "the entry is still there but you can never find it" moment.

A HashMap stores the key's hash in the Node at insertion and uses it to pick the bin. If you later mutate a field that participates in hashCode, the key now hashes to a different bin, but the node stays where it was. get(key) looks in the new bin, finds nothing, and returns null; containsKey is false; remove does nothing; yet size() still counts it and iteration still shows it. The entry is orphaned.

The contract (see the OOP section on equals/hashCode): equal objects must have equal hash codes; unequal objects may collide. Override both or neither, use the same fields in both, and make those fields effectively immutable — records give you this for free. Analogy: filing a folder under the customer's surname and then letting them change their surname; the folder does not move.

class Point { int x, y;
    Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof Point p && p.x == x && p.y == y; }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(x, y); }
}
var map = new HashMap<Point, String>();
Point p = new Point(1, 1);
map.put(p, "one");
p.x = 2;                       // hash changes; node stays in old bin
map.get(p);                    // null
map.containsKey(new Point(1, 1)); // false: right bin, but equals fails (x is 2)
map.size();                    // 1 — the entry is orphaned
map.remove(p);                 // null, nothing removed
Interview angle: "What if I override equals but not hashCode?" Two equal keys land in different bins, so put stores duplicates and get with an equal-but-not-same instance fails. "Can I use a List as a map key?" Yes, but never mutate it afterwards; List.hashCode depends on contents. Records and String are the safe choices.

Pitfalls

  • JPA entities as HashSet members: the id is null before persist and assigned after, so hashCode based on id changes mid-life. Use a business key or a stable UUID.
  • TreeMap has the same problem with compareTo fields: mutation breaks the tree invariant silently.
  • Arrays use identity hashCode/equals: int[] keys never match another array with the same contents.

Likely follow-ups

  • Does HashMap rehash keys on get? (It recomputes hash(key) for the argument, but uses the cached hash for stored nodes — that mismatch is the bug.)
  • Why is String a good key? (Immutable, and it caches its hash in a field after the first call.)

LinkedHashMap: Insertion/Access Order and the 5-line LRU

Why interviewers ask: "design an LRU cache" is a top-5 coding question; knowing that the JDK already ships one in LinkedHashMap shows depth, and explaining how it does it shows internals.

LinkedHashMap extends HashMap and its Entry extends HashMap.Node with two extra references, before and after, threading every entry into one doubly-linked list. The hash table still gives O(1) lookup; the list gives a predictable iteration order. By default the order is insertion (re-putting an existing key does not move it). With the constructor flag accessOrder = true, every get/put/compute on an existing key unlinks the entry and re-links it at the tail, so the head is always the least recently used entry.

The hook protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry eldest) is called after every insertion; returning true evicts the head. Override it to cap the size and you have a working LRU in five lines. Analogy: a queue at a coffee shop where anyone who orders again walks to the back of the line; when the shop is full, whoever is at the front gets asked to leave.

class LruCache<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> {
    private final int capacity;
    LruCache(int capacity) {
        super(16, 0.75f, true);          // accessOrder = true
        this.capacity = capacity;
    }
    @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) {
        return size() > capacity;
    }
}
Interview angle: Show the 5-line version first, then say "in an interview you usually want me to build it: a HashMap<K, Node> plus a hand-rolled doubly-linked list with sentinel head/tail — same O(1) design". Mention that LinkedHashMap is not thread-safe; production caches use Caffeine (window-TinyLFU), not raw LRU.

Pitfalls

  • In access-order mode get is a structural modification: iterating and calling get throws ConcurrentModificationException.
  • Wrapping in Collections.synchronizedMap makes it safe but serialises every get (the list relink is a write).
  • removeEldestEntry is called only on insertion, not on get; you cannot use it for time-based expiry.

Likely follow-ups

  • Extra memory versus HashMap? (Two references per entry plus the head/tail fields.)
  • How would you make it LFU? (Frequency buckets, each a linked set; O(1) LFU is a known follow-up design.)
  • Does putIfAbsent on an existing key move it? (In access-order mode, yes: any access of an existing mapping counts.)

TreeMap/TreeSet and the NavigableMap APIs

Why interviewers ask: "find the latest price at or before time t" and "count events in a range" are solved in one line with floorEntry/subMap; candidates who reach for a sorted list plus binary search lose time.

TreeMap is a red-black tree: a self-balancing binary search tree whose height stays ≤ 2·log₂(n+1), so get, put, remove are O(log n). Keys are ordered by Comparable natural order or a supplied Comparator; the map uses only that ordering, never equals/hashCode. A comparator that returns 0 for two keys makes them the same key, even if equals says otherwise — "consistent with equals" matters here.

The NavigableMap interface adds neighbour lookups: floorKey(k) (greatest ≤ k), ceilingKey(k) (least ≥ k), lowerKey/higherKey (strict), firstEntry/lastEntry, pollFirstEntry, and range views: headMap(to), tailMap(from), subMap(from, to), with inclusive-flag overloads. Views are live and writable within their range. Analogy: a paper dictionary — you can open to the nearest word even if the exact one is missing, and tear out a page range.

// Time-based lookup: latest known price at or before a timestamp
TreeMap<Long, BigDecimal> prices = new TreeMap<>();
prices.put(1000L, new BigDecimal("10.0"));
prices.put(2000L, new BigDecimal("12.5"));
Map.Entry<Long, BigDecimal> e = prices.floorEntry(1500L); // 1000 → 10.0

// Range query: events between t1 (inclusive) and t2 (exclusive)
NavigableMap<Long, String> window = events.subMap(t1, true, t2, false);
int count = window.size();                 // O(n in range), view is live

// TreeSet with comparator: careful, compare()==0 means "duplicate"
TreeSet<String> byLength = new TreeSet<>(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length));
byLength.addAll(List.of("aa", "bb", "c"));  // size 2! "bb" dropped
TreeSet<String> fixed = new TreeSet<>(
    Comparator.comparingInt(String::length).thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder()));
Interview angle: Classic uses: consistent hashing ring (ceilingKey(hash), wrap to firstKey()), calendar/booking conflicts (floorEntry/ceilingEntry around a new interval), leaderboard top-k with descendingMap(), and "sliding window median" with two TreeMaps as multisets.
NeedCallReturns
Largest key ≤ kfloorKey(k) / floorEntry(k)null if none
Smallest key ≥ kceilingKey(k) / ceilingEntry(k)null if none
Strictly below / abovelowerKey(k) / higherKey(k)null if none
Keys in [a, b)subMap(a, b)Live view

Reverse iterationdescendingMap() / descendingKeySet()Live view

Pitfalls

  • null keys are rejected (natural ordering cannot compare null); TreeSet.add(null) throws NPE.
  • subMap views throw IllegalArgumentException if you insert a key outside the range.
  • Comparator inconsistent with equals makes TreeSet violate the Set contract; contains and HashSet.contains disagree.
  • Performance: constant factors are much worse than HashMap (pointer chasing, comparator calls). Only pay for it when you need order.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why red-black rather than AVL? (Fewer rotations on insert/delete; lookups slightly slower than AVL but writes cheaper — a good general-purpose trade.)
  • How would you get the k-th smallest key? (Not supported in O(log n); TreeMap has no subtree sizes. Use an order-statistic tree or a Fenwick tree.)
  • ConcurrentSkipListMap? (The concurrent sorted map: lock-free skip list, same NavigableMap API, O(log n) expected.)

Sets: HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet, EnumSet/EnumMap

Why interviewers ask: "how is HashSet implemented?" is a one-liner they expect instantly; EnumSet separates people who read the JDK from those who do not.

HashSet is literally a HashMap<E, Object> where every value is the same shared static final Object PRESENT. add(e) is map.put(e, PRESENT) == null. So everything about HashMap applies: hash spreading, treeify, resize, null allowed, no order. LinkedHashSet wraps a LinkedHashMap (insertion order, slightly more memory), and TreeSet wraps a TreeMap (sorted, O(log n), NavigableSet API: floor, ceiling, headSet, tailSet).

EnumSet and EnumMap exploit the fact that enum constants have a dense ordinal(). EnumSet is a bit vector — a single long for ≤ 64 constants (RegularEnumSet), a long[] beyond (JumboEnumSet) — so contains, add, union and intersection are single bitwise ops. EnumMap is an Object[] indexed by ordinal: no hashing, no boxing, iteration in declaration order. Analogy: a checklist with one fixed checkbox per option, instead of a bag you have to search.

enum Perm { READ, WRITE, EXEC, ADMIN }
EnumSet<Perm> rw = EnumSet.of(Perm.READ, Perm.WRITE);   // bits 0b0011
EnumSet<Perm> all = EnumSet.allOf(Perm.class);
EnumSet<Perm> rest = EnumSet.complementOf(rw);           // EXEC, ADMIN
rw.contains(Perm.EXEC);                                  // (bits >> 2 & 1) == 0 → false

EnumMap<Perm, Integer> count = new EnumMap<>(Perm.class);
count.merge(Perm.READ, 1, Integer::sum);                 // array[0] += 1
SetBackingOrdernullPick when
HashSetHashMapNoneYesDefault membership test
LinkedHashSetLinkedHashMapInsertionYesDedupe while keeping order
TreeSetTreeMapSortedNoRange / neighbour queries
EnumSetlong bit vectorOrdinalNoAny set of enum constants (flags)
Interview angle: "Remove duplicates from a list preserving order" → new ArrayList<>(new LinkedHashSet<>(list)). "Replace an int bit-flag field with something type-safe" → EnumSet: Effective Java Item 36.

Pitfalls

  • Set.of(...) throws IllegalArgumentException on duplicate elements at construction — a surprise in tests.
  • EnumSet.noneOf(Perm.class) is required for an empty set; there is no public constructor.
  • HashSet of mutable objects has the same orphaning problem as HashMap keys.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why does HashSet not just store keys in a custom table? (Reuse: the map already solves hashing, resize and treeify; the cost is one shared value reference per entry.)
  • Is EnumMap thread-safe? (No; wrap with Collections.synchronizedMap or use it read-only.)

PriorityQueue: Binary Heap and the Top-K Pattern

Why interviewers ask: top-K, merge K sorted lists, Dijkstra, task scheduling — all heap problems. They also love "is the iteration sorted?" (no).

A PriorityQueue is a binary min-heap stored in a plain array queue[]: the children of index i are 2i+1 and 2i+2, the parent is (i-1)/2. The only invariant is parent ≤ children; siblings are unordered. offer appends at the end and sifts up (swap with parent while smaller) — O(log n). poll takes index 0, moves the last element to the root, and sifts down — O(log n). peek is O(1). remove(Object) and contains are O(n) linear scans.

Because siblings are unordered, iterating or printing the queue is not sorted; only repeated poll() is. For a max-heap pass Comparator.reverseOrder() or a custom comparator. Analogy: a tournament bracket — you always know the champion at the top, but the rest of the bracket is not a ranking.

// Top-K largest: keep a MIN-heap of size k; the root is the k-th largest
static List<Integer> topK(int[] nums, int k) {
    PriorityQueue<Integer> heap = new PriorityQueue<>();   // min-heap
    for (int n : nums) {
        heap.offer(n);
        if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();   // drop the smallest
    }
    List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>(heap);   // NOT sorted
    out.sort(Comparator.reverseOrder());
    return out;                                   // O(n log k)
}
// Max-heap of tasks by priority then age
record Task(int priority, long createdAt) {}
PriorityQueue<Task> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(
    Comparator.comparingInt(Task::priority).reversed()
              .thenComparingLong(Task::createdAt));
Interview angle: "Top-K from a stream of a billion numbers" — min-heap of size k, O(n log k) time and O(k) memory; explain why a min-heap for the largest K (the root is the weakest survivor). "Merge K sorted lists" — heap of (value, listIndex), O(N log K).

Pitfalls

  • Not stable: equal-priority elements come out in arbitrary order. Add a sequence number to the comparator for FIFO among ties.
  • Mutating an element's priority while it is in the queue silently corrupts the heap; remove, change, re-offer.
  • null elements are rejected. toString()/iterator() show array order, not priority order.

Likely follow-ups

  • Build a heap from n elements? (new PriorityQueue<>(collection) uses heapify, O(n), not n × offer.)
  • Thread-safe version? (PriorityBlockingQueue; DelayQueue for time-ordered tasks.)
  • Why not a TreeSet? (Heap has better constants and O(1) peek; TreeSet allows removal of arbitrary elements in O(log n) and no duplicates.)

ConcurrentHashMap: Java 8 Design

Why interviewers ask: the second most asked internals question after HashMap. They want to hear "no segments any more", "CAS on empty bin, synchronized on the head node", and the computeIfAbsent pitfall.

Java 7's CHM used 16 segments, each a small hash table with its own ReentrantLock — 16-way write concurrency. Java 8 rewrote it: one Node[] table like HashMap, and the lock granularity dropped to a single bin. Inserting into an empty bin is a lock-free CAS on the array slot. Inserting into a non-empty bin does synchronized (headNode) — the head node object is the monitor, so writers to different bins never contend. Reads are lock-free: val and next are volatile, so get never blocks.

Bookkeeping is lock-free too. sizeCtl is a volatile int that encodes state: negative while resizing (with the number of helper threads), otherwise the next resize threshold. size() does not read a single counter — that would be a hot spot — but sums a baseCount plus striped CounterCell[], exactly the LongAdder design; the value is an estimate under concurrent updates (mappingCount() returns a long). Resize is cooperative: the thread that triggers it allocates the new table, and any thread that touches a bin already moved finds a ForwardingNode (hash −1) and helps transfer other bins before continuing. Iterators are weakly consistent: never throw ConcurrentModificationException, reflect some but not necessarily all concurrent updates.

computeIfAbsent, merge and compute run the function inside the bin lock, so they are atomic and the function runs at most once per key. The flip side: the function must be short and must not touch the same map. A recursive computeIfAbsent (memoised Fibonacci is the classic) either throws IllegalStateException: Recursive update (Java 9+) or deadlocks/loops (Java 8). null keys and values are forbidden because get(k) == null must unambiguously mean "absent" in a concurrent world — containsKey then get is not atomic. Analogy: instead of one lock on the whole warehouse (Hashtable) or 16 zone locks (Java 7), every shelf has its own tiny padlock, and an empty shelf can be claimed with a sticky note (CAS).

ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> hits = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
hits.computeIfAbsent(url, k -> new LongAdder()).increment();   // atomic, once per key
hits.merge(url, 1L, Long::sum);   // alternative with Long values

// PITFALL: recursive update inside computeIfAbsent
Map<Integer, Long> memo = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
long fib(int n) {
    if (n < 2) return n;
    return memo.computeIfAbsent(n, k -> fib(k - 1) + fib(k - 2)); // IllegalStateException (9+) / hang (8)
}
// FIX: look up first, compute outside, then putIfAbsent
long fibOk(int n) {
    if (n < 2) return n;
    Long v = memo.get(n);
    if (v != null) return v;
    long r = fibOk(n - 1) + fibOk(n - 2);
    memo.putIfAbsent(n, r);
    return r;
}
HashtableCollections.synchronizedMapConcurrentHashMap
LockingEvery method synchronized on the tableEvery method on one mutex (wrapper)CAS + per-bin monitor for writes; lock-free reads
Reads scale?NoNoYes
IterationFail-fast; must lock externallyFail-fast; must synchronized (map) manuallyWeakly consistent, no lock
NullsNoWhatever the wrapped map allowsNo
Compound opsNot atomic unless you lockNot atomic unless you lockputIfAbsent, compute*, merge atomic per key
VerdictLegacy, neverOnly to wrap a special map (e.g. LinkedHashMap LRU)Default
Interview angle: "Is if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v) safe on a CHM?" No — check-then-act across two calls; use putIfAbsent. "Is size() exact?" Under concurrent writes it is a snapshot estimate; for exact counts you would need external coordination. "Why can't I put null?" Because get returning null must mean absent; with nulls you would need containsKey + get, which is racy.

Pitfalls

  • Long-running or blocking work inside compute* holds the bin lock and stalls every other key sharing that bin. Compute outside, then putIfAbsent.
  • Iteration order can differ between two iterations; a bulk op like forEach(parallelismThreshold, …) may run on ForkJoin threads.
  • keySet() on a CHM returns a view that supports add only via keySet(defaultValue); newKeySet() is the concurrent Set.

Likely follow-ups

  • Does CHM treeify bins? (Yes, TreeBin at 8 with the same 64-bin minimum; TreeBin holds its own read-write lock so readers proceed during rotation.)
  • What is the concurrency level parameter now? (Ignored except as a sizing hint; Java 8 has no segments.)
  • Concurrent sorted map? (ConcurrentSkipListMap.)

Java 8 vs 17

Java 8 introduced the segment-free design, compute*/merge, mappingCount(), newKeySet(), and the parallel bulk methods. Java 9 made the recursive computeIfAbsent case fail fast with IllegalStateException("Recursive update") instead of looping. Nothing structural changed through 17.

CopyOnWriteArrayList / CopyOnWriteArraySet

Why interviewers ask: to see whether you can articulate the read-mostly trade-off and know that iteration is a snapshot — the reason it fits listener/observer lists and nothing else.

Every mutation (add, set, remove) copies the entire backing array under a lock and swaps in the new one via a volatile reference. Reads and iteration touch the array reference once and then work on an immutable snapshot: no locks, no ConcurrentModificationException, and writes made during iteration are invisible to that iterator. Writes are O(n) in time and allocate O(n) garbage, so this is for collections with many reads, rare writes, small size: event listeners, plugin registries, feature flags. CopyOnWriteArraySet is a thin wrapper that checks contains before add (so O(n) add, no hashing).

Analogy: a printed phone directory — everyone reads their own copy freely; publishing an update means reprinting the whole book.

private final List<Listener> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

void fire(Event e) {
    for (Listener l : listeners) l.on(e);   // snapshot: safe even if l.on() unregisters itself
}
// Iterator.remove() throws UnsupportedOperationException — the snapshot is immutable
// Use listeners.remove(l) directly instead
Interview angle: "Why not Collections.synchronizedList for listeners?" You would have to hold the lock during the whole callback loop (or copy manually), and a listener that deregisters itself would deadlock or throw CME. COW gives lock-free, exception-free iteration and makes self-removal safe.

Pitfalls

  • Using it as a general thread-safe list with frequent writes: O(n) per write plus GC pressure; a 10k-element list with 1k writes/s copies 10M references per second.
  • iterator.remove(), set(), add() on the iterator throw UnsupportedOperationException.
  • size() during iteration may differ from what the iterator sees.

Likely follow-ups

  • Is addIfAbsent atomic? (Yes, under the write lock.)
  • Memory model guarantee? (Writers publish via a volatile array reference: readers see a fully constructed array, happens-before established.)

Fail-Fast vs Fail-Safe Iterators and modCount

Why interviewers ask: everyone has hit ConcurrentModificationException in a single-threaded loop; they want the mechanism (modCount), the correct fix, and the "why did it not throw this time?" edge case.

Every java.util collection keeps a transient int modCount incremented on each structural modification (add/remove/clear — not set). An iterator captures expectedModCount = modCount when created and compares them in next() (and in ArrayList's remove()). A mismatch throws ConcurrentModificationException. This is a best-effort check meant to catch bugs, not a thread-safety mechanism: it works single-threaded and can miss concurrent races, since modCount is not volatile.

The correct ways to remove while iterating: Iterator.remove() (which resets expectedModCount), Collection.removeIf(predicate) (Java 8, does one compaction pass on ArrayList), ListIterator.add/set, or iterating over a copy. Concurrent collections (ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentLinkedQueue) have weakly consistent ("fail-safe") iterators: they never throw and may or may not show concurrent updates. Analogy: counting people in a room while someone keeps opening the door — fail-fast stops and complains; fail-safe finishes the count it started and shrugs.

List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b", "c", "d"));
for (String s : list) {          // Iterator it = list.iterator(); expected = modCount
    if (s.equals("b")) {
        list.remove(s);          // modCount++  → expected != modCount
    }
}                                // it.hasNext(): cursor != size; it.next(): checkForComodification()

// Same loop, but removing "c" instead of "b": NO exception!
// After removing "c", size == 3 and cursor == 3 → hasNext() is false, loop exits quietly.

// Correct:
list.removeIf(s -> s.equals("b"));
Iterator<String> it = list.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) if (it.next().equals("b")) it.remove();
  1. The enhanced for creates an ArrayList.Itr whose expectedModCount copies the current modCount (0).
  2. next() first calls checkForComodification() — equal, fine — and returns "a", advancing cursor to 1.
  3. Second next() returns "b" with cursor = 2. The condition matches.
  4. list.remove("b") shifts the array and increments modCount to 1. The iterator still has expected = 0.
  5. hasNext() only checks cursor != size: 2 ≠ 3, so the loop continues.
  6. next() runs checkForComodification(): modCount (1) != expected (0) — CME thrown here, not at the remove.
  7. The silent case: removing the second-to-last element makes cursor == size, so hasNext() returns false and next() — the only place that checks — never runs. The bug hides until the data changes.
  8. Iterator.remove() performs the removal and sets expectedModCount = modCount, so the next next() passes. removeIf does the whole thing in one pass without an iterator.
Fail-fastWeakly consistent ("fail-safe")
CollectionsArrayList, HashMap, TreeMap, LinkedList… all java.utilConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentLinkedQueue, ConcurrentSkipListMap
On modification during iterationThrows CME (best effort)Never throws; may or may not reflect the change
MemoryNo copySnapshot (COW) or traverses live structure (CHM)
GuaranteeNone — a bug detectorSees elements that existed at creation; each element at most once
Interview angle: "Can CME happen in single-threaded code?" Yes — the walkthrough above is single-threaded. "Can it fail to happen in multi-threaded code?" Also yes: modCount is a plain int and the check runs only in next(). Never rely on CME for correctness.

Pitfalls

  • Streams over a collection are backed by its spliterator: mutating the source inside forEach throws CME too.
  • map.keySet().remove(k) inside a for-each over the map is the same bug; use entrySet().removeIf or an explicit iterator.
  • LinkedHashMap in access-order mode: a plain get inside a loop is a structural modification.

Likely follow-ups

  • Does set(i, x) on an ArrayList bump modCount? (No — not structural; safe in a loop.)
  • How does removeIf avoid O(n²)? (Marks matches in a BitSet, then compacts in one arraycopy pass.)

Comparable vs Comparator, Stable Sorts and Sort Algorithms

Why interviewers ask: "sort employees by department, then salary descending, nulls last" is a warm-up that reveals fluency with the Java 8 comparator combinators; the algorithm question checks depth.

Comparable<T> is implemented by the class (compareTo) and defines its one natural order — String, Integer, LocalDate all have one. Comparator<T> is an external strategy object you pass to sort, TreeMap, PriorityQueue, max; a type can have many. Java 8 made comparators composable: Comparator.comparing(keyExtractor), .thenComparing(...), .reversed(), comparingInt/Long/Double (avoid boxing), nullsFirst/nullsLast(cmp), naturalOrder(), reverseOrder().

Algorithms: Arrays.sort(Object[]) and List.sort/Collections.sort use TimSort — a stable merge/insertion hybrid, O(n log n) worst case, O(n) on already-sorted runs. Arrays.sort(int[]) and other primitive overloads use dual-pivot quicksort — faster, in-place, but not stable (irrelevant for primitives, since equal values are indistinguishable). Stable means equal elements keep their input order, which is what makes "sort by salary, then sort by department" produce department-grouped, salary-ordered output. Analogy: Comparable is a person's alphabetical surname; Comparator is any seating chart you invent for the evening.

record Employee(String dept, String name, Double salary) {}

List<Employee> sorted = employees.stream().sorted(
    Comparator.comparing(Employee::dept)
              .thenComparing(Employee::salary, Comparator.nullsLast(Comparator.reverseOrder()))
              .thenComparing(Employee::name)).toList();

// Beware: reversed() applies to EVERYTHING built so far
Comparator<Employee> wrong = Comparator.comparing(Employee::dept)
        .thenComparing(Employee::salary).reversed();     // reverses dept too
Comparator<Employee> right = Comparator.comparing(Employee::dept)
        .thenComparing(Employee::salary, Comparator.reverseOrder());

// Type inference trap: lambda in comparing() needs a hint
Comparator<Employee> c = Comparator.comparing((Employee e) -> e.salary()).reversed();
CallAlgorithmStableComplexity
Arrays.sort(int[]/long[]/double[]…)Dual-pivot quicksort (with insertion/merge fallbacks)n/aO(n log n) avg; worst mitigated
Arrays.sort(Object[]), List.sort, Collections.sortTimSortYesO(n log n) worst, O(n) best
Arrays.parallelSortParallel merge sort over ForkJoinYes (objects)O(n log n); wins above ~8k elements
Stream.sorted()Buffers into array then TimSortYes for ordered streamsO(n log n)
Interview angle: "Your compareTo returns a.value - b.value; what is wrong?" Integer overflow flips the sign for large magnitudes; use Integer.compare. "TimSort threw IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract?" Your comparator is not transitive or not antisymmetric (e.g. comparing doubles with < and NaN, or a random comparator). TimSort detects it; older sorts silently produced garbage.

Pitfalls

  • Natural order of String is lexicographic by UTF-16 code unit: "Z" < "a", "10" < "9". Use String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER or a Collator for humans.
  • A comparator inconsistent with equals is fine for sorting a list but breaks TreeSet/TreeMap semantics.
  • Collections.sort(list) on a LinkedList copies to an array, sorts, and writes back via a ListIterator.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why not quicksort for objects? (Stability is part of the List.sort contract; comparisons on objects are expensive, and TimSort minimises them on partially ordered data.)
  • Should a record implement Comparable? (Only if there is one obvious natural order; otherwise supply comparators.)

Immutable vs Unmodifiable: List.of, unmodifiableList, copyOf, Stream.toList

Why interviewers ask: "is Collections.unmodifiableList immutable?" No — and explaining the difference between a view and a copy is the whole point.

Collections.unmodifiableList(src) (Java 1.2) returns a view: mutators throw UnsupportedOperationException, but changes to src show through. It is a read-only window, not a guarantee. List.of(...)/Set.of/Map.of (Java 9) build genuinely immutable collections: compact (field-based for 0–2 elements, array-based beyond), null-hostile (NPE on construction and even on contains(null)), and Set.of/Map.of reject duplicates with IllegalArgumentException. Their iteration order for sets/maps is randomised per JVM run to stop code depending on it.

List.copyOf(coll) (Java 10) returns an immutable copy, but if the argument is already an immutable List.of-style list it returns it as-is (no copy). Stream.toList() (Java 16) returns an unmodifiable list that allows nulls, unlike Collectors.toUnmodifiableList(). Collectors.toList() gives an ArrayList in practice but the spec does not promise mutability. Analogy: unmodifiable is a glass wall in front of the shelf — you cannot touch it, but the owner can rearrange it; immutable is a photograph of the shelf.

List<String> src = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a"));
List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(src);
src.add("b");
view.size();                 // 2 — the view reflects the change
view.add("c");               // UnsupportedOperationException

List<String> snap = List.copyOf(src);   // true copy, immutable
src.add("z");
snap.size();                 // 2

List.of("a", null);          // NullPointerException
List.of("a").contains(null); // NullPointerException (surprising)
Stream.of("a", null).toList();                        // OK: [a, null]
Stream.of("a", null).collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList()); // NPE
Set.of("a", "a");            // IllegalArgumentException: duplicate element
FactorySinceCopy or viewNullsNotes
Collections.unmodifiableXxx1.2ViewAs sourceSource can still change
List.of / Set.of / Map.of9ImmutableRejectedDuplicates rejected in Set/Map; randomised set order
List.copyOf / Set.copyOf / Map.copyOf10Immutable copy (no-op if already immutable)RejectedPreferred defensive copy
Stream.toList()16UnmodifiableAllowedReplaces collect(toList()) in most code
Collectors.toUnmodifiableList()10UnmodifiableRejected
Interview angle: "How do you return a collection from a domain object safely?" return List.copyOf(items) in the getter, or store List.copyOf in the constructor and return the field directly. Records do not deep-copy their components — a record holding an ArrayList is still mutable through it.

Pitfalls

  • Immutable collections of mutable objects are shallowly immutable — the elements can still change.
  • Jackson deserialises into ArrayList; serialising a List.of is fine, but code that later mutates a deserialised list may assume immutability that is not there, or vice versa.
  • Arrays.asList is neither: fixed size, but set works.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why are List.of collections null-hostile? (Leaves room for future optimisations and value types; encourages Optional.)
  • Are they thread-safe? (Yes — immutable objects are safely publishable and shareable.)

Java 8 vs 17

Java 8 has only Collections.unmodifiableXxx and Collections.emptyList; Arrays.asList was the common shortcut. 9 added of, 10 copyOf and toUnmodifiableList, 16 Stream.toList().

Arrays and Collections Utilities Interviewers Ask About

Why interviewers ask: quick-fire API knowledge, plus a couple of traps (binarySearch on unsorted input, array hashCode).

Arrays works on raw arrays: sort (algorithms above), binarySearch (input must be sorted; returns -(insertionPoint) - 1 when absent), fill, copyOf/copyOfRange, asList, stream, equals/deepEquals, hashCode/deepHashCode, toString/deepToString. Arrays themselves inherit identity hashCode/equals/toString from Object — int[] printed is [I@1b6d3586, and two arrays with equal contents are not equals. That is why array-keyed maps fail and why Arrays.hashCode(arr) exists.

Collections works on collections: sort (delegates to List.sort, stable), reverse, shuffle (Fisher–Yates, optional Random for reproducibility), frequency, max/min (with comparator), nCopies(n, x) (immutable list of the same reference), swap, rotate, disjoint, emptyList/singletonList, and the synchronizedXxx/unmodifiableXxx wrappers.

int[] a = {5, 1, 4};
Arrays.sort(a);                            // [1, 4, 5]
int i = Arrays.binarySearch(a, 3);         // -2  → insertion point = -(i) - 1 = 1
a.hashCode() == new int[]{1,4,5}.hashCode();          // false (identity)
Arrays.hashCode(a) == Arrays.hashCode(new int[]{1,4,5}); // true
Arrays.equals(new int[][]{{1}}, new int[][]{{1}});   // false: compares inner refs
Arrays.deepEquals(new int[][]{{1}}, new int[][]{{1}}); // true

List<String> grid = new ArrayList<>(Collections.nCopies(3, "."));  // mutable copy
Collections.shuffle(grid, new Random(42));  // deterministic in tests
Collections.frequency(List.of(1, 2, 1), 1); // 2
Interview angle: "Why does my HashSet<int[]> not dedupe?" Identity hash. Convert to List<Integer>, a record, or a String key. "How do I insert into a sorted list?" Collections.binarySearch then list.add(-(idx) - 1, x) — O(n) shift, but O(log n) search.

Pitfalls

  • Arrays.asList(1, 2, 3) returns List<Integer>, but Arrays.asList(new int[]{1,2,3}) returns List<int[]> of size 1.
  • Collections.nCopies returns the same reference n times: a list of 3 StringBuilders is one builder.
  • Collections.sort on a list from List.of throws UnsupportedOperationException.

Likely follow-ups

  • Complexity of Collections.shuffle? (O(n), Fisher–Yates; on a non-RandomAccess list it copies to an array first.)
  • Arrays.equals vs Objects.equals on arrays? (Objects.equals uses identity for arrays.)

Choosing the Right Collection: Decision Table

Why interviewers ask: system design and coding rounds both start here. The strong answer names the requirement first ("I need ordered iteration and O(1) lookup"), then the class.

Work through the requirements in order: duplicates allowed? ordering needed (none / insertion / sorted)? access pattern (index / key / ends / min-max)? thread safety? Only then pick a class. Analogy: choose the container by what you will do with the contents every day, not by what fits today.

RequirementSingle-threadedConcurrentNotes
Ordered sequence, index access, duplicatesArrayListCopyOnWriteArrayList (read-mostly) / Collections.synchronizedListPresize if known
Unique elements, no orderHashSetConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()Good hashCode required
Unique, insertion orderLinkedHashSetWrap in synchronizedSetDedupe preserving order
Unique, sorted, range queriesTreeSetConcurrentSkipListSetO(log n)
Key → value, no orderHashMapConcurrentHashMapDefault
Key → value, insertion/access order (LRU)LinkedHashMapsynchronizedMap wrapper, or CaffeineremoveEldestEntry
Key → value, sorted, floor/ceilingTreeMapConcurrentSkipListMapTime-series, consistent hashing
Enum keys / enum flagsEnumMap / EnumSetWrap or use read-onlyArray / bit vector
FIFO queueArrayDequeConcurrentLinkedQueue (unbounded) / ArrayBlockingQueue, LinkedBlockingQueue (blocking)Never LinkedList
LIFO stackArrayDequeConcurrentLinkedDequeNot Stack
Priority / min-maxPriorityQueuePriorityBlockingQueueDelayQueue for time
Counting occurrencesHashMap<K,Integer> + mergeConcurrentHashMap<K,LongAdder>Or Collectors.groupingBy(…, counting())
Fixed, never changesList.of / Map.ofSame — immutable is thread-safeDefensive copies via copyOf
Interview angle: A good answer sounds like: "Order lookups by id are the hot path, so HashMap<OrderId, Order>; the ids are exposed to multiple request threads, so ConcurrentHashMap; and reports need ids sorted, which is a one-off stream().sorted(), not a reason to pay TreeMap on every write."

Pitfalls

  • Choosing TreeMap "because we sometimes sort" — sort on read instead unless range queries are frequent.
  • Reaching for synchronizedMap by reflex; it serialises reads. ConcurrentHashMap is the default concurrent map.
  • Using Vector/Hashtable/Stack in new code.

Likely follow-ups

  • Bounded producer/consumer queue? (ArrayBlockingQueue: fixed array, single lock; LinkedBlockingQueue: two locks, optional bound.)
  • Multimap or bidirectional map? (Not in the JDK; Map<K, List<V>> with computeIfAbsent, or Guava.)

Collections API by Version: 8 → 17 → 21

Why interviewers ask: "what changed in collections since Java 8?" checks that you have actually used newer JDKs and not just read about them.

Java 8 gave Map its most useful methods: getOrDefault, putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent/computeIfPresent/compute, merge, forEach, replaceAll, plus Collection.removeIf, List.sort, List.replaceAll, Iterable.forEach, and streams. Java 9 added the immutable factories List.of, Set.of, Map.of (up to 10 pairs), Map.ofEntries(Map.entry(k, v), …) for more. 10: copyOf. 16: Stream.toList(). Nothing else structural in 17.

// Word count, Java 8 style, three ways
Map<String, Integer> wc = new HashMap<>();
wc.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum);                       // preferred
wc.compute(word, (k, v) -> v == null ? 1 : v + 1);
wc.put(word, wc.getOrDefault(word, 0) + 1);

// Grouping without null checks
Map<String, List<Order>> byCustomer = new HashMap<>();
byCustomer.computeIfAbsent(o.customerId(), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(o);

// Java 9 immutables
Map<String, Integer> ports = Map.of("http", 80, "https", 443);
Map<String, Integer> many = Map.ofEntries(Map.entry("a", 1), Map.entry("b", 2));
VersionAdditionWhy it matters
8Map.merge/compute*/getOrDefault, removeIf, List.sort, Comparator combinatorsReplaces most manual null-check-then-put code
9List.of/Set.of/Map.of/ofEntries, Map.entryCheap immutables; null-hostile
10copyOf, Collectors.toUnmodifiableXxxDefensive copies in one call
16Stream.toList()Shorter, unmodifiable, null-tolerant
19HashMap.newHashMap(expected)Correct presizing
21SequencedCollection/SequencedSet/SequencedMapgetFirst/getLast/reversed/addFirst on any ordered collection

Pitfalls

  • merge with a function returning null removes the key — a feature that surprises people.
  • computeIfAbsent on a HashMap with a mapping function that modifies the same map throws ConcurrentModificationException since Java 9.

Likely follow-ups

  • Map.of limit? (10 key-value pairs; use ofEntries beyond.)
  • Difference between compute and merge? (merge receives old and new values and never sees null-old; compute receives key and possibly-null old value.)

Java 21 preview

SequencedCollection (JEP 431) retrofits List, Deque, LinkedHashSet, SortedSet and their map counterparts with getFirst(), getLast(), removeFirst(), removeLast(), addFirst(), addLast() and reversed() — so list.get(list.size() - 1) becomes list.getLast() and LinkedHashMap.firstEntry() finally exists (it also makes the LRU eldest lookup a one-liner).

A HashMap bin holds 9 colliding entries but the table has 32 buckets. What happens on the next insert into that bin?

b. treeifyBin checks MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY = 64 first; below that it calls resize() on the theory that a bigger table will spread the keys. a is only true once the table has ≥ 64 bins. The threshold is 8 (d).

During a Java 8 HashMap resize from 16 to 32, a node with hash …0011 0101 (bit 4 set) currently in bin 5 goes to:

c. The new mask exposes one more bit, hash & oldCap (16). It is set, so the node joins the hi list at oldIndex + oldCap. No key is rehashed (b); the cached hash is reused. a would be the lo list if that bit were 0.

Two threads call put on a plain HashMap in Java 17. Which outcome is impossible?

d. The infinite loop came from Java 7's head insertion during transfer(). Java 8's tail insertion and lo/hi split preserve order, so no cycle forms. Lost updates (a), drift in size (b) and torn structures (c) all remain possible: the map is still not thread-safe.

You put a key into a HashMap, then mutate a field used in its hashCode. What does map.size() report and what does map.get(sameKeyObject) return?

b. Bin selection uses the hash computed now for the argument, but the stored node sits in the bin chosen at insertion. The map never re-examines stored keys (a), and equals is only consulted within the chosen bin (c).

In a LinkedHashMap constructed with accessOrder = true, what does this print?
m.put("a",1); m.put("b",2); m.put("c",3); m.get("a"); System.out.println(m.keySet());

a. In access-order mode get relinks the entry at the tail (most recent). b would be correct for the default insertion-order mode. Order is fully specified (d is HashMap).

Which ConcurrentHashMap statement is correct?

c. The Java 8 design. a is Java 7. b is wrong: reads are lock-free via volatile fields (a TreeBin has an internal lock but readers rarely block). d: size() sums baseCount and counter cells without a global lock, so it is an estimate under concurrent writes.

Why does memo.computeIfAbsent(n, k -> fib(k-1) + fib(k-2)) on a ConcurrentHashMap fail?

b. computeIfAbsent holds the bin monitor (or a reservation node) while running the function; a nested computeIfAbsent on a key in the same bin is detected (Java 9+) or hangs (Java 8). HashMap also forbids it (d) with a ConcurrentModificationException.

Which loop over List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a","b","c")) throws ConcurrentModificationException?

d. Removing "a" leaves cursor 1, size 2 → hasNext() true → next() checks modCount and throws. b is the silent trap: removing the second-to-last element makes cursor == size, so the loop exits before next() runs. a: set is not structural. c is the correct idiom.

What does this print? PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(List.of(5, 1, 4, 2)); System.out.println(pq);

c. toString walks the backing array, which satisfies only the heap property (parent ≤ children). The root is the minimum; the rest is not sorted. To get sorted output you must poll() repeatedly. The collection constructor exists and heapifies in O(n) (d).

Which is the best production choice for a listener registry that is iterated on every event and modified a few times at startup?

b. Read-mostly, small, iterated constantly: COW gives lock-free snapshot iteration and lets a listener unregister itself mid-dispatch. a requires holding the lock for the entire iteration (or you get CME). c works but offers no indexed access and weaker ordering guarantees for a listener list. d is the slowest and most error-prone.

Practice

Implement an LRU cache with LinkedHashMap, then explain how you would do it by hand

Implement LruCache<K, V> with V get(K) and void put(K, V), both O(1), evicting the least recently used entry when capacity is exceeded. First using LinkedHashMap, then describe (or code) the data structures you would use if the interviewer forbids it.

Tests: LinkedHashMap access order, removeEldestEntry, doubly-linked list + hash map design
Hint 1
The three-argument LinkedHashMap constructor has an accessOrder flag. What does get do to the order when it is true?
Hint 2
For the manual version: a HashMap<K, Node> gives O(1) lookup, and a doubly-linked list with sentinel head and tail gives O(1) unlink and append; each node stores key and value so eviction can remove from the map.
Reveal solution
// 1. JDK version
class LruCache<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> {
    private final int capacity;
    LruCache(int capacity) { super(capacity * 4 / 3 + 1, 0.75f, true); this.capacity = capacity; }
    @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> e) { return size() > capacity; }
}

// 2. Manual version: HashMap + doubly-linked list with sentinels
class Lru<K, V> {
    private final class Node { K k; V v; Node prev, next; Node(K k, V v) { this.k = k; this.v = v; } }
    private final Map<K, Node> map = new HashMap<>();
    private final Node head = new Node(null, null), tail = new Node(null, null); // head.next = LRU
    private final int cap;
    Lru(int cap) { this.cap = cap; head.next = tail; tail.prev = head; }

    public V get(K k) {
        Node n = map.get(k);
        if (n == null) return null;
        unlink(n); addLast(n);                 // mark as most recently used
        return n.v;
    }
    public void put(K k, V v) {
        Node n = map.get(k);
        if (n != null) { n.v = v; unlink(n); addLast(n); return; }
        if (map.size() == cap) { Node lru = head.next; unlink(lru); map.remove(lru.k); }
        n = new Node(k, v); addLast(n); map.put(k, n);
    }
    private void unlink(Node n) { n.prev.next = n.next; n.next.prev = n.prev; }
    private void addLast(Node n) { n.prev = tail.prev; n.next = tail; tail.prev.next = n; tail.prev = n; }
}

Reasoning. LinkedHashMap with accessOrder = true moves an entry to the tail on every get/put, and removeEldestEntry runs after each insert, so the JDK version is complete in five lines. The manual version reproduces exactly that: the hash map locates a node in O(1) and the sentinel-terminated list makes unlink/addLast branch-free. Storing the key in the node is what allows eviction to remove the map entry. Neither is thread-safe; for concurrent use, wrap in a lock or use Caffeine. Follow-up they usually ask: LFU (frequency-bucketed lists) and TTL (a timestamp per node checked on get, or a DelayQueue for active expiry).

Predict the output: mutable key in a HashMap

import java.util.*;

class Key {
    String id;
    Key(String id) { this.id = id; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof Key k && k.id.equals(id); }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return id.hashCode(); }
}
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<Key, Integer> m = new HashMap<>();
        Key k = new Key("A");
        m.put(k, 1);
        k.id = "B";
        System.out.println(m.get(k));                 // 1
        System.out.println(m.get(new Key("A")));      // 2
        System.out.println(m.get(new Key("B")));      // 3
        m.put(new Key("B"), 2);
        System.out.println(m.size());                 // 4
        for (Key x : m.keySet()) System.out.print(x.id + " ");  // 5
    }
}

What are printed on lines 1–5? Assume "A".hashCode() and "B".hashCode() land in different bins (they do: 65 and 66 in a 16-bucket table → bins 1 and 2).

Tests: cached hash in Node, bin selection vs equals, orphaned entries
Hint 1
The node stored at put time remembers hash 65 (bin 1). After the mutation, what does hash(k) compute, and which bin does get search?
Hint 2
In line 2 the lookup reaches the right bin. What does equals compare there?
Reveal solution

Output:

null
null
null
2
B B

Line 1: k.id is now "B", so hash(k) = 66 → bin 2. The node lives in bin 1. null.
Line 2: new Key("A") hashes to bin 1, finds the node, compares cached hash (65 == 65 ✓), then equals: "A".equals(k.id) where k.id is "B" → false. null.
Line 3: new Key("B") → bin 2, empty. null. The original entry is now unreachable by any lookup.
Line 4: put(new Key("B"), 2) goes to bin 2, finds nothing, inserts. Two nodes → 2.
Line 5: Iteration walks the table and prints both keys' current ids: the orphaned key (mutated to "B") and the new "B". So B B — a map that appears to contain the same key twice.

Lesson: the map stores the hash at insertion and never revisits it. Keys must be immutable in the fields that feed hashCode/equals; use a record or a final field.

Fix the bug: ConcurrentModificationException while cleaning a map

Map<String, Session> sessions = new HashMap<>();   // populated elsewhere

void expire(Instant now) {
    for (String id : sessions.keySet()) {
        Session s = sessions.get(id);
        if (s.expiresAt().isBefore(now)) {
            sessions.remove(id);
            audit.log("expired " + id);
        }
    }
}

This throws ConcurrentModificationException intermittently (and sometimes silently skips sessions). Explain both symptoms and give three correct rewrites, noting which you would ship if expire is called from a scheduler thread while request threads add sessions.

Tests: modCount, Iterator.remove, removeIf, concurrent collections
Hint 1
sessions.remove(id) bumps modCount; the keySet() iterator checks it in next(). What if the removed entry happened to be the last one the iterator would have visited?
Hint 2
The multi-threaded requirement changes the data structure, not just the loop.
Reveal solution

Why it throws: HashMap.remove during a keySet() for-each increments modCount; the iterator's next next() sees the mismatch and throws. Why it sometimes does not: if the removed entry was the last one to be visited, hasNext() returns false and next() is never called; and with two threads the non-volatile modCount may simply be missed. "Silently skips" comes from the concurrent case: a request thread's put during iteration can trigger a resize that the iterator walks inconsistently.

// Fix 1: explicit iterator (single-threaded)
for (Iterator<Map.Entry<String, Session>> it = sessions.entrySet().iterator(); it.hasNext(); ) {
    Map.Entry<String, Session> e = it.next();
    if (e.getValue().expiresAt().isBefore(now)) { it.remove(); audit.log("expired " + e.getKey()); }
}

// Fix 2: removeIf (single-threaded, cleanest when no side effect per element)
sessions.entrySet().removeIf(e -> e.getValue().expiresAt().isBefore(now));

// Fix 3: concurrent map — the one to ship for the scheduler scenario
ConcurrentMap<String, Session> sessions = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
void expire(Instant now) {
    sessions.forEach((id, s) -> {
        if (s.expiresAt().isBefore(now) && sessions.remove(id, s)) audit.log("expired " + id);
    });
}

Reasoning. Fixes 1 and 2 keep the iterator and modCount in sync, so they are correct only if no other thread touches the map. Fix 3 uses a weakly consistent traversal that never throws, and remove(key, value) is atomic: if a request thread replaced the session between the check and the remove, the conditional removal fails and nothing is logged — no lost sessions. Also note the original does a redundant get per key; iterate entrySet() instead. If audit logging must not run under contention, collect expired ids first and log after.

Design question: which collection would you choose, and why?

For each scenario name the collection, the reason in terms of operations and complexity, and one alternative you rejected.

  1. Rate limiter: per-API-key request counts in a service handling 50k req/s across 200 threads; counts reset every minute.
  2. Price history: "what was the price of SKU X at time T?" where updates arrive out of order and queries ask for the latest price at or before T.
  3. Order processing: incoming orders must be processed by priority (VIP first), then by arrival time among equals; producers and consumers run on different threads.
Tests: mapping requirements to data structures, concurrency awareness, NavigableMap, heaps
Hint 1
Scenario 2 is a "floor" query. Scenario 3 has two ordering criteria and a tie-breaking requirement that a heap does not give for free.
Reveal solution

1. Rate limiter: ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder>, with counts.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new LongAdder()).increment(). Lock-free reads, per-bin locking for the first insert only, and LongAdder stripes the hot counter across cells so 200 threads do not CAS-contend on one AtomicLong. Reset by swapping the whole map reference (volatile field) each minute rather than clearing it under load. Rejected: Collections.synchronizedMap (one lock for everything), HashMap<String, Integer> + merge on a CHM (works but boxes a new Long per increment and CAS-retries on hot keys).

2. Price history: per SKU, a TreeMap<Instant, BigDecimal> (or ConcurrentSkipListMap if written concurrently). Out-of-order inserts are O(log n) and land in the right place; the query is floorEntry(T) in O(log n). Rejected: a sorted ArrayList with binary search — O(n) inserts on out-of-order updates; HashMap — no way to find "at or before". If history is large and mostly append-only, a time-bucketed structure or a database with a (sku, ts) index is the scaled version.

3. Order processing: PriorityBlockingQueue<Order> with Comparator.comparingInt(Order::priorityRank).thenComparingLong(Order::sequence), where sequence comes from an AtomicLong at enqueue time. The heap gives O(log n) offer/poll; the explicit sequence gives FIFO among equal priorities, which a heap does not guarantee on its own; blocking semantics let consumers wait without spinning. Rejected: one LinkedBlockingQueue per priority level with consumers polling high first (simple, but starvation logic lives in the consumer and adding a level means code changes); TreeSet (needs external locking, duplicates need care).

5️⃣ Exceptions & Error Handling

Exceptions are where "it compiles" and "it behaves" diverge: a finally that quietly swallows a failure, a resource whose close() hides the real error, a stack trace the JIT stopped recording. The path here is hierarchy → control-flow semantics (try/catch/finally, try-with-resources) → designing your own exceptions → what they cost → how to layer, log and read them in production.

The Hierarchy: Throwable, Error, Exception, RuntimeException

Why interviewers ask: "checked vs unchecked" is the opening question of nearly every Java round; the follow-up ("which would you use for X, and why did Spring go unchecked?") is what separates candidates.

Everything you can throw extends Throwable. It has two children: Error (the JVM is in trouble: OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError, NoClassDefFoundError; you generally do not catch these) and Exception (something the program can reason about). Inside Exception, the subtree under RuntimeException is unchecked; everything else under Exception is checked. Error and its subclasses are unchecked too.

Checked means the compiler forces the caller to either catch it or declare it in throws. Analogy: a checked exception is a form you must sign before leaving the counter; an unchecked one is a fire alarm, nobody signs for it, it just propagates.

The classic guidance (Effective Java, Item 70): use checked exceptions for conditions the caller can realistically recover from (file not found, insufficient funds), and unchecked for programming errors (null argument, index out of range, illegal state). In practice modern frameworks (Spring, Hibernate, JDBC wrappers, most of the JDK since NIO) lean unchecked: checked exceptions do not compose with lambdas, they leak through every intermediate signature, and 95% of callers cannot do anything useful with a SQLException except roll back and report. Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy exists precisely to translate checked JDBC failures into unchecked, meaningful ones.

KindBase typeCompiler enforces?Typical examplesCatch it?
Errorjava.lang.ErrorNoOutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError, NoClassDefFoundError, AssertionErrorAlmost never; log at top level and let the process fail/restart
CheckedException (not RuntimeException)Yes: catch or declareIOException, SQLException, ClassNotFoundException, InterruptedException, ParseExceptionYes, when you can recover or translate
UncheckedRuntimeExceptionNoNullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException, IndexOutOfBoundsException, ClassCastException, ArithmeticException, UnsupportedOperationExceptionUsually only at a boundary (controller advice, job runner)
Interview angle: "Is InterruptedException a good checked exception?" It is the textbook example of a recoverable condition (restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() and exit), yet it is also the one people swallow most. "Why is NumberFormatException unchecked when bad input is clearly recoverable?" Because it extends IllegalArgumentException: the JDK treats un-validated input as a caller bug. Know both sides of the debate; the interviewer wants judgement, not a rule.

Pitfalls

  • catch (Exception e) also catches every RuntimeException, including NPEs you wanted to see. catch (Throwable t) additionally catches OutOfMemoryError, hiding a dying JVM.
  • Checked exceptions in a public API are a permanent contract: adding one later breaks every caller. Unchecked ones let you evolve, at the cost of discoverability.
  • "Unchecked = ignore it" is wrong: unchecked exceptions still crash threads, kill scheduled tasks silently (ScheduledExecutorService stops rescheduling) and roll back Spring transactions.

Likely follow-ups

  • Which exceptions roll back a Spring @Transactional method by default? (Unchecked and Error; checked exceptions commit unless rollbackFor is set.)
  • Can you throw a checked exception without declaring it? (Yes via "sneaky throw" generics or Unsafe; the check is a compiler rule, not a JVM rule.)
  • Is Throwable itself checked? (Yes: anything not under RuntimeException or Error is checked.)

try / catch / finally Semantics and the "Pending Return"

Why interviewers ask: the "what does this print?" with a return in finally is a staple, and it exposes whether you know how the JVM stores a return value before running the cleanup block.

Execution order: the try body runs; if it throws, the first matching catch (top to bottom, by type) runs; then finally always runs, whether the try completed normally, returned, threw, or the catch itself threw. The only things that skip finally are System.exit(), Runtime.halt(), a JVM crash, or the thread being killed. An infinite loop in try also never reaches it, obviously.

When a return expr; executes inside try or catch, the JVM evaluates expr immediately, parks the value (conceptually a hidden local; in bytecode the expression is stored before the inlined finally code runs), runs finally, then returns the parked value. So finally mutating the variable you returned changes nothing, but mutating the object that value references is visible. If finally itself does return (or throws), it replaces the pending return and discards any in-flight exception. That is why javac warns "finally clause cannot complete normally" and every style guide forbids it.

Catch order matters: a subtype after its supertype is a compile error ("exception has already been caught"). Multi-catch catch (IOException | SQLException e) handles alternatives that are not subtypes of one another; the parameter is implicitly final, so you cannot reassign e. Analogy: the return value is a letter already sealed in an envelope; finally is the cleanup crew that can tidy the room but cannot change what is in the envelope, unless it rudely swaps the whole envelope.

static int f() {
    try {
        System.out.println("try");
        throw new IllegalStateException("boom");
    } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
        System.out.println("catch");
        return 1;
    } finally {
        System.out.println("finally");
    }
}
static int g() {
    try {
        return 1;
    } finally {
        return 2;              // overrides: caller sees 2, warning from javac
    }
}
static int h() {
    int x = 1;
    try {
        return x;              // value 1 is parked NOW
    } finally {
        x = 99;                // too late: does not affect the parked 1
    }
}
  1. f() enters the try, prints try, throws. The JVM looks for a handler in this frame's exception table.
  2. The catch matches. catch is printed and return 1 evaluates to 1, which is parked; the exception is now fully handled.
  3. finally runs and prints finally. It has no return, so it completes normally.
  4. The parked 1 is returned. Output order is try, catch, finally.
  5. g() parks 1 and jumps to finally.
  6. finally executes its own return 2: the pending 1 is discarded. Had the try thrown instead, that exception would have vanished the same way.
  7. h(): return x copies the value 1 into the pending slot.
  8. x = 99 updates the local, not the parked copy. h() returns 1. If x were a StringBuilder and finally appended to it, the caller would see the append, because the reference was copied, not the object.
Interview angle: "Does finally run after return?" Yes. "After System.exit(0) inside try?" No, the JVM halts. "Can a finally lose an exception?" Yes, if it returns or throws; the original is gone with no record, unlike try-with-resources which records it as suppressed. "Can I catch FileNotFoundException after IOException?" Compile error: the second catch is unreachable.

Pitfalls

  • return/throw/break/continue inside finally: silently discards exceptions. Sonar and Error Prone flag it; javac emits a warning only with -Xlint:finally.
  • A catch that throws while finally also throws: only the finally exception survives.
  • Multi-catch alternatives must not be related by subclassing (IOException | FileNotFoundException is a compile error) and the variable is effectively final.
  • Catching a checked exception that the try body cannot throw is a compile error ("exception X is never thrown in body of corresponding try statement"), except for Exception/Throwable, which are always allowed.

Likely follow-ups

  • How is finally implemented in bytecode? (javac duplicates the finally code onto every exit path: normal, each return, and a catch-all handler; the exception table has an any entry.)
  • Is try without catch legal? (Yes with finally or with resources.)
  • What happens to an exception thrown in a static initializer? (Wrapped in ExceptionInInitializerError; see the compiler-rules card below.)

try-with-resources, Close Order and Suppressed Exceptions

Why interviewers ask: "two resources, the body throws, close() throws too: which exception does the caller see?" tests whether you understand the desugaring instead of memorising syntax.

Any type implementing AutoCloseable (close() throws Exception) or its IO-flavoured child Closeable (close() throws IOException, expected to be idempotent) can be declared in the resource list. Resources are initialised left to right and closed in reverse order, each one closed only if its initialisation succeeded, and closed before any catch or finally attached to the same statement runs.

If the body throws B and a close() then throws C, the body exception is the primary one and C is attached via B.addSuppressed(C); you read it with getSuppressed(), and printStackTrace prints it as Suppressed: .... If the body succeeds and close() throws, that close exception is the primary. Compare with a hand-written finally { r.close(); }, where the close exception would silently replace the body's. Analogy: the primary exception is the incident report; suppressed exceptions are attachments stapled to it, not separate reports.

Since Java 9 you can use an existing effectively final variable: try (conn) { ... } instead of try (Connection c = conn). The compiler desugars each resource into nested try/finally with a null-check and a catch that calls addSuppressed; you can see the generated shape with javap -c.

// What the compiler roughly generates for try (Res r = open()) { body(); }
final Res r = open();
Throwable primary = null;
try {
    body();
} catch (Throwable t) {
    primary = t;
    throw t;
} finally {
    if (r != null) {
        if (primary != null) {
            try { r.close(); } catch (Throwable c) { primary.addSuppressed(c); }
        } else {
            r.close();          // body succeeded: a close failure is the primary exception
        }
    }
}
Real-world: JDBC: try (var conn = ds.getConnection(); var ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql); var rs = ps.executeQuery()) closes rs, then ps, then conn, exactly the order JDBC requires. With Spring's JdbcTemplate you never write this, but interviewers expect you to know what it is doing for you.

Pitfalls

  • The resource variable is implicitly final; you cannot reassign it in the body.
  • A catch attached to try-with-resources runs after the resources are closed, so you cannot use the resource in the catch block meaningfully.
  • Suppressed exceptions vanish if someone wraps the primary in a new exception without passing it as cause: always chain.
  • Throwable subclasses created with enableSuppression=false silently drop addSuppressed calls.

Likely follow-ups

  • Are streams AutoCloseable? (Yes; you only need to close ones backed by IO such as Files.lines.)
  • Does try-with-resources need a catch? (No; exceptions from the body or from close() propagate, with the close exception declared as checked if close() declares it.)
  • What if close() throws a checked Exception? (You must catch or declare it; prefer narrowing close() in your own types, like Closeable does.)

Java 8 vs 17

Java 9 allows try (existingEffectivelyFinalVar); on Java 8 you had to introduce a new variable try (Res r = existing). Suppressed exceptions and multi-catch exist since Java 7.

Rules the Compiler and JVM Enforce: Overriding, Constructors, Static Init

Why interviewers ask: "can an overriding method throw a broader checked exception?" and "why did the second call throw NoClassDefFoundError instead of the real error?" are cheap questions with a high miss rate.

Overriding: an overriding method may throw fewer or narrower checked exceptions than the method it overrides, never broader or new ones, because callers holding a supertype reference only prepared for the declared set. Unchecked exceptions are unrestricted. Constructors are not overridden, so a subclass constructor may declare more, but it must declare everything the super(...) it invokes can throw. An interface's default method follows the same rule as any method.

Static initialisation: if a static initializer or static field initializer throws an unchecked exception, the JVM wraps it in ExceptionInInitializerError and marks the class erroneous. Every subsequent use of that class throws NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class X, with the original cause nowhere in sight on older JDKs (Java 17+ attaches the original ExceptionInInitializerError as the cause; check your JDK). Static initializers cannot throw checked exceptions at all, which is why you see static { try { ... } catch (IOException e) { throw new UncheckedIOException(e); } }.

class Config {
    static final int PORT = Integer.parseInt(System.getProperty("port"));
    static void ping() { System.out.println("ping " + PORT); }
}
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try { Config.ping(); }
        catch (Throwable t) { System.out.println("1: " + t); }
        try { Config.ping(); }
        catch (Throwable t) { System.out.println("2: " + t); }
    }
}
  1. The first static call is an active use: the JVM must run Config's static initialisation before ping.
  2. <clinit> runs. With no -Dport, parseInt(null) throws NumberFormatException: Cannot parse null string.
  3. The JVM wraps it: ExceptionInInitializerError with getCause() = the NFE, and marks the class erroneous. ping never runs.
  4. Line 8 prints 1: java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError; its cause tells you exactly what went wrong.
  5. Second call: the JVM does not retry initialisation. An erroneous class fails immediately.
  6. Line 10 prints 2: java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class Config. In production the first error is often buried in an early log, and every later request shows only this one. Search the logs for the first occurrence.
