Interview angle: "Object.clone() declares CloneNotSupportedException; can my override drop it?" Yes: narrowing to no checked exceptions is allowed and recommended (Effective Java Item 13). "Why does Spring fail an app with NoClassDefFoundError for a class that is clearly in the jar?" Almost always a static initializer that failed earlier, e.g. a logger or a MessageDigest.getInstance in a static field.

Pitfalls

  • Static fields initialised from environment/config are a time bomb: fail fast in main or a Spring bean instead, where the error is visible and the class stays usable.
  • catch (Throwable) around a static call and then continuing: the next call throws a different, less helpful error.
  • A lambda or anonymous class can only throw checked exceptions permitted by the functional interface's method (usually none).

Likely follow-ups

  • What if the static initializer throws an Error (not Exception)? (Passed through unwrapped; the class is still marked erroneous.)
  • Can main declare throws Exception? (Yes; an uncaught exception prints the trace via the default UncaughtExceptionHandler and the thread ends with exit code 1.)

Designing Custom Exceptions

Why interviewers ask: every service has a SomethingException; they want to see whether yours carries useful context, chains its cause, and stays out of a 40-class hierarchy.

Decide checked vs unchecked deliberately (see the hierarchy card); most service code extends RuntimeException. Carry structured context as final fields (entity id, error code, HTTP status hint) rather than only baking it into the message: a global handler can then map code to a response body and metrics without parsing strings. Always provide a constructor that accepts a cause so the original stack trace survives translation, and keep the exception immutable.

Prefer one or two base types per module plus an error-code enum over deep class hierarchies: a hierarchy forces callers to know dozens of types, while a code is data you can log, count and localise. Throwable is Serializable, so declare serialVersionUID if the exception may cross an RMI/HTTP-session boundary (otherwise it is noise; many teams suppress the warning). Analogy: a good exception is an incident ticket: severity, an id you can search for, the root cause attached, and no essay in the title.

public enum ErrorCode {
    ORDER_NOT_FOUND(404), INSUFFICIENT_STOCK(409), PAYMENT_DECLINED(402);
    public final int httpStatus;
    ErrorCode(int httpStatus) { this.httpStatus = httpStatus; }
}

public class OrderException extends RuntimeException {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
    private final ErrorCode code;
    private final String orderId;

    public OrderException(ErrorCode code, String orderId, String message) {
        this(code, orderId, message, null);
    }
    public OrderException(ErrorCode code, String orderId, String message, Throwable cause) {
        super(message + " [code=" + code + ", orderId=" + orderId + "]", cause);
        this.code = Objects.requireNonNull(code);
        this.orderId = orderId;
    }
    public ErrorCode code() { return code; }
    public String orderId() { return orderId; }
}

// usage at a boundary (Spring):
// @ExceptionHandler(OrderException.class)
// ResponseEntity<Problem> handle(OrderException e) {
//     return ResponseEntity.status(e.code().httpStatus).body(Problem.of(e.code(), e.getMessage()));
// }
Interview angle: "Why not just throw IllegalArgumentException("order not found")?" Because the API layer cannot distinguish it from an NPE-like programmer error, cannot map it to 404, and tests would assert on message strings. "Why an enum instead of subclasses?" Codes are data; they show up in dashboards and in the JSON contract. Subclasses are worth it only when callers genuinely handle them differently.

Pitfalls

  • Losing the cause: throw new OrderException("db failed") inside a catch, without e, deletes the SQL state and the driver's stack frames.
  • Putting PII (emails, card numbers) in messages: messages end up in logs, APM tools and sometimes HTTP responses.
  • Mutable exceptions or exceptions with heavy fields (an entire request object) retained by logging frameworks.
  • Naming: end with Exception, never Error (reserved by convention for JVM-level failures).

Likely follow-ups

  • Should custom exceptions be final? (Often yes for leaf types; keeps the set of catchable types explicit.)
  • How do you version error codes in an API? (Never reuse or rename a code; add new ones; document in the OpenAPI spec.)
  • Where does getLocalizedMessage() fit? (Override for user-facing text; keep getMessage() technical.)

What an Exception Costs (and Why Not to Use Them for Control Flow)

Why interviewers ask: "exceptions are slow" is a meme; the interviewer wants the precise reason (stack capture) and to see that you know the escape hatches.

The expensive part is construction, not throwing or catching: Throwable's constructor calls fillInStackTrace(), a native walk of the entire thread stack that records every frame. Cost grows with stack depth: in a Spring MVC request 100+ frames deep, capturing a trace can cost on the order of tens of microseconds, versus nanoseconds for a normal return. Unwinding to a handler is comparatively cheap, and a throw/catch in the same JIT-compiled method can even be turned into a jump.

The JIT does not optimise across exception-based control flow the way it does across returns: the exceptional path is treated as cold, inlining decisions assume it rarely happens, and hot exception paths deoptimise. So never use exceptions for expected outcomes ("user not found", "end of iteration", "invalid number in a parser loop"). Return Optional, a sealed result type, a boolean, or a sentinel instead. Analogy: pulling the fire alarm to get everyone out of a meeting works, but it is not how you should end meetings.

When you genuinely need a cheap exception (a framework signalling exception, a parser inside a hot loop), use the protected constructor Throwable(String, Throwable, boolean enableSuppression, boolean writableStackTrace) with writableStackTrace=false, or override fillInStackTrace() to return this. Reactor, Kotlin coroutines and many frameworks do this for their internal exceptions.

// Cheap signalling exception: no stack capture, no suppression bookkeeping
public final class StopIteration extends RuntimeException {
    public static final StopIteration INSTANCE = new StopIteration();
    private StopIteration() {
        super("stop", null, /*enableSuppression*/ false, /*writableStackTrace*/ false);
    }
}

// Better than throwing for an expected outcome:
Optional<Integer> parse(String s) {
    try { return Optional.of(Integer.parseInt(s)); }      // fine for rare bad input
    catch (NumberFormatException e) { return Optional.empty(); }
}
// ...but if 30% of inputs are bad, validate with a regex/loop first.
OperationRough costDominated by
Normal return~1 nsnothing
new Exception() with stack trace~1–50 µs (depth dependent)fillInStackTrace walking frames
new Exception() with writableStackTrace=false~ cost of an object allocationallocation only
throw + catch (pre-built exception)sub-µshandler lookup, unwinding frames
Interview angle: "Is Integer.parseInt in a loop with try/catch acceptable?" For rare failures yes; for a CSV where half the cells are blank, pre-check. "Why did my hot NPE lose its stack trace?" -XX:+OmitStackTraceInFastThrow (default on): after a few thousand throws of the same implicit exception at the same site, C2 replaces it with a pre-allocated, trace-less instance. Great for throughput, terrible for debugging; see the stack-trace card.

Pitfalls

  • Micro-benchmarking exceptions with a shallow stack shows them as cheap; production stacks are deep.
  • Pre-allocated singleton exceptions are shared across threads: never addSuppressed or setStackTrace on them (hence enableSuppression=false).
  • Logging frameworks re-walk and format the trace on every log call; a hot "warn with exception" line is often the real cost.

Likely follow-ups

  • Does getStackTrace() cost extra? (Yes: it lazily converts the native backtrace into StackTraceElement[] on first call.)
  • What about StackWalker? (Java 9 API that walks lazily and can stop early; much cheaper than new Throwable().getStackTrace() for "who called me".)

Exception Translation, Layering and "Log Once at the Boundary"

Why interviewers ask: it is the design question hidden in a language question: which layer is allowed to know about SQLException, and why does your log show the same stack trace four times?

Translate at layer boundaries: a repository catches infrastructure exceptions (SQLException, IOException, HTTP client errors) and rethrows a domain exception with the original as cause. Callers above never import java.sql.*; swapping Postgres for DynamoDB then touches one layer. Spring does this for you with DataAccessException: @Repository beans get a PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor proxy that maps vendor SQL states to DuplicateKeyException, DataIntegrityViolationException, QueryTimeoutException and so on, all unchecked.

Handle or propagate, never both: catch (E e) { log.error(..., e); throw e; } ("log and rethrow") is the most common anti-pattern in code reviews. Each layer that does it produces one more copy of the same trace, and the boundary handler logs it again. Rule: an exception is logged exactly once, at the place that finally handles it (the @ControllerAdvice, the message-listener error handler, the job runner, the thread's uncaught-exception handler). Intermediate layers may add context by wrapping, not by logging. Analogy: each department forwards the complaint up with a note attached; only the ombudsman at the top writes it into the public register.

// Repository: translate, keep the cause, do not log
public Order save(Order o) {
    try {
        return jdbc.insert(o);
    } catch (DuplicateKeyException e) {
        throw new OrderException(ErrorCode.DUPLICATE_ORDER, o.id(), "order already exists", e);
    }
}

// Boundary: the ONLY place that logs
@RestControllerAdvice
class ApiErrors {
    @ExceptionHandler(OrderException.class)
    ResponseEntity<Problem> onOrder(OrderException e) {
        log.warn("order failure code={} id={}", e.code(), e.orderId(), e);   // e last → trace printed
        return ResponseEntity.status(e.code().httpStatus).body(Problem.of(e));
    }
}

Pitfalls

  • catch (Exception e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } in every layer: three wrappers deep, the boundary has to unwrap to find the real type.
  • Leaking DataAccessException, WebClientResponseException or HttpClientErrorException into service interfaces couples your domain to a library.
  • Logging at WARN/ERROR inside retry loops: a transient timeout with 5 retries produces 5 error traces and a false alert.
  • Swallowing (catch (Exception ignored) {}) is the worst version: the failure is not logged anywhere, and the caller proceeds with bad state.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why is DataAccessException unchecked? (Callers rarely recover; translation would otherwise force throws everywhere.)
  • How do you keep the correlation id in the log line? (MDC/ThreadContext populated by a filter; the boundary handler logs within the same thread.)
  • Where do you log in a Kafka consumer? (In the container's error handler after retries are exhausted, then dead-letter.)

Checked Exceptions in Lambdas, Streams and CompletableFuture

Why interviewers ask: "why won't this stream compile?" is a practical daily annoyance, and the async part (which wrapper exception do you get from join() vs get()) is a reliable trap.

Function, Supplier, Consumer and friends declare no checked exceptions, so a lambda body that calls Files.readString does not compile inside map(...). Options, in order of preference: (1) handle inside the lambda and return an Optional/result object; (2) wrap in an unchecked exception, ideally a specific one such as UncheckedIOException (the JDK's own choice in Files.lines); (3) define a ThrowingFunction interface plus a small unchecked(...) adapter; (4) "sneaky throw", which uses generic inference to throw a checked exception undeclared. Sneaky throw is legal but surprises callers (a checked exception with no throws clause), so keep it out of public APIs.

Async: an exception thrown inside a CompletableFuture stage completes it exceptionally. join() rethrows it wrapped in unchecked CompletionException; get() wraps it in checked ExecutionException (and can throw InterruptedException). In exceptionally/handle, the argument may or may not be a CompletionException depending on which stage failed, so unwrap with getCause() defensively. Executors behave similarly: Future.get() gives ExecutionException, while execute(Runnable) lets the exception reach the thread's uncaught handler and, in a ScheduledExecutorService, silently cancels further runs.

@FunctionalInterface
interface ThrowingFunction<T, R, E extends Exception> { R apply(T t) throws E; }

static <T, R> Function<T, R> unchecked(ThrowingFunction<T, R, ?> f) {
    return t -> {
        try { return f.apply(t); }
        catch (IOException e) { throw new UncheckedIOException(e); }
        catch (Exception e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); }
    };
}
List<String> bodies = paths.stream().map(unchecked(Files::readString)).toList();

// Sneaky throw: compiles, throws IOException without declaring it
@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
static <E extends Throwable> RuntimeException sneaky(Throwable t) throws E { throw (E) t; }

// CompletableFuture wrapping
CompletableFuture<String> cf = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("x"); });
try { cf.join(); } catch (CompletionException e) { /* e.getCause() is the ISE */ }
try { cf.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { /* checked; cause is the ISE */ } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
Interview angle: "What happens to an exception in a parallel stream?" It propagates to the caller of the terminal operation after the other tasks finish or are abandoned; other elements' exceptions are lost (only one is rethrown). "How do you cancel a scheduled task that keeps dying?" It already cancelled itself: any thrown exception stops the periodic schedule; wrap the runnable in a try/catch that logs.

Pitfalls

  • Catching InterruptedException in a lambda and doing nothing: always restore the interrupt flag.
  • exceptionally(ex -> ...) placed before the failing stage does not see the failure; ordering of stages matters.
  • Wrapping in a bare RuntimeException hides the type from the boundary handler; use UncheckedIOException or your domain exception.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why does Callable declare throws Exception but Runnable not? (Callable was designed for executors with Future.get() to carry the failure; Runnable predates it.)
  • Difference between handle and whenComplete? (handle can recover and return a new value; whenComplete observes and keeps the original outcome.)

Reading Stack Traces and the Two JVM Flags That Change Them

Why interviewers ask: you will be handed a 60-line trace and asked "where is the bug?"; knowing to jump to the last Caused by and the first frame of your package is the whole skill.

A trace prints the outermost exception first, then each Caused by: down to the root cause. Frames run from the throw site (top) to main/thread start (bottom). "... 23 more" means those frames are identical to the enclosing trace and were elided. Reading recipe: (1) go to the last Caused by, that is the root; (2) within it, find the first frame in your package (skip jdk.internal, org.springframework, $$Proxy, reflect); (3) then read upward to see who called it. Suppressed: blocks come from try-with-resources.

Two flags change what you see. -XX:+OmitStackTraceInFastThrow (on by default in server-class JVMs) lets C2 replace frequently thrown implicit exceptions (NPE, ArrayIndexOutOfBounds, ClassCast, ArithmeticException) at a hot site with a pre-allocated instance that has no stack trace and no message. In production logs this looks like java.lang.NullPointerException with nothing below it. Fix: restart with -XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow, or search the logs for the first occurrence, which still had the trace. Helpful NullPointerExceptions (JEP 358, Java 14, on by default since 15 via -XX:+ShowCodeDetailsInExceptionMessages) give messages like Cannot invoke "String.length()" because "order.customer" is null; local variable names appear only if the class was compiled with -g, otherwise you see <local4>.

org.springframework.dao.DataIntegrityViolationException: could not execute statement
    at org.springframework.orm.jpa.vendor.HibernateJpaDialect.convertHibernateAccessException(...)
    at com.acme.order.OrderService$$SpringCGLIB$$0.place(<generated>)      <- proxy, skip
    at com.acme.order.api.OrderController.create(OrderController.java:41)   <- your frame (caller)
    ... 58 more
Caused by: org.hibernate.exception.ConstraintViolationException: could not execute statement
    at org.hibernate.exception.internal.SQLStateConversionDelegate.convert(...)
    ... 71 more
Caused by: org.postgresql.util.PSQLException: ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "uk_order_ref"
    at org.postgresql.core.v3.QueryExecutorImpl.receiveErrorResponse(QueryExecutorImpl.java:2675)
    at com.acme.order.OrderRepository.insert(OrderRepository.java:88)        <- ROOT: first frame of your code
    ... 80 more
Symptom in logsLikely causeAction
NullPointerException with no frames, repeated thousands of timesOmitStackTraceInFastThrow kicked inFind the first occurrence; or run with -XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow
NPE message says "<local3>" is nullClass compiled without -g (Maven/Gradle default includes it; shaded or obfuscated jars may not)Rebuild with debug info or map the slot with javap -l
Trace ends in ... N more with no line numbersFrames elided as duplicates, or -g:noneRead the enclosing trace for the elided frames
Same trace 4 times per requestlog-and-rethrow in every layerLog once at the boundary

Pitfalls

  • log.error("failed: " + e) logs only toString(); pass the exception as the last argument so the trace is printed.
  • e.printStackTrace() writes to stderr, bypassing your logging pipeline and correlation ids.
  • Async traces (CompletableFuture, reactive) stop at the executor; enable Reactor's Hooks.onOperatorDebug()/checkpoints or keep context manually.

Likely follow-ups

  • Does OmitStackTraceInFastThrow affect explicit throw new NullPointerException()? (No; only JVM-generated implicit exceptions.)
  • How do you get the root cause programmatically? (Loop getCause() until null; Spring's NestedExceptionUtils.getMostSpecificCause, Guava's Throwables.getRootCause.)

Errors You Will Meet in Production

Why interviewers ask: "we saw OutOfMemoryError in the logs; what do you do?" checks whether you know there are six different OOMs with six different fixes, and that most of them mean "restart, then diagnose", not "catch and continue".

Errors signal that the JVM itself, not your logic, is in an abnormal state. The pragmatic policy: let them propagate to a top-level handler that logs and lets the orchestrator restart the process (-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError or -XX:+CrashOnOutOfMemoryError exist for exactly this), and capture a heap dump on the way out (-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=...). Catching an OOM to "free something and retry" occasionally works for a single huge allocation (Requested array size exceeds VM limit) but is unreliable elsewhere, because any code path, including the logger, may fail to allocate.

Error (message)MeaningTypical causeRecoverable?First action
OutOfMemoryError: Java heap spaceHeap exhausted after a full GCLeak (static map, listener, ThreadLocal), unbounded cache, oversized batchNoHeap dump, MAT/JFR, dominator tree
OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded>98% time in GC recovering <2% heapSame as above, caught earlier by the collectorNoSame; do not disable the check
OutOfMemoryError: MetaspaceClass metadata space fullClassloader leak on redeploy, runtime bytecode generation (proxies, Groovy, reflection inflation)NoCount loaded classes, check -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize
OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native threadOS refused a threadThread leak, unbounded executors, container pid/ulimit limits, huge -XssNoThread dump; bound the pools; virtual threads (21)
OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memoryOff-heap NIO buffers exhaustedNetty/gRPC buffers not released, -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize too smallNoNetty leak detector, raise limit
StackOverflowErrorOne thread's stack fullUnbounded recursion, cyclic toString/equals/JPA bidirectional mapping, deep Spring bean cyclesPer-thread, often yesFix recursion; -Xss only as a stopgap
NoClassDefFoundErrorClass known at compile time is missing or erroneous at runtimeDependency scope/version mismatch, failed static init (see compiler-rules card)No (fix the deployment)Find the first ExceptionInInitializerError or check the jar
ExceptionInInitializerErrorStatic initializer threwConfig read in a static field, missing resourceNo (class is dead)Read getCause()
AssertionErrorassert failedOnly when running with -ea (off by default)Bug; do not catchNever use assert for input validation in production
UnsupportedClassVersionErrorBytecode newer than the runtimeCompiled with 17, run on 11NoAlign --release and runtime
Interview angle: "Would you ever catch StackOverflowError?" Rarely; a parser or serializer guarding against hostile deeply nested input may catch it in one specific place to fail that request, since the stack is per-thread and fully unwound afterwards. "What is the first thing you look at for an OOM?" The message: it tells you which of the six memory areas is exhausted, and each has a different tool.

Pitfalls

  • catch (Throwable t) in a request loop keeps a JVM with a corrupted state serving errors forever; prefer crash-and-restart.
  • Container memory limit hit before the heap limit: the kernel OOM-kills the process with no Java error at all. Size -Xmx below the container limit (or use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage).
  • assert statements with side effects: they vanish without -ea.

Likely follow-ups

  • How do you get a heap dump from a running pod? (jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/h.hprof or jmap -dump; JFR for continuous profiling.)
  • Does -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError run finally blocks? (No, the JVM exits immediately; that is the point.)

Java 8 vs 17

Java 9: effectively-final variables in try-with-resources, StackWalker. Java 14/15: helpful NPE messages (opt-in in 14, default in 15+). Java 17: NoClassDefFoundError from a failed initializer now records the original cause (check your JDK). Container awareness (MaxRAMPercentage, cgroup limits) arrived in 8u191/10, so most Java 17 OOMs are heap leaks rather than mis-sized heaps. Java 21 preview: virtual threads make "unable to create native thread" largely a thing of the past and change stack-trace shape for async code.

What does this print?
try { return "A"; } finally { System.out.print("F"); } ... called and the result printed after it

c. The return value "A" is parked, then finally runs and prints F, then the method returns and the caller prints A. a forgets that finally always runs; b has the order wrong because finally executes before the method actually returns.

A finally block contains return 0;. The try block throws an IOException. What does the caller observe?

b. An abrupt completion of finally (return, throw, break) replaces whatever was pending, including an in-flight exception. It compiles (javac only warns with -Xlint:finally), so c is wrong; there is no "suppressed" mechanism outside try-with-resources, so a is wrong.

try (A a = new A(); B b = new B()) { throw new RuntimeException("body"); } where both close() methods throw. Which is true?

a. The body exception is primary; resources close in reverse order (B then A) and each close failure is added via addSuppressed, so getSuppressed() is [B's, A's]. Every resource is still closed (d wrong). b describes what a hand-written finally { close(); } would do.

The try body completes normally, but close() throws IOException. What reaches the caller?

d. Suppression only applies when there is already a primary exception from the body. With no body exception, the close failure is the exception, unwrapped and checked, so the enclosing method must catch or declare IOException.

A hot code path throws thousands of NPEs per second and the logs show java.lang.NullPointerException with no stack frames. Why?

b. The JIT's fast-throw optimisation drops both the trace and the message for hot implicit exceptions. Compiling without -g (d) only removes local variable names/line numbers, and helpful NPE messages (c) affect the message text, not the frames.

A static field initializer throws. The first call to the class reports ExceptionInInitializerError. The second call reports what?

c. The JVM marks the class erroneous and never retries (a wrong). ClassNotFoundException (b) is for classes that cannot be found; this one was found but failed to initialise.

Which is the best production shape for a repository that catches SQLException?

a. Translate at the boundary, keep the cause, log once where it is handled. b multiplies traces; c discards the cause and type; d leaks JDBC into the web layer and forces throws everywhere.

An overriding method in a subclass wants to declare throws Exception while the superclass method declares throws IOException. Result?

d. Callers through the supertype reference only handle IOException, so widening would break them. Unchecked exceptions are unrestricted, and constructors are exempt because they are not overridden; c describes a rule Java does not have.

Practice

Predict the output: return, finally and a shared StringBuilder

public class T {
    static String run() {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        try {
            sb.append("A");
            throw new RuntimeException("x");
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            sb.append("B");
            return sb.toString();
        } finally {
            sb.append("C");
            System.out.print(sb + " ");
        }
    }
    static int num() {
        try { throw new IllegalStateException(); }
        finally { return 42; }
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.print(run() + " ");
        System.out.println(num());
    }
}

What is printed? Then: what changes if run() returned sb (a StringBuilder) and main printed it?

Tests: pending return value, finally ordering, exception swallowed by return-in-finally
Hint 1
return sb.toString() evaluates the expression before finally runs. What is the string at that moment?
Hint 2
Does anyone ever see the IllegalStateException in num()?
Reveal solution

Output: ABC AB 42

run(): try appends A and throws; catch appends B; return sb.toString() evaluates to "AB" and parks it. Then finally appends C and prints "ABC " (the builder is now ABC). The method returns the parked "AB", which main prints with a space. num(): the IllegalStateException is in flight when finally executes return 42, which replaces it; the exception is gone forever and 42 is printed.

Variant: if run() returned sb itself, the parked value is a reference; finally mutates the same object, so main would print ABC ABC 42. Pass-by-value of the reference, exactly as in the JVM section's walkthrough.

What the interviewer wants to hear: "return in finally is a bug; it swallows exceptions. javac warns with -Xlint:finally and static analysers flag it."

Predict the output: open/close order and suppressed exceptions

class Res implements AutoCloseable {
    private final String name;
    Res(String name) { this.name = name; System.out.print("open " + name + " "); }
    @Override public void close() {
        System.out.print("close " + name + " ");
        throw new IllegalStateException("close-" + name);
    }
}
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (Res a = new Res("A"); Res b = new Res("B")) {
            throw new RuntimeException("body");
        } catch (Exception e) {
            System.out.print("| " + e.getMessage());
            for (Throwable s : e.getSuppressed()) System.out.print(" +" + s.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

What is printed? Then: what is printed if the body is empty (no throw)?

Tests: reverse close order, primary vs suppressed, catch runs after close
Hint 1
Resources close in reverse declaration order, and all of them close even if one close() throws.
Hint 2
Suppressed exceptions are appended in the order addSuppressed is called.
Reveal solution

Output: open A open B close B close A | body +close-B +close-A

A then B are opened. The body throws "body", which becomes primary. B closes first (reverse order) and throws; that exception is attached as suppressed[0]. A closes and throws; attached as suppressed[1]. Only then does the catch run, seeing the primary with both suppressed exceptions in close order.

Empty body: open A open B close B close A | close-B +close-A. With no primary from the body, B's close exception becomes the primary, and A's close failure is suppressed onto it. This reversal (body failure primary, otherwise first close failure primary) is the point of the question.

Code review: refactor this exception handling

You are reviewing a service method in a Spring Boot order service. List every problem and rewrite it.

public OrderDto place(PlaceOrderRequest req) {
    try {
        Customer c = customerClient.find(req.customerId());     // may throw HttpClientErrorException.NotFound
        Order o = new Order(c, req.items());
        try {
            inventory.reserve(o.items());                       // throws InsufficientStockException (checked)
        } catch (Exception e) {
            log.error("reserve failed", e);
            throw new RuntimeException(e);
        }
        try {
            return mapper.toDto(repo.save(o));
        } catch (DataIntegrityViolationException dup) {
            log.error("duplicate", dup);
            throw dup;
        }
    } catch (Exception e) {
        log.error("place failed", e);
        return null;
    }
}

// elsewhere, in the same class:
boolean exists(String id) {
    try { repo.getById(id); return true; }
    catch (EntityNotFoundException e) { return false; }
}
Tests: catching Exception, swallowing, log-and-rethrow, exceptions for control flow, translation, cause chaining
Hint 1
Count how many times a single duplicate-key failure is logged before it leaves this method. Then ask what the caller does with null.
Hint 2
exists() forces the JPA provider to build an entity and an exception (with stack capture) just to answer a boolean. Is there a query that answers it directly?
Reveal solution

Problems found

  1. Outer catch (Exception e) { return null; } swallows everything, including the two exceptions the inner blocks carefully rethrew and any NPE. The controller gets null, which becomes a 200 with an empty body or an NPE somewhere else; and the @Transactional proxy (if present) commits because no exception escaped.
  2. Log-and-rethrow twice: "reserve failed" and "duplicate" are each logged here and then again by the outer catch, and would be logged a third time by the controller advice if the outer catch did not eat them. One failure, three traces.
  3. catch (Exception) around reserve catches far more than InsufficientStockException and wraps it in a bare RuntimeException: the boundary can no longer map it to HTTP 409 without unwrapping.
  4. Infrastructure types leak: HttpClientErrorException.NotFound from the customer client and DataIntegrityViolationException from Spring Data are not translated into domain vocabulary.
  5. exists() uses an exception for control flow: getById (a lazy reference) throws EntityNotFoundException on first access; on a hot path that is a full stack capture per miss. Use repo.existsById(id).

Rewrite

@Transactional
public OrderDto place(PlaceOrderRequest req) {
    Customer c = customerClient.find(req.customerId())
            .orElseThrow(() -> new OrderException(ErrorCode.CUSTOMER_NOT_FOUND, null,
                                                   "customer " + req.customerId() + " not found"));
    Order o = new Order(c, req.items());
    try {
        inventory.reserve(o.items());
    } catch (InsufficientStockException e) {
        throw new OrderException(ErrorCode.INSUFFICIENT_STOCK, o.id(), "cannot reserve", e);
    }
    try {
        return mapper.toDto(repo.save(o));
    } catch (DataIntegrityViolationException e) {
        throw new OrderException(ErrorCode.DUPLICATE_ORDER, o.id(), "order already exists", e);
    }
}

boolean exists(String id) { return repo.existsById(id); }

// CustomerClient: translate the HTTP client exception once, at the adapter
public Optional<Customer> find(String id) {
    try { return Optional.of(rest.getForObject("/customers/{id}", Customer.class, id)); }
    catch (HttpClientErrorException.NotFound e) { return Optional.empty(); }
}

// Boundary: the only log statement, one line per failure
@ExceptionHandler(OrderException.class)
ResponseEntity<Problem> onOrder(OrderException e) {
    log.warn("order failure code={} orderId={}", e.code(), e.orderId(), e);
    return ResponseEntity.status(e.code().httpStatus).body(Problem.of(e));
}

Why this is better: no null contract; every failure is a typed domain exception with a code and a cause; @Transactional rolls back on any of them (unchecked); the trace appears exactly once, at the boundary, with the correlation id from MDC; infrastructure exceptions stay in the adapter that produced them; and the existence check is a cheap SELECT COUNT. If the interviewer pushes on "what if the customer service is down (5xx)?" answer: that is a different code (CUSTOMER_SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, 503) plus retry/circuit breaker at the adapter, still logged once.

6️⃣ Java 8+ Functional: Lambdas, Streams, Optional, CompletableFuture

Almost every Java interview has a "write a stream that…" moment, and the seniors are separated by what they know about laziness, parallelism and CompletableFuture threading. The path here: lambdas and method references first, then how a pipeline actually executes, the collectors toolbox, Optional, parallel and primitive streams, the classic interview tasks, async composition, and finally functional idioms and java.time.

Lambdas & Functional Interfaces

Why interviewers ask: "why must a captured variable be effectively final?" and "is a lambda an anonymous inner class?" are quick tests of whether you understand what the compiler actually emits.

A functional interface has exactly one abstract method (SAM); default and static methods do not count, nor do Object methods like equals. @FunctionalInterface is optional but makes the compiler fail if someone adds a second abstract method. A lambda is an expression whose target type is inferred from context: the same x -> x * 2 can be a Function<Integer,Integer> or an IntUnaryOperator.

Capture: a lambda may read local variables only if they are effectively final. The reason is memory lifetime: locals live in a stack frame that dies when the method returns, while the lambda may run later on another thread. The compiler therefore copies the value into the lambda object; allowing later writes would create two diverging copies. Analogy: you can photocopy a document for a colleague, but they cannot see edits you make to the original afterwards, so Java simply forbids the edits. Fields and array elements are not locals, so mutating them is allowed (and is the classic data-race source).

Compilation: a lambda is not an inner class. javac desugars the body into a private synthetic method and emits an invokedynamic call site; at first execution LambdaMetafactory spins a tiny class implementing the interface. Consequences: no Foo$1.class files, a non-capturing lambda is a cached singleton, and this inside a lambda means the enclosing instance (in an anonymous class it means the anonymous object).

int base = 10;                       // effectively final: captured by value
Function<Integer, Integer> add = x -> x + base;
// base++;                          // would make the lambda a compile error

Supplier<List<String>> fresh = ArrayList::new;
Predicate<String> blank = String::isBlank;
BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer> max = Math::max;
IntBinaryOperator sum = (a, b) -> a + b;        // no boxing
Runnable r = () -> System.out.println(this);   // this == enclosing object, not the lambda
FamilySignatureTypical usePrimitive variants
Function<T,R> / BiFunction<T,U,R>R apply(T)map, convertersIntFunction, ToIntFunction, IntToLongFunction
UnaryOperator<T> / BinaryOperator<T>T apply(T[,T])reduce, replaceAllIntUnaryOperator, IntBinaryOperator
Supplier<T>T get()lazy values, factories, orElseGetIntSupplier, BooleanSupplier
Consumer<T> / BiConsumer<T,U>void accept(T)forEach, Map.forEachIntConsumer, ObjIntConsumer
Predicate<T> / BiPredicateboolean test(T)filter, removeIfIntPredicate, LongPredicate
Interview angle: "Why do primitive specializations exist?" Because Function<Integer,Integer> boxes on every call; IntUnaryOperator avoids the allocation. The same reason IntStream exists.

Pitfalls

  • Working around "effectively final" with a one-element array or AtomicInteger inside a stream is a code smell: use reduce/collect instead.
  • Checked exceptions cannot escape a Function: you must wrap them (or write your own ThrowingFunction), which is why streams and IO mix badly.
  • Overload ambiguity: submit(() -> foo()) on an ExecutorService picks Callable if foo() returns a value, Runnable otherwise.

Likely follow-ups

  • Can a lambda be serialized? (Only if the target interface is Serializable; it uses SerializedLambda and is fragile across versions.)
  • Is a lambda allocated every time? (Non-capturing: one cached instance. Capturing: usually a new object per evaluation, often escape-analysed away.)
  • Does a lambda add a stack frame? (Yes, the synthetic lambda$main$0 method shows in stack traces.)

Method References: the Four Kinds

Why interviewers ask: mostly to see whether you can explain why String::length is a Function<String,Integer> even though length() takes no arguments.

A method reference is shorthand for a lambda that only forwards its arguments. The trick is which argument becomes the receiver. For an unbound instance reference (String::length) the first lambda parameter is the receiver; for a bound reference (str::equals, System.out::println) the receiver is evaluated once, when the reference is created.

KindSyntaxEquivalent lambda
StaticInteger::parseInts -> Integer.parseInt(s)
Bound instanceprefix::concats -> prefix.concat(s) (receiver fixed now)
Unbound instanceString::toUpperCases -> s.toUpperCase() (receiver = first arg)
ConstructorArrayList::new, int[]::new() -> new ArrayList<>(), n -> new int[n]
When a lambda is clearer: when arguments are reordered, when you would otherwise need a cast to fix overload ambiguity (Integer::toString is ambiguous between static and instance forms), or when the reference hides a side effect like list::add inside map.

Pitfalls

  • this::helper and obj::method capture the receiver strongly; storing such references in a long-lived registry leaks the object.
  • A bound reference on a null receiver throws NullPointerException at creation, not at first call.

Likely follow-ups

  • Can you reference a varargs or generic method? (Yes; type inference from the target type handles it.)
  • Is super::method allowed? (Yes, it is a bound reference to the superclass implementation.)

Stream Pipeline Anatomy: Lazy, Fused, One Element at a Time

Why interviewers ask: the "predict the output with peek" question exposes whether you think a stream runs stage by stage (wrong) or element by element (right). It also explains why limit makes infinite streams safe.

A pipeline is source → zero or more intermediate operations → one terminal operation. Intermediate ops (filter, map, limit…) only build a chain of stage objects and are lazy: nothing runs until the terminal op (collect, forEach, count…) pulls. Then each element travels vertically through every stage before the next element starts, a technique called loop fusion. Analogy: an assembly line, not a batch process; each car goes through all stations before the next car enters, and the line stops the moment the order is filled.

Stages are stateless (map, filter) or stateful (sorted, distinct, limit, skip). A full-barrier stateful op like sorted must see every upstream element before emitting the first, which breaks fusion and makes an infinite stream hang. Short-circuit ops (limit, findFirst, anyMatch) tell the source to stop pulling early. A stream is single-use: a second terminal call throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed.

var out = Stream.of("a", "bb", "ccc", "dddd")
    .peek(s -> System.out.print("F" + s.length() + " "))
    .filter(s -> s.length() % 2 == 0)
    .peek(s -> System.out.print("M" + s.length() + " "))
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .findFirst();
// prints: F1 F2 M2   → findFirst short-circuits after "bb"; "ccc"/"dddd" never read
Interview angle: "Does Stream.iterate(1, i -> i + 1).map(...).limit(5) terminate?" Yes, because limit pulls only 5. Move a sorted() before the limit and it never terminates.

Pitfalls

  • peek is for debugging; the JDK may skip it entirely when the count can be computed from the source (e.g. list.stream().peek(...).count() on Java 9+ prints nothing).
  • Ordering matters for cost: put filter before map/sorted so expensive stages see fewer elements.
  • A stream over a collection is not a snapshot; modifying the source during the terminal op throws ConcurrentModificationException (or worse).

Likely follow-ups

  • Why does sorted().findFirst() still process everything? (Sorting is a full barrier; it cannot know the minimum without seeing all elements.)
  • Is distinct() stateful? (Yes, it keeps a HashSet of seen elements; on ordered parallel streams it is expensive.)
  • Can you close a stream? (It is AutoCloseable; only matters for IO sources like Files.lines, so use try-with-resources there.)

Intermediate Operations Cheat-Sheet

Why interviewers ask: map vs flatMap is the single most common stream question; takeWhile/dropWhile and mapMulti show you kept up past Java 8.

flatMap is for the one-to-many case: the function returns a stream per element and the results are concatenated, so Stream<List<Order>> becomes Stream<Order>. map would give you a stream of lists. Analogy: map replaces every box with another box; flatMap opens every box and pours the contents onto one conveyor.

OpStateful?What it doesNote
map(f)No1 → 1 transformmapToInt/Long/Double to leave boxing
flatMap(f)No1 → 0..n, f returns a StreamThe inner stream is closed after use
mapMulti(c) (16)No1 → 0..n via a BiConsumer(elem, downstream)Cheaper than flatMap when most elements yield 0–1 results (no per-element Stream)
filter(p)Nokeep if predicate truePlace early
distinct()Yes (set)drop duplicates by equals/hashCodeOrder-preserving for ordered streams
sorted() / sorted(cmp)Yes (barrier)full sort, stableInfinite stream hangs
peek(c)Noside effect per elementDebug only, may be elided
limit(n) / skip(n)Yes (counter)first n / all but first nlimit is short-circuiting; both are costly on ordered parallel streams
takeWhile(p) / dropWhile(p) (9)Yesprefix while true / drop prefix while trueUnlike filter, stops at the first failure
boxed(), asLongStream()Noprimitive ↔ object streamsIntStream.boxed() gives Stream<Integer>
List<List<Integer>> nested = List.of(List.of(1, 2), List.of(3), List.of());
List<Integer> flat = nested.stream().flatMap(List::stream).toList();        // [1, 2, 3]

// same with mapMulti: push results directly into the downstream consumer
List<Integer> flat2 = nested.stream()
    .<Integer>mapMulti((list, sink) -> list.forEach(sink)).toList();

Stream.of(2, 4, 5, 6).takeWhile(n -> n % 2 == 0).toList();                   // [2, 4]  (stops at 5)
Stream.of(2, 4, 5, 6).filter(n -> n % 2 == 0).toList();                      // [2, 4, 6]

Pitfalls

  • flatMap in Java 8 was not lazy for the inner stream (fixed in 10): flatMap(x -> infinite).findFirst() hung.
  • sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()) on a stream of records without a comparator throws ClassCastException at runtime, not compile time.

Likely follow-ups

  • How do you flatten Optionals inside a stream? (.flatMap(Optional::stream) since 9.)
  • Difference between Stream.concat and flatMap? (Concat joins two streams; flatMap joins n streams produced per element.)

Terminal Ops & Collectors: reduce, toMap, groupingBy

Why interviewers ask: "group by department and give me the highest-paid per department" is the canonical whiteboard task. Knowing toMap's duplicate-key exception and the parallel contract of reduce marks a senior.

reduce folds elements into one value: reduce(identity, accumulator, combiner). The identity must be a true identity (0 for sum, "" for concat) and the accumulator associative, because a parallel stream reduces chunks independently and merges them with the combiner. collect is the mutable version: a Collector is a bundle of supplier (new container), accumulator (add one element), combiner (merge two containers) and finisher.

groupingBy(classifier, mapFactory, downstream) builds a Map<K, D> where the downstream collector decides what each bucket holds: toList() by default, or counting(), mapping(f, toSet()), summingInt, averagingDouble, maxBy(cmp) (yields Optional), collectingAndThen(maxBy(...), Optional::get) to unwrap. partitioningBy(pred) is a two-key special case that always has both true and false keys. teeing(c1, c2, merger) (12) runs two collectors over the same elements and merges their results.

record Emp(String name, String dept, int salary) {}
var emps = List.of(new Emp("Ann", "ENG", 120), new Emp("Bob", "OPS", 90),
                   new Emp("Cid", "ENG", 150), new Emp("Dee", "OPS", 80));

Map<String, Emp> topPaid = emps.stream().collect(
    Collectors.groupingBy(Emp::dept,
        Collectors.collectingAndThen(
            Collectors.maxBy(Comparator.comparingInt(Emp::salary)),
            Optional::get)));
// {ENG=Cid, OPS=Bob}
  1. The collector's supplier creates an empty HashMap. Downstream containers are created lazily per key.
  2. Ann: classifier gives ENG; no bucket yet, so a fresh maxBy state is created and Ann becomes its current max.
  3. Bob: new key OPS, new bucket.
  4. Cid: bucket ENG exists; maxBy compares 150 vs 120 and keeps Cid.
  5. Dee: bucket OPS; 80 loses to 90, nothing changes.
  6. Elements exhausted. The finisher of collectingAndThen unwraps each Optional<Emp>. Result: {ENG=Cid, OPS=Bob}.
// toMap: duplicate keys throw IllegalStateException unless you pass a merge function
Map<String, Integer> salaryByDept = emps.stream().collect(
    Collectors.toMap(Emp::dept, Emp::salary, Integer::sum, TreeMap::new));

Map<Boolean, Long> highEarners = emps.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(e -> e.salary() > 100, Collectors.counting()));

String names = emps.stream().map(Emp::name).collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "[", "]"));

double avgOfMinMax = emps.stream().collect(Collectors.teeing(
    Collectors.minBy(Comparator.comparingInt(Emp::salary)),
    Collectors.maxBy(Comparator.comparingInt(Emp::salary)),
    (min, max) -> (min.get().salary() + max.get().salary()) / 2.0));

int total = emps.stream().map(Emp::salary).reduce(0, Integer::sum); // prefer mapToInt().sum()
Collectors.toList()Stream.toList() (16)
MutabilityUnspecified (currently ArrayList)Unmodifiable; add throws
NullsAllowedAllowed (unlike List.of)
Use whenYou will mutate the resultDefault choice for returned values
Interview angle: "Why does toMap throw and groupingBy not?" toMap maps each key to one value, so a collision is ambiguous; groupingBy is designed for many values per key. Also: toMap rejects null values with NullPointerException.

Pitfalls

  • reduce("", String::concat) is O(n²); use joining. Likewise reduce(new ArrayList<>(), ...) mutating the identity breaks the parallel contract: use collect.
  • groupingBy classifier returning null throws NPE; map to a sentinel first.
  • groupingByConcurrent gives an unordered ConcurrentHashMap: faster in parallel, but bucket lists are not in encounter order.

Likely follow-ups

  • How do you write a custom collector? (Collector.of(supplier, accumulator, combiner[, finisher], characteristics); IDENTITY_FINISH, UNORDERED, CONCURRENT.)
  • What does reduce(accumulator) without identity return? (Optional<T>, empty for an empty stream.)
  • How do you group into a LinkedHashMap to keep order? (Three-arg groupingBy(f, LinkedHashMap::new, downstream).)

Optional, Used Correctly

Why interviewers ask: Optional misuse is everywhere in real code bases; asking "where should Optional not appear?" quickly shows whether you read the API's intent.

Optional<T> is a return-type container meant to force callers to handle absence. Create with Optional.of(nonNull), ofNullable(maybeNull), empty(). Transform with map (wraps the result), flatMap (function already returns an Optional), filter. Unwrap with orElse(value), orElseGet(supplier), orElseThrow() (10, replaces the no-arg get()), ifPresentOrElse(consumer, runnable) (9), or(supplier) (9) to chain fallbacks, and stream() (9) to use inside flatMap.

The eager trap: orElse(expensive()) evaluates expensive() always, even when the value is present; orElseGet(() -> expensive()) evaluates it only when empty. With a DB call or logging inside, this is a real bug, not a style point. Analogy: orElse is buying a spare tyre before every trip; orElseGet is calling roadside assistance only when you actually get a flat.

Optional<User> user = repo.findById(id);

String city = user.map(User::address)          // Optional<Address>
                  .flatMap(Address::city)      // city() itself returns Optional<String>
                  .filter(c -> !c.isBlank())
                  .orElseGet(() -> geo.lookupCity(ip));   // lazy fallback

User u = user.orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException(id));
user.ifPresentOrElse(audit::seen, () -> log.warn("no user {}", id));
Optional<User> fallback = user.or(() -> cache.get(id));

// BAD: if (user.isPresent()) { return user.get(); }  → same as null check, no gain
PlaceVerdictWhy
Method return typeYesCommunicates "may be absent" in the signature
FieldNoNot Serializable, extra allocation, still can be null itself
Method parameterNoCaller writes Optional.ofNullable(x) ceremony; overload or a nullable param is clearer
Collection element / map valueNoJust omit the element; an empty List already means "nothing"
Return of a collection-typed methodReturn the empty collectionOptional<List<T>> is a double negative

Pitfalls

  • Optional.of(null) throws NPE immediately; use ofNullable when the value may be null.
  • Optional is a value-based class: never synchronize on it or compare with ==.
  • Optional.get() without a check is the same as a null dereference with a worse exception name (NoSuchElementException).

Likely follow-ups

  • OptionalInt vs Optional<Integer>? (Primitive variant returned by IntStream.max() etc.; no map on it.)
  • Does JPA/Spring Data support Optional returns? (Yes, Optional<T> findById; that is the canonical use.)

Parallel Streams: ForkJoin Splitting, the Common Pool, and When Not To

Why interviewers ask: "just add .parallel()" is the most common performance mistake they have seen in production. They want you to explain the cost model and the shared-pool hazard.

parallel() hands the source's Spliterator to the common ForkJoinPool. trySplit() recursively halves the data until chunks are small (roughly size / (4 × parallelism)), each leaf runs the fused pipeline sequentially, and results are merged with the collector's combiner. Splitting is O(1) for arrays, ArrayList, IntStream.range; it is poor for LinkedList, Stream.iterate, BufferedReader.lines (unknown size, must batch) and useless for anything IO-bound because the pool has only cores − 1 workers (-Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism to change) and a blocked worker is a lost core for every parallel stream in the JVM.

Analogy: splitting a deck of cards among four dealers is fast; splitting a chain necklace means walking link by link to find the middle. Rule of thumb from the JDK team: worth it when N × Q (elements × cost per element) is large, say over ~10 000 for cheap operations. Lambdas must be side-effect free and non-interfering; forEach runs in any order, forEachOrdered restores encounter order at a cost; findAny is cheaper than findFirst because it need not honour order.

// Isolate a heavy parallel job from the common pool (undocumented but widely used trick)
ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool(8);
long hits = pool.submit(() -> ids.parallelStream().filter(this::cpuHeavy).count()).get();
pool.shutdown();

// Ordering: forEach may interleave, forEachOrdered restores encounter order
List.of(1, 2, 3, 4).parallelStream().forEachOrdered(System.out::print);   // 1234
Interview angle: "A REST endpoint uses parallelStream to call a downstream service per item. What happens under load?" All requests share one pool of cores − 1 threads blocked on HTTP; throughput collapses and unrelated parallel code stalls. Use an explicit executor with CompletableFuture (or virtual threads) instead.

Pitfalls

  • Collectors.toMap and groupingBy merge maps per chunk: correct but not free; toConcurrentMap/groupingByConcurrent use one shared ConcurrentHashMap and are faster when order is irrelevant.
  • limit/skip/findFirst on ordered parallel streams need coordination and often run slower than sequential; call unordered() if you do not care.
  • parallel() and sequential() are pipeline-wide flags; the last call wins for the whole pipeline, not per stage.

Likely follow-ups

  • Which thread runs the terminal operation? (The caller participates; it helps run tasks rather than only waiting.)
  • Why is the common pool sized cores − 1? (The submitting thread counts as the extra worker.)
  • Is ArrayList safe to write inside forEach on a parallel stream? (No: data race and lost updates; use collect.)

Primitive Streams, Boxing, and Performance Realism

Why interviewers ask: "is a stream slower than a loop?" deserves a nuanced answer: usually a little, mostly because of boxing and allocation, and it matters only in hot loops.

IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream avoid the Integer wrapper per element. Get one with IntStream.range(0, n) / rangeClosed, mapToInt, String.chars(), Arrays.stream(int[]). They have sum(), average() (returns OptionalDouble), max(), and summaryStatistics() which gives count/min/max/sum/avg in one pass. Stream.iterate(seed, f) and generate(supplier) create infinite streams that need limit; iterate(seed, hasNext, next) (9) is the for-loop form.

Reality check: a for loop over an int[] beats Arrays.stream(a).sum() by a small constant factor; list.stream().map(Integer::intValue).reduce(0, Integer::sum) is noticeably worse because of boxing on every step. For business code, per-element cost (DB, JSON, HTTP) dwarfs all of this and readability should win.

IntSummaryStatistics st = orders.stream().mapToInt(Order::amount).summaryStatistics();
// st.getMin(), st.getMax(), st.getAverage(), st.getSum(), st.getCount()

double avg = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 100).average().orElse(0);        // 50.5
List<Integer> squares = IntStream.range(0, 5).map(i -> i * i).boxed().toList();
List<Integer> evens = Stream.iterate(0, i -> i < 20, i -> i + 2).toList();  // Java 9 three-arg
Stream.generate(UUID::randomUUID).limit(3).forEach(System.out::println);

Pitfalls

  • IntStream.max() returns OptionalInt; there is no map on it and no collect(Collectors...) on IntStream (only the 3-arg collect), so call boxed() first.
  • Stream.iterate(1, i -> i * 2) overflows silently; primitive overflow is not an exception.
  • average() of an empty stream is empty, not 0; and sum() of an IntStream can overflow: use mapToLong for money-like totals.

Likely follow-ups

  • How do you sum BigDecimals? (reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add), no primitive stream exists.)
  • What does chars() return? (IntStream of UTF-16 code units, not Stream<Character>.)

Common Stream Interview Tasks

Why interviewers ask: these are the ten-minute screeners. The point is fluency: you should be able to type them without pausing to remember the collector.

Two ideas cover most of them: a frequency map (groupingBy(identity, LinkedHashMap::new, counting())) and dedupe by property (toMap with a "keep first" merge, or a TreeSet with a comparator). Everything else is a comparator, a limit, or a flatMap away.

TaskCode
Word frequencywords.stream().collect(groupingBy(w -> w, LinkedHashMap::new, counting()))
Top-3 by frequencyfreq.entrySet().stream().sorted(Map.Entry.<String,Long>comparingByValue().reversed()).limit(3).toList()
Second highest numbernums.stream().distinct().sorted(reverseOrder()).skip(1).findFirst()
Dedupe by property, keep firstemps.stream().collect(toMap(Emp::email, e -> e, (a, b) -> a, LinkedHashMap::new)).values()
Dedupe by property (alt)emps.stream().collect(toCollection(() -> new TreeSet<>(comparing(Emp::email))))
Flatten nested listslists.stream().flatMap(List::stream).toList()
Group then sort each groupgroupingBy(Emp::dept, collectingAndThen(toList(), l -> l.stream().sorted(comparing(Emp::name)).toList()))
First non-repeated chars.chars().mapToObj(c -> (char) c).collect(groupingBy(c -> c, LinkedHashMap::new, counting())).entrySet().stream().filter(e -> e.getValue() == 1).map(Map.Entry::getKey).findFirst()
Count vowelss.toLowerCase().chars().filter(c -> "aeiou".indexOf(c) >= 0).count()
Join sorted namesemps.stream().map(Emp::name).sorted().collect(joining(", "))
Max salary per dept as Map<String,Integer>toMap(Emp::dept, Emp::salary, Integer::max)
Anagram groupswords.stream().collect(groupingBy(w -> { char[] a = w.toCharArray(); Arrays.sort(a); return new String(a); }))
Interview angle: after you write the one-liner they usually ask "and without streams?" or "and for 100 GB of words?". Have the loop version ready, and talk about Files.lines (lazy, needs closing) plus a bounded HashMap/external sort for the big case.

Pitfalls

  • Second highest with sorted().skip(1) without distinct() returns the max when it is duplicated.
  • Map.Entry.comparingByValue().reversed() needs the explicit type witness <String,Long> or inference fails: a classic compile error under pressure.

Likely follow-ups

  • How would you find the top-k without sorting everything? (A min-heap of size k: O(n log k).)
  • Why LinkedHashMap::new? (Default HashMap loses insertion order; the interviewer often expects "first occurrence" semantics.)

CompletableFuture: Composing Async Calls

Why interviewers ask: the "aggregate three microservice calls in parallel with a timeout and fallback" problem is a staple; and "which thread runs thenApply?" separates people who have debugged it in production from people who have read a tutorial.

CompletableFuture<T> is a Future you can complete manually and chain callbacks on. supplyAsync(supplier, executor) starts work; always pass an executor, because the default is the common ForkJoinPool with cores − 1 threads, which is wrong for blocking IO. thenApply(f) maps the value (map); thenCompose(f) chains when f itself returns a future (flatMap, avoids CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>>); thenCombine(other, biFn) joins two independent futures; allOf(...) returns CompletableFuture<Void> that completes when all do (you then join() each), anyOf when the first does.

Threading rule: a non-async callback (thenApply) runs on whichever thread completes the previous stage; if that stage is already complete when you attach the callback, it runs immediately on your thread. thenApplyAsync(f, executor) always re-submits. Errors: an exception thrown in any stage completes the stage exceptionally and skips downstream thenApplys until an exceptionally(fn) (recover), handle((v, ex) -> ...) (recover or transform both paths) or whenComplete (observe, do not change). Inside those, the throwable is usually wrapped in a CompletionException; join() rethrows CompletionException (unchecked) while get() throws checked ExecutionException. orTimeout(d, unit) (9) fails after a delay; completeOnTimeout(value, d, unit) substitutes a default instead.

ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(32);   // sized for blocking calls

CompletableFuture<Stock>  inv   = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> inventory.get(id), io);
CompletableFuture<Price>  price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> pricing.get(id), io)
        .thenCompose(p -> fx.convertAsync(p, currency));          // returns a CF: flatMap
CompletableFuture<List<Review>> reviews = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> reviewSvc.top(id), io)
        .orTimeout(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
        .exceptionally(ex -> List.of());                          // fallback

CompletableFuture<ProductPage> page = inv.thenCombine(price, ProductPage::partial)
        .thenCombine(reviews, ProductPage::withReviews);

ProductPage result = page.join();     // or .get(200, MILLISECONDS) for a checked, bounded wait
MethodInput → outputRuns when
thenApply(f)T → USuccess; completing thread
thenCompose(f)T → CF<U>Success; flattens
thenCombine(cf, f)(T, U) → VBoth succeed
exceptionally(f)Throwable → TFailure only
handle(f)(T, Throwable) → UAlways; can recover
whenComplete(c)(T, Throwable) → voidAlways; passes result through

Pitfalls

  • Calling join() inside a callback that runs on the same small pool can deadlock the pool (all threads waiting on tasks that need a thread).
  • allOf(...).join() then f.join() each: forgetting the second step returns Void; forgetting allOf and joining sequentially still works but hides an exception in a later future until you reach it.
  • Exceptions in supplyAsync are wrapped in CompletionException when observed via exceptionally, but not wrapped when the stage that threw is the one you attached to; code that does ex instanceof TimeoutException must check ex.getCause() too.
  • cancel(true) does not interrupt the running task (unlike FutureTask); it only completes the future with CancellationException.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is a CompletionStage? (The interface with the composition methods; CompletableFuture adds completion and blocking.)
  • How do you complete manually? (complete(v), completeExceptionally(ex); useful to bridge callback APIs.)
  • How does Spring's @Async relate? (It can return CompletableFuture; the executor is the configured TaskExecutor.)

Java 21 preview

Virtual threads make plain blocking code (executor.submit(() -> client.call()) on newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) as scalable as callback chains, and structured concurrency (StructuredTaskScope, preview) gives the same "fan out, join, timeout" shape with readable stack traces. Expect "would you still use CompletableFuture?" as a follow-up.

Functional Design Idioms (and When Not to Stream)

Why interviewers ask: design questions like "replace this strategy hierarchy" or "validate with a chain of rules" are cleanly solved with function composition; the seniors also know when a for loop is the better answer.

Function.andThen(g) is "f then g"; compose(g) is "g then f". Predicate.and/or/negate and the static Predicate.not(p) (11) build rule chains. Currying turns a two-argument function into a function returning a function: Function<Integer, Function<Integer, Integer>> add = a -> b -> a + b;. A strategy becomes a Map<String, Function<Order, Money>> of lambdas instead of a class per case. Comparator.comparing(keyFn).thenComparing(...).reversed(), with nullsFirst/nullsLast, replaces hand-written compareTo.

Predicate<Order> valid = Order::hasItems;
valid = valid.and(o -> o.total().signum() > 0).and(Predicate.not(Order::isCancelled));

Function<String, String> clean = String::strip;
Function<String, String> normalise = clean.andThen(String::toLowerCase);   // strip then lowercase

Map<String, UnaryOperator<BigDecimal>> discounts = Map.of(
    "VIP",  p -> p.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.8")),
    "NONE", UnaryOperator.identity());
BigDecimal price = discounts.getOrDefault(tier, UnaryOperator.identity()).apply(base);

Comparator<Emp> bySalaryDescThenName = Comparator.comparingInt(Emp::salary).reversed()
        .thenComparing(Emp::name, Comparator.nullsLast(Comparator.naturalOrder()));
Prefer a loop whenBecause
The body throws checked exceptionsEvery lambda needs a wrapper; the stream hides the real exception in UncheckedIOException
You need early exit with a value plus a side effectfindFirst + peek tricks are harder to read than break
You will debug it with breakpointsStepping through lambdas and stack traces full of ReferencePipeline$3$1.accept is slow
Index-based logic or two collections in lockstepStreams have no zip; IntStream.range(0, n) workarounds are noise
Mutating shared stateStreams promise side-effect freedom; a loop is honest about it

Pitfalls

  • Comparator.comparing(Emp::salary).reversed() works, but Comparator.comparing(e -> e.salary()).reversed() fails inference: use a method reference or the explicit type.
  • Composing functions that capture heavy objects keeps them alive as long as the composed function lives.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is the difference between andThen on Function and on Consumer? (Consumer's runs both side effects in order; Function's pipes the value.)
  • How do you make a lambda-based strategy testable? (Inject the map/function; each lambda is unit-testable in isolation.)

java.time: Immutable Dates, Zones and DST Pitfalls

Why interviewers ask: "why was SimpleDateFormat a bug in your service?" and "how do you store timestamps?" are practical questions with clear right answers.

Everything in java.time is immutable and thread-safe: plusDays returns a new object. Instant is a point on the UTC timeline (what you store and log); LocalDate/LocalTime/LocalDateTime have no zone (a birthday, a store opening time); ZonedDateTime = local date-time + ZoneId with DST rules; OffsetDateTime = local + fixed offset (what ISO strings and JDBC TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE use). Duration is machine time (seconds/nanos); Period is calendar time (years/months/days), so "plus 1 month" is a Period.

DateTimeFormatter is immutable and safe to share as a static final; SimpleDateFormat keeps mutable state in a Calendar field, so sharing it across threads silently produces wrong dates. Analogy: Instant is the GPS coordinate; ZonedDateTime is the street address, which changes meaning when the city renames streets (DST).

static final DateTimeFormatter F = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm");   // safe to share

Instant now = Instant.now();                                        // store this (UTC)
ZonedDateTime ny = now.atZone(ZoneId.of("America/New_York"));      // display in user zone
ZonedDateTime beforeDst = ZonedDateTime.of(2026, 3, 8, 1, 30, 0, 0, ZoneId.of("America/New_York"));
beforeDst.plusHours(1);        // 03:30 EDT: 02:30 does not exist that night
beforeDst.plusDays(1);         // next day 01:30, a 23-hour "day"

Period p = Period.between(LocalDate.of(2020, 2, 29), LocalDate.of(2026, 2, 28)); // P5Y11M30D
Duration d = Duration.between(now, now.plusSeconds(90));                         // PT1M30S
long epochMs = now.toEpochMilli();
TypeHas zone?Use forDB column
InstantUTCEvents, audit, created_atTIMESTAMP (UTC) / epoch millis
LocalDateNoBirthdays, due datesDATE
LocalDateTimeNoWall-clock in a known local contextTIMESTAMP (ambiguous across zones!)
ZonedDateTimeYes (rules)Scheduling "9am Chicago" recurring eventsStore instant + zone id separately
OffsetDateTimeFixed offsetAPI payloads, JDBC/JPATIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE

Pitfalls

  • Pattern letters: YYYY is week-based year (wrong around New Year), yyyy is the calendar year; MM is month, mm is minutes.
  • LocalDateTime for a future meeting across a DST change gives the wrong instant; keep the zone until the last moment.
  • java.util.Date is mutable and zone-less but prints in the JVM default zone, which is why "it works on my laptop" and not in the UTC container.

Likely follow-ups

  • How do you unit test time-dependent code? (Inject a Clock; Clock.fixed(...) in tests.)
  • Instant.now() resolution? (Microseconds on Linux with Java 15+, milliseconds before.)
  • How do you convert legacy Date? (date.toInstant() / Date.from(instant).)

Java 8 vs 17

Java 8 introduced java.time, lambdas and streams. Since then: Optional.or/ifPresentOrElse/stream, takeWhile/dropWhile, Stream.iterate 3-arg and ofNullable (9); orTimeout/completeOnTimeout (9); Predicate.not (11); Collectors.teeing (12); Stream.toList and mapMulti (16); tzdata updates and the Clock precision improvements. Java 8's flatMap was not lazy for the inner stream (fixed in 10).

What does this print? Stream.of("a","bb","ccc").peek(s -> System.out.print(s + " ")).map(String::length).filter(n -> n > 1).findFirst();

b. Elements flow one at a time: "a" is peeked, mapped to 1, filtered out; "bb" is peeked, mapped to 2, passes, and findFirst short-circuits, so "ccc" is never pulled. a assumes stage-by-stage execution; d only applies when the JDK can skip the traversal entirely (e.g. count() on a sized source).

Why must a local variable captured by a lambda be effectively final?

c. Captured values are copied into the lambda object; the frame's variable does not outlive the method. a is wrong (lambdas use invokedynamic, not inner classes, though inner classes have the same rule for the same reason). d overstates it: captured object references can still be mutated unsafely.

Stream.iterate(1, i -> i + 1).sorted().limit(3).toList() …

a. sorted is a full barrier; it cannot emit anything until upstream is exhausted, which never happens. Moving limit(3) before sorted() fixes it. The JDK does not reorder stages (d), and it does not detect the pre-sorted property of an iterate source (b).

list.stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(Emp::dept, Emp::name)) with two employees in ENG:

d. Without a merge function toMap refuses duplicates. Pass (a, b) -> a for b, (a, b) -> b for a, or use groupingBy(Emp::dept, mapping(Emp::name, toList())) for c.

Which is the production-correct way to fetch a default from the database only when the value is missing?

b. orElse's argument is evaluated eagerly, so a hits the DB every time. c is correct but is the anti-pattern the API exists to remove. d does not compile unless loadDefault returns an Optional.

A service does ids.parallelStream().map(httpClient::fetch).toList() for 200 ids. Under concurrent requests the whole JVM slows down. Why?

c. The common pool is JVM-wide and tiny; IO-bound tasks should go to a dedicated executor (or virtual threads). a is not how ForkJoin works; ArrayList (d) splits in O(1).

Which thread runs f in cf.thenApply(f) when cf is already completed at the moment thenApply is called?

a. Non-async dependents run on the completing thread if the stage is still pending, otherwise synchronously on the thread attaching them. c is the pending case; b requires thenApplyAsync.

reduce(new ArrayList<>(), (list, e) -> { list.add(e); return list; }, (a, b) -> { a.addAll(b); return a; }) on a parallel stream is wrong because…

d. Each chunk starts from the same list object, so parallel accumulators race. collect(ArrayList::new, List::add, List::addAll) creates a fresh container per chunk. b is wrong: the 3-arg reduce allows a different result type.

What is the key difference between thenCompose and thenApply?

b. It is flatMap for futures. Combining two independent futures (c) is thenCombine. Threading (a) is identical for the non-async variants.

A shared static SimpleDateFormat occasionally produces dates from the wrong year under load. The fix that best matches Java 17 practice is…

c. DateTimeFormatter is thread-safe by design; the others work but keep the legacy API (a serialises all callers, b leaks in thread pools if not removed, d allocates needlessly).

Practice

Predict the output: laziness, short-circuit and peek

List<String> names = List.of("Ann", "Bob", "Cid", "Dee", "Eve");
Stream<String> s = names.stream()
    .peek(n -> System.out.print("P:" + n + " "))
    .filter(n -> n.length() == 3)
    .map(n -> { System.out.print("M:" + n + " "); return n.toUpperCase(); })
    .limit(2);
System.out.print("| ");
List<String> out = s.toList();
System.out.print("| " + out + " ");
System.out.println(s.count());
Tests: laziness, per-element flow, short-circuiting, single-use streams
Hint 1
Nothing before toList() prints anything, so the first thing on the line is | .
Hint 2
Every name has 3 letters, so the filter never drops anything; how many elements does limit(2) need to pull?
Reveal solution

Output: | P:Ann M:Ann P:Bob M:Bob | [ANN, BOB] followed by IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed thrown by s.count().

The pipeline is built lazily, so | prints first. toList() pulls Ann through peek → filter → map → limit, then Bob; after the second element limit signals completion and Cid, Dee, Eve are never read (no P:Cid). The result is printed, then calling a second terminal operation on the same Stream object throws. Follow-up they will ask: replace filter with sorted() and all five P: lines appear before any M:.

Write the stream: top-paid per department, and top-3 word frequency

Given record Emp(String name, String dept, int salary) and a List<Emp>: (a) produce Map<String, Emp> of the highest-paid employee per department; (b) also produce Map<String, Double> of average salary per department, sorted by department name. Then (c) given a String text, return the 3 most frequent words (case-insensitive, ties broken alphabetically) as List<String>.

Tests: groupingBy with downstream collectors, maxBy, collectingAndThen, TreeMap factory, sorting map entries
Hint 1
maxBy yields an Optional; wrap it in collectingAndThen(..., Optional::get). Alternatively toMap(Emp::dept, e -> e, BinaryOperator.maxBy(comparingInt(Emp::salary))).
Hint 2
For the frequency map use groupingBy(w -> w, counting()), then stream the entrySet() with a comparator on value descending, then key ascending.
Reveal solution
// (a) top-paid per department
Map<String, Emp> top = emps.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Emp::dept,
    Collectors.collectingAndThen(
        Collectors.maxBy(Comparator.comparingInt(Emp::salary)), Optional::get)));

// (a, alternative) toMap with a max merge: no Optional to unwrap
Map<String, Emp> top2 = emps.stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(Emp::dept, e -> e,
    BinaryOperator.maxBy(Comparator.comparingInt(Emp::salary))));

// (b) average per department, sorted by department
Map<String, Double> avg = emps.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Emp::dept,
    TreeMap::new, Collectors.averagingInt(Emp::salary)));

// (c) top-3 words
List<String> top3 = Arrays.stream(text.toLowerCase().split("\\W+"))
    .filter(w -> !w.isBlank())
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(w -> w, Collectors.counting()))
    .entrySet().stream()
    .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed()
            .thenComparing(Map.Entry.comparingByKey()))
    .limit(3)
    .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
    .toList();

Reasoning: groupingBy creates one downstream container per key; maxBy keeps a running max, so it is O(n) with no sorting. The TreeMap::new factory gives ordered keys without a separate sort. For the word count, sorting the entry set is O(k log k) in the number of distinct words; for very large inputs mention a size-3 min-heap instead. The explicit <String, Long> witness is needed because reversed() breaks inference.

Fix the bug: parallel stream with a shared ArrayList

List<Integer> evens = new ArrayList<>();
int[] counter = {0};
IntStream.range(0, 100_000).parallel()
    .filter(i -> i % 2 == 0)
    .forEach(i -> { evens.add(i); counter[0]++; });
System.out.println(evens.size() + " " + counter[0]);   // expected 50000 50000

In production this prints values like 49871 49903, sometimes throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, and the list order is random. Explain and fix it properly.

Tests: side effects in parallel pipelines, non-thread-safe collections, stateful lambdas, correct use of collectors
Hint 1
ArrayList.add is a read-modify-write of size and the backing array; several ForkJoin workers call it concurrently.
Hint 2
Wrapping the list in Collections.synchronizedList makes it correct but serialises every add and still leaves the ordering random. The stream API has a construct designed for exactly this.
Reveal solution

Diagnosis: the lambda passed to forEach has side effects on shared mutable state. ArrayList is not thread-safe: two workers can read the same size, write the same slot (lost update → fewer than 50 000) or race the grow-array logic (→ ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException). counter[0]++ is a non-atomic increment. forEach on a parallel stream also makes no ordering promise.

// Correct: let the collector own the mutable state; one container per chunk, merged at the end
List<Integer> evens = IntStream.range(0, 100_000).parallel()
    .filter(i -> i % 2 == 0)
    .boxed()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());          // encounter order preserved: 0, 2, 4, ...
long count = evens.size();                  // or IntStream...filter().count() directly

// If you truly need a side-effecting sink: forEachOrdered + a thread-safe target,
// but at that point a sequential stream is almost always faster.

Why this is the right fix: collect uses a supplier to create a fresh ArrayList per leaf task, accumulates without contention, and merges with addAll in the combiner; the result keeps encounter order. Using AtomicInteger plus synchronizedList would be correct but contended, defeating the purpose of parallelism. Also point out that for 100k cheap integers the parallel version probably loses to a plain sequential stream: the fork/join and merge overhead exceeds the work.

CompletableFuture: three services in parallel with timeout and fallback

Implement ProductPage load(String id) that calls inventory.stock(id), pricing.price(id) and reviews.top(id) (all blocking clients, ~50–200 ms each). Requirements: run them in parallel; the whole call must return within 300 ms; if reviews fail or time out, use an empty list; if inventory or pricing fail, propagate a ServiceException (unwrapped, not CompletionException); do not use the common ForkJoin pool.

Tests: supplyAsync with executor, thenCombine, orTimeout, exceptionally, exception unwrapping, bounded get
Hint 1
Per-branch policy goes on the branch (reviews.orTimeout(...).exceptionally(...)); the overall budget goes on the combined future (get(300, MILLISECONDS) or orTimeout).
Hint 2
join() throws CompletionException; get() throws ExecutionException. Either way the real cause is getCause().
Reveal solution
private final ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(64,
        r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "io-"); t.setDaemon(true); return t; });

public ProductPage load(String id) {
    var stock = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> inventory.stock(id), io);
    var price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> pricing.price(id), io);
    var revs  = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> reviews.top(id), io)
            .orTimeout(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
            .exceptionally(ex -> { log.warn("reviews degraded: {}", ex.toString()); return List.<Review>of(); });

    CompletableFuture<ProductPage> page = stock
            .thenCombine(price, (s, p) -> new ProductPage(id, s, p, List.of()))
            .thenCombine(revs, ProductPage::withReviews);
    try {
