        return page.get(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    } catch (TimeoutException e) {
        page.cancel(true);                                     // stop dependents; clients keep running
        throw new ServiceException("product page timed out", e);
    } catch (ExecutionException e) {
        Throwable cause = e.getCause();
        if (cause instanceof CompletionException ce && ce.getCause() != null) cause = ce.getCause();
        throw cause instanceof ServiceException se ? se : new ServiceException("upstream failed", cause);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        throw new ServiceException("interrupted", e);
    }
}

Reasoning: an explicit, generously sized executor keeps blocking calls off the common pool. thenCombine expresses "wait for both" without allOf + manual joins. Only the reviews branch has a fallback, so failures in stock/price propagate through the chain and surface once in get. The bounded get gives the end-to-end budget; the per-branch orTimeout is tighter so a slow reviews call degrades rather than fails the page. Cancelling the future does not interrupt the HTTP call: mention per-request client timeouts as the real safety net. Interviewers often follow up with "how would this look with virtual threads?": three Futures from newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() and plain get calls, same shape, simpler stack traces.

7️⃣ Concurrency & the Java Memory Model

Concurrency is where senior Java interviews are decided: not "do you know synchronized" but "can you explain why a field read in a loop never sees an update, what a thread pool does when its queue is full, and which lock ConcurrentHashMap actually takes". The path here goes from threads and the memory model, through locks, atomics and the classic failure modes, to the executor and java.util.concurrent tools you use daily, and ends with virtual threads.

Thread Lifecycle & States

Why interviewers ask: reading a thread dump is a real on-call skill; "what is the difference between BLOCKED and WAITING?" separates people who have debugged a hang from those who have not.

A Thread is in exactly one Thread.State: NEW (created, start() not called), RUNNABLE (eligible to run or running; the JVM does not distinguish "ready" from "on a CPU"), BLOCKED (waiting to enter a synchronized block owned by another thread), WAITING (parked indefinitely: Object.wait(), Thread.join(), LockSupport.park()), TIMED_WAITING (same with a timeout: sleep(ms), wait(ms), tryLock(t)) and TERMINATED. A thread never returns to NEW; calling start() twice throws IllegalThreadStateException.

Interruption is cooperative: t.interrupt() sets a flag; blocking methods (sleep, wait, join, BlockingQueue.take) notice it, clear the flag and throw InterruptedException. Plain running code must poll Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted(). Analogy: interruption is a tap on the shoulder, not a trapdoor; the thread decides what to do about it. Daemon threads do not keep the JVM alive; a pool of non-daemon threads that is never shut down keeps your app running after main returns.

StateEntered byLeaves whenThread dump shows
BLOCKEDContending for a monitor (synchronized)Monitor is released and this thread wins it- waiting to lock <0x…>
WAITINGwait(), join(), park(), lock.lock()notify/unpark/target ends- parking to wait for …
TIMED_WAITINGsleep, wait(ms), tryLock(t), awaitTerminationTimeout or wake-upTIMED_WAITING (sleeping)
Thread t = new Thread(() -> {
    while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {   // cooperative check
        try { doUnitOfWork(); Thread.sleep(100); }
        catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // restore the flag, then exit
            return;
        }
    }
});
t.setDaemon(false);        // keeps the JVM alive until it finishes
t.start();                 // NEW → RUNNABLE
t.interrupt();             // sets flag; sleep() throws InterruptedException
t.join();                  // caller WAITING until t is TERMINATED
Interview angle: "Why is swallowing InterruptedException a bug?" Because the flag is cleared when it is thrown; if you catch and continue, the pool or caller that asked you to stop never finds out. Either rethrow or re-set the flag. "Why is Thread.stop() deprecated?" It releases every monitor mid-operation, leaving shared state half-updated.

Pitfalls

  • Thread.sleep(0) and Thread.yield() are scheduler hints, not synchronization; they never make writes visible.
  • Lock-based ReentrantLock.lock() shows as WAITING (parked), not BLOCKED; grep for both in dumps.
  • A thread whose run() throws dies silently unless an UncaughtExceptionHandler is set; in pools the exception is captured by the Future and never printed.

Likely follow-ups

  • What does run() without start() do? (Executes on the calling thread, no new thread.)
  • Priority? (setPriority is a hint most OSes ignore; do not design around it.)
  • How do you get a thread dump? (jstack <pid>, jcmd <pid> Thread.print, or kill -3.)

Runnable vs Thread vs Callable/Future

Why interviewers ask: a warm-up that reveals whether you think in "tasks submitted to executors" (good) or "threads I create by hand" (2005).

Runnable is a task: void run(), no result, no checked exceptions. Thread is the worker that executes a task; extending it couples your logic to one specific thread and blocks you from extending anything else. Callable<V> is a task that returns V and may throw a checked exception; you get its result through a Future<V>, whose get() blocks (WAITING) until done and rethrows the task's exception wrapped in ExecutionException.

Analogy: Runnable is a to-do note, Callable is a to-do note with a return envelope, Thread is the person, ExecutorService is the team you hand notes to. An executor wraps every submitted task in a FutureTask, which is both a Runnable (the worker runs it) and a Future (you wait on it).

ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);

Future<Integer> f = pool.submit(() -> {          // Callable<Integer>
    if (Math.random() < 0.1) throw new IOException("flaky");
    return 42;
});
try {
    Integer v = f.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);        // blocks up to 2s
} catch (ExecutionException e) {
    Throwable real = e.getCause();                 // the IOException
} catch (TimeoutException e) {
    f.cancel(true);   // interrupt the worker if it is still running
}
pool.submit(() -> System.out.println("fire-and-forget")); // Runnable → Future<?> of null
pool.shutdown();                                  // no new tasks; finish queued ones
RunnableCallable<V>
Methodvoid run()V call() throws Exception
ResultNone (side effects only)Value via Future.get()
Checked exceptionsNot allowedAllowed; surface as ExecutionException
Submit withexecute(r) or submit(r)submit(c), invokeAll, invokeAny

Pitfalls

  • execute(runnable) lets an exception reach the thread's uncaught handler (printed, thread replaced); submit(runnable) silently stores it in the Future nobody calls get() on. Log inside the task.
  • cancel(true) only interrupts; a task that ignores interruption keeps running.
  • Future.get() without a timeout on a request thread is how you turn one slow dependency into a full thread-pool exhaustion.

Likely follow-ups

  • Difference between shutdown() and shutdownNow()? (Graceful vs interrupt workers and return the unstarted queue.)
  • Why prefer implementing Runnable over extending Thread? (Separation of task and execution; one task can run on any executor; you keep inheritance free.)

The Java Memory Model: Happens-Before, Visibility, Reordering, volatile

Why interviewers ask: every other concurrency answer stands on this. "Does this loop ever terminate?" and "why is volatile not enough for count++?" are the two most common senior-round probes.

Each core has its own caches and store buffers, and the JIT reorders and hoists instructions freely as long as the single-threaded result is unchanged. So without synchronization there is no guarantee that a write by thread A is ever seen by thread B, nor that B sees A's writes in the order A made them. The JMM (JLS §17) defines exactly when visibility is guaranteed through the happens-before (HB) relation: if action X happens-before Y, then X's effects are visible to Y.

HB edges you can rely on: program order within one thread; monitor unlock → subsequent lock of the same monitor; volatile write → subsequent volatile read of the same field; Thread.start() → everything in the started thread; everything in a thread → join() returning; executor submit → task start; Future.get() returning after task completion; and it is transitive. A conflicting access with no HB edge between them is a data race, and racy reads may return stale values indefinitely.

volatile gives two things: every read goes to the coherent value (no register/cached copy), and piggybacking: all writes made before a volatile write become visible to a thread after it reads that volatile (the write acts as a release, the read as an acquire fence). It does not give atomicity for compound actions like i++ (read-modify-write). One bonus it does give: non-volatile long/double writes may tear into two 32-bit halves on 32-bit JVMs; volatile guarantees a single atomic 64-bit write. Analogy: volatile is a shared whiteboard everyone reads directly; a normal field is a sticky note each person may have copied to their desk yesterday.

class Publisher {
    private int data;                 // plain
    private volatile boolean ready;   // publish through this

    void producer() { data = 42; ready = true; }          // write data, then release
    void consumer() {
        while (!ready) { Thread.onSpinWait(); }           // acquire
        System.out.println(data);                         // guaranteed 42
    }
}
// NOT safe: volatile int count; count++;  → read, add, write = 3 steps; lost updates
// Safe alternatives: AtomicInteger, LongAdder, synchronized, or a lock
Interview angle: "Is volatile slower?" A volatile read on x86 is essentially free (loads are already acquire); a volatile write costs a full fence (lock addl / mfence), roughly tens of nanoseconds, plus it forbids surrounding reorderings. "Where is a data race acceptable?" Benign races on immutable-once values, e.g. String.hash caching: any thread computes the same value, so a stale read is only a wasted recomputation.

Pitfalls

  • volatile on a reference makes the reference visible, not the object's internals: volatile List<X> list; list.add(x) is still a race.
  • Reordering is real on ARM (Graviton, Apple Silicon); code that "worked" for years on x86 laptops fails in production on weaker memory models.
  • final fields have their own guarantee: a correctly constructed object's final fields are visible to any thread that sees the reference, even without synchronization. Non-final fields are not.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is a memory barrier? (A CPU instruction preventing reordering of loads/stores across it; volatile and monitors compile down to them.)
  • Does synchronized also give visibility? (Yes: unlock → lock is an HB edge, so all writes inside the block are visible to the next holder.)
  • What is safe publication? (Making an object visible to other threads only via volatile, final, a lock, a concurrent collection, or thread start.)

Java 9+

VarHandle exposes finer modes: getOpaque/setOpaque, getAcquire/setRelease, and full volatile. Library code (e.g. ConcurrentHashMap) now uses these instead of Unsafe.

synchronized, Intrinsic Locks & wait/notify

Why interviewers ask: "why must wait() be in a loop?", "what does synchronized on a static method lock?", and "how does the JVM implement it?" are asked in nearly every Java round.

Every object has a monitor: an owner, a recursion count, an entry set (threads BLOCKED trying to get in) and a wait set (threads that called wait()). synchronized(obj) acquires the monitor of obj; a synchronized instance method locks this; a synchronized static method locks the Class object, so instance and static synchronized methods do not exclude each other. Monitors are reentrant: the owner can re-enter (count++), which is why a synchronized method can call another one on the same object.

wait() atomically releases the monitor and parks the thread in the wait set; it must be called while holding the monitor or you get IllegalMonitorStateException. notify() moves one arbitrary waiter to the entry set; notifyAll() moves all. A woken thread must re-acquire the monitor before wait() returns, and by then the condition may be false again (another thread consumed the item) or the wake may be spurious. Therefore: always wait() in a while loop. Analogy: a meeting room with one key. wait() is stepping out and hanging the key back; notify() is shouting "room's free" into the hallway, but you still have to grab the key before you re-enter.

Implementation (HotSpot): the lock state lives in the object header's mark word. An uncontended lock is a thin/lightweight lock (a CAS to point the mark word at a lock record on the thread's stack). Under contention it inflates to a heavyweight ObjectMonitor with OS-level parking. Biased locking (skipping the CAS for a single-thread owner) was disabled by default in Java 15 and removed in 18.

class Mailbox {
    private final Queue<String> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final int capacity = 10;

    public synchronized void put(String s) throws InterruptedException {
        while (q.size() == capacity) wait();     // loop, never if
        q.add(s);
        notifyAll();            // wake consumers (and producers; they re-check)
    }
    public synchronized String take() throws InterruptedException {
        while (q.isEmpty()) wait();
        String s = q.poll();
        notifyAll();
        return s;
    }
}
Interview angle: "notify or notifyAll?" With one condition and identical waiters notify is fine; with mixed waiters (producers and consumers on one monitor) notify can wake a producer when a consumer was needed, and everyone hangs. Default to notifyAll or, better, use Condition objects with a ReentrantLock, one per condition. "What is lost wake-up?" A notify issued before the other thread calls wait is not remembered; the while re-check under the lock is what prevents it.

Pitfalls

  • Synchronizing on a String literal, boxed Integer, or Boolean: these are interned/cached, so unrelated code shares your lock. Lock on a private final Object.
  • synchronized(this) in a public class lets callers lock you out; prefer a private lock object.
  • Holding a monitor while doing I/O or calling unknown code (listeners) invites deadlock and starves other threads.
  • Changing the lock object (synchronized(list) then list = new ArrayList()) means different threads lock different objects.

Likely follow-ups

  • Is synchronized fair? (No; the JVM may let a barging thread win over waiting ones.)
  • Can a thread be interrupted while BLOCKED on a monitor? (No; only wait/sleep/park respond. ReentrantLock.lockInterruptibly() fixes that.)
  • What does the bytecode look like? (monitorenter/monitorexit with an implicit exception-handler exit; synchronized methods use the ACC_SYNCHRONIZED flag instead.)

Race Conditions, Atomicity & CAS: AtomicInteger, ABA, LongAdder

Why interviewers ask: "implement a thread-safe counter without locks" then "what is ABA?" is a standard escalation; it tests whether you understand what the hardware actually gives you.

A race condition is when correctness depends on the relative timing of threads. The two classic shapes are read-modify-write (count++ = load, add, store; two threads interleave and one update is lost) and check-then-act (if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v); both threads pass the check). Neither is fixed by volatile, because the problem is atomicity, not visibility.

Compare-and-swap (CAS) is a single CPU instruction (lock cmpxchg on x86, LL/SC on ARM): "if the memory location still holds expected, write newValue and tell me it worked". AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() is a loop: read current, compute +1, CAS; on failure (someone else won), retry. No thread ever blocks, so no deadlock and no context switch: this is lock-free. Under heavy contention many retries burn CPU, which is why LongAdder splits the count into per-thread cells and sums on sum(): use it for metrics counters, AtomicLong when you need the exact value after every update.

The ABA problem: CAS only compares values. If the value went A → B → A while you were computing, your CAS succeeds even though the world changed underneath, which breaks lock-free stacks and pools that reuse nodes. Fix: AtomicStampedReference (value + version stamp) or AtomicMarkableReference. Analogy: CAS is checking that the parking spot still has the same car before you tow it; ABA is the car leaving and an identical one parking there.

// What AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet does (conceptually)
int incrementAndGet() {
    while (true) {
        int cur = get();                         // volatile read
        if (compareAndSet(cur, cur + 1)) return cur + 1;   // one CPU instruction
    }                                            // else: lost the race, retry
}

AtomicInteger hits = new AtomicInteger();
hits.incrementAndGet();
hits.updateAndGet(x -> Math.max(x, 10));        // any pure function, retried on conflict
hits.accumulateAndGet(5, Integer::sum);

LongAdder metrics = new LongAdder();             // striped: cheap increments
metrics.increment();  long snapshot = metrics.sum();

AtomicStampedReference<Node> top = new AtomicStampedReference<>(null, 0);
int[] stamp = new int[1];
Node old = top.get(stamp);
top.compareAndSet(old, newNode, stamp[0], stamp[0] + 1);   // fails if version moved
Interview angle: "When do you pick a lock over CAS?" When the critical section is more than one variable, when it does I/O, or when contention is so high that spinning wastes cores. "Is compareAndSet volatile?" Yes: it has full volatile read/write semantics, so it also publishes prior writes.

Pitfalls

  • Two atomics do not make a compound action atomic: if (a.get() > 0) b.increment() is still check-then-act.
  • LongAdder.sum() is not a snapshot under concurrent updates; do not use it for "exactly once" logic.
  • AtomicReference<List> makes the pointer swap atomic, not the list's contents: pair it with immutable values (copy-on-write).

Likely follow-ups

  • Lock-free vs wait-free? (Lock-free: some thread always makes progress; wait-free: every thread finishes in bounded steps. CAS loops are lock-free.)
  • How does ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent avoid check-then-act? (It locks the bin and runs the function once; see the CHM card.)
  • Where is the atomic field updater useful? (AtomicIntegerFieldUpdater avoids one object per counter in hot classes, e.g. Netty's ref counts.)

ReentrantLock, ReadWriteLock, StampedLock: Fairness & tryLock

Why interviewers ask: "when would you use ReentrantLock instead of synchronized?" has a precise answer, and StampedLock's optimistic read is a favourite "have you read the docs" probe.

ReentrantLock is the explicit-lock version of a monitor with extras: tryLock() (never blocks) and tryLock(timeout), lockInterruptibly(), an optional fair mode (FIFO hand-off; slower, but no starvation), multiple Conditions per lock (notEmpty, notFull) and lock acquisition in one method with release in another. The price: you must unlock() in a finally, and forgetting it is a permanent hang. Both are built on AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS): a volatile state int plus a CLH queue of parked waiters.

ReentrantReadWriteLock lets many readers in concurrently but a writer needs exclusivity. It pays off only when reads vastly outnumber writes and hold the lock for a while; the reader-count bookkeeping makes it slower than a plain lock for short critical sections, and writers can starve under a stream of readers in non-fair mode. StampedLock (Java 8) adds optimistic reading: tryOptimisticRead() returns a stamp without locking; you read your fields, then validate(stamp) tells you whether a writer intervened. No CAS on the read path at all. It is not reentrant and has no Condition. Analogy: optimistic read is glancing at a scoreboard and checking the "last updated" clock after; if the clock moved, look again.

class Point {
    private final StampedLock sl = new StampedLock();
    private double x, y;

    double distanceFromOrigin() {
        long stamp = sl.tryOptimisticRead();          // no lock, just a version
        double cx = x, cy = y;                          // read into locals first
        if (!sl.validate(stamp)) {                      // a writer got in?
            stamp = sl.readLock();
            try { cx = x; cy = y; } finally { sl.unlockRead(stamp); }
        }
        return Math.hypot(cx, cy);
    }
    void move(double dx, double dy) {
        long stamp = sl.writeLock();
        try { x += dx; y += dy; } finally { sl.unlockWrite(stamp); }
    }
}

ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(true);   // fair
if (lock.tryLock(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
    try { /* critical section */ } finally { lock.unlock(); }
} else { /* back off, log, or fail fast: no deadlock possible */ }
synchronizedReentrantLockReentrantReadWriteLockStampedLock
ReentrantYesYesYesNo
Try / timeoutNoYesYesYes
Interruptible waitNolockInterruptiblyYesYes
Fairness optionNoYesYesNo
ConditionsOne (wait set)ManyWrite lock onlyNone
Best forShort sections, defaultTimeouts, multiple conditionsRead-heavy, long readsRead-mostly tiny state, max throughput
Interview angle: "Is ReentrantLock faster than synchronized?" Not any more; since Java 6 monitor performance is comparable and synchronized gets JIT lock elision and coarsening. Choose ReentrantLock for features, not speed. Also note synchronized pins virtual threads before Java 24 while ReentrantLock does not (see virtual threads card).

Pitfalls

  • Calling lock() inside the try: if it throws, finally unlocks a lock you never held (IllegalMonitorStateException). Lock before try.
  • Upgrading a read lock to a write lock with ReentrantReadWriteLock deadlocks (writer waits for readers, including itself). Release then acquire, or use StampedLock.tryConvertToWriteLock.
  • Optimistic reads must copy fields to locals before validate and must never dereference partially-read state (you may be reading torn data).

Likely follow-ups

  • What does fair mode cost? (Every acquire goes through the queue; throughput drops noticeably; use only when starvation is observed.)
  • How does Condition.await() differ from wait()? (Same semantics, but per-condition wait sets and it works with the explicit lock; still loop.)

Deadlock, Livelock & Starvation: Detection and Prevention

Why interviewers ask: "we had a service freeze at 3am; how do you find out why and prevent it?" is the scenario question. They want the four conditions, the lock-ordering fix, and the jstack output you would look for.

Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and a circular wait. Java monitors give you the first three for free, so deadlocks are always about the fourth: T1 holds A and wants B while T2 holds B and wants A. Prevention is therefore about breaking the cycle: acquire locks in a global order (sort by System.identityHashCode or a business key such as account id), use tryLock with timeout and back off, hold one lock at a time (open calls: never invoke unknown code while holding a lock), or restructure so only one thread owns the state.

Detection: jstack prints "Found one Java-level deadlock" with the cycle for monitors and ReentrantLocks; programmatically ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads(). Recovery is impossible without killing threads, which is why prevention matters. Livelock is the polite version: threads keep responding to each other (both back off, both retry, both collide again) and none progresses; fix with randomised backoff. Starvation is one thread never getting CPU or a lock because others keep winning (unfair locks, a writer under constant readers, priority abuse); fix with fair locks or bounded queues. Analogy: deadlock is two cars nose to nose on a one-lane bridge; livelock is two people in a corridor both stepping the same way forever; starvation is always losing the coin toss.

void transfer(Account from, Account to, long amount) {
    Account first  = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to;   // global lock order
    Account second = from.id() < to.id() ? to   : from;
    synchronized (first) {
        synchronized (second) {
            from.debit(amount); to.credit(amount);
        }
    }
}
// Alternative with timeouts (ReentrantLock in Account):
boolean transferWithTimeout(Account from, Account to, long amt) throws InterruptedException {
    for (int attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt++) {
        if (from.lock.tryLock(50, MILLISECONDS)) {
            try {
                if (to.lock.tryLock(50, MILLISECONDS)) {
                    try { from.debit(amt); to.credit(amt); return true; }
                    finally { to.lock.unlock(); }
                }
            } finally { from.lock.unlock(); }
        }
        Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(5, 20));   // jitter vs livelock
    }
    return false;
}
Interview angle: "What does the deadlocked thread dump look like?" Two threads in BLOCKED, each with - locked <0x1> and - waiting to lock <0x2> in mirrored order, then a "Found one Java-level deadlock" summary. "Can a single thread deadlock?" With reentrant locks no; with a non-reentrant StampedLock or by calling Future.get() on a task queued in the same single-thread pool, yes (see the practice problem).

Pitfalls

  • Lock ordering by hashCode can collide; use a unique id or fall back to a global tie-breaker lock when hashes are equal.
  • Hidden lock acquisition: a synchronized method that calls a listener that calls back into another synchronized object. Open calls only.
  • Database row locks deadlock the same way (two transactions updating rows in opposite order); the fix is identical: order the updates.

Likely follow-ups

  • How does the JVM detect deadlock but not fix it? (It walks the monitor owner graph on request; breaking it would require killing a thread mid-critical-section.)
  • Livelock example in Java? (Two threads each releasing and retrying tryLock in lock-step; add random backoff.)
  • Starvation in a thread pool? (Long tasks hogging all workers; use separate pools per workload, or bulkheads.)

ExecutorService & Thread Pool Internals: Core, Max, Queue, Rejection, Sizing

Why interviewers ask: "why did our pool never grow beyond 8 threads even though max was 100?" is a real production bug that catches most candidates; pool sizing is the follow-up.

ThreadPoolExecutor decides what to do with a submitted task in a fixed order: (1) fewer than corePoolSize threads alive → start a new thread even if others are idle; (2) otherwise offer to the workQueue; (3) only if the queue refuses (bounded and full) and fewer than maximumPoolSize threads → start a non-core thread; (4) otherwise invoke the RejectedExecutionHandler. Non-core threads die after keepAliveTime idle. The consequence: with an unbounded queue (LinkedBlockingQueue default) step 3 never happens and maximumPoolSize is meaningless. That is exactly what Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) builds, and newCachedThreadPool is the opposite (SynchronousQueue, core 0, max Integer.MAX_VALUE: unlimited threads under load).

Rejection policies: AbortPolicy (default, throws RejectedExecutionException), CallerRunsPolicy (the submitting thread runs the task: natural backpressure), DiscardPolicy, DiscardOldestPolicy. Sizing: for CPU-bound work, cores (or cores + 1); for blocking work, cores × (1 + wait/compute), e.g. 8 cores, tasks that wait 90 ms per 10 ms of CPU → 8 × 10 = 80 threads. Or by Little's law: threads = target throughput × mean latency. Analogy: core threads are full-time staff, the queue is the waiting room, max threads are temps you only call when the waiting room is full, and the rejection policy is what the receptionist says when even the temps are busy.

ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
        8, 32,                                   // core, max
        60, TimeUnit.SECONDS,                    // keepAlive for non-core
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(500),           // bounded, so max matters
        new ThreadFactoryBuilder().setNameFormat("order-svc-%d").build(),
        new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
pool.allowCoreThreadTimeOut(false);

// Graceful shutdown idiom
pool.shutdown();
if (!pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
    List<Runnable> dropped = pool.shutdownNow();   // interrupts workers
}
// Executors factory cheat sheet:
// newFixedThreadPool(n)     core=max=n, LinkedBlockingQueue (unbounded)  → OOM risk in queue
// newCachedThreadPool()     core=0, max=MAX_VALUE, SynchronousQueue      → thread explosion
// newSingleThreadExecutor() core=max=1, unbounded queue, serial order
// newScheduledThreadPool(n) DelayedWorkQueue; fixed core, effectively unbounded
// newWorkStealingPool()     ForkJoinPool with parallelism = cores
Interview angle: "Which Executors factory would you use in production?" None: build ThreadPoolExecutor yourself with a bounded queue, a naming ThreadFactory, and an explicit rejection policy (Alibaba's Java guidelines forbid the factories for this reason). "How do you observe a pool?" Expose getActiveCount(), getQueue().size(), getCompletedTaskCount() as metrics; Spring's ThreadPoolTaskExecutor wraps the same class.

Pitfalls

  • A worker that throws in execute() dies and is replaced (thread name counter increments: a clue in logs). In submit() the exception is swallowed into the Future.
  • In ScheduledExecutorService, one exception silently cancels all future runs of that periodic task. Wrap the body in try/catch.
  • prestartAllCoreThreads() if cold-start latency matters; otherwise threads are created lazily on demand.
  • Nested submissions to the same bounded pool (task waits on subtask) deadlock once workers are all waiting: see the practice problem.

Likely follow-ups

  • Difference between execute and submit? (Return type and exception handling; submit wraps in FutureTask.)
  • Why is SynchronousQueue "size 0"? (Each offer succeeds only if a consumer is already waiting; it hands off, it does not store.)
  • What is ctl inside ThreadPoolExecutor? (One AtomicInteger packing run state in 3 high bits and worker count in 29 bits, updated by CAS.)

CompletableFuture: Composition, Async Variants & Exception Handling

Why interviewers ask: fan-out/fan-in ("call three services, combine, with a timeout") is the standard microservice question, and thenApply vs thenCompose vs thenApplyAsync is the follow-up that reveals whether you know which thread runs your callback.

A CompletableFuture<T> is a Future you can complete manually and, more importantly, chain without blocking. thenApply(fn) maps the value (like Stream.map); thenCompose(fn) takes a function returning another CompletableFuture and flattens it (like flatMap): use it when the next step is itself async, or you end up with CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<X>>. thenCombine(other, biFn) joins two independent futures; allOf/anyOf fan in many (note allOf returns CompletableFuture<Void>; collect results with join() afterwards).

Which thread? supplyAsync(s) without an executor uses ForkJoinPool.commonPool(). A non-async continuation (thenApply) runs on whichever thread completes the previous stage, or on the caller thread if the stage was already complete. thenApplyAsync(fn, executor) always hops to the given pool. Exceptions propagate down the chain, skipping stages, until an exceptionally(fn) (recover with a value), handle((v, ex) → …) (always runs, can transform either path) or whenComplete (side-effect only, rethrows). The exception you see is usually wrapped in CompletionException. Analogy: a CompletableFuture is a promise slip with a "when this arrives, do X" list stapled to it; thenCompose is when X itself hands back another slip.

ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16);

CompletableFuture<User> user =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> userClient.get(id), io);       // stage A
CompletableFuture<List<Order>> orders =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> orderClient.byUser(id), io);   // stage B

CompletableFuture<Profile> profile = user
    .thenCombine(orders, Profile::new)                                  // stage C
    .thenCompose(p -> enrichAsync(p, io))                               // stage D (async→flatten)
    .exceptionally(ex -> Profile.fallback(id))                          // stage E
    .orTimeout(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);                             // Java 9

Profile result = profile.join();                                        // unchecked
  1. Both supplyAsync calls submit immediately; nothing blocks. Passing io keeps the common pool free for CPU work.
  2. thenCombine does not run yet. A finished first; C waits for B. Whichever completes last will execute the Profile::new lambda on its own thread.
  3. B completes on io-2, so C runs on io-2. With thenCombineAsync(..., executor) it would hop instead.
  4. enrichAsync returns its own future; thenCompose adopts it as stage D. With thenApply here you would get a nested future and join() twice.
  5. Suppose D throws. Stages between the failure and the first exceptionally/handle are skipped; E receives the exception and returns a fallback, turning the chain back into a normal completion.
  6. orTimeout arms a single shared scheduler thread. If the deadline hits first, downstream sees TimeoutException, but the HTTP call in D keeps running unless you cancel it yourself.
  7. join() (unchecked) or get() (checked ExecutionException) collects the result. In a reactive/servlet-async stack you would return the future instead of joining.
MethodInputReturnsUse when
thenApplyT → UCF<U>Synchronous transform
thenComposeT → CF<U>CF<U>Next step is async (flatMap)
thenCombineCF<V>, (T,V) → UCF<U>Two independent results
thenAccept / thenRunT → void / RunnableCF<Void>Terminal side effect
exceptionallyThrowable → TCF<T>Recover with fallback
handle(T, Throwable) → UCF<U>Transform both paths
whenComplete(T, Throwable) → voidCF<T>Logging/metrics; passes result through
Interview angle: "Fetch 50 product prices in parallel with a 1 s budget." List<CF<Price>> via supplyAsync on a bounded pool, allOf(arr).orTimeout(1, SECONDS), then futures.stream().filter(CF::isDone).filter(f -> !f.isCompletedExceptionally()).map(CF::join) to keep partial results. Mention that allOf fails fast on the first exception only in the sense that its result is exceptional; the other tasks keep running.

Pitfalls

  • Blocking (join, JDBC, HTTP) inside supplyAsync on the common pool starves parallel streams and every other user of the common pool. Always pass an executor for I/O.
  • exceptionally placed before the failing stage catches nothing: position matters.
  • ThreadLocal context (MDC, security context) does not follow the chain across pools; propagate explicitly or use a context-aware executor wrapper.
  • cancel(true) on a CompletableFuture does not interrupt the running task; it just completes the future with CancellationException.

Likely follow-ups

  • What if the future is already complete when you call thenApply? (The function runs synchronously on the calling thread.)
  • How do you do "first successful of N"? (anyOf returns the first completed, including failures; wrap each with handle or use a manual complete() race.)
  • Java 8 alternative to orTimeout? (A scheduled task that calls completeExceptionally.)

ConcurrentHashMap Internals: CAS Bins, Locking on the Head, Striped Size

Why interviewers ask: the default follow-up to "HashMap internals" for senior candidates. The trap answer is "it uses 16 segments"; that was Java 7. They want the Java 8 design: CAS on empty bins, synchronized on the first node otherwise, and how size() stays cheap.

Java 8 replaced the segment array with the same Node<K,V>[] table shape as HashMap (power-of-two, lists that treeify at 8, resize at 0.75) and made each bin its own lock. putVal: if the bin is empty, CAS the new node in (casTabAt) — no lock at all; if it is occupied, synchronized (firstNodeOfBin) and walk/append. Reads (get) take no lock: Node.val and Node.next are volatile, and the table is read with a volatile-acquire (tabAt). Since two threads only contend when they hit the same bin, throughput scales with the table size instead of a fixed 16.

Size: incrementing one shared counter per put would serialise every writer. Instead addCount tries a CAS on baseCount; on contention it falls back to a striped CounterCell[] (the same idea as LongAdder), and size()/mappingCount() sums base + all cells: cheap, but only an estimate under concurrent updates. Resize is cooperative: a resizing thread splits the table into stripes and each bin it finishes is replaced by a ForwardingNode (hash −1); any writer that hits a ForwardingNode helps transfer (helpTransfer) before retrying, while readers simply follow it to the new table.

Contract differences from HashMap: no null keys or values (a null from get must unambiguously mean absent, since there is no locked containsKey-then-get window); iterators are weakly consistent (never throw ConcurrentModificationException, may or may not reflect concurrent updates); computeIfAbsent/merge/compute are atomic per key and run the function while holding the bin lock. Analogy: a hotel where every room has its own lock instead of one lock on the corridor; the room count is kept on a few tally boards the clerks add up when asked.

ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> hits = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
hits.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new LongAdder()).increment();   // atomic per key

// WRONG: check-then-act, two threads can both put
if (!hits.containsKey(key)) hits.put(key, new LongAdder());

// merge for "put or combine"
Map<String, Integer> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
counts.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum);

// Bulk parallel ops (Java 8): threshold = min elements per task
long total = counts.reduceValuesToLong(1_000, Integer::longValue, 0L, Long::sum);
Set<String> live = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();                 // concurrent Set
HashMapCollections.synchronizedMapConcurrentHashMap
LockingNoneOne monitor for every callCAS + per-bin monitor; lock-free reads
null key/valueBoth allowedBoth allowedNeither
IteratorFail-fast (CME)Fail-fast; you must sync manually while iteratingWeakly consistent, never CME
Compound opsNot atomicNot atomic across callscompute*, merge, putIfAbsent atomic per key
size()ExactExactEstimate under writes
Interview angle: "Why no null values?" With HashMap you can disambiguate get == null with containsKey; in a concurrent map another thread may remove the key between those two calls, so the ambiguity would be unresolvable. Doug Lea rejected nulls for that reason. "Java 7 vs 8?" Java 7 Segment<K,V> extends ReentrantLock, 16 by default (concurrencyLevel), so at most 16 concurrent writers; Java 8 locks per bin and the parameter is only used as a sizing hint.

Pitfalls

  • The computeIfAbsent function must not touch the same map (recursive computation on the same bin throws IllegalStateException: Recursive update since Java 9, or hung/corrupted in 8).
  • Long-running functions in compute hold the bin lock and block other keys that share the bin; keep them cheap.
  • Wrapping synchronizedMap does not make iteration safe: you must synchronized (map) { for (...) }.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why does get need no lock? (Volatile fields on Node give happens-before from the writer's volatile store; a reader sees a consistent node or the old chain.)
  • What is sizeCtl? (Volatile control field: negative while resizing (encodes resizer count), otherwise the next resize threshold.)
  • Where would you still use synchronizedMap? (Almost never; perhaps when you need null values or a custom map type like LinkedHashMap for LRU.)

CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier, Semaphore, Phaser

Why interviewers ask: "wait for N workers to finish", "limit concurrent calls to a downstream to 10", and "all threads must reach a point before any continues" are the three scenarios; naming the right primitive fast is the test.

All four are built on AQS. CountDownLatch(n): one-shot gate; countDown() from anyone, await() blocks until the count reaches 0, then stays open forever. CyclicBarrier(n, action): parties call await() and all release together when the n-th arrives; the barrier resets for the next round and can run an action at the trip point; if one party breaks (interrupt/timeout) all others get BrokenBarrierException. Semaphore(permits): a counter of permits; acquire() blocks when 0, release() adds one (any thread, not just the acquirer). With 1 permit it is a non-reentrant mutex; with N it is a rate/concurrency limiter (bulkhead). Phaser: a reusable barrier where parties can register and deregister dynamically and phases are numbered; use for multi-round algorithms with a changing participant set. Analogy: latch = the starting gun (fires once); barrier = "everyone at the trailhead before we hike"; semaphore = parking spots; phaser = a relay race with rounds where runners may join or leave.

ReusableWho waitsTypical useGotcha
CountDownLatchNoWaiters; counters never waitStart signal; wait for N tasks; test harnessMissing countDown on exception path hangs await forever: put it in finally
CyclicBarrierYes (auto reset)All partiesIterative parallel algorithms, simulationsParty count must match exactly; one timeout breaks everyone
SemaphoreYesAcquirers when permits = 0Bounded concurrency to a resource, connection poolsrelease without acquire inflates permits; not reentrant
PhaserYes (phases)Registered partiesDynamic parties, tiered barriersMore API surface; arriveAndDeregister vs arriveAndAwaitAdvance confusion
// Bulkhead: at most 10 concurrent calls to a slow downstream
Semaphore permits = new Semaphore(10, true);
Response call(Request r) throws InterruptedException {
    if (!permits.tryAcquire(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) throw new TooBusyException();
    try { return client.send(r); } finally { permits.release(); }
}

// Wait for N workers (latch), each counting down in finally
CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(workers.size());
for (Runnable w : workers) pool.execute(() -> { try { w.run(); } finally { done.countDown(); } });
if (!done.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) log.warn("timed out; {} still running", done.getCount());

// Barrier with a per-round merge step
CyclicBarrier round = new CyclicBarrier(4, () -> mergePartialResults());
// each of the 4 worker threads: compute(); round.await();   // repeat per iteration
Interview angle: "Test that 100 threads hit a method at the same instant." Start latch (1) + done latch (100): workers await the start latch, main calls countDown() once, then awaits the done latch. "How do you rate-limit vs limit concurrency?" Semaphore limits in-flight calls; a token bucket (Guava RateLimiter, Resilience4j) limits calls per second. Different questions.

Pitfalls

  • CountDownLatch.await() without timeout in production code is a hang waiting to happen; always use the timed overload and log.
  • A Semaphore does not track ownership: thread A can release what B acquired. That is a feature for hand-off patterns and a bug otherwise.
  • Fair semaphores (new Semaphore(n, true)) prevent starvation of waiting callers at a throughput cost.

Likely follow-ups

  • Latch vs Future.get for waiting on N tasks? (invokeAll or CompletableFuture.allOf is cleaner; latch is for non-task events.)
  • What is Exchanger? (Two threads swap objects at a rendezvous; double-buffering between producer and consumer.)
  • How would you implement a latch yourself? (Extend AQS: tryAcquireShared returns 1 when state is 0; tryReleaseShared decrements by CAS.)

ThreadLocal & Memory Leaks in Thread Pools

Why interviewers ask: "why did request A see user B's security context?" and "why does Metaspace/heap grow on every redeploy?" both trace back to ThreadLocal in pooled threads.

A ThreadLocal<T> gives each thread its own independent value. The value is not stored in the ThreadLocal: each Thread object holds a ThreadLocalMap whose keys are weak references to the ThreadLocal and whose values are strong references. The ThreadLocal instance is just the key. Uses: per-thread caches of non-thread-safe objects (the classic SimpleDateFormat before DateTimeFormatter), request context (MDC logging, Spring's SecurityContextHolder, TransactionSynchronizationManager, RequestContextHolder).

The leak: in a thread pool, threads live forever. If you set() and never remove(), the value stays reachable through the worker's map. Even if the ThreadLocal key is garbage collected (weak), the strong value lingers as a "stale entry" until the map happens to expunge it on a later access. In app servers this pins the web app's class loader (the value's class belongs to it) and leaks the whole deployment. The second failure is context bleed: the next request on the same worker reads the previous request's value. Rule: every set() gets a remove() in finally, typically in a filter/interceptor. Analogy: a hot-desk with a drawer; if you leave your files in the drawer, the next person at that desk finds them, and the building never empties.

public final class RequestContext {
    private static final ThreadLocal<String> TENANT = new ThreadLocal<>();
    public static void set(String tenant) { TENANT.set(tenant); }
    public static String get() { return TENANT.get(); }
    public static void clear() { TENANT.remove(); }
}

// Servlet filter: bind for the request, unbind no matter what
public void doFilter(ServletRequest req, ServletResponse res, FilterChain chain) throws IOException, ServletException {
    RequestContext.set(resolveTenant(req));
    try { chain.doFilter(req, res); }
    finally { RequestContext.clear();   // pooled thread goes back clean }
}

// Propagation to another pool must be explicit: capture on submit, restore in task
String tenant = RequestContext.get();
pool.submit(() -> { RequestContext.set(tenant); try { work(); } finally { RequestContext.clear(); } });
Interview angle: "Does a ThreadLocal value follow a CompletableFuture to another thread?" No. Nor does it follow @Async or a parallel stream. Spring Security's context and MDC need a TaskDecorator or Micrometer's context propagation. "InheritableThreadLocal?" Copies the parent's value when a new thread is created; useless with pools because workers were created long ago.

Pitfalls

  • withInitial(Supplier) is convenient but still needs remove() if the value is heavy or class-loader-bound.
  • Tomcat logs "The web application created a ThreadLocal ... but failed to remove it" on undeploy: that is this leak.
  • Virtual threads: millions of threads × one ThreadLocal value each = a lot of memory; and pooling objects per virtual thread makes no sense. See ScopedValue.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why weak keys but strong values? (So an unreferenced ThreadLocal can be collected; values cannot be weak without risking premature loss.)
  • What does expungeStaleEntries do? (On set/get/remove, scans for entries with a null key and drops them; opportunistic, not guaranteed.)

Java 21+

ScopedValue (preview in 21, finalized later; check your JDK) is an immutable, inherited-by-structured-concurrency replacement: ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "acme").run(() -> …): bound for a lexical scope, automatically unbound, no remove() to forget.

ForkJoinPool, Work Stealing & Parallel Stream Pitfalls

Why interviewers ask: ".parallel() made it slower" and "parallel stream with JDBC calls hung the app" are common war stories; they want you to explain the common pool and when parallelism pays.

ForkJoinPool is a pool specialised for divide-and-conquer: a RecursiveTask splits work (fork()), computes the small pieces, and join()s results. Each worker has its own deque: it pushes/pops its own forked subtasks LIFO (cache-friendly, smallest tasks first) and, when empty, steals from the tail of another worker's deque FIFO (largest remaining chunk, so the thief has plenty to do before stealing again). A worker that calls join() on an unfinished task does not idle; it runs other tasks meanwhile, so nested parallelism does not exhaust threads the way it does in ThreadPoolExecutor.

The common pool (ForkJoinPool.commonPool()) has parallelism cores − 1 (the calling thread contributes as the last worker) and is shared by every parallel stream and every CompletableFuture.*Async call without an explicit executor in the JVM. Parallel streams win when the source splits well (ArrayList, arrays, IntStream.range), elements are many (rule of thumb: N × cost per element ≳ 100 µs total), and operations are stateless and CPU-bound. They lose with LinkedList/Stream.iterate sources (poor splitting), limit/findFirst (ordering constraints), boxing, or any blocking I/O, which parks common-pool workers and stalls everyone. Analogy: work stealing is a kitchen where an idle cook grabs the biggest unstarted ticket from a colleague's rail, not the one they are already plating.

class SumTask extends RecursiveTask<Long> {
    static final int THRESHOLD = 10_000;
    final long[] a; final int lo, hi;
    SumTask(long[] a, int lo, int hi) { this.a = a; this.lo = lo; this.hi = hi; }
    @Override protected Long compute() {
        if (hi - lo <= THRESHOLD) { long s = 0; for (int i = lo; i < hi; i++) s += a[i]; return s; }
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        SumTask left = new SumTask(a, lo, mid), right = new SumTask(a, mid, hi);
        left.fork();                       // push to own deque
        return right.compute() + left.join(); // compute one side yourself, join the other
    }
}
long total = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(new SumTask(data, 0, data.length));

// Isolating a parallel stream from the common pool (undocumented but widely used trick)
ForkJoinPool own = new ForkJoinPool(8);
List<R> out = own.submit(() -> items.parallelStream().map(this::cpuHeavy).toList()).get();
// Tune common pool: -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism=N
Interview angle: "Why compute right directly instead of forking both?" Forking both then joining both wastes one task's worth of scheduling and doubles deque traffic; fork one, compute the other. "Is parallelStream().forEach(list::add) safe?" No: ArrayList.add is not thread-safe; use collect(toList()), which merges per-thread containers.

Pitfalls

  • Blocking inside the common pool (HTTP, JDBC, Future.get) starves parallel streams across the whole JVM; if you must, wrap in ForkJoinPool.managedBlock or use a dedicated executor.
  • forEach on a parallel stream loses encounter order; forEachOrdered restores it at a cost.
  • Parallel reduce needs an associative combiner and an identity that is truly an identity; (a, b) -> a - b gives different results per run.
  • In a servlet container, parallel streams inside request handling compete with each other for cores − 1 threads; measure before enabling.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why LIFO for own tasks and FIFO for stealing? (Locality for the owner, large chunks for the thief, fewer steal attempts.)
  • What is Spliterator? (The splitting iterator streams use; trySplit quality determines parallel speedup.)
  • How does a virtual thread scheduler relate? (It is a ForkJoinPool in FIFO mode; see next card.)

Virtual Threads (Java 21): Carriers, Pinning, When Not to Use Them

Why interviewers ask: it is the biggest concurrency change since Java 5, and "so should we drop reactive/WebFlux?" is the architecture question behind it. They also want the two caveats: pinning and CPU-bound work.

A virtual thread is a java.lang.Thread whose stack lives on the heap as a continuation, scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of carrier platform threads (a ForkJoinPool, parallelism = cores by default). When the virtual thread blocks in a JDK blocking call (Socket read, BlockingQueue.take, sleep, ReentrantLock), it unmounts: its frames are copied to the heap and the carrier picks up another virtual thread. Millions of them cost only heap; a blocked platform thread costs an OS thread and roughly 1 MB of stack reservation. The programming model stays the plain "thread per request", blocking style, which is the entire point: throughput of async code with the readability and stack traces of synchronous code.

Pinning: in Java 21, a virtual thread that blocks while inside a synchronized block or method, or inside a native call/JNI, cannot unmount and holds its carrier hostage. With few carriers and many pinned threads, throughput collapses to that of a small platform pool. Detect with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full (21) or the jdk.VirtualThreadPinned JFR event; fix by switching hot-path monitors to ReentrantLock. JDK 24 (JEP 491) removes this limitation for synchronized, but check your runtime. Do not use virtual threads for CPU-bound work (no benefit; the carrier pool is already cores-sized), do not pool them (they are cheap and disposable, one per task), and do not cache expensive objects in ThreadLocal per virtual thread. Analogy: platform threads are salaried employees who sit idle while waiting on a reply; virtual threads are tickets that a handful of employees pick up whenever a reply arrives.

// One virtual thread per task; no pool sizing, no queue
try (ExecutorService vt = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    List<Future<Price>> futures = skus.stream()
        .map(sku -> vt.submit(() -> priceClient.fetch(sku)))   // blocking HTTP is fine
        .toList();
    for (Future<Price> f : futures) prices.add(f.get());
}   // close() waits for all tasks

Thread.ofVirtual().name("ingest-", 0).start(() -> consume(queue));
Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> audit(event));

// Pinning hazard (Java 21): the carrier is stuck while this blocks
synchronized (cache) { value = remoteCall();  // use ReentrantLock instead }

// Spring Boot 3.2+: spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true switches Tomcat and @Async to virtual threads
Platform threadVirtual thread
Backed by1:1 OS threadContinuation on heap, mounted on a carrier
Cost~1 MB stack reserve, slow to createFew hundred bytes upward, cheap to create
BlockingBlocks the OS threadUnmounts; carrier reused
Daemon / priorityConfigurableAlways daemon; priority ignored
Good forCPU-bound, few threadsI/O-bound, many concurrent tasks
Interview angle: "Virtual threads vs reactive (WebFlux)?" Same throughput goal, different cost: reactive requires rewriting to non-blocking APIs and loses stack traces; virtual threads keep blocking code. Reactive still wins for backpressure-native streaming and very hot paths; for typical CRUD services virtual threads plus a JDBC driver are simpler. Note that connection pools (HikariCP) still bound concurrency: 10 000 virtual threads waiting on 20 connections is a queue, not parallelism.

Pitfalls

  • Rate limits that relied on "the pool has 200 threads" disappear; add explicit Semaphores in front of scarce resources.
  • Thread dumps with millions of virtual threads need jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json; jstack does not list them.
  • Thread.currentThread().getId() is no longer a small stable number; do not use it as a shard key.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is structured concurrency? (StructuredTaskScope, preview: fork subtasks, join or fail as a unit, cancellation propagates; check your JDK for status.)
  • How many carriers? (jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism, default cores; the scheduler can temporarily add carriers when threads pin in file I/O.)
  • Does Object.wait() pin? (In 21 yes; JEP 491 in 24 fixes it along with synchronized.)

Producer–Consumer with BlockingQueue

Why interviewers ask: the pattern behind every thread pool, log appender and message pipeline; "implement producer-consumer" is the most common live-coding concurrency task and the queue choice reveals whether you think about backpressure.

A BlockingQueue<E> decouples producers from consumers with four flavours of each operation: throws (add/remove), returns special value (offer/poll → false/null), blocks (put/take), blocks with timeout (offer(e, t, u)/poll(t, u)). A bounded queue (ArrayBlockingQueue, LinkedBlockingQueue(cap)) gives backpressure: when consumers fall behind, put blocks producers instead of letting memory grow until OOM. LinkedBlockingQueue uses two locks (put and take) so producers and consumers do not contend with each other; ArrayBlockingQueue uses one lock with two Conditions but no per-element allocation. SynchronousQueue holds nothing (hand-off), PriorityBlockingQueue is unbounded and ordered, DelayQueue releases elements when their delay expires, LinkedTransferQueue lets a producer wait until a consumer has received the item.

Shutdown is the part candidates miss: consumers blocked in take() never see a boolean flag. Use a poison pill sentinel (one per consumer) or interrupt() the consumers and let take() throw. Analogy: a sushi conveyor belt with a fixed number of plates; the chef waits when the belt is full, diners wait when it is empty, and closing time is announced by a "last plate" marker.

BlockingQueue<Event> buf = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1_000);   // bounded = backpressure
Event POISON = new Event("__EOF__");

Runnable producer = () -> {
    try {
        for (Event e : source) buf.put(e);            // blocks when full
        for (int i = 0; i < CONSUMERS; i++) buf.put(POISON);   // one pill per consumer
    } catch (InterruptedException ie) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
};
Runnable consumer = () -> {
    try {
        for (Event e; (e = buf.take()) != POISON; ) handle(e);   // blocks when empty
    } catch (InterruptedException ie) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
};
// Never: while (!buf.isEmpty()) buf.poll();   → busy-spins and races with producers
QueueBoundedOrderingLocksPick when
ArrayBlockingQueueYes (fixed)FIFO1 lock, 2 conditions, optional fairKnown capacity, low allocation
LinkedBlockingQueueOptionalFIFO2 locks (put/take)High throughput, separate producer/consumer contention
SynchronousQueue0Hand-offLock-freeDirect hand-off; cached pools
PriorityBlockingQueueNoComparator1 lockPriority scheduling (beware unbounded)
DelayQueueNoBy delay expiry1 lockTimeouts, scheduled retries
Interview angle: "What if the producer is faster forever?" Bounded queue + offer(e, 100ms) and drop/log, or apply backpressure upstream (HTTP 429). "Multiple consumers and ordering?" A single queue with N consumers loses per-key ordering; partition into N queues by key hash (the Kafka consumer model).

Pitfalls

  • LinkedBlockingQueue with no capacity is unbounded; it is the default in newFixedThreadPool and the usual cause of "heap full of queued Runnables".
  • size() on LinkedBlockingQueue is accurate but drainTo/iteration are weakly consistent; do not branch on isEmpty().
  • Batching consumers should take() one then drainTo(batch, max) the rest; polling in a loop with a tiny timeout wastes CPU.

Likely follow-ups

  • How do you implement it with wait/notify or Condition? (See the bounded-buffer practice problem below.)
  • Which queue does ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor use? (DelayedWorkQueue, a heap keyed by trigger time.)
  • Difference between put and add on a full queue? (put blocks; add throws IllegalStateException; offer returns false.)

Thread A sets a plain boolean done = true; thread B loops while (!done) {}. Which statement is correct?

c. Without volatile or a lock, the read is a data race and may legally be hoisted into if (!done) while (true). Cache coherence (a) is a hardware property that says nothing about compiler reordering, and A terminating (b) only creates an edge for a thread that join()s it. d is not a thing; races are silent.

Two threads each run for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) counter++; where counter is volatile int. What is guaranteed at the end?

b. Each ++ is three steps; both threads can read the same value and one increment is lost, any number of times. Volatile solves visibility, not atomicity (a). The hardware (c) does not change the fact that the three steps are separate instructions. Use AtomicInteger or synchronized.

Why must wait() be called inside a while loop rather than an if?

d. notify moves the waiter to the entry set; it competes for the lock and another thread may consume the item first. Spurious wake-ups are also permitted by the spec. a is wrong: calling wait without the monitor throws IllegalMonitorStateException; c is backwards: wait releases it.

You create new ThreadPoolExecutor(4, 50, 60, SECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()). Under sustained load, how many threads will the pool run?

a. Non-core threads are created only when the queue rejects a task; an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue never does, so tasks pile up in memory while 4 threads work. b describes what most people assume (and what a bounded queue would do). Threads are never pre-started without prestartAllCoreThreads (c).

In production, which rejection policy gives natural backpressure when a bounded pool is saturated?

c. Running the task on the caller stalls the producer for one task's duration, throttling submission without losing work. AbortPolicy (a, the default) is right when the caller has a fallback, but immediate retries just hammer a saturated pool. b and d lose tasks silently, which is acceptable only for best-effort work like metrics.

What does ConcurrentHashMap (Java 8+) lock when two threads put keys that hash to different, non-empty bins?

b. Java 8 locks per bin on the head Node. Segments (c) were the Java 7 design. CAS alone (d) is used only for an empty bin and for the counter; appending to a chain uses synchronized.

A lock-free stack pops node A by CAS(top, A, A.next). Between reading A and the CAS, another thread pops A, pops B, and pushes A back. What happens?

d. CAS compares the reference only; top == A again so it succeeds with the old next captured before B was removed. Fix with AtomicStampedReference (version stamp). a/c describe what people wish CAS did; no exception (b) is ever raised.

Which line correctly chains an async call that itself returns a CompletableFuture<Order> after a user lookup?

a. thenCompose flattens the nested future into CompletableFuture<Order>. b yields CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Order>>. c starts the order fetch before the user id is known. d returns CompletableFuture<Void> and discards the order.

A Spring Boot app on Java 21 with virtual threads enabled shows poor throughput under load. JFR reports many jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events. Most likely cause?

c. In Java 21 a virtual thread that blocks while holding a monitor cannot unmount, so the small carrier pool is exhausted. Replace the hot-path synchronized with ReentrantLock (or upgrade to JDK 24+). Pooling (a) is an anti-pattern for virtual threads; blocking I/O (b) is exactly what they are for; the carrier pool defaults to the core count (d).

In a web app running on a thread pool, a request filter calls CURRENT_USER.set(user) on a ThreadLocal and never calls remove(). What are the consequences?

b. Pooled threads outlive requests; the ThreadLocalMap value is strongly referenced by the thread until overwritten or removed. Context bleed is a security bug; the retained value pins classes on redeploy. Nothing is thrown (c) and the pool does not know or care (d).

Practice

Fix the bug: broken double-checked locking singleton

This singleton occasionally hands out an object whose fields are still default (zero/null) on multi-core machines. Explain why and fix it in two different ways.

public class ConfigRegistry {
    private static ConfigRegistry instance;
    private final Map<String, String> props;

    private ConfigRegistry() { props = loadFromDisk(); }

    public static ConfigRegistry get() {
        if (instance == null) {
            synchronized (ConfigRegistry.class) {
                if (instance == null) {
                    instance = new ConfigRegistry();
                }
            }
        }
        return instance;
    }
}
Tests: JMM reordering, safe publication, volatile, class-init idiom
Hint 1
instance = new ConfigRegistry() is three actions: allocate, run constructor, store reference. Which of these may the JIT reorder, and what does the first unsynchronized if see?
Hint 2
Java gives a special guarantee for final fields and another for class initialization. One of them makes this example accidentally safe on JDK 5+; the other gives the idiomatic fix without any lock code.
Reveal solution

Why it breaks: the JIT may publish the reference to instance before the constructor's writes are visible (store reordering). Thread B passes the outer if (instance == null) check without ever entering synchronized, so it has no happens-before edge with thread A's constructor, and reads a partially constructed object. (With only final fields, as written here, the final-field freeze semantics actually rescue it; add one non-final field and it is broken for real.)

Fix 1: volatile reference. The volatile write becomes a release, the outer read an acquire, so anyone who sees the non-null reference sees a fully constructed object.

private static volatile ConfigRegistry instance;   // rest unchanged

Fix 2 (preferred): initialization-on-demand holder. Class initialization is guaranteed by the JVM to be thread-safe and lazy; no volatile, no lock code, and the JIT can treat the read as a constant after init.

public class ConfigRegistry {
    private ConfigRegistry() { /* … */ }
    private static class Holder { static final ConfigRegistry INSTANCE = new ConfigRegistry(); }
    public static ConfigRegistry get() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }
}
// Or simply: public enum ConfigRegistry { INSTANCE; ... }  — also serialization-safe

Interviewer follow-up: "Why was DCL broken before Java 5?" The old JMM did not define volatile as a release/acquire fence, so even volatile did not fix it. JSR-133 (Java 5) did.

Predict the output: a visibility bug that "works on my laptop"

public class Stopper {
    private static boolean running = true;
    private static int ticks = 0;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Thread worker = new Thread(() -> {
            while (running) { ticks++; }
            System.out.println("stopped at " + ticks);
        });
        worker.start();
        Thread.sleep(200);
        running = false;
        worker.join(2_000);
        System.out.println("alive=" + worker.isAlive() + " ticks>0=" + (ticks > 0));
    }
}

What can this print? Give every legal outcome, say which one you would expect on a server JVM, and fix it with the smallest change.

Tests: data races, JIT hoisting, join with timeout, what main is allowed to observe
Hint 1
The worker reads running in a hot loop with no synchronization; after C2 compiles the loop, what does the read become?
Hint 2
join(2_000) returns after two seconds even if the worker is still running. What does main read for ticks, and is that value guaranteed?
Reveal solution

Legal outcomes:

  • Most likely on HotSpot server (C2): the loop is JIT-compiled with the read of running hoisted out; the worker never sees false. After 2 s join times out and main prints alive=true ticks>0=true (or ticks>0=false: main's read of ticks is also a race, and the worker's increments may not be visible to main at all). The JVM then hangs forever because worker is non-daemon. "stopped at" is never printed.
  • Possible (interpreter, -Xint, or if a safepoint/deopt happens to reload the field): worker stops, prints stopped at N, main prints alive=false ticks>0=true. This is the "works on my laptop" run.

Nothing else is legal: ticks can never go backwards within the worker, and main cannot observe a value the worker never wrote. But main is permitted to observe 0 for ticks even after 200 ms of increments, because there is no happens-before edge from the worker to main until join() returns because the thread terminated (a timed-out join creates no edge).

Smallest fix: private static volatile boolean running = true;. That makes the worker terminate promptly; join then returns on termination, which does give main a happens-before edge, so ticks > 0 becomes guaranteed true too (all of the worker's writes are visible after a successful join). ticks itself needs no volatile because only the worker writes it and main reads it only after the join edge. Bonus: on the interrupt-based version, worker.interrupt() plus checking isInterrupted() is the idiomatic stop signal.

Implement: a bounded buffer with ReentrantLock and two Conditions

Implement BoundedBuffer<T> with void put(T) (blocks while full) and T take() (blocks while empty) without using java.util.concurrent queues. Producers must not wake other producers, and consumers must not wake other consumers. Then explain what changes if you use synchronized + wait/notify.

Tests: condition variables, spurious wake-ups, lock discipline, signal vs signalAll
Hint 1
One lock, two conditions: notFull for producers, notEmpty for consumers. Each side awaits on its own condition and signals the other.
Hint 2
Use a circular array with putIdx, takeIdx, count; the state you check in the while loop is count == items.length / count == 0.
Reveal solution
public final class BoundedBuffer<T> {
    private final Object[] items;
    private int putIdx, takeIdx, count;
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition notFull  = lock.newCondition();
    private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();

    public BoundedBuffer(int capacity) { items = new Object[capacity]; }

    public void put(T t) throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            while (count == items.length) notFull.await();   // loop: spurious wake-ups
            items[putIdx] = t;
            putIdx = (putIdx + 1) % items.length;
            count++;
            notEmpty.signal();                 // wake one consumer only
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public T take() throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            while (count == 0) notEmpty.await();
            T t = (T) items[takeIdx];
            items[takeIdx] = null;             // let GC reclaim
            takeIdx = (takeIdx + 1) % items.length;
            count--;
            notFull.signal();                  // wake one producer only
            return t;
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
}

Why two conditions: with a single wait set you must notifyAll(), waking every producer and consumer on every operation, most of which re-check and go back to sleep (thundering herd). Separate conditions let each operation signal() exactly one thread of the right kind. Because each await is guarded by a while, a spurious wake-up or an interrupted waiter is harmless.

With synchronized: replace lock/conditions with synchronized methods and wait(); you lose the two-condition split, so you must use notifyAll(). Using notify() there can deadlock: a producer might wake another producer while a consumer stays asleep, and the buffer stays full. This is essentially ArrayBlockingQueue's design (it also adds interruptible/timed variants and an optional fair lock).

Diagnose: the thread pool that deadlocks with no locks in sight

An order service uses a shared ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8). Under a spike of 20 concurrent orders, the service stops responding; a thread dump shows all 8 workers WAITING in FutureTask.get, CPU near 0%, no synchronized anywhere, no "Java-level deadlock" reported by jstack. Explain the mechanism and propose three fixes, ranking them.

Future<Receipt> placeOrder(Order o) {
    return pool.submit(() -> {
        Future<Boolean> stock = pool.submit(() -> inventory.reserve(o));   // subtask, same pool
        Future<Price>   price = pool.submit(() -> pricing.quote(o));       // subtask, same pool
        return new Receipt(o, stock.get(), price.get());                    // parent waits
    });
}
Tests: thread starvation deadlock, pool isolation, ForkJoin vs TPE, reading dumps
Hint 1
Where are the 16+ subtasks when all 8 workers are busy being parents? Who is supposed to run them?
Hint 2
jstack only reports cycles through monitors and Locks. A Future.get() waiting on a task that is still in a queue is a wait-for edge the JVM cannot see.
Reveal solution

Mechanism: thread-starvation deadlock. 20 parent tasks arrive; 8 start on the workers and each submits 2 children to the same pool, then blocks in get(). The 16 children (plus 12 waiting parents) sit in the unbounded queue. All 8 workers are parents waiting for children that can only run on those same 8 workers. Nobody holds a lock, so jstack sees only 8 threads parked in FutureTask.get → LockSupport.park; the cycle goes through the queue, not through monitors. Every request after that queues forever; the heap slowly fills with queued tasks.

Fixes, best first:

  1. Do not block a worker on work from its own bounded pool. Compose instead of joining: CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(reserve, pool).thenCombine(supplyAsync(quote, pool), Receipt::new). The parent submits and returns; no worker ever waits. Same pool, zero risk.
  2. Separate pools per tier (bulkheads): parents on orderPool, children on ioPool. A parent can then safely block, and a slow inventory service cannot starve order intake. Size ioPool for its blocking ratio and give both bounded queues with CallerRunsPolicy or AbortPolicy so saturation is visible instead of silent.
  3. Use a pool whose workers help while waiting. ForkJoinPool.join() lets a worker execute other queued tasks while its child is pending (and on Java 21, a virtual-thread-per-task executor removes the fixed worker count altogether, so blocking is cheap). Ranked last because it hides the design smell rather than removing it, and ForkJoinPool is a poor fit for blocking I/O children.

What to say about detection: alert on queue.size() growth with activeCount == maximumPoolSize and completed-task rate ≈ 0; that signature is starvation deadlock even when jstack is silent. A Future.get(timeout) on the parent would have turned the hang into a timeout with a stack trace.

8️⃣ Design Patterns & SOLID in Java

Patterns are the vocabulary interviewers use to check whether you can shape code, not just write it. The path here: SOLID first (the "why"), then the creational trio (Singleton, Factory, Builder), the behavioural workhorses (Strategy, Observer, Template, Chain, Command/State), the structural wrappers that everybody confuses (Decorator/Proxy/Adapter/Facade), and finally dynamic proxies, which is the bridge to how Spring actually works.

SOLID with Before/After Java

Why interviewers ask: every "how would you refactor this service?" question is a SOLID question in disguise. They want a concrete smell and a concrete fix, not the acronym recited.

Single responsibility: a class has one reason to change. Open/closed: add behaviour by adding classes, not editing a switch. Liskov: a subtype must be usable wherever the supertype is promised (no "throws UnsupportedOperationException" overrides). Interface segregation: many small role interfaces beat one fat one. Dependency inversion: depend on abstractions, and let someone else (Spring) inject the concrete thing.

Analogy: a restaurant. One chef per station (S), a new dish is a new recipe card not a rewrite of the kitchen (O), any sous-chef can cover any station they are certified for (L), the dishwasher does not need the full menu training (I), the chef orders "tomatoes" from a supplier interface, not from a specific farm (D).

// BEFORE: violates S (formats + persists), O (switch grows), D (news up its own repo)
class ReportService {
    private final JdbcReportRepo repo = new JdbcReportRepo();
    String render(Report r, String fmt) {
        switch (fmt) { case "CSV": return toCsv(r); case "PDF": return toPdf(r); default: throw new IllegalArgumentException(fmt); }
    }
}

// AFTER: one renderer per format (S), new format = new bean (O), repo injected (D)
interface ReportRenderer { String format(); String render(Report r); }
record CsvRenderer() implements ReportRenderer { public String format() { return "CSV"; } public String render(Report r) { return "..."; } }

class ReportService {
    private final ReportRepo repo;                      // abstraction, not JdbcReportRepo
    private final Map<String, ReportRenderer> renderers;
    ReportService(ReportRepo repo, List<ReportRenderer> all) {   // Spring injects every bean
        this.repo = repo;
        this.renderers = all.stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(ReportRenderer::format, r -> r));
    }
    String render(long id, String fmt) {
        var r = Optional.ofNullable(renderers.get(fmt)).orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException(fmt));
        return r.render(repo.load(id));
    }
}
PrincipleSmell you nameFix you proposeWhere Spring shows it
SRPOrderService validates, prices, emails, logs to Kafka (800 lines)Split into OrderValidator, PricingService, OrderNotifier; compose@Controller / @Service / @Repository layering
OCPswitch (paymentType) repeated in 4 methodsStrategy per type + registry map; add a class, never edit the switchInjecting List<PaymentHandler>; HandlerMapping chain
LSPReadOnlyList extends ArrayList overriding add to throwCompose: wrap and expose only a read interface; or List.copyOfJpaRepository extends CrudRepository without weakening contracts
ISPOne Repository with 40 methods; every test stubs all 40Role interfaces: OrderReader, OrderWriterCrudRepository vs PagingAndSortingRepository split
DIPnew SmtpMailer() inside the service; untestableConstructor-inject a Mailer interface; test with a fakeConstructor injection, @Primary/@Qualifier to pick the impl
Interview angle: "Which SOLID principle does java.util.Stack extends Vector break?" LSP/ISP: a stack exposes get(int) and insertElementAt, so callers can violate the stack invariant. The JDK's own Javadoc recommends ArrayDeque instead.

Pitfalls

  • Over-applying OCP produces an interface for every class with exactly one implementation. Say so: "I add the abstraction when the second implementation or the first test needs it."
  • "SRP" is not "one method per class"; it is one actor that requests changes.
  • Field injection (@Autowired on a field) hides DIP violations because you cannot see the dependency list; constructor injection makes them explicit and final.

Likely follow-ups

  • Is Square extends Rectangle an LSP violation? (Yes if setWidth must keep the sides equal: code written against Rectangle breaks. Use immutable value types instead.)
  • How does DIP differ from dependency injection? (DIP is the principle "depend on abstractions"; DI is one mechanism to satisfy it; IoC container is the tool.)
  • Where does Java 17 help? (Sealed interfaces make closed hierarchies explicit, records remove boilerplate that used to hide responsibilities.)

Singleton: Eager, DCL, Holder, Enum

Why interviewers ask: it is the cheapest way to test whether you understand the Java Memory Model. "Write a thread-safe singleton" is really "explain why volatile is needed in double-checked locking".

Intent: exactly one instance, globally reachable.
