Five ways, in order of increasing correctness-per-line: eager (static final X INSTANCE = new X(), safe because class init is guarded by the JVM), lazy synchronized (correct, but every call takes a lock), double-checked locking (lock only on the slow path; needs volatile), initialization-on-demand holder (a nested static class whose init the JVM serialises for you: lazy, lock-free, no volatile), and enum (one line; the JVM guarantees one instance per class loader, and the serialization and reflection loopholes are closed).

Why volatile? INSTANCE = new Config() is three actions: allocate, run constructor, store the reference. Without volatile the JIT may store the reference before the constructor finishes. A second thread passes the first null check, and reads a half-built object. volatile forbids that reordering (a release store paired with an acquire load), so a non-null reference means a fully constructed object.

Analogy: DCL is checking whether the meeting room is booked before walking to reception; the holder idiom is a room that only gets built the first time someone opens the door, and the JVM is the contractor guaranteeing nobody enters a half-built room.

public final class Config {
    private static volatile Config INSTANCE;      // volatile: no store reordering
    private Config() { load(); }

    public static Config get() {
        Config c = INSTANCE;                      // 1st read: no lock (fast path)
        if (c == null) {
            synchronized (Config.class) {
                c = INSTANCE;                     // 2nd read, now under the lock
                if (c == null) {
                    INSTANCE = c = new Config();  // construct, then publish
                }
            }
        }
        return c;
    }
}
  1. T1 and T2 both call get() for the first time; both see INSTANCE == null.
  2. T1 wins the monitor; T2 blocks at the synchronized entry.
  3. Under the lock T1 re-reads: still null, so it is the one allowed to construct.
  4. T1 allocates @1 and runs the constructor. The volatile write is ordered after construction completes.
  5. T1 publishes INSTANCE = @1 and releases the monitor.
  6. T2 acquires the lock, re-reads @1, skips the if and returns the same instance.
  7. Every later caller (T3) takes the fast path: a single volatile read, no monitor.
// Holder idiom: lazy AND lock-free, no volatile needed (JVM serialises class init)
public final class Registry {
    private Registry() {}
    private static final class Holder { static final Registry INSTANCE = new Registry(); }
    public static Registry get() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }   // Holder is initialised on first call
}

// Enum: Effective Java item 3. Serialization returns the same constant; reflection cannot call the ctor.
public enum Clock { INSTANCE; public long now() { return System.currentTimeMillis(); } }
Interview angle: "Is a Spring bean a singleton?" A singleton-scoped bean is one instance per ApplicationContext, enforced by the container, not by the class. Two contexts (or two class loaders in Tomcat) give two instances. That is the answer to "singleton vs Spring singleton".
VariantLazy?Locking costSurvives reflection / serialization?Verdict
Eager static finalNo (at class init)NoneNo / no (unless readResolve)Fine when cheap to build
Synchronized getterYesEvery callNo / noCorrect but slow under contention
DCL + volatileYesFirst call onlyNo / noCorrect since Java 5; verbose
Holder classYesNone (class-init lock, once)No / noBest plain-class option
enumAt enum class initNoneYes / yesEffective Java's recommendation

Pitfalls

  • DCL without volatile was broken before Java 5 and is still wrong today: the reordering is legal under the JMM, and it shows up as an intermittent NPE on a field of a "non-null" object.
  • Testability: a static getInstance() is hard-wired global state; tests cannot swap it. Prefer letting the container hold the one instance and inject it.
  • Multiple class loaders (app servers, OSGi) each get their own singleton. "One per JVM" is really "one per class loader".
  • Reflection: ctor.setAccessible(true) creates a second instance of any class-based singleton; a private ctor can throw if INSTANCE != null, but the enum is the only airtight variant.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why the second null check? (Two threads can both pass the first one; without the re-check under the lock you build two instances.)
  • Can I use a local variable in DCL? (Yes; the c local above avoids a second volatile read on the fast path, which is the version in Effective Java.)
  • How does the JVM make the holder idiom safe? (JLS 12.4.2: class initialization takes an init lock, other threads wait until it completes; the resulting write is visible.)

Factory Method & Abstract Factory

Why interviewers ask: "how do you create the right implementation without a switch in every caller?" and "why does List.of exist when there are constructors?"

Intent: put object creation behind a method so callers depend on an interface, not on new ConcreteThing(). Static factory (Effective Java item 1) is the simplest form: a named method that can cache, return a subtype, or return an interface (List.of returns a hidden immutable class; Integer.valueOf caches -128..127; Calendar.getInstance picks a locale-specific subclass). Factory Method is the GoF version: subclasses decide what to create (Collection.iterator(), AbstractList subclasses returning their own iterator). Abstract Factory creates a family of related objects so they stay consistent (DocumentBuilderFactory, a ThemeFactory producing matching buttons and dialogs).

The modern Java 17 shapes: a Map<String, Supplier<T>> registry (open for extension, no switch) and a sealed interface + exhaustive switch expression when the set is closed by design and you want the compiler to complain when a case is missing.

Analogy: static factory = ordering "a coffee" at the counter and letting the barista choose the cup; abstract factory = ordering a "breakfast set" and getting a matching plate, cup, and cutlery.

// 1) Registry factory: adding a new type never touches this class (OCP)
public final class ParserFactory {
    private static final Map<String, Supplier<Parser>> REGISTRY = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(Map.of(
        "json", JsonParser::new,
        "csv",  CsvParser::new));
    public static void register(String type, Supplier<Parser> s) { REGISTRY.put(type, s); }
    public static Parser create(String type) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(REGISTRY.get(type)).map(Supplier::get)
                       .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("No parser: " + type));
    }
}

// 2) Sealed + switch: closed set, compiler enforces exhaustiveness
sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}
record Circle(double r) implements Shape {}
record Square(double s) implements Shape {}
static Shape parse(String spec) {
    var parts = spec.split(":");
    return switch (parts[0]) {
        case "circle" -> new Circle(Double.parseDouble(parts[1]));
        case "square" -> new Square(Double.parseDouble(parts[1]));
        default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException(spec);
    };
}
Interview angle: Effective Java's four advantages of static factories over constructors: they have names (BigInteger.probablePrime), they need not create a new object (Boolean.valueOf), they can return a subtype (EnumSet.of returns RegularEnumSet or JumboEnumSet depending on size), and the returned class can vary by input. In Spring, a @Bean method is a factory method; FactoryBean<T> is the abstract-factory-ish hook.
FormWho decides the concrete typeJDK / Spring exampleUse when
Static factoryThe method bodyList.of, Optional.of, Executors.newFixedThreadPoolNaming, caching, hiding impl class
Factory Method (GoF)A subclass overrideIterable.iterator(), ThreadFactory.newThreadFramework code that must create user-defined objects
Abstract FactoryA factory objectDocumentBuilderFactory, SSLSocketFactory, Spring BeanFactoryFamilies that must stay consistent
Registry mapA lookup keySpring injecting Map<String, Handler> keyed by bean namePlugins, many types, open set

Pitfalls

  • Static factories are not subclassable and are easy to miss in Javadoc; use conventional names (of, from, valueOf, getInstance, newInstance).
  • A switch factory is fine for a sealed set; it is a smell for an open set (you edit it for every new type).
  • Class.forName(name).newInstance()-style "reflection factories" lose compile-time safety and break under GraalVM native image without hints.

Likely follow-ups

  • Simple factory vs Factory Method? (Simple factory is a static helper; Factory Method defers creation to subclasses; interviewers accept either if you name the distinction.)
  • How does Spring choose among several beans of one interface? (@Primary, @Qualifier, or inject the Map<String, T> and pick at runtime.)

Builder

Why interviewers ask: "how do you construct an object with 8 optional fields safely?" and "records or builders?" is a common Java 17 follow-up.

Intent: separate construction of a complex object from its representation. The telescoping constructor problem: new Pizza(12, true, false, true, null, 2) where nobody remembers which boolean is which. A fluent builder names each part, allows any order, and validates everything once in build(), producing an immutable object with final fields.

Records vs builders: a record is the right tool when all components are required and there are few (up to ~5). A builder wins when many are optional, defaults are needed, or validation spans fields. They combine: a record with a nested static Builder that calls the canonical constructor. Lombok @Builder generates the same code; know that it is generated, not magic, and that @Builder on a record is supported in recent Lombok (check your version).

public record HttpCall(String url, String method, Duration timeout, Map<String, String> headers) {
    public HttpCall {                                   // compact ctor: validate + defensively copy
        Objects.requireNonNull(url, "url");
        headers = Map.copyOf(headers);
    }
    public static Builder builder(String url) { return new Builder(url); }

    public static final class Builder {
        private final String url;                       // required: taken in the builder ctor
        private String method = "GET";                  // optional with defaults
        private Duration timeout = Duration.ofSeconds(10);
        private final Map<String, String> headers = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        private Builder(String url) { this.url = url; }
        public Builder method(String m) { this.method = m; return this; }
        public Builder timeout(Duration d) { this.timeout = d; return this; }
        public Builder header(String k, String v) { headers.put(k, v); return this; }
        public HttpCall build() {
            if (timeout.isNegative()) throw new IllegalStateException("timeout < 0");
            return new HttpCall(url, method, timeout, headers);
        }
    }
}
var call = HttpCall.builder("https://api").method("POST").header("Accept", "json").build();
In the JDK / Spring: StringBuilder (a builder of strings), HttpRequest.newBuilder(), Stream.builder(), Locale.Builder, ProcessBuilder; Spring's UriComponentsBuilder, MockMvcBuilders, RestClient.builder(), ResponseEntity.status(...).body(...).

Pitfalls

  • Builders are mutable; never share one across threads or reuse it after build() unless you document that it copies state.
  • Validate in build() (or the record's compact constructor), not in each setter, so cross-field rules can be checked together.
  • A builder with all-required fields is just a verbose constructor; use a record or the "staged builder" idiom where each step returns the next interface.

Likely follow-ups

  • How do you make the built object immutable? (final fields, defensive copies of collections, no setters; Map.copyOf / List.copyOf.)
  • Builder vs Factory? (Factory chooses which type; Builder assembles one type step by step.)

Java 8 vs 17

Records (16+) with compact constructors eliminate most hand-written value classes; the builder remains for optional-heavy configuration objects. Map.of/List.copyOf (9/10+) make the defensive copy a one-liner.

Strategy

Why interviewers ask: it is the answer to almost every "we have a growing if/else on type" refactoring question, and the natural place to show Spring's List<T>/Map<String,T> injection.

Intent: define a family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface and pick one at runtime. In Java 17 the strategy can be a class (when it needs dependencies), a lambda (Comparator is a strategy), or an enum constant with a body (fixed, serializable set of strategies). Spring turns every implementation into a bean and hands you all of them as a List (ordered by @Order) or a Map keyed by bean name; you build your own map keyed by a domain key.

Analogy: a payment terminal. The checkout code says "charge 500"; whether that is card, UPI or wallet is a plugged-in module chosen by the key on the request.

public interface PaymentStrategy { String key(); PaymentResult pay(PaymentRequest r); }

@Component class UpiStrategy implements PaymentStrategy {
    public String key() { return "UPI"; }
    public PaymentResult pay(PaymentRequest r) { /* call UPI gateway */ return PaymentResult.ok(); }
}

@Service class CheckoutService {
    private final Map<String, PaymentStrategy> byKey;
    CheckoutService(List<PaymentStrategy> strategies) {          // Spring injects ALL implementations
        byKey = strategies.stream().collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableMap(PaymentStrategy::key, s -> s));
    }
    PaymentResult pay(PaymentRequest r) {
        var s = byKey.get(r.method());
        if (s == null) throw new UnsupportedOperationException(r.method());
        return s.pay(r);
    }
}

// Lambda strategies: Comparator IS the pattern
enum Discount implements UnaryOperator<BigDecimal> {           // enum strategies: fixed set, switchable
    NONE  { public BigDecimal apply(BigDecimal p) { return p; } },
    TEN   { public BigDecimal apply(BigDecimal p) { return p.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.90")); } }
}
In the JDK / Spring: Comparator, ThreadPoolExecutor.RejectedExecutionHandler (AbortPolicy, CallerRunsPolicy), Collector; Spring PlatformTransactionManager, HttpMessageConverter list, AuthenticationProvider list in Spring Security.

Pitfalls

  • Duplicate keys blow up toMap at startup with IllegalStateException: Duplicate key. Good: fail fast. Make the message clear.
  • Strategies with state must be stateless or thread-safe: they are singletons shared by all requests.
  • Do not inject the Map<String, PaymentStrategy> Spring provides directly if your key is a domain value: it is keyed by bean name, which couples business logic to class names.

Likely follow-ups

  • Strategy vs State? (Same shape; Strategy is chosen by the client, State changes itself as transitions happen.)
  • Strategy vs Template Method? (Composition vs inheritance; Strategy swaps the whole algorithm, Template fixes the skeleton and varies steps.)
  • How to order strategies when several could apply? (@Order/Ordered on beans, then a supports(req) method and first-match; that is Chain of Responsibility.)

Observer / Listener

Why interviewers ask: event-driven design inside a process (before you reach Kafka), plus two traps: iterating listeners while one unregisters, and leaks from listeners never removed.

Intent: one-to-many dependency; when the subject changes, all registered observers are notified without the subject knowing their concrete types. Push model: the event carries the data (OrderPlaced(orderId, total)). Pull model: the event says "something changed", observers query the subject. Push with an immutable event record is the modern default.

In the JDK: java.beans.PropertyChangeSupport (the reusable subject), java.util.Observable (deprecated since 9: a class, not an interface, and not thread-safe), Swing listeners, Flow.Subscriber (reactive streams, with backpressure). In Spring: publish an ApplicationEvent (any object since 4.2) via ApplicationEventPublisher, receive with @EventListener; synchronous by default, @Async to decouple, @TransactionalEventListener to fire after commit.

public record OrderPlaced(long orderId, BigDecimal total) {}

public final class OrderEvents {
    private final List<Consumer<OrderPlaced>> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); // safe iteration
    public Runnable subscribe(Consumer<OrderPlaced> l) {
        listeners.add(l);
        return () -> listeners.remove(l);       // return the unsubscribe handle: prevents leaks
    }
    public void publish(OrderPlaced e) {
        for (var l : listeners) {
            try { l.accept(e); } catch (RuntimeException ex) { log.warn("listener failed", ex); } // isolate
        }
    }
}

// Spring flavour
@Component class InventoryListener {
    @EventListener
    @TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)   // only after the order really committed
    public void on(OrderPlaced e) { reserve(e.orderId()); }
}
Interview angle: "Why CopyOnWriteArrayList?" Notification iterates while listeners may subscribe/unsubscribe on other threads; an ArrayList would throw ConcurrentModificationException. Writes are rare, reads are every event: exactly COW's sweet spot.

Pitfalls

  • Leaks: a short-lived object that registers on a long-lived subject is kept alive forever. Unsubscribe in close(), or use WeakReference-based listeners with care.
  • One slow or throwing listener blocks or breaks the others in a synchronous loop: catch per listener, or dispatch asynchronously.
  • Ordering: do not rely on the order listeners were added unless you sort them (@Order works on Spring @EventListener).
  • Spring @EventListener on the same bean that publishes goes through the proxy: self-invocation rules apply (see Dynamic Proxy below).

Likely follow-ups

  • Observer vs pub/sub (Kafka)? (Observer is in-process and synchronous with direct references; pub/sub adds a broker, durability, and decoupling in time.)
  • Why is java.util.Observable deprecated? (It is a class, so you cannot extend anything else; setChanged API is clunky; no generics; not thread-safe.)

Decorator vs Proxy vs Adapter vs Facade

Why interviewers ask: the four look identical in UML (a class holding a reference to another). The question tests whether you can name the intent: add behaviour, control access, translate interface, or simplify a subsystem.

Decorator wraps an object of the same interface to add responsibilities, stackable at runtime: new BufferedInputStream(new GZIPInputStream(new FileInputStream(f))). The client chose the layers. Proxy also implements the same interface but exists to control access: lazy loading (Hibernate entity proxies), security checks, remote calls (Feign), caching, logging; the client usually does not know it holds a proxy. Adapter converts one interface to another the client expects: Arrays.asList(T[]) makes an array look like a List; InputStreamReader adapts bytes to chars. Facade is a single simple entry point over a messy subsystem: Executors.newFixedThreadPool hides ThreadPoolExecutor's 7-argument constructor; JdbcTemplate hides connection/statement/result-set juggling.

Analogy: Decorator is putting a coat over a jacket (still you, warmer); Proxy is your assistant answering the phone for you; Adapter is a travel plug; Facade is the hotel concierge who talks to the kitchen, laundry and taxis for you.

// Decorator: same interface, wraps, adds a responsibility, stackable
record RetryingClient(HttpClientPort delegate, int attempts) implements HttpClientPort {
    public Response send(Request r) {
        RuntimeException last = null;
        for (int i = 0; i < attempts; i++) {
            try { return delegate.send(r); } catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; }
        }
        throw last;
    }
}
// Adapter: different interfaces; translate
record LegacyPaymentAdapter(LegacySoapGateway legacy) implements PaymentGateway {
    public PaymentResult charge(Money m) {
        var resp = legacy.doCharge(m.amount().toPlainString(), m.currency().getCurrencyCode());
        return resp.code() == 0 ? PaymentResult.ok() : PaymentResult.failed(resp.message());
    }
}
var client = new RetryingClient(new LoggingClient(new RealClient()), 3);   // decorators compose
PatternInterfaceIntentClient knows?JDK / Spring
DecoratorSame as wrappedAdd behaviour, layer freelyYes (it builds the stack)java.io streams, Collections.synchronizedList, Collections.checkedList
ProxySame as targetControl access: lazy, security, remote, cache, loggingUsually noCollections.unmodifiableList (protection proxy), Hibernate lazy entities, Spring AOP, Feign
AdapterDifferent: target ≠ adapteeMake incompatible interfaces workYes (it wants the target interface)Arrays.asList, InputStreamReader, Executors.callable(Runnable), Spring HandlerAdapter
FacadeNew, simpler oneHide a subsystem behind one entry pointYesExecutors, Files, JdbcTemplate, RestTemplate
Interview angle: "Is Collections.unmodifiableList a decorator or a proxy?" Argue it: same interface, wraps the target, but its purpose is to restrict (a protection proxy) rather than to add. Both answers are accepted if you state the intent-based criterion; the trap is calling it an adapter.

Pitfalls

  • Decorator stacks break identity: equals/hashCode of the wrapper vs the wrapped object; instanceof checks on the outer object fail for the inner type.
  • Forgetting to close the outermost stream only: closing the outer decorator closes the chain; closing inner ones separately double-closes.
  • Adapter with hidden partial support (Arrays.asList().add) violates LSP for the target interface; document or use a full copy.
  • Facades that leak: if callers still need the subsystem types (e.g. return ThreadPoolExecutor), the facade is not hiding anything.

Likely follow-ups

  • Bridge vs Adapter? (Bridge is designed up front to separate abstraction from implementation, e.g. JDBC Driver; Adapter is retrofitted.)
  • How do you decorate a Spring bean? (Define the decorator as the @Primary bean and inject the original via @Qualifier; or use AOP which is a proxy.)

Dynamic Proxy: JDK vs CGLIB, and Why @Transactional Sometimes Does Nothing

Why interviewers ask: it is the mechanism behind Spring AOP, @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, Mockito mocks, Feign clients, and JPA repositories. Explaining it correctly answers a dozen Spring "why did my annotation not work?" questions in one go.

java.lang.reflect.Proxy generates, at runtime, a class ($Proxy0) that implements a list of interfaces. Every method call on it is routed to one InvocationHandler.invoke(proxy, method, args), where you can do anything before/after and then method.invoke(target, args). It needs an interface: the generated class extends java.lang.reflect.Proxy, so it cannot also extend your class.

CGLIB (bundled into Spring as spring-core repackaged) proxies a class by generating a subclass at runtime that overrides every non-final public/protected method and calls a MethodInterceptor. Therefore it cannot proxy final classes or final/private/static methods, and needs a visible no-arg constructor path (Spring uses Objenesis to skip constructors). Spring Boot 2+ defaults to CGLIB even for interface-backed beans (spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true) so that injecting by concrete class works.

The consequence interviewers love: self-invocation. Inside a bean, this.saveAll() calls the method on the raw object, not on the proxy, so @Transactional/@Cacheable on saveAll is silently ignored. Analogy: the proxy is a receptionist in front of your office; visitors go through her, but when you talk to yourself in the room she never hears it.

interface Repo { void save(Object o); }

static <T> T timed(Class<T> iface, T target) {
    InvocationHandler h = (proxy, method, args) -> {
        long t0 = System.nanoTime();
        try {
            return method.invoke(target, args);            // delegate to the real object
        } catch (InvocationTargetException e) {
            throw e.getCause();                             // unwrap: rethrow the target's exception
        } finally {
            System.out.printf("%s took %d us%n", method.getName(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000);
        }
    };
    return iface.cast(Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, h));
}
Repo repo = timed(Repo.class, new JdbcRepo());     // repo.getClass() == class com.sun.proxy.$Proxy0
Who uses it: Spring AOP (JdkDynamicAopProxy / CglibAopProxy), Spring Data repositories (an interface with no implementation: the proxy's handler builds the query from the method name), Feign and Retrofit (interface → HTTP call), Mockito (mock(List.class) is a ByteBuddy subclass proxy; final needs the inline mock maker), JDBC connection pools (HikariCP proxies Connection so close() returns to the pool), java.rmi.
JDK ProxyCGLIB / ByteBuddy
RequiresAt least one interfaceNon-final class, non-final methods
Generated typeextends Proxy implements Iextends Target
Inject asInterface onlyClass or interface
Private/final/static methodsN/A (interface methods only)Not intercepted, run un-advised
Spring Boot defaultOnly if spring.aop.proxy-target-class=falseYes (since Boot 2.0)

Pitfalls

  • Self-invocation: @Transactional on a private method or called via this does nothing. Fix: move it to another bean, inject yourself lazily (@Lazy self-reference), or use TransactionTemplate explicitly.
  • Fields on a CGLIB proxy are not initialised (the ctor is skipped): never read fields of an injected bean directly; call methods.
  • method.invoke wraps exceptions in InvocationTargetException; forgetting to unwrap changes the exception type callers see.
  • equals/hashCode/toString go through the handler too: handle Object methods explicitly or infinite recursion/"proxy equals proxy" bugs appear.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why does @Transactional not roll back on a checked exception? (Spring's default is RuntimeException/Error only; use rollbackFor. It is decided in the proxy's after-advice.)
  • Can AspectJ avoid these limits? (Yes: compile-time/load-time weaving modifies the bytecode itself, so self-invocation and private methods are advised. Spring AOP is proxy-based by design.)
  • Performance? (A reflective invoke costs tens of nanoseconds after JIT inlining of the accessor; CGLIB uses FastClass indices, similar. Not a bottleneck next to a DB call.)

Java 8 vs 17

Since Java 16 strong encapsulation blocks CGLIB from defining classes in java.* packages and from deep reflection on JDK internals; Spring's repackaged CGLIB uses MethodHandles.Lookup.defineClass and works on 17 without --add-opens for your own classes.

Template Method vs Strategy

Why interviewers ask: to see whether you default to inheritance or composition, and whether you can explain why JdbcTemplate takes a callback instead of asking you to subclass it.

Intent: an abstract class fixes the skeleton of an algorithm (a final method) and lets subclasses fill in steps via abstract or hook methods (with a default, often empty, body). AbstractList is the JDK poster child: implement get(int) and size() and you get iterator, indexOf, equals, subList for free. AbstractQueuedSynchronizer asks you for tryAcquire/tryRelease. Servlet's HttpServlet.service() dispatches to doGet/doPost.

Spring's JdbcTemplate is the same idea done with composition: the fixed steps (get connection, create statement, iterate, close, translate exceptions) are in the template, and the varying step (RowMapper) is passed as a lambda. That is Template Method's intent delivered through Strategy's mechanism, and it is what "prefer composition over inheritance" looks like in practice: no subclass, testable in isolation, combinable at runtime.

abstract class ImportJob {
    public final Report run(Path file) {                 // template: fixed order, cannot be overridden
        var rows = read(file);
        var valid = rows.stream().filter(this::isValid).toList();
        persist(valid);
        afterPersist(valid.size());                        // hook with default body
        return new Report(rows.size(), valid.size());
    }
    protected abstract List<Row> read(Path file);
    protected abstract void persist(List<Row> rows);
    protected boolean isValid(Row r) { return true; }      // hook: optional override
    protected void afterPersist(int n) {}
}
// Composition alternative: same skeleton, steps as strategies
record ImportPipeline(Function<Path, List<Row>> reader, Predicate<Row> valid, Consumer<List<Row>> sink) {
    Report run(Path f) { var rows = reader.apply(f); var ok = rows.stream().filter(valid).toList(); sink.accept(ok); return new Report(rows.size(), ok.size()); }
}
Template MethodStrategy
MechanismInheritance; subclass overrides stepsComposition; object holds an interface
VariesIndividual steps; skeleton fixedThe whole algorithm
Change at runtimeNo (type fixed at construction)Yes (swap the reference)
TestingNeed a concrete subclassMock or lambda per step
ExamplesAbstractList, HttpServlet, AQS, JUnit @BeforeEach lifecycleJdbcTemplate + RowMapper, Comparator

Pitfalls

  • Calling an overridable method from a constructor: the subclass's override runs before its fields are initialised (Effective Java item 19).
  • Fragile base class: adding a step to the template silently changes every subclass; keep the skeleton final and small.
  • Deep template hierarchies (AbstractBaseServiceImpl) are the "enterprise Java" smell; two levels max.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is a hook method? (A non-abstract method with a default body that subclasses may override to plug into the skeleton.)
  • Can Java 8 default methods replace Template Method? (Partly: an interface with default methods calling abstract ones is a template without state; it cannot hold fields.)

Chain of Responsibility

Why interviewers ask: every web request you have ever served went through one (servlet filters, Spring Security's FilterChainProxy, interceptors), and it is the natural follow-up to "which strategy applies when several might?"

Intent: pass a request along a chain of handlers; each either handles it, enriches it and passes on, or stops the chain. Two flavours. First-match: handlers are tried in order until one accepts (exception mapping, discount rules, auth providers). Pipeline: every handler runs and calls next (servlet Filter.doFilter(req, res, chain), Spring HandlerInterceptor, OkHttp interceptors, Spring Security's ~15 filters where UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter may short-circuit with a 401). The classic GoF form links handlers via a next field; modern Java prefers an ordered List<Handler> and a loop, which Spring can populate.

Analogy: airport security. Passport check, bag scan, body scan, gate. Any station can send you back; each adds a stamp; you reach the gate only if all pass.

interface DiscountRule { Optional<BigDecimal> apply(Order o); }          // first-match flavour

@Component @Order(1) class LoyaltyRule implements DiscountRule {
    public Optional<BigDecimal> apply(Order o) { return o.customer().isGold() ? Optional.of(new BigDecimal("0.10")) : Optional.empty(); }
}
@Component @Order(2) class BulkRule implements DiscountRule {
    public Optional<BigDecimal> apply(Order o) { return o.items() > 50 ? Optional.of(new BigDecimal("0.05")) : Optional.empty(); }
}
@Service class Pricing {
    private final List<DiscountRule> rules;                                  // Spring injects in @Order order
    Pricing(List<DiscountRule> rules) { this.rules = rules; }
    BigDecimal discount(Order o) {
        return rules.stream().map(r -> r.apply(o)).flatMap(Optional::stream).findFirst().orElse(BigDecimal.ZERO);
    }
}

// Pipeline flavour: each stage decides whether to continue (servlet-filter shape)
interface Stage { void handle(Request req, Runnable next); }
static void run(List<Stage> stages, Request req) {
    Runnable[] step = new Runnable[stages.size() + 1];
    step[stages.size()] = () -> {};                                           // end of chain
    for (int i = stages.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { int k = i; step[k] = () -> stages.get(k).handle(req, step[k + 1]); }
    step[0].run();
}
Interview angle: "How does Spring Security decide whether a request is authenticated?" A SecurityFilterChain bean is a Chain of Responsibility: filters like BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter try to authenticate; AuthorizationFilter at the end decides; ExceptionTranslationFilter catches and converts to 401/403. Ordering is the whole design, which is why addFilterBefore exists.

Pitfalls

  • Unhandled fallthrough: if no handler accepts, decide explicitly (default handler, exception, or Optional.empty()). Silent no-op is the classic bug.
  • Ordering by accident: rely on @Order/Ordered, not on classpath scanning order.
  • A handler that swallows exceptions from next hides failures downstream; filters must rethrow or translate deliberately.

Likely follow-ups

  • Chain vs Decorator? (Both pass calls along; Decorator always delegates and adds, Chain may stop and each link is a peer, not a wrapper.)
  • How do you unit test one filter? (Call it with a mock chain and assert whether chain.doFilter was invoked.)

Command, Iterator, State

Why interviewers ask: quick checks. Command via "how would you implement undo?", Iterator via "why ConcurrentModificationException?", State via "model an order lifecycle so invalid transitions are impossible".

Command turns a request into an object: Runnable/Callable submitted to an executor is a command; add undo() and keep a Deque for undo/redo; persist commands and you have an event log. Iterator decouples traversal from structure; JDK iterators are fail-fast: they record modCount at creation and throw ConcurrentModificationException on a best-effort basis if the collection changed underneath (remove via iterator.remove() or removeIf; CopyOnWriteArrayList/ConcurrentHashMap iterators are weakly consistent instead). State makes an object's behaviour depend on its state with each state as its own type; in Java 17 an enum with a transition method (or a sealed interface per state) keeps the rules in one place and makes illegal moves impossible to compile or throw immediately.

enum OrderState {
    NEW      { OrderState on(Event e) { return switch (e) { case PAY -> PAID; case CANCEL -> CANCELLED; default -> illegal(e); }; } },
    PAID     { OrderState on(Event e) { return switch (e) { case SHIP -> SHIPPED; case CANCEL -> CANCELLED; default -> illegal(e); }; } },
    SHIPPED  { OrderState on(Event e) { return e == Event.DELIVER ? DELIVERED : illegal(e); } },
    DELIVERED, CANCELLED;                                   // terminal: default on() throws
    enum Event { PAY, SHIP, DELIVER, CANCEL }
    OrderState on(Event e) { return illegal(e); }
    OrderState illegal(Event e) { throw new IllegalStateException(this + " cannot " + e); }
}

// Command with undo
interface Command { void execute(); void undo(); }
final class Editor {
    private final Deque<Command> done = new ArrayDeque<>();
    void run(Command c) { c.execute(); done.push(c); }
    void undo() { if (!done.isEmpty()) done.pop().undo(); }
}
PatternIntentJDKInterview probe
CommandRequest as an object: queue, log, undoRunnable, Callable, ExecutorService.submit, Swing ActionUndo stack; retry queue; the outbox pattern is persisted commands
IteratorTraverse without exposing structureIterator, Iterable (for-each), Spliterator, StreamFail-fast modCount; remove during iteration; weakly consistent iterators
StateBehaviour changes with internal stateThread.State (read-only), ReentrantLock/AQS internalsOrder/payment lifecycle; replace status-if chains

Pitfalls

  • Fail-fast is best-effort, not guaranteed: single-threaded list.remove(x) inside a for-each may or may not throw depending on position (removing the second-to-last element skips the check).
  • State stored as a String column and checked with equals in five services is the anemic version; centralise transitions in the domain type.
  • Undo needs commands to capture enough state to reverse; "undo delete" must keep the deleted object.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why does Iterator.remove() not throw? (It updates the iterator's expected modCount after the removal.)
  • State vs Strategy? (Identical structure; State transitions itself and the set is closed, Strategy is chosen externally.)

Object Pool & Flyweight

Why interviewers ask: "why pool connections but not StringBuilders?" checks whether you know what is expensive on the JVM today (I/O handshakes, threads) versus what is nearly free (small short-lived objects).

Object Pool reuses instances that are costly to create or limited by the outside world: DB connections (a TCP + TLS + auth handshake can cost 10-50 ms; HikariCP keeps, say, 10 warm and hands out proxies whose close() returns them), threads (ThreadPoolExecutor: creating an OS thread costs ~1 MB reserved stack and a syscall), HTTP connections (keep-alive pools in HttpClient/OkHttp), and large direct ByteBuffers (Netty's pooled allocator). Flyweight shares immutable intrinsic state so millions of logical objects are backed by few real ones: Integer.valueOf caches -128..127 (upper bound tunable with -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax), Boolean.TRUE, the String pool for literals and intern(), Character cache, enum constants, Font glyphs in Swing.

When pooling hurts: for small short-lived objects, allocation is a pointer bump in the thread-local allocation buffer (TLAB) and death in the young generation is free; a pool adds synchronisation, keeps objects alive into the old generation, and risks state leaking between users. Escape analysis may even scalar-replace the allocation entirely. Rule: pool for external resources and OS-level things; do not pool plain Java objects unless a profiler says so.

Integer a = 127, b = 127, c = 128, d = 128;
System.out.println(a == b);              // true  (cached flyweight, same reference)
System.out.println(c == d);              // false (two boxes) — always use equals()
String s1 = "java", s2 = "java", s3 = new String("java");
System.out.println(s1 == s2);            // true  (literal pool)
System.out.println(s1 == s3.intern());   // true  (interned into the pool)

// HikariCP in Spring Boot: pool sizing is a Little's-law question, not "as many as possible"
// spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=10   (cores * 2 + spindles is the usual starting point)
// spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=30000  (ms to wait for a free connection before failing)
ResourcePoolCost savedDanger if unbounded
DB connectionHikariCP, Tomcat JDBCHandshake ms, DB-side session memoryDB max_connections exhausted
ThreadThreadPoolExecutorStack allocation, OS schedulingOOM: unable to create native thread
HTTP connectionHttpClient, OkHttp, Apache HCTCP/TLS handshake, HTTP/2 multiplexingSocket exhaustion (TIME_WAIT)
Small objectsDo not poolNothing: TLAB bump allocationSlower + leaked state

Pitfalls

  • Leaking a pooled connection (no try-with-resources) starves the pool; Hikari's leakDetectionThreshold logs the stack trace of the borrower.
  • Pool size larger than DB cores often lowers throughput (context switching, lock contention on the DB). Measure.
  • String.intern() on high-cardinality data (user IDs) bloats the string table; it lives in native memory and is only worth it for a small repeated vocabulary.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why does Hikari hand out a proxy connection? (So close() returns to the pool and a closed proxy cannot be reused by the old holder: Proxy pattern again.)
  • Virtual threads and thread pools? (Java 21: do not pool virtual threads; they are cheap; pool the underlying resources instead.)

Java 21 preview

Virtual threads (JEP 444) invert the thread-pool advice: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() creates one per task; the pooling concern moves to the JDBC pool, which becomes the real concurrency limit.

Anti-patterns Interviewers Probe

Why interviewers ask: "tell me about a codebase you improved" is graded on whether you can name the smell, the cost, and the pattern that fixes it, in that order.

Patterns are the fixes; anti-patterns are the recurring diseases. The most-asked five: a God object that knows everything (one OrderService with 60 dependencies), an anemic domain model (entities are getter/setter bags and every rule lives in a service, so invariants are enforced nowhere), service locator (Registry.get(Mailer.class) hides dependencies and kills testability; DI makes them explicit), singleton abuse (global mutable state via getInstance(), shared across tests), and premature abstraction (IFooService + FooServiceImpl for one implementation, an abstract factory for one product, a plugin system nobody plugs into).

The refactoring vocabulary interviewers expect: Extract Class toward SRP, Replace Conditional with Polymorphism toward Strategy/State, Introduce Parameter Object toward Builder/records, Move Method from service into entity toward a rich domain model, Replace Constructor with Factory.

Anti-patternHow you spot itWhat it costsRefactor toward
God objectClass > 1000 lines, 15+ constructor args, every PR touches itMerge conflicts, untestable, one bug takes down all featuresSRP split by use case; Facade if callers need one entry; domain events to decouple
Anemic domain modelEntities with only getters/setters; OrderService.validate(order) everywhereInvariants duplicated and skipped; "how can status be SHIPPED with no address?"Move behaviour into the entity (order.ship()), State pattern, value objects as records
Service locatorServiceRegistry.get(X.class) inside methods; static ApplicationContext holderHidden dependencies, NPE at runtime instead of wiring error at startupConstructor injection; ObjectProvider<T> only for optional/lazy cases
Singleton abuseConfig.getInstance().set(...) in tests; order-dependent test failuresGlobal mutable state, test pollution, no per-tenant configurationContainer-managed singleton bean with immutable state; pass config as an object
Premature abstractionInterface with one impl, generic "framework" packages, AbstractBaseEntityManagerFactoryBeanIndirection tax on every read; abstraction shaped by guesswork, wrong when the 2nd impl arrivesRule of three: extract when the second concrete case exists; keep records/final classes until then
Boolean parameter explosionsend(msg, true, false, true)Unreadable call sites, combinatorial branchesBuilder, enums, or separate methods
Interview angle: "Is Spring's ApplicationContext.getBean() a service locator?" Yes, and that is why calling it from business code is discouraged: it works, but you lose compile-time wiring checks and make the class untestable without a container. Use it only at composition roots and in framework glue.

Pitfalls

  • Reflexively splitting a god class into OrderServiceA/B/C by size rather than by responsibility just distributes the mess.
  • Rich domain model does not mean entities call repositories; keep persistence out of the entity, put orchestration in an application service.
  • Naming a pattern you did not need ("we used Abstract Factory") is a red flag; explain the problem first, then the pattern.

Likely follow-ups

  • How do you refactor safely? (Characterisation tests first, small steps behind the same interface, strangler approach for large modules.)
  • When is a singleton fine? (Stateless or immutable, e.g. a Clock, a cache of immutable config; and still better as an injected bean.)

In double-checked locking, what does removing volatile from the INSTANCE field risk?

c. The reference store may be reordered before the constructor's field writes; a reader on the lock-free fast path can observe a half-built object. a is prevented by the second check under the lock, not by volatile. d is the tempting one: the lock protects only threads that enter it, and the fast path never does.

Which singleton variant is safe against both deserialization and reflection creating a second instance?

d. The JVM special-cases enums: deserialization resolves to the existing constant and Constructor.newInstance refuses enum types. a is the best plain-class option for laziness but a setAccessible constructor call still produces a second object.

A bean annotated @Transactional on saveAll() calls this.saveAll() from another public method of the same class. What happens?

b. Advice lives in the proxy; this is the raw target, so the interceptor never runs. d confuses the JDK-vs-CGLIB choice with self-invocation: both proxy types have the same limitation. Fix by moving the method to another bean or injecting a lazy self-reference.

Why can a JDK Proxy.newProxyInstance proxy not be injected into a field typed as the concrete class JdbcRepo?

a. Java has single inheritance and the proxy's superclass is already taken. That is exactly why Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB subclass proxies (proxy-target-class=true). b would be the CGLIB limitation, not the JDK one.

Collections.unmodifiableList(list) returns an object that implements List, holds the original, and throws on mutators. Which classification is most defensible?

c. Same interface plus access control is Proxy's intent; "decorator that subtracts" is also accepted. a is the common trap: Adapter requires two different interfaces, and here both sides are List.

What does this print?

List<String> l = Arrays.asList("a", "b");
l.set(0, "z");
l.add("c");
System.out.println(l);
b. Arrays.asList is an adapter over the array: set writes through (so c is wrong), but the array cannot grow, so add throws. List.of would throw on both.

A service has switch (paymentType) in four different methods and a new type is added every quarter. Best production refactor?

d. Open set, growing, four call sites: Strategy plus a registry means a new type is one new bean and zero edits (OCP). c is the tempting modern answer, but sealed types are for closed sets and still require editing every switch. b couples via inheritance and cannot be swapped at runtime.

Which of these should you generally NOT pool on a modern JVM?

a. Young-generation allocation is a TLAB pointer bump and short-lived garbage is free to collect; a pool adds locking, promotes objects to old gen, and can leak state between users. The other three wrap expensive OS or network resources with real limits.

Practice

Implement: thread-safe bounded cache with a pluggable eviction Strategy

Write Cache<K, V> with get(K), put(K, V), and a fixed capacity. Eviction must be a Strategy so LRU can be swapped for FIFO (or LFU) without touching the cache. The cache must be safe for concurrent callers. Then answer: what would you use in production instead?

interface EvictionPolicy<K> {
    void onAccess(K key);      // a hit on an existing key
    void onInsert(K key);      // a brand-new key was added
    void onRemove(K key);      // key removed (evicted or explicit)
    K victim();                // which key to evict next (null if none)
}
Tests: Strategy, encapsulation of ordering state, locking granularity Time: 25 min
Hint 1
Keep the data in a plain HashMap; keep the ordering in the policy. For LRU, a LinkedHashSet gives O(1) remove + re-add to the tail; its first element is the least recently used.
Hint 2
Both the map and the policy must change atomically, so one lock around each operation is the correct first answer. A ConcurrentHashMap alone does not help because the policy's state is not lock-free.
Reveal solution
final class LruPolicy<K> implements EvictionPolicy<K> {
    private final LinkedHashSet<K> order = new LinkedHashSet<>();     // head = LRU, tail = MRU
    public void onAccess(K k) { if (order.remove(k)) order.add(k); }
    public void onInsert(K k) { order.add(k); }
    public void onRemove(K k) { order.remove(k); }
    public K victim() { return order.isEmpty() ? null : order.iterator().next(); }
}
final class FifoPolicy<K> implements EvictionPolicy<K> {
    private final ArrayDeque<K> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    public void onAccess(K k) {}                                        // FIFO ignores hits
    public void onInsert(K k) { q.addLast(k); }
    public void onRemove(K k) { q.remove(k); }
    public K victim() { return q.peekFirst(); }
}

public final class Cache<K, V> {
    private final int capacity;
    private final Map<K, V> data = new HashMap<>();
    private final EvictionPolicy<K> policy;
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

    public Cache(int capacity, EvictionPolicy<K> policy) {
        if (capacity <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity");
        this.capacity = capacity; this.policy = Objects.requireNonNull(policy);
    }
    public Optional<V> get(K key) {
        lock.lock();
        try {
            V v = data.get(key);
            if (v != null) policy.onAccess(key);
            return Optional.ofNullable(v);
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
    public void put(K key, V value) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(value);
        lock.lock();
        try {
            if (data.put(key, value) != null) { policy.onAccess(key); return; }   // overwrite = hit
            policy.onInsert(key);
            if (data.size() > capacity) {
                K victim = policy.victim();
                data.remove(victim);
                policy.onRemove(victim);
            }
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
}
var cache = new Cache<String, byte[]>(1_000, new LruPolicy<>());

Why this shape. The cache owns storage and the invariant size ≤ capacity; the policy owns only the ordering. Swapping LruPolicy for FifoPolicy changes zero lines in Cache: that is the Strategy requirement. The single lock makes "update map + update policy" atomic; a ConcurrentHashMap would only protect half of the state.

Follow-up answers. (1) A shortcut for LRU only: new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) with removeEldestEntry overridden, wrapped in Collections.synchronizedMap; it is not pluggable. (2) Production: Caffeine (W-TinyLFU admission, striped buffers so reads do not contend on one lock, expireAfterWrite, async loading) via Spring @Cacheable with CaffeineCacheManager. (3) To reduce contention with this design: lock striping by key hash, or a ReadWriteLock does not help because get mutates the LRU order; Caffeine solves it by recording accesses in a lock-free ring buffer and replaying them.

Refactor: replace a god-class switch on type with Strategy + Factory

This class grows a new case in every method whenever a payment method is added, and the product team has three more planned. Refactor so that adding a method touches no existing class. Keep it Spring-friendly.

@Service
public class PaymentService {
    public BigDecimal fee(String type, BigDecimal amt) {
        switch (type) {
            case "CARD":   return amt.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.02"));
            case "UPI":    return BigDecimal.ZERO;
            case "WALLET": return amt.compareTo(new BigDecimal("1000")) > 0 ? new BigDecimal("5") : BigDecimal.ZERO;
            default: throw new IllegalArgumentException(type);
        }
    }
    public void pay(String type, BigDecimal amt) {
        switch (type) { case "CARD": cardGateway.charge(amt); break; case "UPI": upi.collect(amt); break; /* ... */ }
    }
    public String receipt(String type, BigDecimal amt) {
        switch (type) { case "CARD": return "Card ****" + last4; case "UPI": return "UPI " + vpa; /* ... */ default: return ""; }
    }
}
Tests: OCP, Replace Conditional with Polymorphism, Spring collection injection Time: 20 min
Hint 1
The three switches all branch on the same key: that is one missing type. Every case label across the three methods becomes one method on one class.
Hint 2
The "factory" is a map from key to strategy. Let Spring build the list of implementations; the service builds the map in its constructor and fails fast on duplicates.
Reveal solution
public interface PaymentMethod {
    String key();                                   // "CARD", "UPI", ...
    BigDecimal fee(BigDecimal amt);
    void pay(BigDecimal amt);
    String receipt(BigDecimal amt);
}

@Component
class CardPayment implements PaymentMethod {
    private final CardGateway gateway;
    CardPayment(CardGateway gateway) { this.gateway = gateway; }      // each strategy owns its own deps
    public String key() { return "CARD"; }
    public BigDecimal fee(BigDecimal amt) { return amt.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.02")); }
    public void pay(BigDecimal amt) { gateway.charge(amt); }
    public String receipt(BigDecimal amt) { return "Card ****" + gateway.last4(); }
}
@Component
class UpiPayment implements PaymentMethod { /* key() = "UPI", fee = ZERO, ... */ }

@Component
class PaymentMethodFactory {                                          // Factory = registry map
    private final Map<String, PaymentMethod> byKey;
    PaymentMethodFactory(List<PaymentMethod> methods) {
        byKey = methods.stream().collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableMap(PaymentMethod::key, m -> m)); // dup key → startup failure
    }
    PaymentMethod forType(String type) {
        var m = byKey.get(type);
        if (m == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown payment type: " + type);
        return m;
    }
}

@Service
public class PaymentService {                                         // now stable: no switch anywhere
    private final PaymentMethodFactory factory;
    PaymentService(PaymentMethodFactory factory) { this.factory = factory; }
    public BigDecimal fee(String type, BigDecimal amt) { return factory.forType(type).fee(amt); }
    public void pay(String type, BigDecimal amt) { factory.forType(type).pay(amt); }
    public String receipt(String type, BigDecimal amt) { return factory.forType(type).receipt(amt); }
}

What changed and why. The three switches were three views of one missing abstraction. Each former case label is now a cohesive class with its own dependencies (SRP), and adding CryptoPayment is a new @Component with no edits elsewhere (OCP). PaymentService depends on the interface and the factory (DIP). Unit tests can construct PaymentMethodFactory with a list of fakes: no Spring context needed.

Points to raise in the interview. Keying by key() rather than by Spring bean name keeps domain vocabulary out of class names. If the set of methods were truly closed by law (say, exactly 3 forever), a sealed interface with exhaustive switch expressions is a legitimate alternative, but the prompt says it is growing, so Strategy wins. If some methods are unavailable per region, replace the map lookup with a first-match chain (supports(request)), which is Chain of Responsibility.

Scenario: which pattern? Five rapid-fire cases

For each scenario name the pattern, one JDK or Spring example, and the one-line reason. Say the alternative you rejected if two patterns look similar.

  1. Every call to an external HttpClientPort must retry 3 times with exponential backoff; the call sites must not change.
  2. An HttpRequest has 2 required and 9 optional fields (headers, timeouts, body, auth). Constructing one is error-prone.
  3. When an order is placed, inventory, email, and analytics must all react, and more reactors will be added without touching the order code.
  4. A vendor's legacy SOAP client exposes doCharge(String amount, String ccy); your code is written against PaymentGateway.charge(Money).
  5. Every incoming API request must pass authentication, then rate limiting, then request validation; any step can reject the request.
Tests: Recognising intent, not UML shape Time: 10 min
Hint 1
Ask two questions per scenario: "same interface or different?" and "am I adding behaviour, controlling access, creating, or notifying?"
Reveal solution
#PatternExampleWhy (and what you rejected)
1Decorator (a Proxy is also accepted)Resilience4j Retry.decorateSupplier; Spring Retry's proxy for @RetryableSame interface, wraps the target, adds behaviour, call sites untouched. Decorator if you compose it explicitly; Proxy if the framework injects it transparently. Rejected Chain: there is no list of peers deciding.
2BuilderHttpRequest.newBuilder().uri(u).timeout(d).header(k, v).build()Many optional parts, validation at build(), immutable result. Rejected telescoping constructors and setters (mutable, no validation point).
3ObserverSpring ApplicationEventPublisher + @EventListener / @TransactionalEventListenerOne subject, many independent reactors added without editing the subject. Rejected Chain (reactors do not stop each other) and Strategy (all run, not one).
4AdapterArrays.asList, InputStreamReader; a LegacyPaymentAdapter implements PaymentGatewayTwo different interfaces must be reconciled. Rejected Facade: you are not simplifying a subsystem, you are translating one call.
5Chain of ResponsibilityServlet Filter chain, Spring Security SecurityFilterChain, HandlerInterceptorOrdered handlers, each may pass on or short-circuit. Rejected Decorator: handlers are peers with an order, not layers around one target, and rejection ends the pipeline.

Bonus scenarios interviewers add: "one instance of a config loader" (Singleton, ideally as a Spring bean or enum); "walk a tree without exposing its nodes" (Iterator); "queue user actions and support undo" (Command); "order status rules scattered across services" (State); "hide JDBC boilerplate" (Facade + Template: JdbcTemplate); "thousands of identical map tiles" (Flyweight).

9️⃣ I/O, NIO & Serialization

Every service reads files, sockets, or both, and most production incidents in this area are the same three bugs: an unclosed stream, a missing charset, and "why does my thread-per-request server fall over at 5k connections?". The path here is streams → the modern Files API → how NIO multiplexes sockets with one thread → the ByteBuffer dance behind it → what frameworks build on top → Java serialization and why you mostly avoid it → the charset rules that make the first bug disappear.

Byte Streams vs Character Streams (and the Decorator Stack)

Why interviewers ask: the byte/char split plus the decorator design is the whole of java.io; if you know which class sits where, you can explain the "garbled accented characters" bug and the "unclosed file handle" bug in one breath.

java.io has two parallel hierarchies. Byte streams (InputStream/OutputStream) move raw 8-bit bytes: files, sockets, images, zip entries. Character streams (Reader/Writer) move 16-bit chars and exist only so text decoding happens in exactly one place. The two are joined by bridges: InputStreamReader and OutputStreamWriter, which take a Charset. Analogy: bytes are the shipping container; a Reader is the customs officer who knows which language the labels are written in.

Everything else is the Decorator pattern: you wrap a raw stream in layers that add behavior. BufferedInputStream/BufferedReader add an internal buffer (8 KB by default in OpenJDK, check your JDK) so a file is read in large chunks instead of one syscall per byte. DataInputStream adds readInt()/readUTF() for binary protocols; ObjectInputStream adds Java serialization; GZIPInputStream adds decompression. Closing the outermost wrapper closes the whole chain.

The #1 bug: new InputStreamReader(in) without a charset uses the platform default, which on Java 8–17 varies per OS and per LANG setting. A file written on a UTF-8 Linux box and read on a Windows-1252 JVM produces mojibake. Always pass StandardCharsets.UTF_8 explicitly.

// Text: bytes → decoded chars → buffered lines. One charset, one close.
try (var reader = new BufferedReader(
        new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream("orders.csv"), StandardCharsets.UTF_8))) {
    String line;
    while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {
        process(line);
    }
} // try-with-resources closes reader → InputStreamReader → FileInputStream

// Binary: copy a stream without ever decoding it (Java 9+ transferTo)
try (InputStream in = socket.getInputStream();
     OutputStream out = new BufferedOutputStream(new FileOutputStream("upload.bin"))) {
    in.transferTo(out);
}
LayerByte sideCharacter sideAdds
Source/sinkFileInputStream, Socket.getInputStream(), ByteArrayInputStreamFileReader (avoid: no charset before Java 11), StringReaderWhere bytes/chars come from
BridgeInputStreamReader(in, charset) / OutputStreamWriter(out, charset)Decoding/encoding, exactly once
BufferingBufferedInputStreamBufferedReader (readLine, lines())Fewer syscalls; line reading
Typed dataDataInputStream, ObjectInputStreamPrintWriter (printf, never throws IOException)Primitives / objects / formatted text
TransformGZIPInputStream, CipherInputStream—Compression, encryption
Interview angle: "Why is reading a 1 GB file with FileInputStream.read() in a loop slow?" Each unbuffered read() is a native call; wrap in BufferedInputStream or read into a byte[8192] yourself. "What happens if you forget close()?" The OS file descriptor stays open until the object is finalized/GC'd; under load you hit Too many open files (ulimit, often 1024) long before GC runs.

Pitfalls

  • FileReader/FileWriter before Java 11 have no charset parameter at all; use the bridge classes or Files.newBufferedReader(path, UTF_8).
  • Reading bytes one at a time as char ((char) in.read()) silently breaks any non-ASCII text; multibyte UTF-8 sequences must go through a Reader.
  • PrintWriter swallows IOException; you must call checkError() to know a write failed.
  • Flushing: a BufferedOutputStream that is closed via try-with-resources flushes; one that is abandoned after an exception may lose its last 8 KB.

Likely follow-ups

  • Which design pattern is java.io? (Decorator; each wrapper extends the same abstract base and delegates to the wrapped instance.)
  • Difference between flush() and close()? (flush pushes buffered data down the chain; close flushes then releases the OS handle.)
  • How do you read a classpath resource? (getClass().getResourceAsStream("/x.txt") returns an InputStream; it is a jar entry, not a File.)

java.nio.file: Files & Path (the API you should actually use)

Why interviewers ask: writing new File(...) in 2024 signals Java 6 habits. Files/Path give one-liners for the common cases and lazy streams for the big ones, and the "must close Files.lines" detail is a favorite gotcha.

Path (create with Path.of("a", "b.txt") since Java 11, or Paths.get) is an immutable, OS-independent path value; Files is the static utility class that does the I/O. Small files: Files.readString(path) and Files.writeString(path, text) (Java 11, UTF-8 by default) and Files.readAllLines/readAllBytes load everything into memory. Large files: Files.newBufferedReader(path, UTF_8) and Files.lines(path) stream lazily. Analogy: readString is bringing the whole box home; lines is reading one letter at a time at the post office.

Files.lines returns a Stream<String> backed by an open file handle: it is one of the few streams you must close, so put it in try-with-resources. Files.walk(dir) is the same for directory trees (depth-first, lazy). Files.move(src, dst, ATOMIC_MOVE) renames atomically on the same filesystem, the standard trick for "write to a temp file then publish". WatchService registers a directory for ENTRY_CREATE/MODIFY/DELETE events (inotify on Linux, polling on macOS, so latency differs).

Path dir = Path.of("/var/data");
Path cfg = dir.resolve("app.yml");

String yaml = Files.readString(cfg);                       // UTF-8 default (11+)
Files.writeString(dir.resolve("out.txt"), "hello\n",
        StandardOpenOption.CREATE, StandardOpenOption.APPEND);

// lazy: the file is opened here and closed by try-with-resources
try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(dir.resolve("big.log"), StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {
    long errors = lines.filter(l -> l.contains("ERROR")).count();
}

try (Stream<Path> tree = Files.walk(dir)) {
    List<Path> jars = tree.filter(p -> p.toString().endsWith(".jar")).toList();
}

// publish atomically: readers see either the old file or the complete new one
Path tmp = Files.createTempFile(dir, "cfg", ".tmp");
Files.writeString(tmp, newYaml);
Files.move(tmp, cfg, StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
NeedUseMemoryClose?
Whole small text fileFiles.readString / readAllLinesEntire fileNo
Whole small binary fileFiles.readAllBytesEntire fileNo
Line-by-line, any sizeFiles.lines / newBufferedReaderOne buffer (8 KB) + current lineYes
Directory treeFiles.walk / Files.findOpen dir handles per depthYes
Random access / huge binaryFileChannel + MappedByteBufferOS page cacheYes
Real world: config hot-reload = WatchService on the config directory + atomic move by the writer, so the reader never parses a half-written file. Log shipping = Files.lines with a filter, never readAllLines on a 20 GB log.

Pitfalls

  • Files.lines(path) outside try-with-resources leaks a file descriptor per call; the stream's close() is what closes the file.
  • Files.walk follows no symlinks by default and throws UncheckedIOException mid-stream on an unreadable directory; catch it or use Files.walkFileTree with a visitor for control.
  • ATOMIC_MOVE across filesystems (e.g. /tmp on tmpfs to /var) throws AtomicMoveNotSupportedException: create the temp file in the target directory.

Likely follow-ups

  • File vs Path? (File returns booleans on failure and has no symlink/attribute support; Path throws specific IOExceptions and works with any FileSystem, including zip files.)
  • Is Files.lines parallel-friendly? (Yes since Java 9 it splits by byte ranges for files, but order is not preserved with parallel().)

Java 8 vs 17

Files.readString/writeString and Path.of arrived in Java 11; InputStream.readAllBytes/transferTo in 9. On Java 8 you use new String(Files.readAllBytes(p), UTF_8) and Paths.get.

Blocking I/O vs NIO: One Thread, Many Connections

Why interviewers ask: this is the mechanism behind Netty, Tomcat's NIO connector, Kafka's network layer, and every "how would you handle 100k idle websocket connections" system-design follow-up. Knowing why a selector scales where threads do not is the whole point.

Blocking I/O (ServerSocket.accept() then socket.getInputStream().read()) parks the calling thread until data arrives. To serve N clients you need N threads (thread-per-connection). Each platform thread costs a stack (1 MB reserved by default, -Xss) and a kernel scheduling slot, so 10k mostly-idle connections means 10k mostly-parked threads and heavy context switching. Analogy: one waiter standing at each table staring at the customer until they order.

NIO (Java 1.4, java.nio.channels) flips it: a SocketChannel can be non-blocking (configureBlocking(false)), so read() returns immediately with 0 bytes if nothing is there. You register many channels with one Selector, saying which event you care about (OP_ACCEPT, OP_READ, OP_WRITE, OP_CONNECT). selector.select() blocks once, on behalf of all of them, and returns the set of SelectionKeys that are ready. Under the hood it is epoll on Linux / kqueue on macOS: the kernel tells you which sockets have data instead of you asking each one. One waiter watching the whole room, walking only to tables that raise a hand.

The pattern is the readiness loop (the "Reactor" pattern): select → iterate ready keys → for each, do a short non-blocking read/write → back to select. The one rule that makes it work: never block inside the loop. A slow database call in a handler stalls every connection on that selector, which is why Netty gives you separate event-loop groups and why "don't block the event loop" is a mantra in WebFlux.

Blocking I/O (java.io)NIO (java.nio)
UnitStream (one direction)Channel (bidirectional) + Buffer
Threads for N idle connsN1 selector thread (plus a small worker pool)
Wait mechanismThread blocked in read()One thread blocked in select() (epoll/kqueue)
Code complexityLinear, easyState machine per connection, partial reads
Best forFew connections, CPU-bound handlers, or virtual threadsMany mostly-idle connections (chat, push, proxies)
Interview angle: "Tomcat is blocking, right?" No: since Tomcat 8 the default connector is NIO. A few poller threads run selectors; when a request is fully readable it is handed to the worker pool (server.tomcat.threads.max, 200 by default) where your blocking servlet/Spring MVC code runs. So Spring MVC still needs one thread per in-flight request, but not per idle keep-alive connection.

Pitfalls

  • Forgetting iterator.remove() on selectedKeys() makes the same key look ready forever.
  • Registering OP_WRITE permanently: a socket is almost always writable, so the loop spins at 100% CPU. Register it only while you have pending output, then deregister.
  • One read() rarely gives you a whole message. You must accumulate into a per-connection buffer and parse by length prefix or delimiter.
  • Blocking inside the handler (JDBC call, Thread.sleep) freezes every channel on that selector.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is the C10K problem? (Serving 10k concurrent connections; thread-per-connection hits memory and scheduler limits, multiplexing solves it.)
  • Is NIO faster for a single connection? (No; often slightly slower. It wins on scalability, not latency.)
  • How does Netty avoid the single-loop bottleneck? (A boss group accepts, N worker event loops each own a selector; each channel is pinned to one loop so handlers need no locks.)

Java 21 preview

Virtual threads (JEP 444) make thread-per-connection cheap again: a blocked virtual thread unmounts from its carrier, and the JDK's socket implementation uses a hidden poller (epoll) internally. You write blocking java.io code and get NIO-like scalability; the selector stays relevant for frameworks and for zero-copy paths.

ByteBuffer Mechanics: position / limit / capacity, flip, direct & mapped

Why interviewers ask: "why do you call flip()?" is the quickest way to check whether someone has used NIO or only read about it, and direct vs heap buffers leads into off-heap memory and zero-copy, which matter for Kafka, Netty and gRPC.

A ByteBuffer is a byte[] (or an off-heap block) plus three cursors: capacity (fixed size), position (next index to read/write), limit (first index that must not be touched). Invariant: 0 ≤ position ≤ limit ≤ capacity. The same buffer is used for writing into it (channel reads, put) and reading out of it (get, channel writes); flip() switches from the first mode to the second by setting limit = position; position = 0. Analogy: you write on a tape, then rewind to the start and stop the tape at the last thing you wrote.

After reading out, clear() resets to an empty write mode (position 0, limit = capacity) without erasing bytes; compact() moves the unread bytes to the front and positions after them, which is what you want when a channel read gave you half a message. rewind() sets position 0 keeping limit; mark()/reset() bookmark a position.

Heap buffers (allocate) wrap a byte[]; a socket write copies them to a temporary native buffer because the GC may move the array. Direct buffers (allocateDirect) live in native memory, skip that copy, and are the right choice for long-lived I/O buffers, but they are expensive to allocate and freed only when the wrapper is GC'd (bounded by -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize). FileChannel.map() gives a MappedByteBuffer: the file's pages become your buffer via mmap, so reads are page-cache hits with no syscall. FileChannel.transferTo(pos, count, socketChannel) is zero-copy: on Linux it becomes sendfile, moving file bytes to the socket inside the kernel without ever entering user space, which is how Kafka serves consumers.

ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocate(8);        // capacity 8

buf.put((byte) 'H').put((byte) 'i').put((byte) '!');

buf.flip();                                      // switch to read mode

byte b1 = buf.get();                             // 'H'
byte b2 = buf.get();                             // 'i'

buf.compact();                                   // keep unread '!' at front

buf.put((byte) '?');                             // append after '!'

buf.clear();                                     // ready to fill from scratch
  1. allocate(8): position 0, limit = capacity = 8. Ready to be written into.
  2. Three puts advance position to 3. Limit is still 8: a get() now would read garbage at index 3.
  3. flip() fences the readable region: limit becomes 3, position rewinds to 0. This is the step people forget, then wonder why channel.write(buf) sends 0 bytes or 8 bytes of junk.
  4. Two gets move position to 2. remaining() (limit − position) is 1: the unread '!'.
  5. compact() copies the unread byte to the front and sets position just after it, limit back to capacity. Old bytes at 1..2 are stale but harmless. This is the idiom after a partial protocol read.
  6. New data is appended after the leftover, so a subsequent flip() yields !? in order. Nothing was lost.
  7. clear() resets the cursors only. The bytes are still there; the next put overwrites them. Use clear() when you have consumed everything, compact() when you have not.
// Typical channel read/write loop with one buffer per connection
ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(64 * 1024);     // long-lived → direct
int n = channel.read(buf);                                 // fills from position to limit
if (n == -1) { channel.close(); return; }
buf.flip();                                                // read mode
while (buf.hasRemaining() && tryParseOneMessage(buf)) { /* handle */ }
buf.compact();                                             // keep the partial tail

// Zero-copy file → socket (Linux: sendfile)
try (FileChannel file = FileChannel.open(path, StandardOpenOption.READ)) {
    long pos = 0, size = file.size();
    while (pos < size) pos += file.transferTo(pos, size - pos, socketChannel);
}
Heap (allocate)Direct (allocateDirect)Mapped (FileChannel.map)
Backed bybyte[] on Java heapmalloc-style native memoryOS page cache (mmap)
Socket/file I/OExtra copy to a native bufferWritten directly by the kernelNo read syscalls at all
Allocation costCheap (TLAB)Expensive; pool themExpensive; map once
Freed byGCGC of the wrapper (Cleaner); -XX:MaxDirectMemorySizeUnmap on GC; no explicit unmap API before Java 22
Use forShort-lived parsingNetty/HTTP buffers, per-connection buffersHuge files, random access, IPC (Chronicle, LMDB)
Interview angle: "Kafka claims zero-copy: what does that mean?" A consumer fetch is served with FileChannel.transferTo from the log segment to the socket; the data goes page cache → NIC via sendfile with no copy into the JVM heap, which is why a broker can push several GB/s while its heap stays small. (With TLS enabled the kernel must hand bytes to user space for encryption, so zero-copy is lost.)

Pitfalls

  • Writing a buffer to a channel without flip() sends the empty region between position and limit, usually zero bytes, with no error.
  • OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory under load: direct buffers are released only when their Java wrapper is collected; if the heap is roomy, GC rarely runs and native memory piles up. Pool buffers (Netty's PooledByteBufAllocator) instead of allocating per request.
  • Byte order: ByteBuffer defaults to big-endian; reading a little-endian binary format needs buf.order(ByteOrder.LITTLE_ENDIAN).
  • Mapping a file you then truncate causes a SIGBUS-style JVM crash (InternalError), not an exception.

Likely follow-ups

  • flip() vs rewind()? (rewind only resets position; flip also sets limit to the old position.)
  • Why does String.getBytes() plus ByteBuffer.wrap not need flip? (wrap creates a buffer already in read mode: position 0, limit = array length.)
  • Where does the Foreign Function & Memory API fit? (Java 22's MemorySegment replaces direct buffers with explicit, deterministic deallocation via Arena.)

NIO.2 Async Channels & Why Netty / Tomcat / WebFlux Exist

Why interviewers ask: the practical question is "Spring MVC or WebFlux for this service?", and the honest answer depends on knowing what each runs on: a thread pool fed by Tomcat's NIO poller, or Netty's event loops.

Java 7's NIO.2 added asynchronous channels: AsynchronousFileChannel and AsynchronousSocketChannel. Instead of a readiness loop you start an operation and get either a Future<Integer> or a callback (CompletionHandler.completed/failed) run on a hidden thread pool (AsynchronousChannelGroup). It is a Proactor rather than Reactor model. For files this is the only truly async option in the JDK (regular FileChannel is not selectable); for sockets almost nobody uses it directly, because the raw selector API is verbose and the async API's threading is hard to reason about.

That gap is why Netty exists: an opinionated selector loop (NioEventLoopGroup, or epoll native transport), pooled direct buffers (ByteBuf with reference counting), and a ChannelPipeline of handlers for framing, TLS, HTTP/2. It underpins gRPC-java, Reactor Netty, Vert.x, Cassandra's driver, Elasticsearch transport. Tomcat solved the same problem for the servlet world: its NIO connector uses poller threads with selectors to wait for request bytes, then dispatches each complete request to a bounded worker thread pool, where your blocking servlet code runs.

So in Spring MVC (Tomcat NIO + thread pool) a request occupies a worker thread for its whole duration, including while it waits on JDBC or a downstream HTTP call; throughput is capped near threads.max / avg latency. In Spring WebFlux (Reactor Netty) a handful of event-loop threads (default = CPU cores) run non-blocking handlers, and a request holds no thread while waiting on a reactive client (R2DBC, WebClient). It wins when the service is I/O-bound fan-out with many concurrent slow calls; it loses when you have any blocking call in the path (JDBC, JPA, a synchronous SDK), which you must hoist onto Schedulers.boundedElastic() or you stall the loop.

// NIO.2 async file read with a callback (rarely written by hand, but know the shape)
try (var ch = AsynchronousFileChannel.open(path, StandardOpenOption.READ)) {
    ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocate(4096);
    ch.read(buf, 0, buf, new CompletionHandler<Integer, ByteBuffer>() {
        public void completed(Integer bytes, ByteBuffer b) { b.flip(); handle(b); }
        public void failed(Throwable t, ByteBuffer b) { log.error("read failed", t); }
    });
    // caller thread is free; completed() runs on the channel group pool
}
Spring MVC (Tomcat NIO)Spring WebFlux (Reactor Netty)
Waiting for bytes on socketPoller thread + selector (no worker used)Event loop + selector
Running your handlerWorker pool, 200 threads by default; blocking is fineEvent loop threads (= cores); blocking is forbidden
Waiting on DB / downstreamThread parked (JDBC, RestTemplate)No thread held (R2DBC, WebClient)
Max in-flight requests≈ worker threadsBounded by memory, not threads
DebuggabilityStack traces make senseAssembly-time traces; needs checkpoint()/BlockHound
Pick whenCRUD over JDBC/JPA, moderate concurrency, team familiarityAPI gateway, SSE/websocket push, high fan-out to slow services
Interview angle (system design): "We have 20k concurrent mobile clients holding long-polling connections to a Spring MVC service; CPU is idle but it stops responding." Tomcat's 200 workers are all parked in the long-poll wait. Options: async servlet (DeferredResult/SseEmitter release the worker), WebFlux, or Java 21 virtual threads (spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true) so parking is cheap.

Pitfalls

  • Calling a blocking JDBC repository from a WebFlux controller works in tests and collapses under load: every event loop thread ends up parked in the driver.
  • Mixing: spring-boot-starter-web plus spring-boot-starter-webflux on one classpath silently runs MVC on Tomcat; WebFlux annotations still work but you get none of the non-blocking benefit.
