  • Netty ByteBuf is reference counted; forgetting release() in a handler leaks direct memory (enable -Dio.netty.leakDetection.level=paranoid in tests).

Likely follow-ups

  • Reactor vs Proactor? (Reactor: notified when ready, you do the read. Proactor: you submit the read, notified when done. Selector is Reactor; NIO.2 async and Windows IOCP are Proactor.)
  • Does WebFlux use fewer threads than MVC for CPU-bound work? (Yes, but it is no faster; the benefit is only for I/O waits.)
  • What does server.tomcat.max-connections (default 8192) limit vs threads.max? (Open sockets held by the poller vs concurrently executing requests.)

Java Serialization: Serializable, serialVersionUID, transient, and Why You Mostly Avoid It

Why interviewers ask: it is still everywhere under the hood (HTTP session replication, RMI, Hazelcast/Ehcache defaults, Spring Security's SecurityContext in sessions) and it has been the root of the worst Java CVEs. The interviewer probes whether you know the rules and the risks.

Serializable is a marker interface: ObjectOutputStream.writeObject walks the object graph reflectively and writes every non-static, non-transient field of every Serializable class in the hierarchy. Static fields belong to the class, not the instance, so they are never written; transient fields are skipped and come back as their defaults (null/0/false). A non-serializable superclass is handled by calling its no-arg constructor on deserialization; a serializable class's own constructor is not called. Analogy: a photo of a room: you get the furniture, not the lights that were on (statics) or the sticky notes you marked "do not copy" (transient).

serialVersionUID is a version stamp checked on read. If you do not declare it the JVM computes one from the class's shape (fields, methods, modifiers), so a harmless refactor like adding a method changes it and every stored/blob/cached instance fails with InvalidClassException. Declare private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L; and bump it only on incompatible changes. You can hook the process with private void writeObject(ObjectOutputStream) / readObject(ObjectInputStream) (call defaultWriteObject() then add extras, e.g. re-derive a transient cache), replace the deserialized instance with readResolve() (the classic way to keep a singleton a singleton), or take full control with Externalizable (public no-arg constructor required, you write every field).

The security problem: readObject instantiates whatever class name is in the byte stream, as long as it is on the classpath. Attackers chain existing library classes whose readObject/hashCode/toString do something dangerous ("gadget chains", e.g. Commons-Collections InvokerTransformer) into remote code execution. Java 9 added ObjectInputFilter (allow/deny lists by class name, depth, array size) and Java 17 lets you set a JVM-wide filter factory; Java 21 disables serialization of some risky JDK internals. In practice: never deserialize untrusted bytes, prefer JSON (Jackson) or Protobuf/Avro for wire formats, and if you must use Java serialization, set a filter. Records (Java 16) serialize cleanly: their state is restored through the canonical constructor, so invariants are re-validated and readObject tricks do not apply.

public final class Session implements Serializable {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 3L;   // declare it; bump on incompatible change
    private static int liveCount;                      // static: never serialized
    private final String userId;
    private transient Cache cache;                     // rebuilt on read, not written

    private void readObject(ObjectInputStream in) throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException {
        in.defaultReadObject();                        // restore userId
        cache = Cache.forUser(userId);                 // re-derive transient state
    }
}

// Only accept what you expect (Java 9+): allow our package, reject everything else
ObjectInputFilter filter = ObjectInputFilter.Config.createFilter(
        "com.acme.session.*;java.base/*;!*;maxdepth=10");
try (var in = new ObjectInputStream(bytes)) {
    in.setObjectInputFilter(filter);
    Session s = (Session) in.readObject();
}
MechanismWhat it doesTypical use
transientField skipped; default value on readCaches, sockets, passwords, non-serializable members
writeObject/readObjectPrivate hooks around default (de)serializationRe-derive transient state, validate, encrypt a field
readResolve()Returns a replacement instance after readSingletons, enums (built-in), canonical instances
ExternalizableYou write/read every field; public no-arg ctor calledCompact custom formats, performance
ObjectInputFilterReject classes/depth/size before instantiationAny deserialization of data you did not just write
Interview angle: "Your Spring Boot app stores User in the HTTP session on Redis; after a deploy every user is logged out with InvalidClassException. Why?" No explicit serialVersionUID, the class changed, the computed UID no longer matches the bytes in Redis. Fix: declare the UID, or better, store JSON in the session (GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer).

Pitfalls

  • Referencing a non-Serializable field (a Logger, a Connection) throws NotSerializableException at write time; mark it transient or make it static.
  • Enums serialize by name only; readResolve is implicit. Singletons implemented as classes without readResolve yield a second instance after deserialization.
  • Serialization exposes private fields as a public API: the stream format is now something you must keep compatible.
  • ObjectInputStream without a filter on network input is a remote-code-execution surface (Log4Shell's JNDI vector ended in deserialization too).

Likely follow-ups

  • Is a serializable subclass of a non-serializable parent OK? (Yes, if the parent has an accessible no-arg constructor; its fields are re-initialized by that constructor, not restored.)
  • Why does Jackson not need Serializable? (It uses getters/fields and creates objects through constructors; no bytecode-level class resolution from the stream.)
  • What about Serializable lambdas? (Only if the target interface is serializable; captured variables must be too. Rarely a good idea.)

Java 8 vs 17

ObjectInputFilter is Java 9 (backported to 8u121). Java 17 added ObjectInputFilter.Config.setSerialFilterFactory for per-stream, context-aware filters. Records (16) always deserialize via the canonical constructor.

Charsets & Encodings: file.encoding, getBytes(), BOM, and String memory

Why interviewers ask: encoding bugs are the ones that only appear in production on the one Windows box or the one container without LANG set. They also want to know you understand a String is chars, not bytes.

A String is a sequence of UTF-16 code units; bytes only exist at the boundary (file, socket, getBytes()), and a Charset defines the mapping. UTF-8 is variable-width (1 byte ASCII, 2–4 bytes otherwise) and is the de facto standard for files, JSON, HTTP. ISO-8859-1/Windows-1252 are single-byte and silently corrupt anything outside Western Europe. UTF-16 is what char is; surrogate pairs mean "😀".length() == 2 while codePointCount is 1.

The trap is the default charset. Up to Java 17, Charset.defaultCharset() comes from the OS locale (file.encoding): UTF-8 on modern Linux/macOS, but Cp1252 on Windows and often ANSI_X3.4-1968 (ASCII) in minimal Docker images with no locale. Every overload without an explicit charset (new String(bytes), str.getBytes(), new FileReader, new InputStreamReader(in), new PrintStream(out)) uses it. JEP 400 (Java 18) made UTF-8 the default everywhere; on Java 17 you get the same by starting the JVM with -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8, or just always passing StandardCharsets.UTF_8.

A BOM (byte order mark, EF BB BF for UTF-8) is what Windows Notepad and Excel prepend; Java's UTF-8 decoder does not strip it, so the first field of a CSV becomes "\uFEFFid" and your header check fails. Memory: since Java 9 compact strings store Latin-1-only strings as 1 byte per char and everything else as 2 bytes, so an ASCII 1 M-char string is ~1 MB, not 2 MB.

String s = "café";
System.out.println(s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8).length);       // 5  (é = 2 bytes)
System.out.println(s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.ISO_8859_1).length);  // 4
System.out.println(s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_16).length);      // 10 (2-byte BOM + 4 chars × 2)

byte[] utf8 = s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
String wrong = new String(utf8, StandardCharsets.ISO_8859_1);        // "cafÃ©"  ← classic mojibake
String right = new String(utf8, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);             // "café"

// Java 17: what is the JVM using right now? (Java 18+: always UTF-8)
System.out.println(Charset.defaultCharset());
// Strip a UTF-8 BOM defensively when reading user-uploaded CSV
if (line.startsWith("\uFEFF")) line = line.substring(1);
CharsetBytes per charCoversNotes
US-ASCII1128 charsDefault in many bare containers on Java ≤17: non-ASCII becomes ?
ISO-8859-11Western EuropeNever fails to decode, which is why corruption is silent
UTF-81–4All of UnicodeASCII-compatible; use it unless a spec says otherwise
UTF-162 or 4All of UnicodeJava's in-memory char; getBytes(UTF_16) adds a BOM
Real world: a service passes tests on macOS, then in the eclipse-temurin:17-jre image customer names come out as ???. The image has no LANG, the default charset is ASCII, and new String(body) in a legacy helper decoded the request with it. Fix: pass the charset, or add -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 (or ENV LANG=C.UTF-8) to the image; upgrading to 18+ fixes it structurally.

Pitfalls

  • String.length() is UTF-16 units, not characters or bytes: never use it to size a byte buffer or to validate a DB VARCHAR(n) in bytes.
  • new String(bytes, 0, n) on a chunk that ends mid-multibyte sequence corrupts the boundary; decode through a Reader or CharsetDecoder that keeps state across chunks.
  • System.out uses stdout.encoding (Java 19+) / the console charset, so printing looks fine in an IDE and wrong in a terminal, or vice versa.
  • HTTP: Content-Type: application/json is UTF-8 by spec, but text/plain without charset= is not; set it explicitly on responses.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why is UTF-8 ASCII-compatible and UTF-16 not? (UTF-8 encodes 0–127 as the same single byte; UTF-16 uses 2 bytes for everything.)
  • How do you count real characters? (codePointCount, or BreakIterator for grapheme clusters like flags and combined emoji.)
  • Does -XX:-CompactStrings exist? (Yes, it disables the Latin-1 optimization; almost never needed.)

Java 18+

JEP 400: Charset.defaultCharset() is UTF-8 on every platform; -Dfile.encoding=COMPAT restores the old behavior. Java 19 split out stdout.encoding/stderr.encoding for the console.

Java 8 → 17 I/O Cheat Sheet

Why interviewers ask: "what changed since 8?" is the standard way to check whether you have actually worked on a modern JDK. For I/O the answer is short and concrete.

Most additions are convenience methods that remove boilerplate you used to write (or copy from Apache Commons IO / Guava). The one behavioral change, default UTF-8, is Java 18, so on 17 you still pass charsets explicitly.

VersionAdditionReplaces
9InputStream.readAllBytes(), readNBytes(), transferTo(OutputStream)Manual byte[8192] copy loops, IOUtils.copy
9ObjectInputFilter (JEP 290)Custom resolveClass overrides for deserialization safety
9Files.lines parallel splitting; Process API improvements—
11Files.readString/writeString, Path.of, FileReader(File, Charset)new String(Files.readAllBytes(p), UTF_8), Paths.get
11java.net.http.HttpClient (HTTP/1.1 + HTTP/2, sync and async via CompletableFuture)HttpURLConnection; often Apache HttpClient/OkHttp
11Reader.transferTo(Writer), InputStream.nullInputStream()Hand-written copy loops, mock streams

// Java 11 HttpClient: the JDK's answer to "how do I call a REST API without a library"
HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder().connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)).build();
HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://api.example.com/orders/42"))
        .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).GET().build();
HttpResponse<String> res = client.send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()); // UTF-8 per Content-Type
// async variant: client.sendAsync(req, BodyHandlers.ofString()).thenApply(HttpResponse::body)

Likely follow-ups

  • Which of these would you still avoid on Java 17? (Relying on the default charset; it is only fixed in 18.)
  • Is the JDK HttpClient production-ready? (Yes; it is what Spring's JdkClientHttpRequestFactory wraps. It lacks connection-pool tuning knobs that Apache HttpClient exposes.)

Java 18–21

18: UTF-8 default (JEP 400) and the jwebserver tool. 21: virtual threads make blocking java.io scalable; the JDK's socket and file I/O were reworked in 19–21 so a blocked virtual thread releases its carrier.

A UTF-8 file containing café is read with new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(f))) on a Java 17 JVM in a container whose default charset is US-ASCII. What is read?

c. Without an explicit charset the bridge uses Charset.defaultCharset(); the ASCII decoder in InputStreamReader replaces malformed input with ? rather than throwing (b happens only with a CharsetDecoder configured to REPORT). d is what ISO-8859-1 would produce; a is fiction, nothing auto-detects.

Which call leaks a file descriptor if the returned object is not closed?

b. Files.lines is lazy: the file stays open until the Stream is closed, so it belongs in try-with-resources. a and c read eagerly and close internally before returning; d only reads metadata.

In a selector loop, a handler calls channel.write(buf) right after channel.read(buf) returned 5, without flip(). The buffer was freshly allocated with capacity 1024. How many bytes are written?

d. After the read, position = 5 and limit = 1024. write sends remaining() = 1019 bytes starting at position 5, which are the never-written zeros. flip() would have set limit 5, position 0, yielding a. Channels never throw for this (c), which is why the bug is silent.

Why does a single selector thread scale to tens of thousands of idle connections while thread-per-connection does not?

a. Multiplexing removes the per-connection thread (stack memory + context switches). b is false: per-connection latency is not better, often slightly worse. c is an orthogonal optimization. d is backwards: one selector loop is single-threaded, which is exactly why handlers must not block.

After a channel read, you parsed 2 of the 3 messages in the buffer; the third is incomplete. Before the next read(buf) you should call:

c. compact() moves the unread tail to index 0 and sets position after it, so the next read appends and the partial message survives. a discards the tail; b would set limit to the current position and shrink the writable region; d keeps the read-mode limit so the read fills only up to it.

A class without an explicit serialVersionUID gains a new private helper method. Instances serialized by the old build are read by the new build. Result?

b. The default UID is a hash of the class's shape including non-private methods and constructors; in practice any structural edit tends to change it. That is why you declare it. a describes what a declared UID buys you. d is thrown at write time for classes that are not Serializable at all.

Your Spring Boot service on Java 17 must accept 30k concurrent long-lived SSE connections that each receive a message every ~30 s. Which is the least appropriate choice?

d. A synchronous handler holds one of ~200 Tomcat workers for the life of the connection; connection 201 waits forever. b releases the worker between events (Tomcat's poller holds the socket). a holds no thread at all. c makes the parked thread cheap.

What does "😀".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8).length return, and what is "😀".length()?

a. An emoji outside the BMP is 4 bytes in UTF-8 and a surrogate pair (two chars) in Java's UTF-16 String, so length() is 2 while codePointCount(0, 2) is 1. c is what people assume length() means.

Practice

Word frequency over a 10 GB log file on a 512 MB heap

You are given /data/access.log (10 GB, UTF-8, one request per line). Print the 10 most frequent words. The JVM runs with -Xmx512m. Write it so it does not OOM, then explain where the memory actually goes and what would still blow up.

Tests: streaming I/O, lazy streams, memory reasoningFollow-up: what if the number of distinct words is also huge?
Hint 1
Anything with readAllLines, readString, or Files.lines(...).toList() materializes 10 GB of Strings. You need a path where at most one line is in memory at a time.
Hint 2
Memory is bounded by the distinct vocabulary, not the file size. The map holds one entry per distinct word; the top-10 needs only a bounded heap (PriorityQueue) at the end.
Reveal solution
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

public class WordFreq {
    private static final Pattern SPLIT = Pattern.compile("[^\\p{L}\\p{Nd}]+");

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Map<String, long[]> counts = new HashMap<>(1 << 16);   // mutable counter avoids boxing churn

        try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(Path.of("/data/access.log"), StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {
            lines.forEach(line -> {
                for (String w : SPLIT.split(line)) {
                    if (w.isEmpty()) continue;
                    counts.computeIfAbsent(w.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT), k -> new long[1])[0]++;
                }
            });
        }

        // bounded top-k: min-heap of size 10, O(V log 10) instead of sorting V entries
        PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<String, long[]>> heap =
                new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingLong(e -> e.getValue()[0]));
        for (var e : counts.entrySet()) {
            heap.offer(e);
            if (heap.size() > 10) heap.poll();
        }
        var top = new ArrayList<>(heap);
        top.sort((a, b) -> Long.compare(b.getValue()[0], a.getValue()[0]));
        top.forEach(e -> System.out.println(e.getKey() + " " + e.getValue()[0]));
    }
}

Where the memory goes. Files.lines wraps a BufferedReader over the file: one 8 KB decode buffer plus the current line String. Each line becomes garbage as soon as the lambda returns, so the young generation churns through 10 GB but the live set never exceeds the map. The map costs roughly (entry ≈ 32 B + String ≈ 40 B + chars + long[1] ≈ 24 B) ≈ 100–120 bytes per distinct word: a 1 M-word vocabulary is ~120 MB, fine on 512 MB. The PriorityQueue is bounded at 10.

What would still OOM. (1) A vocabulary of tens of millions of distinct tokens (UUIDs, session ids in the log). Fix: pre-filter tokens that look like ids, or shard by hash(word) % N into N temp files and count each file separately (external hashing), or use a streaming sketch (Count-Min Sketch + heavy-hitters) if approximate counts are acceptable. (2) A pathological single line of several GB (no newline) would materialize as one String; guard with a max line length or read fixed-size chunks with a CharsetDecoder.

Why not parallel()? Files.lines can split the file by byte offsets (Java 9+), but the shared HashMap is not thread-safe. Use ConcurrentHashMap + LongAdder, or a Collectors.groupingByConcurrent. For a 10 GB file on a local SSD the job is usually CPU-bound on splitting/lowercasing, so parallelism helps; on network storage it does not.

Interviewer probes: "Why long[] instead of merge(w, 1L, Long::sum)?" Both are correct; the array avoids allocating a new Long per increment (values above 127 are not cached). "Why the explicit charset?" Because the log is UTF-8 and the container may default to ASCII on Java 17.

Fix the bug: three defects in a config loader

This helper "works on my machine" but in production it corrupts non-ASCII values, and after a few thousand reloads the process dies with java.io.IOException: Too many open files. Find every bug.

public class ConfigLoader {
    public static String load(String path) throws IOException {
        InputStream in = new FileInputStream(path);
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        int b;
        while ((b = in.read()) != -1) {
            sb.append((char) b);
        }
        if (sb.length() == 0) throw new IOException("empty config: " + path);
        in.close();
        return sb.toString();
    }
}
Tests: resource leaks, byte vs char, charset handling, performance
Hint 1
Follow the control flow when the file is empty: which line never runs? Then follow the control flow when read() throws.
Hint 2
(char) b takes a single byte and treats it as a 16-bit char. What happens to the two UTF-8 bytes of é?
Reveal solution

Bug 1: resource leak. in.close() is skipped when the "empty config" exception is thrown, and also when any read() throws. Each leaked FileInputStream holds an OS file descriptor until GC finalizes it, which under a healthy heap can be minutes; with a 1024 fd ulimit the server eventually cannot open sockets either. Fix: try-with-resources.

Bug 2: bytes read as chars. (char) b maps each byte 0–255 to the Unicode code point with the same number, which is ISO-8859-1 decoding whatever the file's real encoding is. UTF-8 é (C3 A9) becomes "Ã©"; anything outside Latin-1 becomes garbage. Decoding must go through a Reader (or new String(bytes, charset)) so multibyte sequences are assembled.

Bug 3: no explicit charset (the fix for bug 2 must not reintroduce it). new InputStreamReader(in) or new FileReader(path) would use the platform default, which is ASCII/Cp1252 in some environments on Java 17. Pass StandardCharsets.UTF_8.

Bonus: performance. Unbuffered read() makes one native call per byte; a 1 MB config is a million syscalls. Buffering (or reading the whole file at once) fixes it.

public class ConfigLoader {
    public static String load(String path) throws IOException {
        String text = Files.readString(Path.of(path), StandardCharsets.UTF_8); // opens, reads, closes
        if (text.isEmpty()) throw new IOException("empty config: " + path);
        return text;
    }

    // Streaming variant for large files or an arbitrary InputStream:
    public static String load(InputStream raw) throws IOException {
        try (var reader = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(raw, StandardCharsets.UTF_8))) {
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
            char[] buf = new char[8192];
            int n;
            while ((n = reader.read(buf)) != -1) sb.append(buf, 0, n);
            if (sb.isEmpty()) throw new IOException("empty config");
            return sb.toString();
        }
    }
}

Interviewer probes: "Would finally { in.close(); } be enough?" It fixes the leak but is worse than try-with-resources because an exception from close() would mask the original one; try-with-resources attaches it as a suppressed exception. "Why does the corruption only show in production?" Dev machines are UTF-8 and the config there is ASCII-only; the production config has a customer name with an accent and the decoder is different.

Design and implement: a single-threaded NIO echo server, then explain what virtual threads change

Write an echo server on port 9000 that handles thousands of concurrent clients with one thread using Selector. Each client sends newline-terminated lines; the server echoes each line back. Handle partial reads, partial writes, and client disconnects. Then answer: on Java 21 with virtual threads, would you still write it this way?

Tests: selector readiness loop, ByteBuffer state, per-connection state, OP_WRITE disciplineTime: 25–30 min
Hint 1
Three kinds of keys: the listening ServerSocketChannel (OP_ACCEPT) and each client SocketChannel (OP_READ, sometimes OP_WRITE). Attach a per-connection object to the key with key.attach(...).
Hint 2
Do not register OP_WRITE up front. Try to write immediately; only if write() could not drain the buffer, add OP_WRITE to interestOps, and remove it once the buffer is empty.
Reveal solution
public class NioEchoServer {
    /** Per-connection state: what we have read but not yet echoed. */
    static final class Conn {
        final ByteBuffer in = ByteBuffer.allocate(8192);   // write mode between reads
        ByteBuffer out = ByteBuffer.allocate(0);            // read mode: pending echo bytes
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Selector selector = Selector.open();
        ServerSocketChannel server = ServerSocketChannel.open();
        server.bind(new InetSocketAddress(9000));
        server.configureBlocking(false);
        server.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_ACCEPT);

        while (true) {
            selector.select();                                    // blocks once for all channels
            Iterator<SelectionKey> it = selector.selectedKeys().iterator();
            while (it.hasNext()) {
                SelectionKey key = it.next();
                it.remove();                                      // selector never clears it for you
                try {
                    if (key.isAcceptable()) accept(selector, server);
                    if (key.isReadable())   read(key);
                    if (key.isWritable())   write(key);
                } catch (IOException e) {
                    key.cancel(); key.channel().close();          // peer reset, etc.
                }
            }
        }
    }

    static void accept(Selector sel, ServerSocketChannel server) throws IOException {
        SocketChannel client = server.accept();                   // non-null: key said ready
        client.configureBlocking(false);
        client.register(sel, SelectionKey.OP_READ, new Conn());
    }

    static void read(SelectionKey key) throws IOException {
        SocketChannel ch = (SocketChannel) key.channel();
        Conn c = (Conn) key.attachment();
        int n = ch.read(c.in);
        if (n == -1) { key.cancel(); ch.close(); return; }        // client closed
        c.in.flip();                                              // read mode: scan for '\n'
        int lastNl = -1;
        for (int i = c.in.position(); i < c.in.limit(); i++) if (c.in.get(i) == '\n') lastNl = i;
        if (lastNl >= 0) {                                        // echo all complete lines
            ByteBuffer lines = c.in.slice(0, lastNl + 1);
            ByteBuffer merged = ByteBuffer.allocate(c.out.remaining() + lines.remaining());
            merged.put(c.out).put(lines).flip();
            c.out = merged;
            c.in.position(lastNl + 1);
        }
        c.in.compact();                                           // keep the partial tail
        if (c.in.position() == c.in.capacity()) throw new IOException("line too long");
        write(key);
    }

    static void write(SelectionKey key) throws IOException {
        SocketChannel ch = (SocketChannel) key.channel();
        Conn c = (Conn) key.attachment();
        ch.write(c.out);                                          // may write less than remaining()
        if (c.out.hasRemaining()) key.interestOps(SelectionKey.OP_READ | SelectionKey.OP_WRITE);
        else                      key.interestOps(SelectionKey.OP_READ);
    }
}

Why each piece is there. it.remove(): the selected-key set is only ever added to by the selector. configureBlocking(false) on both channels: registering a blocking channel throws IllegalBlockingModeException. read() == -1: orderly close; a reset shows up as an IOException, handled by cancel + close. Per-connection Conn in the attachment is what makes partial reads work: the flip → scan → compact cycle keeps a half line in in until the rest arrives. Writing immediately and registering OP_WRITE only when the socket send buffer is full avoids the classic 100% CPU spin, because a socket is writable almost all the time.

Limits of the design. One thread means one core; Netty runs N such loops and pins each channel to one, so handlers stay lock-free. The allocate per merged output is naive; a real server would use a pooled direct buffer or a queue of buffers. A slow reader who never drains can grow out unboundedly: production code caps pending bytes and drops or throttles the client (backpressure).

What changes with virtual threads (Java 21). The scalability argument for the selector was "threads are expensive". With Thread.ofVirtual() a blocked thread costs a few hundred bytes of heap-allocated stack, and the JDK's blocking socket calls park the virtual thread while an internal poller (epoll) waits on its behalf. So the thread-per-connection version becomes viable again and is far simpler:

try (var server = new ServerSocket(9000);
     var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    while (true) {
        Socket s = server.accept();
        pool.submit(() -> {
            try (s; var in = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(s.getInputStream(), UTF_8));
                 var out = new PrintWriter(new OutputStreamWriter(s.getOutputStream(), UTF_8), true)) {
                String line;
                while ((line = in.readLine()) != null) out.println(line);
            } catch (IOException ignored) { }
        });
    }
}

Partial reads, flip/compact, and OP_WRITE juggling disappear because readLine and println block per connection at no scalability cost. You would still pick the selector when you need zero-copy transferTo, precise control over buffers, or you are inside a framework (Netty) that already does it. The honest answer in an interview: on 21+, default to blocking code on virtual threads for application servers; know the selector for the frameworks you run on.

🔟 Reflection, Annotations & Modules

Every framework you list on your résumé (Spring, Hibernate, Jackson, JUnit, Mockito) is built on the three things in this section: reading a class at runtime, tagging code with metadata, and the module rules that decide what a framework is allowed to touch. Learn the raw Reflection API first, then how annotations carry the metadata frameworks read, then the compile-time alternative, and finally JPMS, which is the reason for every --add-opens flag you have ever copy-pasted.

The Reflection API: inspecting and invoking at runtime

Why interviewers ask: "how does Spring instantiate your class without knowing it at compile time?" has exactly one honest answer. They also probe whether you know reflection's price tag and the Java 9+ access rules that break older libraries.

Reflection lets a running program inspect and manipulate classes it did not know at compile time: obtain a Class object (Foo.class, obj.getClass(), or Class.forName("com.acme.Foo")), then ask it for Field, Method and Constructor objects and read, write or invoke them. Analogy: normal code is a key cut for one lock; reflection is the locksmith's pick that opens any door, slowly, and sometimes sets off the alarm.

The single most-missed detail is the two families of lookup methods. getFields()/getMethods() return only public members, including inherited ones. getDeclaredFields()/getDeclaredMethods() return all members (private, package, protected, public) but only of that class, not superclasses. To find a private field in a parent you walk getSuperclass() yourself, which is what Spring's ReflectionUtils.doWithFields does.

Private members throw IllegalAccessException unless you call setAccessible(true) first. Since Java 9 the JDK enforces strong encapsulation: setAccessible on a member of a package the owning module does not open to you throws InaccessibleObjectException. Your own classpath code lives in the unnamed module, which opens everything, so reflecting on your own classes still works; reflecting into java.base internals (java.lang, sun.nio.ch) needs --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED.

Class<?> c = Class.forName("com.acme.Order");          // loads AND initializes the class
Object o = c.getDeclaredConstructor(String.class).newInstance("A1");

Field id = c.getDeclaredField("id");                     // private field of THIS class only
id.setAccessible(true);                                  // InaccessibleObjectException if module not opened
System.out.println(id.get(o));                           // "A1"

Method total = c.getMethod("total");                     // public, including inherited
Object result = total.invoke(o);                         // checked: InvocationTargetException wraps the real exception

System.out.println(Modifier.isFinal(id.getModifiers())); // decode the int bitmask
System.out.println(Modifier.toString(c.getModifiers())); // "public final"
CallVisibilityInherited members?Typical use
getFields() / getMethods()public onlyYes (superclasses and interfaces)Bean-style introspection of the public surface
getDeclaredFields() / getDeclaredMethods()all modifiersNo, this class onlyDependency injection, ORMs, serializers (walk the hierarchy yourself)
getConstructors() vs getDeclaredConstructors()public vs allConstructors are never inheritedFrameworks prefer the no-arg or the single annotated constructor
Method.invokeruntime access check per call (cached after setAccessible)n/aSlow path: boxing of args, varargs array, exception wrapping
MethodHandle.invokeExactaccess checked once at Lookup timen/aFast path: JIT can inline a constant handle like a direct call
Interview angle: "What does reflection cost?" Three things: (1) speed, since Method.invoke boxes primitives, allocates an Object[] and goes through an accessor the JIT cannot see through, so it is roughly 2 to 10x a direct call and blocks inlining; (2) safety, since a renamed field becomes a runtime NoSuchFieldException instead of a compile error; (3) encapsulation, since it bypasses private. Frameworks pay these once (at startup or first use) and then cache Method objects, or switch to MethodHandle, which is resolved once and then JIT-inlined like a normal call.

Pitfalls

  • getDeclaredFields() does not include a parent's private fields; a naive DI container silently fails to inject fields declared in an abstract base class.
  • The real exception thrown by an invoked method is wrapped in InvocationTargetException; unwrap with getCause() or you log the wrong stack trace.
  • The order of getDeclaredFields() is unspecified (in practice declaration order on HotSpot, but do not rely on it for serialization formats).
  • Reflection on generics only sees erased types, except via getGenericType()/ParameterizedType for declared fields, parameters and superclass signatures (the trick behind Jackson's TypeReference).

Likely follow-ups

  • Can reflection change a final field? (Instance final fields: yes after setAccessible; static final constants and record fields: no, and the JIT may have constant-folded the old value anyway.)
  • Does reflection work on records and sealed types? (Yes: isRecord(), getRecordComponents(), isSealed(), getPermittedSubclasses().)
  • How does obj.getClass() differ from Foo.class? (Runtime class of the instance vs compile-time literal; for a CGLIB proxy getClass() is the generated subclass.)

Java 8 vs 17

Java 8: setAccessible(true) opened anything, including java.lang internals. Java 9 to 15: allowed with a "illegal reflective access" warning (--illegal-access=permit default). Java 16: default became deny. Java 17 removed the --illegal-access flag entirely (JEP 403); only --add-opens works. New in the same window: Class.getRecordComponents() (16) and Class.getPermittedSubclasses()/isSealed() (17), which Jackson and Hibernate use to serialize records and sealed hierarchies.

How Spring Uses Reflection: from classpath scan to proxy

Why interviewers ask: it connects Java fundamentals to Spring behaviour you see every day: slow startup, "why is my @Transactional ignored when called from the same class", and why GraalVM native images need extra configuration.

Spring does not know your classes at compile time. At startup it scans the package under @SpringBootApplication by reading every .class file's bytes (ASM, without loading them), looks for classes carrying @Component (or a meta-annotated variant like @Service), then loads each with Class.forName, picks a constructor, calls newInstance, walks getDeclaredFields() for @Autowired/@Inject, sets them with setAccessible(true) + Field.set, and finally lets each BeanPostProcessor replace the bean with a proxy (JDK dynamic proxy if it has an interface, CGLIB subclass otherwise) that adds @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async or security checks around method calls.

Analogy: a hotel concierge (the container) reads every guest's registration card (annotations), assembles their room (injection), and then answers their phone for them (proxy) so it can add services before passing the call through.

Real-world consequences. Slow startup: a service with 2,000 beans does thousands of Class.forName, constructor and annotation lookups, and generates CGLIB classes at runtime. Spring Boot 3's AOT mode moves the scan and bean-definition building to build time to cut this. GraalVM native image compiles ahead of time with closed-world analysis: it cannot see Class.forName("…") targets or which fields will be accessed reflectively, so it needs reachability metadata (reflect-config.json, or @RegisterReflectionForBinding / RuntimeHintsRegistrar in Spring) or those classes are simply absent from the binary and fail with ClassNotFoundException at runtime.

Pitfalls

  • Self-invocation: this.saveAll() inside the same bean skips the proxy, so @Transactional/@Cacheable on that method does nothing. Inject yourself lazily or move the method to another bean.
  • CGLIB proxies subclass your class: final classes/methods cannot be proxied, and the proxy runs your constructor a second time (with null fields) in older Spring versions, which is why constructors should not do work.
  • Field injection hides dependencies and needs setAccessible; constructor injection is what the reflection story above makes trivially testable.

Likely follow-ups

  • JDK proxy vs CGLIB? (JDK: interface-based, java.lang.reflect.Proxy; CGLIB: subclass, default in Boot since 2.0 via proxyTargetClass=true.)
  • How does Jackson know your fields? (Same API: getDeclaredFields/getters plus annotations like @JsonProperty, cached per class in a serializer.)
  • How does JUnit find @Test methods? (getDeclaredMethods() filtered by isAnnotationPresent(Test.class), then invoke on a fresh instance per test.)

Annotations: declaring them and the Retention trap

Why interviewers ask: "write me a custom annotation and make a framework react to it" is a classic whiteboard task, and forgetting @Retention(RUNTIME) is the most common way to fail it.

An annotation is a typed piece of metadata attached to a declaration. You declare one with @interface; its elements look like methods and may have defaults. Element types are limited to primitives, String, Class, enums, other annotations and one-dimensional arrays of those. Analogy: a sticky note on a document. Who gets to read the note depends on how long it stays attached.

That lifetime is @Retention: SOURCE is thrown away by javac (@Override, Lombok's @Getter); CLASS (the default, easy to forget) is written into the .class file but not loaded into the Class object, so getAnnotation returns null; RUNTIME is what Spring, JPA, JUnit and your own reflective code need. @Target restricts where it may appear (TYPE, METHOD, FIELD, PARAMETER, CONSTRUCTOR, TYPE_USE…). @Inherited makes a class annotation visible through getAnnotation on subclasses (classes only, never methods or interfaces). @Repeatable allows several instances by naming a container annotation. @Documented only affects Javadoc.

Annotations on annotations are meta-annotations, and frameworks use them to compose: Spring's @RestController is declared as @Controller @ResponseBody @interface RestController. Plain Java does not follow that chain (isAnnotationPresent(Controller.class) on your class is false), so Spring's MergedAnnotations walks the meta-annotation graph itself. The same trick gives you @Transactional(readOnly = true) @interface ReadOnlyTx in your own code.

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)            // without this the default is CLASS: invisible to reflection
@Target({ElementType.TYPE, ElementType.METHOD})
@Documented
public @interface Audited {
    String value() default "";                  // @Audited("orders") shorthand for a single element named value
    String[] tags() default {};
    Level level() default Level.INFO;           // enum element
}

@Repeatable(Schedules.class)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface Schedule { String cron(); }

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface Schedules { Schedule[] value(); }   // container required by @Repeatable

// composing, Spring-style: one annotation that "means" two others
@Target(ElementType.TYPE) @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Transactional(readOnly = true) @Service
public @interface ReadOnlyService { }

// reading them
Audited a = OrderService.class.getAnnotation(Audited.class);       // null if absent
Schedule[] s = job.getClass().getAnnotationsByType(Schedule.class); // unwraps the container
boolean hasIt = m.isAnnotationPresent(Audited.class);
Interview angle: "Design @RateLimited(permits=100) for our REST layer." Expected answer: declare it with RUNTIME retention and METHOD/TYPE targets, then either a Spring AOP @Around("@annotation(rateLimited)") aspect or a HandlerInterceptor that reads it via HandlerMethod.getMethodAnnotation. Mention that the annotation itself is inert; something must read it.

Pitfalls

  • Default retention is CLASS, not RUNTIME. The annotation compiles, deploys, and does nothing.
  • @Inherited only works for class-level annotations found via getAnnotation on a subclass; a @Transactional on an interface method is not seen by getAnnotation on the implementing method (Spring handles this with its own lookup).
  • Annotation instances are compared by value; getAnnotation returns a JDK dynamic proxy implementing your interface, so == on two lookups is unreliable.
  • Element values must be compile-time constants; you cannot write @Timeout(config.get()). Spring works around this with ${...} strings evaluated later.

Likely follow-ups

  • Where do type-use annotations go? (ElementType.TYPE_USE, e.g. List<@NonNull String>; read via AnnotatedType, used by Checker Framework.)
  • Why can an annotation not extend another? (The language forbids inheritance for annotation types; composition via meta-annotations replaces it.)
  • What does @FunctionalInterface do at runtime? (Nothing; it is a compile-time check with RUNTIME retention purely for documentation.)

Compile-time Annotation Processing vs Runtime Reflection

Why interviewers ask: "how does Lombok add a getter that is not in your source?" separates people who use the tooling from people who understand it, and the trade-off table below is a common system-design-adjacent question ("why is MapStruct faster than ModelMapper?").

The same annotation can be consumed at two very different moments. Runtime reflection (Spring, JPA/Hibernate, Jackson, JUnit) reads RUNTIME-retained annotations from loaded classes while the program runs. Annotation processing (javax.annotation.processing.Processor, JSR 269) runs inside javac: the compiler discovers processors via META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor, hands them the AST-level model (Element, TypeMirror) of annotated declarations, and lets them generate new source files in additional compilation rounds. Analogy: reflection is a waiter reading your order at the table; annotation processing is a kitchen that pre-cooks dishes the night before based on the printed menu.

MapStruct generates a plain OrderMapperImpl class with hand-written-looking getter/setter calls, so mapping costs nothing at runtime and mistakes are compile errors. Immutables/AutoValue generate value classes. Lombok is the odd one out: standard processors can only add files, but Lombok modifies the compiler's AST of your existing class through internal javac APIs, which is why it needs --add-opens-style hacks on new JDKs and why IDE plugins are required. Dagger and Micronaut take the idea to DI itself: the injector is generated code, which is why they start fast and work on GraalVM without hints.

@SupportedAnnotationTypes("com.acme.Builder")
@SupportedSourceVersion(SourceVersion.RELEASE_17)
public class BuilderProcessor extends AbstractProcessor {
    @Override
    public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment env) {
        for (Element e : env.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Builder.class)) {
            TypeElement type = (TypeElement) e;                       // compile-time model, not a Class
            String name = type.getSimpleName() + "Builder";
            try (Writer w = processingEnv.getFiler()
                    .createSourceFile(type.getQualifiedName() + "Builder").openWriter()) {
                w.write("public class " + name + " { /* generated setters */ }");
            } catch (IOException ex) {
                processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, ex.getMessage(), e);
            }
        }
        return true;   // claimed: no other processor sees @Builder this round
    }
}
Annotation processing (compile time)Reflection (runtime)
ExamplesLombok, MapStruct, Immutables, AutoValue, Dagger, Micronaut, Hibernate JPA metamodelSpring, Hibernate ORM, Jackson, JUnit, Mockito
Retention neededSOURCE is enoughRUNTIME mandatory
Runtime costZero; generated code is ordinary code the JIT inlinesStartup scanning, per-call invoke overhead unless cached or replaced by handles
Error timingCompile error (missing mapping, wrong type)Runtime exception, often on first request
FlexibilityClosed at build; cannot react to config or classes discovered laterCan wire anything present on the classpath, profiles, conditional beans
DebuggabilityGenerated source is readable and steppableStack traces full of invoke/proxy frames
GraalVM nativeWorks out of the boxNeeds reachability metadata
Build complexityProcessor must be on the annotationProcessorPath; IDE support variesJust a jar on the classpath
Interview angle: "MapStruct vs ModelMapper for a hot DTO mapping path?" MapStruct: generated code, ~direct-assignment speed, compile-time errors when a field is missing. ModelMapper: reflection plus name heuristics, orders of magnitude slower on hot paths, silent mismatches. Same story for Dagger vs Spring DI on startup time.

Pitfalls

  • A processor never sees a Class; it sees Element/TypeMirror. Calling Class.forName on the annotated type inside a processor fails because the class is not compiled yet.
  • Processors cannot edit existing classes through the public API; Lombok's AST rewriting is why it occasionally breaks on new JDK releases before an update ships.
  • Generated sources must be in the build's generated-sources dir or incremental builds and IDEs get confused.

Likely follow-ups

  • What are compilation rounds? (Processors run repeatedly until no new files are generated; generated files can themselves be annotated.)
  • Can a processor fail the build? (Yes, Messager.printMessage(ERROR, …) makes javac exit non-zero, a cheap way to enforce architecture rules.)
  • Where do Spring Boot's spring-boot-configuration-processor and the JPA static metamodel come from? (Both are annotation processors generating metadata / Order_ classes.)

MethodHandles, VarHandle and invokedynamic

Why interviewers ask: mostly as a depth probe after "how are lambdas implemented?" or "what replaced sun.misc.Unsafe?". A two-minute answer earns credit; nobody expects you to write invokedynamic bootstraps by hand.

A MethodHandle (Java 7, java.lang.invoke) is a typed, directly executable reference to a method, constructor or field. You get one from a MethodHandles.Lookup, which performs the access check once, at lookup time, using the caller's own privileges; after that invokeExact is a signature-polymorphic call the JIT can inline when the handle is a static final constant. Analogy: Method.invoke shows ID at the door every time; a MethodHandle got a badge once and walks straight in.

VarHandle (Java 9) is the same idea for fields and array elements with explicit memory-ordering modes: get/set (plain), getVolatile, getAcquire/setRelease, compareAndSet, getAndAdd. It is the supported replacement for sun.misc.Unsafe, which the JDK used internally for CAS since Java 5, leaked into every serious library (Netty, Kafka, Guava), and is now being phased out by strong encapsulation.

invokedynamic (Java 7, built for JRuby) is a bytecode instruction whose target is resolved on first execution by a bootstrap method returning a CallSite. Lambdas compile to an invokedynamic that calls LambdaMetafactory, which spins a tiny hidden class implementing the functional interface, once per call site. Since Java 9, "a" + b compiles to an invokedynamic to StringConcatFactory instead of a StringBuilder chain; records' equals/hashCode/toString use ObjectMethods the same way. This is why a lambda is not "an anonymous inner class" and why you cannot find a Foo$1.class for it.

class Counter {
    private volatile int count;
    private static final VarHandle COUNT;
    static {
        try {
            COUNT = MethodHandles.lookup().findVarHandle(Counter.class, "count", int.class);
        } catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) { throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(e); }
    }
    void inc()                          { COUNT.getAndAdd(this, 1); }
    boolean cas(int expect, int update) { return COUNT.compareAndSet(this, expect, update); }
}

// MethodHandle: looked up once, JIT-inlined afterwards
MethodHandle total = MethodHandles.lookup()
        .findVirtual(Order.class, "total", MethodType.methodType(BigDecimal.class));
BigDecimal t = (BigDecimal) total.invokeExact(order);   // exact signature required, no boxing

Pitfalls

  • invokeExact demands the exact call-site signature including the cast on the return; use invoke when you need boxing/adaptation.
  • A handle stored in a non-final field is not inlined; performance benefits assume a static final handle.
  • MethodHandles.privateLookupIn(target, lookup) (Java 9) still respects module opens; it is not a backdoor around encapsulation.

Likely follow-ups

  • Are lambdas cheaper than anonymous classes? (Stateless lambdas are cached singletons; capturing ones allocate per evaluation; neither writes an extra class file.)
  • Why did the JDK reimplement core reflection on method handles? (JEP 416, Java 18: one code path, fewer generated accessor classes.)

Java Platform Module System (JPMS): requires, exports, opens

Why interviewers ask: they want to know whether you understand the Java 9 to 17 migration flags you have had to add (--add-opens), why the JDK itself is now sealed, and whether you have a reasoned answer to "should we modularize our services?".

JPMS (Java 9, Project Jigsaw) adds a layer above packages: a module is a named group of packages with a module-info.java declaring what it requires (dependencies, forming a graph checked at startup, no more missing-jar surprises at runtime) and what it exports (packages visible at compile time and runtime to others; everything else is inaccessible even if public). opens is separate and specifically about deep reflection: an opened package allows setAccessible(true) on its non-public members, which is what Jackson, Hibernate and Spring need on your entities. requires transitive re-exports a dependency to your consumers; uses/provides integrate with ServiceLoader. Analogy: exports is the customer entrance; opens hands the building inspector a master key.

Strong encapsulation is the JDK applying this to itself: java.base exports java.lang but does not open it, so a library that reflects into String.value fails on 16+ unless you run with --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED. Compatibility: anything on the plain classpath lands in the unnamed module, which reads every other module and opens all its packages, so unmodularized apps keep working. A jar with an Automatic-Module-Name manifest entry can sit on the module path as an automatic module without a descriptor.

Who modularizes? Libraries (the JDK, Jackson, SLF4J, Guava with automatic names) because they benefit from a stable public API and being usable in modular consumers. Most applications, and Spring Boot fat jars in particular, do not: the fat-jar launcher uses the classpath, many dependencies still lack descriptors, and the payoff (a smaller runtime via jlink, which assembles a custom JRE containing only the modules you require, useful for slim containers) is attainable with jlink on the JDK modules alone.

module com.acme.app {
    requires org.lib;                    // read edge; not re-exported
    requires transitive java.sql;        // consumers of com.acme.app also read java.sql
    requires static lombok;              // compile-time only (annotation processors)
    exports com.acme.app.api;            // public types visible to everyone
    exports com.acme.app.spi to com.acme.plugins;   // qualified export
    opens com.acme.app.model;            // deep reflection for Jackson / Hibernate
    uses com.acme.app.spi.Plugin;        // ServiceLoader consumer
    provides com.acme.app.spi.Plugin with com.acme.app.DefaultPlugin;
}
Flag / directiveGrantsTypical reason
--add-exports M/P=Tcompile/runtime access to public types of package PUsing a JDK-internal API such as sun.nio.ch (Netty, Kafka)
--add-opens M/P=Tdeep reflection (setAccessible) into PSerializers touching java.lang/java.util internals; Mockito inline mocks; older Groovy/Hibernate
--add-reads M=Ta readability edge missing from the descriptorTest frameworks patching module graphs
--patch-moduleoverlay classes into a moduleUnit tests living in the same package as the module under test

Pitfalls

  • Split packages: two modules (or a jar and a module) containing the same package fail to load. Classic case: javax.annotation shipped by several jars.
  • Automatic-Module-Name jars export everything and read everything, which quietly defeats the purpose if you count on encapsulation.
  • Putting --add-opens in JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS hides the problem; put it in the Launcher-Agent/Add-Opens manifest attribute of an executable jar or fix the library version.

Likely follow-ups

  • Does Spring Boot use modules? (No; it runs from the classpath. The Spring jars carry Automatic-Module-Name so modular apps can require them.)
  • What is jdeps? (JDK tool that lists module dependencies and flags JDK-internal API usage before you migrate.)
  • Why did java.xml.bind (JAXB) disappear? (Java 11 removed the Java EE modules; add the jar as a dependency.)

Class Loading & Reflection Pitfalls

Why interviewers ask: the JDBC Class.forName("com.mysql.jdbc.Driver") idiom is a favourite "why did that line ever work?" question, and "does reflection get faster after warm-up?" tells them whether you have profiled a real service.

Class.forName(name) initializes the class: static initializers run immediately. That is the whole reason the old JDBC idiom worked: the driver's static block called DriverManager.registerDriver(new Driver()). ClassLoader.loadClass(name) and the three-arg Class.forName(name, false, loader) only load; initialization is deferred to first active use (new, static call, static field write). Since JDBC 4 the driver is found through ServiceLoader and the forName line is dead weight (see JVM & Memory for the loading phases).

Reflection caching: the JVM keeps a soft-referenced ReflectionData per class, but every getDeclaredFields() call returns a fresh copy of the array, and getDeclaredMethod(name, …) does a linear search. Well-behaved frameworks look up Method/Field objects once and cache them (Spring's ReflectionUtils declared-method cache, Jackson's serializer cache). Up to Java 17 Method.invoke also uses inflation: the first ~15 calls go through a slow native accessor, after which HotSpot generates a bytecode accessor class (-Dsun.reflect.inflationThreshold), so a single reflective call in a microbenchmark looks far slower than steady state.

SecurityManager, the sandbox that could veto setAccessible and file/network access, was deprecated for removal in Java 17 (JEP 411) and is effectively disabled by default; do not propose it as a security control in a design interview. Isolation today means containers, OS permissions and JPMS encapsulation.

Class.forName("com.acme.Driver");                      // load + link + initialize: static { } runs now
Class.forName("com.acme.Driver", false, loader);       // load + link only
loader.loadClass("com.acme.Driver");                   // load only; init deferred to first use

// cache reflective lookups: do this once per class, not per request
private static final Map<Class<?>, List<Field>> INJECTABLE = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
static List<Field> injectable(Class<?> c) {
    return INJECTABLE.computeIfAbsent(c, k -> {
        List<Field> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Class<?> t = k; t != null && t != Object.class; t = t.getSuperclass())   // walk the hierarchy
            for (Field f : t.getDeclaredFields())
                if (f.isAnnotationPresent(Inject.class)) { f.setAccessible(true); out.add(f); }
        return List.copyOf(out);
    });
}

Pitfalls

  • Static-initializer side effects triggered by Class.forName in one thread while another thread also initializes the same class: the JVM serializes class init, which can deadlock if the two initializers depend on each other.
  • Reflection on a class loaded by a different loader (plugin, web-app) yields a different Class object; Foo.class.isInstance(obj) is false even though the names match.
  • Calling setAccessible(true) on every request instead of once wastes the access-check work and hits InaccessibleObjectException late, in production, on the first request that touches a JDK internal.

Likely follow-ups

  • What does Class.forName use as loader? (The caller's defining loader, which is wrong inside a shared library in an app server; pass the thread context class loader explicitly.)
  • How does a JDBC 4 driver register now? (META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver + ServiceLoader in DriverManager.)

Beyond 17

Java 18 (JEP 416) reimplemented core reflection on top of method handles, removing inflation and the generated accessor classes; Java 21 adds nothing reflection-specific, but the SecurityManager path continues toward removal.

class Base { private String id; } and class Child extends Base { public int n; }. Which call on Child.class returns the id field?

c. getFields() (a) is public-only, and id is private. getDeclaredFields() (b) sees private members but only of Child itself. d throws NoSuchFieldException before setAccessible is ever reached. Walking the hierarchy is the only way, which is exactly what DI containers do.

A @Service bean calls its own @Transactional method via this.persist(order) from a non-transactional public method. What happens?

b. Reflection is used once at startup to build a proxy; the interceptor lives in the proxy, and this is the raw target created by newInstance, so the annotation is never consulted (a). Startup does not validate self-calls (c), and the interface only changes proxy type, not this outcome (d).

Why does a Spring Boot app that works on the JVM fail with ClassNotFoundException when compiled to a GraalVM native image?

d. The AOT compiler includes only what static analysis can reach; a class named in a string or found through component scanning at runtime is invisible unless hinted. Class.forName exists (b) but can only return classes registered in the image. Annotations (a) and modules (c) are unrelated.

@interface Audited {} is declared with no meta-annotations and placed on OrderService. What does OrderService.class.isAnnotationPresent(Audited.class) return?

a. The default is RetentionPolicy.CLASS: recorded in the .class file (so b is tempting; ASM could read it) but never materialized for reflection. d gives the right value for the wrong reason; SOURCE would not even reach the class file. c: @Retention is optional.

Spring's @RestController is meta-annotated with @Controller. For @RestController class Api {}, what does plain Java's Api.class.isAnnotationPresent(Controller.class) return, and why does Spring still treat it as a controller?

c. Java only reports annotations directly present (plus @Inherited class annotations from superclasses, which is about subclassing, not meta-annotation, so b is wrong). a is false. Spring's expansion is a runtime lookup, not compile-time code generation (d).

On Java 17 a library throws InaccessibleObjectException: Unable to make field private final byte[] java.lang.String.value accessible. Which fix is correct?

b. Deep reflection into a private field needs the package opened. --add-exports (c) only grants access to public API, and java.lang is already exported. --illegal-access (a) was removed in Java 17 (JEP 403). java.base is required implicitly (d) and readability is not the problem.

Which statement about Class.forName("com.acme.Driver") vs loader.loadClass("com.acme.Driver") is true?

c. The one-arg Class.forName initializes, which is why the legacy JDBC idiom registered drivers. loadClass and Class.forName(name, false, cl) stop after loading/linking. Options a, b and d each get one of the two wrong.

Practice

Implement a mini dependency injector with @Inject

Write an Injector with <T> T get(Class<T> type). It must create the instance via its no-arg constructor, find every field annotated @Inject (including private fields and fields declared in superclasses), recursively obtain the dependency and set it. Instances must be singletons per type, and a cycle (A needs B, B needs A) must not stack-overflow. Declare the annotation too.

class Repo {}
class Service { @Inject private Repo repo; Repo repo() { return repo; } }
class Controller extends Service { @Inject Repo again; }

Injector inj = new Injector();
Controller c = inj.get(Controller.class);
assert c.repo() != null && c.repo() == c.again;   // singleton, superclass field injected
Tests: annotation declaration, getDeclaredFields hierarchy walk, setAccessible, singleton registry
Hint 1
The annotation is useless without @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) and should be limited with @Target(ElementType.FIELD).
Hint 2
Register the new instance in the map before injecting its fields; then a cycle resolves to the half-built instance instead of recursing forever.
Reveal solution
import java.lang.annotation.*;
import java.lang.reflect.*;
import java.util.*;

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.FIELD)
@interface Inject {}

class Injector {
    private final Map<Class<?>, Object> singletons = new HashMap<>();

    public <T> T get(Class<T> type) {
        Object existing = singletons.get(type);
        if (existing != null) return type.cast(existing);
        try {
            Constructor<T> ctor = type.getDeclaredConstructor();   // no-arg, may be non-public
            ctor.setAccessible(true);
            T instance = ctor.newInstance();
            singletons.put(type, instance);                        // register BEFORE injecting: breaks cycles
            for (Class<?> c = type; c != null && c != Object.class; c = c.getSuperclass()) {
                for (Field f : c.getDeclaredFields()) {
                    if (!f.isAnnotationPresent(Inject.class)) continue;
                    if (Modifier.isStatic(f.getModifiers()) || Modifier.isFinal(f.getModifiers()))
                        throw new IllegalStateException("cannot inject static/final " + f);
                    f.setAccessible(true);
                    f.set(instance, get(f.getType()));
                }
            }
            return instance;
        } catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("cannot create " + type.getName(), e);
        }
    }
}

Reasoning. getDeclaredFields() sees private fields but only of one class, hence the getSuperclass() loop (stop at Object). setAccessible(true) works because both the injector and the target are in the unnamed module. Registering before injection makes A ⇄ B terminate; the cost is that a dependency can observe a partially injected instance, which is exactly the caveat Spring documents for circular references. In an interview, follow up with: constructor injection would reject cycles instead of tolerating them, and the field lookups should be cached per class (see the pitfalls card) because getDeclaredFields() allocates a new array each call.

Implement @Retry(times = 3) with a dynamic proxy

Declare a method-level @Retry annotation with an int times() default 3 element. Write static <T> T withRetry(Class<T> iface, T target) that returns a java.lang.reflect.Proxy implementing iface: methods annotated @Retry are re-invoked on the target up to times attempts when they throw; other methods pass straight through. The original exception (not InvocationTargetException) must reach the caller after the last failed attempt.

interface PaymentClient {
    @Retry(times = 3) String charge(String orderId);
    String status(String orderId);          // no retry
}
PaymentClient flaky = new FlakyClient();   // throws twice, then succeeds
PaymentClient safe = withRetry(PaymentClient.class, flaky);
safe.charge("A1");                         // succeeds on the 3rd attempt
Tests: Proxy.newProxyInstance, InvocationHandler, reading annotations from Method, unwrapping InvocationTargetException
Hint 1
The Method passed to the handler is the interface method, so the annotation must be on the interface (or you must look it up on target.getClass()).
Hint 2
method.invoke wraps whatever the target throws in InvocationTargetException; keep getCause() and rethrow it at the end. An InvocationHandler may throw Throwable.
Reveal solution
import java.lang.annotation.*;
import java.lang.reflect.*;

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
@interface Retry { int times() default 3; }

final class Retrying {
    static <T> T withRetry(Class<T> iface, T target) {
        InvocationHandler h = (proxy, method, args) -> {
            Retry retry = method.getAnnotation(Retry.class);        // interface method: annotation must live there
            int attempts = retry == null ? 1 : Math.max(1, retry.times());
            Throwable last = null;
            for (int i = 1; i <= attempts; i++) {
                try {
                    return method.invoke(target, args);
                } catch (InvocationTargetException e) {
                    last = e.getCause();                                // the real exception
                    if (i < attempts) System.err.println("attempt " + i + " failed: " + last);
                }
            }
            throw last;                                                 // handler may throw Throwable
        };
        Object proxy = Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, h);
        return iface.cast(proxy);
    }
}

Reasoning. The proxy class is generated at runtime and every call lands in invoke(proxy, method, args). method is the interface's Method, which is why the annotation on PaymentClient.charge is found; had it been on FlakyClient.charge you would need target.getClass().getMethod(method.getName(), method.getParameterTypes()), which is the lookup Spring's AnnotationUtils.findAnnotation performs. Unwrapping InvocationTargetException matters for checked exceptions too: the proxy may throw any checked exception declared by the interface method; throwing one that is not declared produces UndeclaredThrowableException. Follow-ups an interviewer may add: only retry on specific exception types, add backoff, and note that equals/hashCode/toString also route through the handler (guard with method.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class). This is a JDK proxy; for a class without an interface Spring would fall back to a CGLIB subclass.

Predict the output: which annotations are visible at runtime?

import java.lang.annotation.*;

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.SOURCE)  @interface Src {}
@interface Cls {}                                        // no @Retention
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) @interface Run {}
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) @Inherited @interface Base {}

@Src @Cls @Run @Base class Parent {}
class Child extends Parent {}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] a) {
        System.out.println(Parent.class.getAnnotations().length);
        System.out.println(Child.class.getAnnotations().length);
        System.out.println(Child.class.getDeclaredAnnotations().length);
        System.out.println(Parent.class.isAnnotationPresent(Cls.class));
    }
}
Tests: retention defaults, @Inherited, getAnnotations vs getDeclaredAnnotations
Hint 1
Only one retention policy survives class loading; count how many annotations carry it.
Hint 2
getAnnotations() includes @Inherited annotations from superclasses; getDeclaredAnnotations() does not.
Reveal solution

Output:

2
1
0
false

Parent: @Src is discarded by javac; @Cls defaults to CLASS retention, so it is in the bytecode (javap -v shows it under RuntimeInvisibleAnnotations) but not in the Class object; @Run and @Base are RUNTIME, giving 2. Child: getAnnotations() adds superclass annotations marked @Inherited, which is only @Base, giving 1; getDeclaredAnnotations() ignores inheritance, giving 0. Finally isAnnotationPresent(Cls.class) is false for the retention reason above. Interview twist: if Parent were an interface and Child implemented it, @Inherited would not apply and the second line would print 0.

1️⃣1️⃣ Java 9 → 17: What Changed (and 8 → 11 → 17 Migration)

Most teams jumped straight from Java 8 to 11 or 17, so interviewers probe two things: do you actually use the post-8 language (records, var, switch expressions, sealed types, pattern matching) and do you know what breaks when you upgrade (modules, removed javax.*, strong encapsulation). The cards go release by release, then dig into the internals people like to ask about, and finish with a migration playbook and a look past 17.

Release Cadence, LTS and Preview vs Incubator vs Standard

Why interviewers ask: "Which Java are you on and why?" is a warm-up that reveals whether you understand LTS, why Spring Boot 3 forces 17, and whether you would ship preview features to production.

Since Java 9 (September 2017) a new feature release ships every 6 months (March and September). Only some are LTS (long-term support) with multi-year security updates from vendors: 8, 11, 17, 21 (and 25). Non-LTS releases (9, 10, 12–16) are effectively unsupported the day the next one lands. Analogy: LTS releases are the train stations where most passengers get on; the other releases are the track between them.

A feature enters the JDK in one of three states. Incubator = an API in a jdk.incubator.* module that can change or vanish (HTTP client in 9, Vector API). Preview = a fully specified language/VM feature that needs --enable-preview at compile and run time, and whose class files only run on that exact JDK version (records in 14–15, sealed classes in 15–16, pattern matching for switch in 17–20). Standard = final, no flags. Never ship preview features: the bytecode is version-locked.

"Java 17 baseline" (Spring Boot 3 / Spring Framework 6, Hibernate 6, Jakarta EE 10) means the library itself is compiled for class-file version 61 and uses records, sealed types and switch expressions internally, so your app cannot run it on 11 at all. It usually arrives together with the javax.* → jakarta.* namespace change.

  • Java 9 (Sep 2017) — Module system (JPMS), jshell, List.of, G1 default, compact strings, multi-release jars.
  • Java 10 (Mar 2018) — var, AppCDS, container awareness, parallel full GC for G1.
  • Java 11 (Sep 2018, LTS) — Standard HTTP client, String/Files helpers, JFR open-sourced, ZGC experimental, Java EE & CORBA modules removed.
  • Java 12 (Mar 2019) — Switch expressions (preview), Shenandoah, Collectors.teeing, default CDS archive.
  • Java 13 (Sep 2019) — Text blocks (preview), yield, dynamic CDS.
  • Java 14 (Mar 2020) — Switch expressions standard, helpful NPEs, records & pattern matching instanceof (preview), CMS removed.
  • Java 15 (Sep 2020) — Text blocks standard, sealed classes (preview), ZGC & Shenandoah production, Nashorn removed.
  • Java 16 (Mar 2021) — Records & pattern matching instanceof standard, Stream.toList(), strong encapsulation on by default.
  • Java 17 (Sep 2021, LTS) — Sealed classes standard, pattern matching for switch (preview), --illegal-access removed, Security Manager deprecated, Apple silicon port, new random generator API.
Interview angle: "We are on 8, should we go to 11 or 17?" Go to 17: 11's window is closing, Spring Boot 2.7 is out of OSS support, and the 11→17 jump is mostly about strong encapsulation, which you fix with the same tooling as the 8→11 jump. Vendors offering LTS builds: Oracle, Eclipse Temurin (Adoptium), Amazon Corretto, Azul Zulu, Microsoft, Red Hat.

Pitfalls

  • "Java 17 has pattern matching for switch." Only as preview (JEP 406). Standard arrives in 21. Be precise about this in interviews.
  • Compiling with --release 17 is safer than -source/-target: it also checks you only use the Java 17 API.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is the class-file major version per release? (8 = 52, 11 = 55, 17 = 61, 21 = 65; "Unsupported class file major version 61" means a bytecode library is too old.)
  • Are non-LTS releases "beta"? (No, they are production quality, just short-lived.)

Java 9: Modules, Collection Factories, Stream/Optional Additions

Why interviewers ask: Java 9 is the release that changed the JDK's shape (modules, G1 default, compact strings). Candidates who know only "List.of" miss the platform-level story.

JPMS (Project Jigsaw) split the JDK into ~70 modules (java.base, java.sql, …) described by module-info.java with requires, exports and opens. Your classpath code runs in the unnamed module, so you rarely write module descriptors, but you inherit the consequences: internal packages such as sun.misc.Unsafe users and reflection into java.base become restricted (see strong encapsulation). rt.jar is gone, replaced by lib/modules; jlink can build a minimal runtime image containing only the modules you need.

Language and API additions are small but you should use them daily: private interface methods (share code between default methods), immutable collection factories (List.of, Set.of, Map.of, Map.ofEntries — null-hostile, unmodifiable, Set.of/Map.of reject duplicate keys with IllegalArgumentException), Optional (ifPresentOrElse, or, stream), Stream (takeWhile, dropWhile, three-arg iterate(seed, hasNext, next), ofNullable), CompletableFuture.orTimeout/completeOnTimeout, InputStream.transferTo, try-with-resources on effectively-final variables, @Deprecated(since, forRemoval) plus the jdeprscan tool.

Under the hood: G1 became the default collector, compact strings store Latin-1 text as one byte per char (byte[] value + coder field) cutting heap for typical apps by 10–20 %, and multi-release jars (META-INF/versions/17/...) let one jar carry version-specific classes.

// Optional and Stream additions you should reach for on 9+
Optional<User> cached = cache.find(id);
cached.ifPresentOrElse(u -> log.info("hit {}", u), () -> log.info("miss"));
User user = cached.or(() -> repo.findById(id)).orElseThrow();

List<Order> firstBatch = orders.stream()
        .takeWhile(o -> o.createdAt().isBefore(cutoff))   // stops at first failure (ordered stream)
        .toList();                                          // Stream.toList() is Java 16

Stream.iterate(1, i -> i <= 1024, i -> i * 2).forEach(System.out::println); // 1,2,4…1024

List<String> roles = List.of("ADMIN", "USER");   // unmodifiable; roles.add() → UnsupportedOperationException

CompletableFuture<Price> price = pricing.quoteAsync(sku)
        .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)          // completes exceptionally
        .exceptionally(ex -> Price.UNAVAILABLE);
try (InputStream in = req.getInputStream(); OutputStream out = Files.newOutputStream(tmp)) {
    in.transferTo(out);
}
AreaJava 9 changeWhat the interviewer really wants
Modulesmodule-info.java, requires/exports/opens, unnamed module, jlinkYou know why reflective access into java.* internals started warning and why rt.jar hacks broke
CollectionsList.of/Set.of/Map.of immutable, null-hostileDifference from Arrays.asList (fixed-size but mutable elements) and Collections.unmodifiableList (a view over a mutable list)
InterfacesPrivate (static) methodsHelpers for default methods without leaking them as API
Streams / OptionaltakeWhile, dropWhile, iterate, ofNullable; ifPresentOrElse, or, streamtakeWhile is ordered-prefix, not filter; Optional.stream() flattens optionals inside flatMap
RuntimeG1 default, compact strings, StackWalker, Process API, VarHandle, string concat via invokedynamicWhy Java 9+ heaps are smaller and why pause behaviour changed versus Parallel GC on 8
Toolsjshell, jdeps, jdeprscan, multi-release jarsHow you diagnose a migration before touching code
Real-world: a Spring Boot fat jar still runs on the classpath, in the unnamed module, on Java 17. Modules matter to you mostly as a consumer: --add-opens, --add-exports and jlink-built container images (~40 MB runtime instead of a full JDK).

Pitfalls

  • Map.of(k1, v1, k1, v2) throws at runtime (duplicate key); List.of(null) throws NPE. Serialising them to JSON is fine, but Jackson deserialises into ArrayList, so do not assume immutability round-trips.
  • Immutable collection factories have unspecified iteration order for Set.of/Map.of (randomised per JVM run) — tests that depend on order become flaky.
  • takeWhile on an unordered parallel stream may keep an arbitrary subset.

Likely follow-ups

  • What does opens add over exports? (exports = compile/run access to public API; opens = deep reflection into non-public members too, what Spring/Hibernate need.)
  • Why did G1 replace Parallel GC as default? (Predictable pauses with regions and concurrent marking; Parallel still wins on raw throughput for batch jobs.)
  • How does Stream.iterate(seed, hasNext, next) differ from iterate(seed, next).limit(n)? (Termination by predicate, like a classic for loop.)

Java 10–11: var, HTTP Client, String/Files Helpers, and the Java EE Removal

Why interviewers ask: 11 is the LTS most companies actually moved to. They test var rules (a favourite trick question) and whether you know that JAXB/javax.annotation vanishing is the number-one 8→11 breaker.

var (Java 10, JEP 286) is local variable type inference, not dynamic typing: the compiler fixes the static type from the initialiser and it never changes. Allowed: local variables with an initialiser, for/enhanced-for variables, try-with-resources, and lambda parameters (11, so you can annotate them). Not allowed: fields, method parameters, return types, var x = null;, array initialisers (var a = {1,2};), lambdas/method refs without a target type, or compound declarations (var a = 1, b = 2;). Trap: var list = new ArrayList<>(); infers ArrayList<Object>, and var hides whether you hold the interface or the implementation — so keep the right-hand side self-describing.

Java 11 (JEP 321) promoted the HTTP Client to java.net.http: HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, synchronous send and asynchronous sendAsync returning CompletableFuture, WebSocket, and body handlers (ofString, ofFile, ofInputStream, ofLines). It finally retires HttpURLConnection for new code.
