Small but daily-use APIs: String.isBlank/lines/strip/stripLeading/stripTrailing/repeat (strip is Unicode-aware, trim only drops ≤ U+0020), Files.readString/writeString, Path.of, Predicate.not, Optional.isEmpty (11) and no-arg Optional.orElseThrow() (10, the "honest" get()), Collectors.toUnmodifiableList/Set/Map and List.copyOf (10). Also: run a single source file directly with java Hello.java, TLS 1.3, Epsilon no-op GC (JEP 318, for benchmarking/short-lived jobs) and ZGC experimental (JEP 333).

The breaker: JEP 320 removed the Java EE and CORBA modules — java.xml.bind (JAXB), java.xml.ws (JAX-WS), java.activation, java.transaction, java.corba and java.xml.ws.annotation (which held javax.annotation.@PostConstruct/@PreDestroy/@Resource/@Generated). Anything that compiled against these on 8 fails on 11 with ClassNotFoundException: javax.xml.bind.JAXBException or "package javax.annotation does not exist" until you add the standalone artefacts. Nashorn was deprecated in 11 and removed in 15.

var client = HttpClient.newBuilder()
        .version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_2)          // falls back to 1.1 automatically
        .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
        .build();                                    // thread-safe; build once, reuse

var request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://api.example.com/items/42"))
        .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))              // per-request read timeout
        .header("Accept", "application/json")
        .GET()
        .build();

// synchronous
HttpResponse<String> resp = client.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
if (resp.statusCode() == 200) System.out.println(resp.body());

// asynchronous: returns CompletableFuture, no thread blocked while waiting
CompletableFuture<String> body = client.sendAsync(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString())
        .thenApply(HttpResponse::body)
        .orTimeout(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

String text = Files.readString(Path.of("config.yaml"));
List<String> nonBlank = text.lines().filter(Predicate.not(String::isBlank)).map(String::strip).toList();
Interview angle: "Does var make Java dynamically typed?" No — the type is inferred once at compile time; var s = "x"; s = 1; fails to compile. "Would you use the JDK HTTP client instead of a library?" For simple calls yes; Spring teams usually prefer RestClient/WebClient for interceptors, codecs and observability, but the JDK client is what they wrap (Spring 6's JdkClientHttpRequestFactory).
Removed / changed in 11Symptom on 11+Fix
java.xml.bind (JAXB)NoClassDefFoundError: javax/xml/bind/JAXBExceptionjakarta.xml.bind:jakarta.xml.bind-api + org.glassfish.jaxb:jaxb-runtime (2.3.x keeps the javax.xml.bind package; 3+/4+ use jakarta.xml.bind)
java.xml.ws.annotation"package javax.annotation does not exist" (@PostConstruct)jakarta.annotation:jakarta.annotation-api (1.3.5 for javax, 2.x for jakarta; Spring supports both)
java.activation, java.transactionMissing javax.activation.DataHandler, javax.transaction.*jakarta.activation-api, jakarta.transaction-api
java.corba, JAX-WSMissing org.omg.*, javax.jwsGlassfish Metro / jakarta.xml.ws-api or, better, stop using CORBA
Nashorn (deprecated 11, removed 15)ScriptEngineManager.getEngineByName("nashorn") returns nullorg.openjdk.nashorn:nashorn-core standalone, or GraalJS

Pitfalls

  • var with the diamond operator (var m = new HashMap<>()) infers Object type arguments; spell the generics out on the right-hand side.
  • var for a chained stream result or a Map.Entry is fine; var hiding a long vs int distinction (var n = 1; is int) causes silent overflow later.
  • The JDK HttpClient has no per-client read timeout — only connectTimeout; set HttpRequest.timeout or you can hang forever on a stalled server.
  • Collectors.toUnmodifiableList() throws NPE on null elements; Stream.toList() (16) allows nulls.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why did Oracle remove JAXB from the JDK? (It belonged to Java EE, which moved to Eclipse as Jakarta EE; keeping it in the JDK tied its release cycle to the platform.)
  • What is the difference between strip() and trim()? (strip uses Character.isWhitespace, so it removes Unicode spaces such as U+2003; trim removes only code points ≤ U+0020.)
  • When is Epsilon GC useful? (Allocation-only benchmarks, extremely short-lived jobs, or proving that your service allocates nothing in the hot path.)

Java 12–15: Switch Expressions, Text Blocks, Helpful NPEs

Why interviewers ask: switch expressions are the first place where the "new Java" semantics differ from C-style Java. Predict-the-output questions target fallthrough, yield, and text-block indentation rules.

Switch expressions (preview 12–13, standard 14, JEP 361) add the case A, B -> value; form: no fallthrough, multiple labels per case, the switch returns a value, and a block body returns via yield. A switch expression must be exhaustive: for int/String that means a default; for an enum, covering every constant is enough and the compiler inserts a hidden default that throws if a new constant appears at run time. You cannot mix arrow and colon forms in one switch, but the old case X: form can still be used inside an expression with yield. Analogy: the old switch is a staircase you fall down unless someone puts a gate (break) on each step; the arrow form gives every step its own door.

Text blocks (preview 13–14, standard 15, JEP 378) start with """ followed by a mandatory newline. The compiler removes incidental indentation: it finds the smallest indentation across all non-blank lines including the line holding the closing """ and strips it, then strips trailing spaces on each line. So moving the closing delimiter left adds indentation to every line. Two escape sequences exist only for text blocks: \ at end of line joins lines (no newline), and \s is a space that survives trailing-space stripping. Use String.formatted(...) (15) instead of String.format for placeholders.

Other items in this window: helpful NullPointerExceptions (JEP 358, on by default from 15): the message now says which reference was null — "Cannot invoke "String.length()" because the return value of "Order.customer()" is null". Records and pattern matching for instanceof previewed in 14, sealed classes in 15. Runtime: Shenandoah (12, low-pause GC from Red Hat), ZGC and Shenandoah production (15), CMS removed (14), default and dynamic CDS archives (12/13), Collectors.teeing (12), String.indent/transform (12), NIO socket reimplementation (13, groundwork for virtual threads). Stream.toList() and standard records came only in 16.

static String oldStyle(int day) {
    String kind = "";
    switch (day) {
        case 6:
        case 7:
            kind = "weekend";
        case 1:
            kind = "monday";
            break;
        default:
            kind = "weekday";
    }
    return kind;
}
static String newStyle(int day) {
    return switch (day) {
        case 6, 7 -> "weekend";
        case 1 -> {
            var s = "mon";
            yield s + "day";
        }
        default -> "weekday";
    };
}
  1. Calling oldStyle(7): jump to the matching label.
  2. case 7 matches; kind = "weekend". So far correct.
  3. Missing break: control falls into case 1 and overwrites kind. This is the bug.
  4. Returns "monday" for a Sunday. The compiler could not help because fallthrough is legal.
  5. newStyle(7): case 6, 7 -> "weekend" yields the value and the switch is done. Returns "weekend".
  6. newStyle(1): block body needs yield to produce the value.
  7. default is mandatory here because int cannot be enumerated. The result is an expression, so it can be assigned or returned directly.
String json = """
        {
          "sku": "%s",
          "qty": %d
        }\
        """.formatted(sku, qty);      // closing """ at same indent as content → no leading spaces
// Result: {\n  "sku": "A1",\n  "qty": 2\n} — the trailing \ removed the final newline

String sql = """
        SELECT id, name \
        FROM users \
        WHERE active = true""";   // one line: "SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE active = true"

String padded = """
        col1\s
        col2\s""";                // \s keeps the trailing space that would otherwise be stripped

enum Level { LOW, MID, HIGH }
int weight(Level l) {
    return switch (l) {             // exhaustive over the enum → no default needed
        case LOW -> 1;
        case MID -> 5;
        case HIGH -> 10;
    };
}
Interview angle: "What happens if someone adds Level.CRITICAL and only recompiles the enum?" The switch expression's synthetic default throws at run time (IncompatibleClassChangeError on 17; MatchException from 21). "Why not just use break discipline?" Because the compiler cannot enforce it; arrow cases make the bug class impossible.

Pitfalls

  • return inside a switch-expression block is a compile error ("attempt to return out of a switch expression"); use yield. Conversely, yield is a contextual keyword — yield as a method name still compiles but a bare statement yield(x); is now parsed as the yield statement.
  • Text block: the closing """ on its own line adds a trailing newline; put it on the last content line to avoid it. Tabs vs spaces mixed in indentation are counted as one whitespace each, so mixing breaks stripping.
  • Old colon-form switch statements still fall through in Java 17; migrating a statement to arrows changes behaviour if fallthrough was intentional.
  • Helpful NPE messages compute lazily and are omitted for code compiled without local variable names (-g:none); they show variable names only when compiled with -g.

Likely follow-ups

  • Can a switch expression throw? (Yes: default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException(...) is a valid arm because throw is treated as an expression result of type "nothing".)
  • Does the arrow form work in a switch statement? (Yes, arrows without a value, e.g. case 1 -> log();, still no fallthrough.)
  • How do you keep JSON/SQL text blocks readable and safe? (Text block for shape, formatted or parameters for values; never concatenate user input into SQL.)

Java 8 vs 17

On 8 a "value-producing switch" needs a mutable local plus break on every branch and a default you hope nobody forgets; on 17 it is an expression that the compiler forces to be exhaustive and fallthrough-free. Multi-line strings on 8 mean + "\n" + chains or external files.

Java 16–17: Records, Pattern Matching for instanceof, Sealed Classes, and the 17 Cleanups

Why interviewers ask: this is "the Java 17 feature set". Records and pattern matching change how you write DTOs and type checks; the 17 removals explain most upgrade tickets.

Records (16, JEP 395) are nominal tuples: record Point(int x, int y) {} generates a canonical constructor, accessors x()/y(), equals/hashCode/toString. They are implicitly final, cannot declare instance fields beyond the components, can implement interfaces, and support a compact constructor for validation/normalisation. Static fields, static methods and nested records are fine; local records (declared inside a method) are implicitly static. Reflection treats them specially (Class.isRecord(), getRecordComponents()), which is how Jackson 2.12+ and Spring bind them without setters.

Pattern matching for instanceof (16, JEP 394): if (o instanceof String s && s.length() > 3) binds s only where the compiler can prove the match. Flow scoping: && is allowed on the right because the left must be true; || is rejected because s might not be bound. The binding is also in scope after if (!(o instanceof String s)) return;. Java 16 additionally forbids a pattern whose type is total on the expression (String s2 on a String) — that is lifted in 21.

Sealed classes (17, JEP 409): sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square closes the hierarchy; every permitted subtype must be final, sealed or non-sealed, and must live in the same module (or same package on the classpath). Records are implicitly final so "sealed interface + records" is the idiomatic algebraic data type; the next card shows why the compiler can then check exhaustiveness. API additions: Stream.toList() (unmodifiable, null-tolerant), Stream.mapMulti (a push-style flatMap without allocating intermediate streams), Unix-domain socket channels, jpackage standard, enhanced pseudo-random generators (17, JEP 356: RandomGenerator.of("L64X128MixRandom"), splittable/jumpable streams, RandomGeneratorFactory), and always-strict floating point (17, JEP 306: strictfp is now the only semantics, the keyword is a no-op).

The 17 cleanups: strong encapsulation of JDK internals is the default (16) and the --illegal-access escape hatch is removed (17, JEP 403); the experimental AOT compiler (jaotc) and Graal JIT were removed (JEP 410) — Graal lives on in GraalVM; Security Manager deprecated for removal (JEP 411, disabled by default from 18, permanently disabled in 24); RMI Activation removed; Apple silicon (macOS/AArch64) port (JEP 391); context-specific deserialization filters (JEP 415); the applet API deprecated for removal.

public record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) implements Comparable<Money> {
    public Money {                                         // compact constructor: validate + normalise
        Objects.requireNonNull(amount); Objects.requireNonNull(currency);
        amount = amount.setScale(currency.getDefaultFractionDigits(), RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);
    }
    public static Money zero(Currency c) { return new Money(BigDecimal.ZERO, c); }
    public Money plus(Money o) {
        if (!currency.equals(o.currency)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch");
        return new Money(amount.add(o.amount), currency);
    }
    @Override public int compareTo(Money o) { return amount.compareTo(o.amount); }
}

static String describe(Object o) {
    if (o instanceof Money m && m.amount().signum() > 0) return "credit " + m;   // && ok
    if (!(o instanceof CharSequence cs)) return "unknown";
    return "text of length " + cs.length();                 // cs in scope: the negated branch returned
}

// mapMulti: emit 0..n elements per input without creating a Stream per element
List<Integer> evensDoubled = List.of(1, 2, 3, 4).stream()
        .<Integer>mapMulti((n, sink) -> { if (n % 2 == 0) sink.accept(n * 2); })
        .toList();                                          // [4, 8]
FeatureStandard sinceOne-line rule to remember
Records16Immutable, final, accessor = component name, no extra instance fields, compact ctor for validation
Pattern matching instanceof16Binding is in scope wherever the match is definitely true (&&, negated-return); never with ||
Sealed classes17Subtypes listed in permits (or same file), each final/sealed/non-sealed
Pattern matching for switch21 (preview in 17)Type patterns as case labels, guards with when, exhaustive over sealed types
Stream.toList()16Unmodifiable, allows null; not the same contract as Collectors.toList()
Strong encapsulation16 default, 17 finalDeep reflection into java.* needs --add-opens; no global switch on 17
Interview angle: "Would you use a record as a JPA entity?" No: entities need a no-arg constructor, mutable state and proxying; records are for DTOs, value objects, projections and map keys. "Does a record with an array or List component stay immutable?" Only shallowly — copy defensively in the compact constructor (items = List.copyOf(items)).

Pitfalls

  • Record equals uses component equality; a double component compares via Double.compare (so NaN equals NaN, unlike ==).
  • Lombok @Value/@Data and records overlap; teams on 17 should default to records and keep Lombok for builders and loggers only. Lombok before 1.18.20 could not even parse records.
  • Stream.toList() silently changes the mutability contract if you replace collect(Collectors.toList()) and later call add.
  • Sealed hierarchies across Maven modules only work when both sides are named JPMS modules; on the classpath the permitted classes must be in the same package.

Likely follow-ups

  • Can a record have a mutable field? (No instance fields other than components; but a component can reference a mutable object, hence defensive copies.)
  • What replaces the Security Manager for sandboxing? (Process isolation: containers, seccomp, separate JVMs; not a Java-level API.)
  • Why remove the experimental AOT compiler? (Little use, heavy maintenance; GraalVM native-image covers the use case.)

Sealed Types + Pattern Matching Switch: Compiler-Checked Exhaustiveness

Why interviewers ask: it is the design-level payoff of Java 17: the compiler, not a runtime default branch, guarantees you handled every case. Senior candidates are expected to explain why sealing enables this and what happens when the hierarchy grows.

With an open hierarchy the compiler cannot know all subtypes, so a switch over types always needs a default. A sealed type gives the compiler the closed list (permits), so a switch with type patterns over it is exhaustive without default — and the moment somebody adds a permitted subtype, every switch that does not handle it becomes a compile error ("the switch expression does not cover all possible input values"). Analogy: a sealed interface is a fixed cast list; the compiler is the stage manager who refuses to start the show if any actor has no lines.

Nuance for 17: type patterns in case labels are preview in 17 (JEP 406, --enable-preview), standard in 21 (JEP 441). On plain 17 you get the sealing and the instanceof patterns, but the exhaustive switch shown below needs preview or Java 21. What sealing already buys on plain 17: documented closed hierarchies, safe downcasts, and reflection via Class.getPermittedSubclasses() so frameworks (Jackson polymorphic types) can enumerate subtypes.

sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square, Triangle {}
record Circle(double r) implements Shape {}
record Square(double side) implements Shape {}
record Triangle(double b, double h) implements Shape {}

// Java 17: needs --enable-preview (JEP 406). Java 21+: standard (JEP 441).
static double area(Shape s) {
    return switch (s) {
        case Circle c   -> Math.PI * c.r() * c.r();
        case Square q   -> q.side() * q.side();
        case Triangle t -> 0.5 * t.b() * t.h();      // remove this line → compile error, not a runtime surprise
    };
}

// Plain Java 17 alternative (no preview): instanceof patterns, but you must supply the fallback yourself
static double area17(Shape s) {
    if (s instanceof Circle c) return Math.PI * c.r() * c.r();
    if (s instanceof Square q) return q.side() * q.side();
    if (s instanceof Triangle t) return 0.5 * t.b() * t.h();
    throw new IllegalStateException("unhandled " + s);   // compiler cannot prove this is dead
}
Real-world: domain events (sealed interface OrderEvent permits Created, Paid, Shipped, Cancelled) and API results (sealed interface Result<T> permits Ok, Err) are the two most common uses. Sealed + records replaces the Visitor pattern for most "operation over a closed set of types" needs.

Pitfalls

  • Adding default to a pattern switch over a sealed type throws away the exhaustiveness guarantee. Leave it out on purpose.
  • A non-sealed subtype reopens that branch: anyone can extend it, so the switch only needs a case for the non-sealed type, not its unknown descendants.
  • Pattern switch on 17 with null input throws NPE unless there is a case null (preview syntax) — the classic switch also NPEs on null, so this is not new, but it surprises people using Object selectors.
  • Case order matters with dominance: case Shape s before case Circle c is a compile error ("this case label is dominated by a preceding case label").

Likely follow-ups

  • Can a sealed class permit a class in another package? (Only inside a named module; on the classpath all permitted subclasses must share the package.)
  • Can enums do this already? (Yes for constants; sealed types add per-subtype data and types, i.e. a sum type with payloads.)
  • What happens if a subtype is compiled later and the switch class is not recompiled? (Runtime MatchException/IncompatibleClassChangeError from the synthetic default — the same separate-compilation caveat as enums.)

Beyond 17

Java 21 adds record patterns so you can destructure inside the case: case Circle(double r) -> Math.PI * r * r, plus guards (case Square q when q.side() == 0 -> 0) and case null.

Under-the-Hood Improvements Interviewers Like

Why interviewers ask: "What actually got faster or cheaper when you moved to 17?" A concrete answer (startup via CDS, memory via compact strings and container limits, diagnostics via JFR) shows you measured rather than just bumped a version number.

Several changes have no syntax but change production behaviour. String concatenation via invokedynamic (9, JEP 280): a + b + c no longer compiles to a StringBuilder chain; javac emits an invokedynamic to StringConcatFactory, letting the JDK pick the fastest strategy at run time (and improve it without recompiling you). Class-Data Sharing: the JDK ships a default CDS archive (12) so core classes are memory-mapped pre-parsed; AppCDS (10, JEP 310) extends this to your classes (-XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa in 13+, then -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa), cutting Spring Boot startup by roughly 20–40 % — Boot 3.3 automates it via -Djarmode=tools extract and a training run.

Container awareness (10, backported to 8u191): the JVM reads cgroup CPU and memory limits instead of the host's, so Runtime.availableProcessors() and default heap (-XX:MaxRAMPercentage, default 25 %) respect the pod. Before 8u191, a 512 MB pod on a 64 GB node got a 16 GB default heap and was OOM-killed. JFR (Flight Recorder) and JMC were open-sourced in 11 (JEP 328): always-on, ~1 % overhead production profiling (-XX:StartFlightRecording). ZGC reached production in 15 (sub-millisecond pauses regardless of heap size, generational in 21); G1 gained parallel full GC (10), abortable mixed collections (12), memory uncommit while idle (12), NUMA awareness (14).

ImprovementReleaseEffect you can quoteFlag / API

Compact strings9Latin-1 strings use 1 byte/char; 10–20 % smaller heaps typical-XX:-CompactStrings disables
Default CDS / AppCDS / dynamic CDS12 / 10 / 13Faster class loading, shared read-only metadata across JVMs on a host-XX:SharedArchiveFile, -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit

Interview angle: "Your pod has 1 CPU and 1 GB; what does the JVM do?" On 10+/8u191+ it sees 1 processor (common pool parallelism 1, G1 may drop to Serial GC below 2 CPUs / 2 GB — check your JDK), and a 256 MB default max heap; set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 explicitly. "How would you profile a latency spike in prod?" Start a JFR recording via jcmd, analyse in JMC.

Pitfalls

  • Container awareness only reads limits, not requests; and cgroup v2 support arrived in 15 (backported to 11.0.16 and 8u372). Older JDKs on cgroup v2 nodes fall back to host values.
  • AppCDS archives are tied to the exact JDK build and classpath; rebuild them in the image build stage, not at deploy time.

Likely follow-ups

  • Should you still write StringBuilder loops? (Yes for loops — indy helps only a single expression; a loop of s += x is still quadratic.)
  • What does JFR cost? (Around 1 % with the default profile; safe to leave on.)

Strong Encapsulation: From Warning (9) to Deny (16) to No Switch at All (17)

Why interviewers ask: the single most common 11→17 failure is java.lang.reflect.InaccessibleObjectException: Unable to make field … accessible: module java.base does not "opens java.lang" to unnamed module. Explaining why it appeared now, and the right fix versus the quick fix, is a senior-level answer.

Modules let java.base declare which packages are exported (public API usable) and opened (deep reflection allowed). Libraries built in the Java 8 era freely called setAccessible(true) on private JDK fields (Gson on java.util internals, old Mockito/ByteBuddy defining classes via ClassLoader.defineClass, Netty and Kryo on java.nio.DirectByteBuffer, Hibernate/Groovy/Lombok on javac internals). Java 9 could not break all of them at once, so it shipped --illegal-access=permit as the default: the first illegal access prints "WARNING: An illegal reflective access operation has occurred" and continues.

Java 16 (JEP 396) flipped the default to deny; Java 17 (JEP 403) removed the option entirely — passing --illegal-access now only prints a warning that it is ignored. The only remaining doors are explicit and per package: --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED on the command line, in JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS, in a jar manifest Add-Opens: attribute (main jar only), or in Maven Surefire's argLine. Analogy: 9–15 left the office doors unlocked with a sign-in sheet; 16 locked them; 17 removed the master key, so every door you need is a named exception on the badge. Note that sun.misc.Unsafe stayed reachable through the jdk.unsupported module on purpose, which is why Netty, Kafka and friends still run without flags.

# 1. Find who touches JDK internals before you upgrade
jdeps --jdk-internals --multi-release 17 -R --class-path 'target/lib/*' target/app.jar

# 2. Unblock while libraries are upgraded (one entry per package in the stack trace)
java --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED \
     --add-opens java.base/java.util=ALL-UNNAMED \
     --add-exports java.base/sun.nio.ch=ALL-UNNAMED \
     -jar app.jar

# Same thing without touching the launch command (picked up by every java invocation)
export JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS="--add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED"

# Maven Surefire / Failsafe for tests
#   <argLine>--add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED</argLine>
Interview angle: "Why does my app work on 11 but not 17 with zero code changes?" Because 11 still defaulted to permit; the warning you saw in the 11 logs was the heads-up. "Is --add-opens a security hole?" It weakens encapsulation for that package only and only for the code you ship; it is not remote-exploitable by itself, but it pins you to JDK internals that can change in any update.

Pitfalls

  • --add-opens in JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS applies to every JVM on the host including build tools; prefer JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS (java launcher only) or the launch script.
  • The manifest Add-Opens attribute is honoured only for the jar launched with -jar, not for jars on the classpath.
  • --add-exports ≠ --add-opens: exports gives compile/link access to public members; reflection on private members still needs opens.
  • Removing --illegal-access did not remove sun.misc.Unsafe; its memory-access methods are deprecated for removal from 23 (JEP 471), which is the next migration wave.

Likely follow-ups

  • How do you open a package from within a named module? (opens pkg to targetModule; in module-info.java.)
  • What is ALL-UNNAMED? (The classpath: every class not in a named module.)
  • Why does Spring/Hibernate work without flags? (They reflect into your classes, which live in the unnamed module and are open to everyone; only reflection into JDK modules is restricted.)

Migration Playbook: 8 → 11 → 17

Why interviewers ask: "Walk me through how you upgraded a service from 8 to 17." They are looking for a repeatable process — inventory, build, test, run, observe — rather than "we bumped the version and fixed errors as they came".

The order matters: fix the build tooling first (Maven 3.8+, Gradle 7.3+ for 17 class files, maven-compiler-plugin with <release>17</release>, Surefire 3.x), then libraries that generate or parse bytecode (they hard-fail on class-file version 61: Lombok 1.18.22+, Mockito 4+/ByteBuddy 1.12+, ASM 9.2+, cglib-based proxies, Jacoco 0.8.7+, Groovy 3.0.9+, Spring 5.3.x or 6), then removed APIs, then runtime flags. Do 8 → 11 → 17 as one project but compile against 11 first: JEP 320 removals surface as compile errors on 11, while 17 issues are mostly reflection at run time, so the two stages fail in different places and are easier to attribute.

Removed or degraded APIs to grep for: javax.xml.bind, javax.annotation (@PostConstruct, @Generated), javax.activation, javax.jws, org.omg.* (all 11); Thread.destroy() and Thread.stop(Throwable) (11), Runtime.runFinalizersOnExit (11); Thread.stop/suspend/resume and ThreadGroup.stop are deprecated-for-removal and throw UnsupportedOperationException from 20; Nashorn (15); sun.misc.BASE64Encoder, sun.reflect.Reflection.getCallerClass (9, use StackWalker); the Extension class loader and URLClassLoader cast (9); SecurityManager (deprecated 17, non-functional 18+); finalize() deprecated for removal (18); RMI Activation (17); Pack200 (14); jaotc (17).

Some behaviour changes silently: the default GC is G1 not Parallel (retune or set -XX:+UseParallelGC for batch), String and Locale data moved to CLDR in 9 (date/number formatting can differ, -Djava.locale.providers=COMPAT to compare), TLS 1.0/1.1 disabled (11.0.11+), Object.finalize timing, and Set.of/HashSet iteration order in tests.

PhaseDoTool / artefact
0. InventoryList JDK-internal usage and deprecated-for-removal APIs across your jar and dependenciesjdeps --jdk-internals, jdeprscan --for-removal --release 17, mvn versions:display-dependency-updates
1. BuildUpgrade Maven/Gradle and every bytecode plugin; set --releaseCompiler, Surefire, Jacoco, Lombok, Spotbugs, Error Prone
2. Compile on 11Add jakarta.xml.bind-api + jaxb-runtime, jakarta.annotation-api, activation; replace NashornCompile errors = complete list of JEP 320 hits
3. Compile on 17Upgrade Mockito/ByteBuddy/ASM users; replace SecurityManager, Thread.stop, finalize"Unsupported class file major version 61" = bytecode lib too old
4. Run tests on 17Fix InaccessibleObjectException: upgrade lib, else --add-opens in Surefire argLineStack trace names the module/package to open
5. Run in stagingCompare GC logs (G1 vs Parallel), heap sizing in containers, locale/date formatting, TLS handshakes-Xlog:gc*, JFR, canary traffic
6. AdoptOnly now: records, var, switch expressions, text blocks, Stream.toList; consider Spring Boot 3 / Jakarta namespace as a separate stepOpenRewrite recipes (UpgradeToJava17, SpringBoot3) automate most of it
Checklist — 8 → 11 → 17
[ ] Build: Maven ≥ 3.8 / Gradle ≥ 7.3, compiler <release>17</release>, Surefire ≥ 3.0
[ ] Bytecode libs: Lombok ≥ 1.18.22, Mockito ≥ 4 (ByteBuddy ≥ 1.12), ASM ≥ 9.2, Jacoco ≥ 0.8.7, Groovy ≥ 3.0.9
[ ] javax.xml.bind / javax.annotation / javax.activation → jakarta.* API + runtime deps
[ ] Nashorn → nashorn-core standalone or GraalJS; CORBA/JAX-WS → standalone or remove
[ ] grep for sun.misc, sun.reflect, com.sun.* (except jdk.unsupported), URLClassLoader casts
[ ] jdeps --jdk-internals on the full classpath; jdeprscan --for-removal
[ ] Thread.stop/suspend/resume, finalize(), SecurityManager, Runtime.exec(String) usages reviewed
[ ] --add-opens entries documented with the library that needs them and a removal ticket each
[ ] GC: keep G1 or explicitly choose; MaxRAMPercentage set for containers
[ ] Locale/date formatting and Set/Map iteration-order assumptions in tests
[ ] Base image: Temurin/Corretto 17 JRE or jlink image; JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS reviewed
[ ] Observability: JFR enabled, GC logs with -Xlog:gc*, dashboards compared before/after
Interview angle: "What surprised you most?" Good answers: the dependency you did not know you had (transitive JAXB via a SOAP client), the test suite that depended on HashSet order, the batch job that got slower on G1 until you set Parallel GC, and the Docker image that still had -Xmx hard-coded from a bare-metal era.

Pitfalls

  • Mixing javax.xml.bind-api 2.3 with jaxb-runtime 3.x or 4.x: the namespaces differ (javax vs jakarta) and you get ClassNotFoundException for the implementation. Keep API and runtime on the same major line.
  • Compiling with -source 8 -target 8 on JDK 17 does not prove Java 8 compatibility: you may call 17-only APIs. Use --release 8 if you still need to ship for 8.
  • Spring Boot 2.x works on 17 (2.5.5+ officially), so "Boot 3 first" is not required; do the JDK upgrade, ship, then do Boot 3 / Jakarta.
  • A --add-opens added "temporarily" in 2021 is still in most launch scripts. Attach an owner and a ticket to each one.

Likely follow-ups

  • Can you run 8-compiled jars on 17 unchanged? (Usually yes — the JVM is backward compatible for bytecode; failures come from removed APIs and reflection, not from bytecode.)
  • How do you keep a library compatible with both 8 and 17? (Multi-release jar: base classes for 8, META-INF/versions/17 overrides; --release per source set.)
  • What about 17 → 21? (Mostly painless: virtual threads are opt-in, SecurityManager and Thread.stop now hard-fail, finalize still works but warns.)

Beyond 17: Java 21 Headlines (Not Part of the 17 Baseline)

Why interviewers ask: to check that you follow the platform and can separate "what we run" from "what is coming". Everything in this card requires Java 21; do not present it as a Java 17 feature.

Java 21 (September 2023, LTS) is the next station after 17. Its headline features are listed below with their JEP numbers so you can label them precisely. Spring Boot 3.2+ supports virtual threads with spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true, which is why many teams plan 17 → 21 as a short follow-up rather than a big project.

Java 21 (beyond 17)

  • Virtual threads (JEP 444, standard): cheap JVM-managed threads for blocking I/O at scale — Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); the "thread-per-request without the thread cost" answer to reactive.
  • Sequenced collections (JEP 431): SequencedCollection/SequencedSet/SequencedMap with getFirst/getLast/addFirst/addLast/reversed() on List, Deque, LinkedHashSet, LinkedHashMap.
  • Record patterns (JEP 440, standard): destructure in instanceof and case: if (o instanceof Point(int x, int y)), nested patterns included.
  • Pattern matching for switch (JEP 441, standard): type patterns, when guards, case null, exhaustiveness over sealed hierarchies — the preview from 17 finalised.
  • String templates (JEP 430, preview): STR."Hello \{name}" — note it was withdrawn in Java 23 for redesign, so do not build on it.
  • Generational ZGC (JEP 439): -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational, much lower memory/CPU overhead than single-generation ZGC (default in 23).
  • Also: unnamed patterns/variables and unnamed classes + instance main (preview), structured concurrency and scoped values (preview), Foreign Function & Memory API (3rd preview, standard in 22), Key Encapsulation Mechanism API, Thread.stop/suspend/resume hard-fail.

Likely follow-ups

  • Do virtual threads make reactive obsolete? (For most CRUD/IO services yes; reactive still wins for backpressure and streaming semantics.)
  • What pins a virtual thread? (synchronized blocks and native frames in 21; fixed for synchronized in 24 via JEP 491.)

What does this print?
int d = 7; String k = ""; switch (d) { case 6: case 7: k = "weekend"; case 1: k = "monday"; break; default: k = "weekday"; } System.out.print(k);

c. case 7 sets k = "weekend", then falls through into case 1 which overwrites it with "monday" before the break. It is an assignment, not concatenation, so b is wrong; fallthrough is legal Java, so d is wrong. The arrow form case 6, 7 -> "weekend" makes this bug impossible.

Inside a block-bodied arm of a switch expression (case 1 -> { … }), how do you produce the arm's value?

b. yield (Java 13+) hands the value to the switch expression. return (a) is a compile error because it would exit the enclosing method from inside an expression; break value (c) was the Java 12 preview syntax that was dropped; Java has no implicit last-expression value (d).

Which text block evaluates to exactly "a\nb" (no trailing newline, no leading spaces)?

d. Closing """ on the last content line means no trailing newline, and the common indentation of the content lines is stripped. a yields "a\nb\n" (the delimiter's own line adds a newline). b moves the minimum indentation to column 0, so the result keeps four leading spaces on each line plus a trailing newline. c does not compile: the opening delimiter must be followed by a line terminator.

sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}. Which declaration of Circle compiles?

b. A permitted subtype must be final, sealed or non-sealed; records are implicitly final. A plain class (a) and an abstract class (c) lack the required modifier. d uses extends on an interface, which never compiles.

A pattern switch over a sealed type has no default and covers every permitted subtype. A new permitted record is added and everything is recompiled. What happens?

c. Exhaustiveness is checked at compile time against the permits list, which is the whole point of sealing. The runtime exception in b only occurs under separate compilation (switch class not recompiled). Pattern switches must be exhaustive whether statement or expression, so d is wrong.

On Java 17 an app fails with InaccessibleObjectException: module java.base does not "opens java.util" to unnamed module. It ran fine on Java 11. Why the difference?

a. JEP 396 (16) made deny the default and JEP 403 (17) removed the switch. java.util is still in java.base (b) and setAccessible still exists (c) — it simply throws for non-opened packages. Recompiling (d) changes nothing; the check happens at run time.

Same failure, caused by an old version of a JSON library. Which fix is best in production?

d. Upgrading removes the dependency on JDK internals for good. a is ignored on 17. b works but leaks into every JVM on the host (build tools included) and hides the debt. c silently changes behaviour.

Which statement about var and these APIs is correct?

b. With no target type, the diamond infers Object. var is for locals only (a). Stream.toList() allows nulls while toUnmodifiableList() throws NPE (c). JAXB left in Java 11 (JEP 320), not 17 (d).

Practice

Modernize this Java 8 code to idiomatic Java 17

Rewrite the following without changing behaviour. Use lambdas/method references, Optional chaining, a record, String.join/streams, and pattern matching. Say which parts need Java 21 (or preview on 17) and give the plain-17 alternative.

public class Legacy {
    public static class Customer {
        private final String id; private final String email;
        public Customer(String id, String email) { this.id = id; this.email = email; }
        public String getId() { return id; }
        public String getEmail() { return email; }
        @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { /* 8 lines */ return false; }
        @Override public int hashCode() { return 0; }
        @Override public String toString() { return "Customer[" + id + "," + email + "]"; }
    }

    static String emailOf(Optional<Customer> c) {
        if (c.isPresent()) { return c.get().getEmail().toLowerCase(); } else { return "n/a"; }
    }

    static String csv(List<Customer> list) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++) {
            if (i > 0) sb.append(",");
            sb.append(list.get(i).getId());
        }
        return sb.toString();
    }

    static void sortByEmail(List<Customer> list) {
        Collections.sort(list, new Comparator<Customer>() {
            @Override public int compare(Customer a, Customer b) { return a.getEmail().compareTo(b.getEmail()); }
        });
    }

    static String describe(Object o) {
        if (o instanceof Integer) { Integer i = (Integer) o; return "int:" + (i + 1); }
        else if (o instanceof String) { String s = (String) o; return "str:" + s.length(); }
        else if (o instanceof Customer) { Customer c = (Customer) o; return "cust:" + c.getId(); }
        else { return "other"; }
    }
}
Tests: records, Optional API, Comparator factories, String.join, pattern matchingTime: 15 min
Hint 1
A record gives you constructor, accessors, equals/hashCode/toString for free — but accessor names become id()/email(), so callers change. Optional.map(...).orElse(...) replaces isPresent/get.
Hint 2
Comparator.comparing(Customer::email); list.stream().map(Customer::id).collect(Collectors.joining(",")). For the type chain, instanceof patterns are standard on 17; a pattern switch is preview on 17 and standard on 21.
Reveal solution
public class Modern {
    public record Customer(String id, String email) {}          // equals/hashCode/toString generated

    static String emailOf(Optional<Customer> c) {
        return c.map(Customer::email).map(String::toLowerCase).orElse("n/a");
    }

    static String csv(List<Customer> list) {
        return list.stream().map(Customer::id).collect(Collectors.joining(","));
        // or: String.join(",", list.stream().map(Customer::id).toList());
    }

    static void sortByEmail(List<Customer> list) {
        list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Customer::email));
    }

    // Java 17 (standard): pattern matching for instanceof
    static String describe(Object o) {
        if (o instanceof Integer i)  return "int:" + (i + 1);
        if (o instanceof String s)   return "str:" + s.length();
        if (o instanceof Customer c) return "cust:" + c.id();
        return "other";
    }

    // Java 21 (or 17 with --enable-preview): pattern matching for switch
    static String describe21(Object o) {
        return switch (o) {
            case Integer i  -> "int:" + (i + 1);
            case String s   -> "str:" + s.length();
            case Customer c -> "cust:" + c.id();
            case null, default -> "other";
        };
    }
}

Reasoning and gotchas. (1) The record changes the accessor names (getId() → id()) and makes equals component-based, which is what the hand-written version presumably intended; if Customer is serialised by an older Jackson (< 2.12) or used as a JPA entity, keep the class. (2) Optional.map short-circuits on empty, so no get() and no NoSuchElementException; note the original also NPEs on a null email — map(String::toLowerCase) skips a null returned from email() because map wraps with ofNullable, which is a small behaviour change worth mentioning. (3) Collectors.joining handles the "no comma before first" logic. (4) Comparator.comparing with a method ref replaces the anonymous class; List.sort replaces Collections.sort. (5) The describe chain keeps the original "null → other" behaviour with instanceof (null never matches); the switch version must add case null explicitly or it throws NPE.

Predict the output: switch expression with yield and pattern matching

enum Level { LOW, MID, HIGH }

static String label(Level lv, Object payload) {
    String base = switch (lv) {
        case LOW -> "low";
        case MID, HIGH -> {
            String s = lv.name().toLowerCase();
            if (payload instanceof Integer i && i > 10) yield s + "+" + i;
            yield s;
        }
    };
    return Character.toUpperCase(base.charAt(0)) + base.substring(1);
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    System.out.println(label(Level.MID, 42) + " " + label(Level.HIGH, "42") + " " + label(Level.LOW, 99));

    int n = 2;
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    switch (n) {
        case 1: sb.append("one");
        case 2: sb.append("two");
        case 3: sb.append("three"); break;
        default: sb.append("many");
    }
    String r = switch (n) { case 1 -> "one"; case 2 -> "two"; default -> "many"; };
    System.out.println(sb + " " + r);
}
Tests: yield, enum exhaustiveness, instanceof pattern with &&, fallthrough
Hint 1
"42" is a String, so the Integer pattern does not match; LOW never reaches the block.
Hint 2
The colon-form switch statement falls through from case 2 into case 3; the expression form does not.
Reveal solution

Output:

Mid+42 High Low
twothree two

label(MID, 42): block arm, s = "mid", payload is an Integer greater than 10 → yield "mid+42", capitalised to Mid+42. label(HIGH, "42"): the pattern does not match a String, so the second yield returns "high" → High. label(LOW, 99): arrow arm returns "low" → Low; the payload is never looked at. The switch over Level needs no default because all constants are covered; if someone adds Level.CRITICAL the method fails to compile.

Second block: the statement switch enters at case 2, appends two, falls through and appends three, then breaks: twothree. The switch expression returns two. Note that the pattern binding i is only in scope after &&; replacing it with || would not compile because i might be unbound.

Scenario: the service fails on Java 17 with InaccessibleObjectException and a missing javax.xml.bind

A Spring Boot 2.7 service was built and tested on Java 8 for years. The platform team switched the base image to eclipse-temurin:17-jre. The container now exits during startup. Two stack traces alternate depending on which bean initialises first:

Caused by: java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: javax/xml/bind/annotation/XmlRootElement
    at com.acme.billing.soap.InvoiceClient.<clinit>(InvoiceClient.java:31)
Caused by: java.lang.ClassNotFoundException: javax.xml.bind.annotation.XmlRootElement

Caused by: java.lang.reflect.InaccessibleObjectException: Unable to make field private final java.util.Comparator
    java.util.TreeMap.comparator accessible: module java.base does not "opens java.util" to unnamed module @3b2c72c2
    at java.base/java.lang.reflect.AccessibleObject.checkCanSetAccessible(AccessibleObject.java:354)
    at com.google.gson.internal.reflect.ReflectionHelper.makeAccessible(ReflectionHelper.java:19)   // gson 2.8.5
    at com.acme.billing.cache.SnapshotSerializer.write(SnapshotSerializer.java:44)

Diagnose both failures, explain why neither appeared on Java 8, propose the fix you would ship this week and the fix you would ship next sprint, and list what else you would check before calling the migration done.

Tests: JEP 320 removals, strong encapsulation, migration processTime: 15 min
Hint 1
Java 8 shipped JAXB inside the JDK; Java 11 removed it. Java 8 had no module system; Java 17 has no --illegal-access switch.
Hint 2
Read the exception: it names the module (java.base), the package to open (java.util) and the caller (gson 2.8.5). Every piece of the fix is in that line.
Reveal solution

Failure 1 — javax.xml.bind. JAXB lived in the java.xml.bind module, deprecated in 9 and removed in 11 (JEP 320). On Java 8 it was implicitly on the bootstrap classpath, so the SOAP client compiled and ran with no declared dependency. It has been broken since 11 — the team simply never ran on 11. Fix: add the API and an implementation with matching namespace. For Spring Boot 2.7 (still javax namespace):

<dependency><groupId>jakarta.xml.bind</groupId><artifactId>jakarta.xml.bind-api</artifactId><version>2.3.3</version></dependency>
<dependency><groupId>org.glassfish.jaxb</groupId><artifactId>jaxb-runtime</artifactId><version>2.3.x</version><scope>runtime</scope></dependency>
<!-- if the SOAP client uses JAX-WS too: jakarta.xml.ws-api 2.3.x + com.sun.xml.ws:jaxws-rt 2.3.x -->

Stay on the 2.3 line: 3.x/4.x switched to jakarta.xml.bind packages and would not satisfy javax.xml.bind.annotation.XmlRootElement. When the service later moves to Boot 3, switch to 4.x and rename imports. Also grep for javax.annotation.PostConstruct and javax.activation, which fell out in the same JEP.

Failure 2 — InaccessibleObjectException. Gson 2.8.5 serialises a TreeMap by reflecting into its private comparator field. On Java 8 there were no module boundaries. On 9–15 this produced only the "illegal reflective access" warning (default --illegal-access=permit). On 16 the default became deny, and on 17 the flag is gone (JEP 403), so setAccessible throws. The message tells you the exact remedy target: module java.base, package java.util, target ALL-UNNAMED.

This week (unblock): in the Dockerfile or launch script, JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS="--add-opens java.base/java.util=ALL-UNNAMED" (or --add-opens in the java command; for tests, Surefire argLine). Expect to repeat for each package a new stack trace names; document each flag with the library that needs it. Do not use JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS (affects every JVM) and do not add --illegal-access=permit (ignored on 17).

Next sprint (real fix): upgrade Gson to 2.10+ which handles JDK types without reflection into java.* (or use TypeAdapters / switch to Jackson, which Boot already manages), then delete the --add-opens. Run jdeps --jdk-internals -R --class-path 'lib/*' app.jar to find the remaining offenders before they surface in production (typical: old Mockito/ByteBuddy, Netty < 4.1.x, Kryo, Ehcache 2, Lombok < 1.18.22).

Before calling it done: build on 17 with <release>17</release> and Surefire 3 (the tests currently run on a Java 8 CI image, which is how this shipped); check bytecode-plugin versions (Jacoco, Lombok, Spotbugs) for "Unsupported class file major version 61"; verify Boot 2.7's supported JDK range (2.7 supports 17; 2.5.5+ is the minimum); compare GC behaviour (Parallel on 8 vs G1 on 17) and container heap sizing (MaxRAMPercentage); confirm TLS 1.0/1.1 partners are not affected; run the locale/date-format tests (CLDR data since 9); look for HashSet/Set.of ordering assumptions; enable JFR and -Xlog:gc* for the canary; and only then start using records/var/switch expressions in the codebase.

1️⃣2️⃣ JVM Tuning, Profiling & Production Troubleshooting

Senior interviews end with "your service is on fire at 2 a.m., what do you do?" This section is the runbook: the flags you set before the fire, how to choose and read a garbage collector, and how to turn a GC log, a heap dump, or a thread dump into a root cause in minutes. The four practice scenarios at the end are the exact shapes those questions take.

The Essential JVM Flags

Why interviewers ask: a dozen flags cover 95% of production JVMs. Knowing which ones to set before an incident (heap dump on OOM, GC logging) is what separates someone who has run services from someone who has read about them.

Flags come in three shapes: -X (non-standard but stable: -Xmx, -Xss, -Xlog), -XX: (HotSpot-specific: -XX:+Flag turns a boolean on, -XX:-Flag off, -XX:Name=value sets a value) and plain -D system properties, which the JVM ignores but your code reads. Analogy: -Xmx is the size of the warehouse, -Xms is how much of it you rent on day one, and -Xss is the size of each worker's desk.

Two flags are non-negotiable in production: -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError (with a -XX:HeapDumpPath on a volume that survives the pod) and -Xlog:gc* to a rotating file. Both cost nothing until the day you need them, and on that day they are the only evidence you have.

FlagWhat it controlsProduction guidance
-Xms / -XmxInitial / maximum heapSet equal in containers: avoids resize pauses and makes RSS predictable. Prefer -XX:MaxRAMPercentage (below) so the value follows the container limit.
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75Max heap as % of container memory limitContainer-aware replacement for -Xmx. Leave the remaining 25–30% for metaspace, threads, direct buffers, code cache. -XX:InitialRAMPercentage is the -Xms twin.
-XssThread stack size (default 1 MB on 64-bit Linux, check your JDK)Lower (256k–512k) to fit more threads; raise only for pathological recursion. It is reserved virtual memory, committed as used.
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSizeCap on class-metadata native memoryUnbounded by default. Set a cap (e.g. 256m) so a class-loader leak fails fast with OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace instead of eating the node.
-XX:+UseG1GC / -XX:+UseZGC / -XX:+UseParallelGC / -XX:+UseSerialGCCollector selectionG1 is the default on server-class machines since Java 9. See the next card for the decision table.
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200Pause-time goal for G1 (default 200 ms)A goal, not a guarantee. G1 shrinks the young generation to hit it, trading throughput. Do not set it to 10 and expect magic.
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
-XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps		Write an .hprof on first OOMAlways on. Path must be a persistent volume in Kubernetes. The dump is heap-sized on disk; plan the volume accordingly.
-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryErrorKill the JVM on the first OOMOn for services behind an orchestrator: a half-dead JVM that keeps answering health checks is worse than a restart. (CrashOnOutOfMemoryError additionally writes a core file.)
-Xlog:gc*:file=/logs/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20mUnified GC logging (Java 9+)Always on, rotated. -Xlog:gc alone gives one line per pause; gc* adds phases, heap regions, ergonomics. -verbose:gc is the old alias.
-XX:+UseStringDeduplicationG1/ZGC merge duplicate char[]/byte[] behind StringsCheap win for apps holding many repeated strings (JSON keys, enums-as-strings).
-XX:+PrintFlagsFinal / jcmd <pid> VM.flagsShow the effective value of every flagFirst command when the "we set 4 GB" story does not match the OOM. Ergonomics may have overridden you.
# A production-ready baseline for a Spring Boot service in a 2 GB container
JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="\
  -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 -XX:InitialRAMPercentage=75 \
  -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 \
  -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m -Xss512k \
  -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError \
  -Xlog:gc*:file=/logs/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m \
  -Djava.security.egd=file:/dev/./urandom"
Interview angle: "Why set -Xms equal to -Xmx?" Growing the heap triggers extra GCs and a Full GC on shrink in older collectors; in a container the memory is reserved for you anyway, so there is nothing to save. "Why does JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS beat editing the Dockerfile CMD?" Every JVM launched in the container picks it up, including sidecar tools, and it is visible in the startup log line Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS.

Pitfalls

  • -Xmx is only the heap. A JVM with -Xmx1g commonly has 1.4–1.6 GB RSS. Size the container for RSS, not the heap.
  • -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis too low starves the young generation, causing more frequent pauses and promotion of short-lived objects into old gen.
  • Setting flags that a collector ignores (e.g. NewRatio with G1's adaptive sizing) silently does nothing. Verify with VM.flags.

Likely follow-ups

  • Where do I put flags in Kubernetes? (JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS env var or JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS; the latter applies only to the java launcher, Java 9+.)
  • How do I change a flag at runtime? (Only "manageable" flags: jcmd <pid> VM.set_flag HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError true. Heap size is not one of them.)
  • What is -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch? (Touch every heap page at startup so the first requests do not pay page-fault cost; slower start, flatter latency.)

Choosing a Garbage Collector

Why interviewers ask: "Which GC would you pick for X?" checks whether you understand the throughput-vs-latency trade-off rather than memorised names. The honest answer usually starts with "G1, until measurements say otherwise".

Every collector makes the same trade: throughput (fraction of CPU spent on application code), latency (worst-case pause length) and footprint (extra memory for headroom, remembered sets, colored pointers). You can have two of the three. Analogy: cleaning a restaurant. Parallel closes the whole restaurant once a night and blitzes it with all staff (fast total, long closure). G1 cleans one dining room at a time within a time budget. ZGC cleans around the guests with almost no closure at all, but needs more cleaners.

The generational hypothesis (most objects die young) is why all of them keep a young generation that is collected often and cheaply by copying survivors, and an old generation that is collected rarely. ZGC became generational in Java 21 (-XX:+ZGenerational); in 17 it is single-generation and pays for that with higher allocation-rate sensitivity.

WorkloadPickWhyKey tunables
Batch / ETL / Spark executor; nobody waits on a single requestParallel -XX:+UseParallelGCHighest throughput; stop-the-world for young and old with all cores. Pauses of seconds are fine.-XX:ParallelGCThreads, -XX:NewRatio/-Xmn, -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis (soft), -XX:GCTimeRatio
Typical REST/gRPC service, heap 2–32 GB, p99 in tens of msG1 (default) -XX:+UseG1GCRegion-based, incremental old-gen ("mixed") collections, concurrent marking, predictable pauses at a pause goal.-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis, -XX:G1HeapRegionSize (raise for humongous objects), -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent (start marking earlier), -XX:G1NewSizePercent, -XX:ParallelGCThreads/ConcGCThreads
Very large heaps (tens of GB to TB) or sub-millisecond pause SLO: trading, gaming, in-memory cachesZGC -XX:+UseZGC (production since 15)Almost everything concurrent, pauses < 1 ms regardless of heap size, at the cost of ~10–15% throughput and more memory headroom.-Xmx (give it headroom), -XX:SoftMaxHeapSize, -XX:ConcGCThreads, -XX:ZCollectionInterval; Java 21: -XX:+ZGenerational
Tiny containers (1 CPU, < 1 GB), CLIs, sidecarsSerial -XX:+UseSerialGCSingle thread, smallest footprint, no GC-thread contention with the app on a 1-CPU quota. HotSpot picks it automatically below 2 CPUs / 2 GB ("client-class").-Xmn, -XX:NewRatio
Low pause, medium heap, OpenJDK-only buildsShenandoah -XX:+UseShenandoahGCRed Hat's concurrent compacting GC, similar goals to ZGC. Not in Oracle builds.-XX:ShenandoahGCHeuristics
Interview angle: "We moved to ZGC and throughput dropped 12%; was that a mistake?" Only if the service was throughput-bound. ZGC's read barriers cost CPU; if your SLO is p99 latency and you had spare CPU, it is the right trade. "When is G1's pause goal unreachable?" When a single object graph is huge (long linked structures make remark expensive) or when humongous allocations (objects > half a region) fragment the heap: raise G1HeapRegionSize or fix the allocation pattern.

Pitfalls

  • Tuning before measuring. Get a week of -Xlog:gc* from the current collector first; most "GC problems" are allocation-rate problems in application code.
  • Choosing ZGC on a 1–2 CPU container: its concurrent threads compete with your request threads and everything gets slower.
  • Copy-pasting flag sets from 2012 blog posts (CMSInitiatingOccupancyFraction, UseConcMarkSweepGC): CMS was removed in Java 14 and the JVM refuses to start with unknown -XX flags.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is a humongous object in G1? (Larger than half a region; allocated directly in old-gen regions, expensive to collect. Common cause: large byte arrays from big HTTP responses.)
  • How does ZGC achieve sub-ms pauses? (Colored pointers plus load barriers let it relocate objects while threads run; only root scanning is paused.)
  • Does G1 ever do a Full GC? (Yes, when it cannot evacuate: "to-space exhausted". It is a single-threaded-ish disaster in 8, parallel since 10, but still a symptom to fix.)

Java 8 vs 17

Java 8 defaulted to Parallel GC; 9 made G1 the default. CMS was deprecated in 9 and removed in 14. ZGC and Shenandoah were experimental in 11 and production-ready in 15. Parallel Full GC for G1 arrived in 10.

Reading a GC Log

Why interviewers ask: a GC log is the cheapest, most decisive evidence about a JVM's health, and reading one aloud is a standard senior-level exercise: "here are six lines, what is happening and is it healthy?"

Each -Xlog:gc line has the same skeleton: timestamp, tags, GC id, the pause or phase name with its cause, then before→after(total) heap and the duration. The three numbers that matter are the heap size after each collection (live data), the pause duration, and the interval between collections (allocation rate). Analogy: an ECG. You look for a regular rhythm (young pauses), the occasional slower beat (mixed), and a flat-line event (Full GC).

A healthy G1 log is a sawtooth with a flat floor: heap climbs between young collections, drops back to about the same live size each time. A rising floor (the "after" value creeping up over hours) means live data is growing: either the working set is legitimately bigger or you have a leak. A Full GC in a G1 log is always worth investigating; it means concurrent marking could not keep up or the heap is simply too small for live data.

[12.412s][info][gc] GC(41) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 612M->118M(1024M) 14.2ms
[13.005s][info][gc] GC(42) Pause Young (Concurrent Start) (G1 Humongous Allocation) 640M->190M(1024M) 21.7ms
[13.006s][info][gc] GC(43) Concurrent Mark Cycle
[13.612s][info][gc] GC(43) Concurrent Mark Cycle 606.1ms
[14.100s][info][gc] GC(44) Pause Young (Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 700M->260M(1024M) 35.4ms
[71.230s][info][gc] GC(180) Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 1010M->905M(1024M) 1840.3ms
  1. A normal young pause. Eden filled up (G1 Evacuation Pause), live objects were copied to survivor/old regions. The "after" value (118M) is roughly the live set. 14 ms is well under the 200 ms goal.
  2. Still a young pause, but Concurrent Start: while evacuating, G1 also scans roots to kick off a marking cycle. The cause, G1 Humongous Allocation, is a hint: something allocated an object larger than half a region (e.g. a multi-MB byte array). Check -XX:G1HeapRegionSize or the code.
  3. The concurrent mark cycle ran for 606 ms while the app kept serving. With gc* you would also see the short Pause Remark and Pause Cleanup inside it. Marking tells G1 which old regions are mostly garbage, so it can collect them cheaply next.
  4. A mixed pause: young regions plus the old regions marking found most profitable (highest garbage ratio). Slightly longer (35 ms) because old regions are evacuated too. This is the normal way G1 keeps old gen in check.
  5. Now read the trend, not one line. The after-GC floor is rising: 118M → 190M → 260M. Across seconds this is normal (a warm-up, a cache filling). Across hours with steady traffic it is the signature of a leak: the live set that survives every collection keeps growing.
  6. Sixty seconds later a Full GC: 1.8 s stop-the-world, and it only recovered 105 MB because 905 MB is genuinely live. Two conclusions: (1) the pause spikes users are seeing are these; (2) either the heap is undersized for the working set, or a leak has filled it. The next step is a heap dump, not a bigger -Xmx.
Interview angle: "Users report latency spikes every few minutes, CPU is low." Low CPU plus periodic spikes says "we are waiting, not computing"; the two candidates are GC pauses and lock/IO waits. The GC log answers in ten seconds: line up the spike timestamps with pause lines. Tools that plot logs for you: GCeasy, GCViewer, or jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000 for a live view.
Symptom in logMeaningUsual fix
Young pauses every < 1 sAllocation rate very highReduce garbage in hot paths (profile allocations with JFR); larger young gen
Pause time creeping up with same heapSurvivors being copied repeatedly, or remembered-set growthCheck promotion; raise MaxTenuringThreshold or heap
"to-space exhausted" / "Evacuation Failure"No free region to copy intoIncrease heap headroom or lower InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent so marking starts earlier
Full GC reclaiming littleLive set ≈ heapHeap dump → leak or legitimately bigger working set
Back-to-back Full GCs, 98% time in GCDeath spiralThis is GC overhead limit exceeded territory; same fix as above

Pitfalls

  • Reading only the pause length. A 200 ms pause every 10 minutes is fine; a 20 ms pause every 200 ms means 10% of wall time is stopped.
  • Forgetting -Xlog "uptime" vs wall time: correlate with request logs using the time decorator, not uptime.
  • Restarting the pod "to fix it" before saving the GC log and taking a heap dump destroys the evidence.

Likely follow-ups

  • What does the gc+heap tag add? (Per-region counts: eden/survivor/old/humongous before and after each pause.)
  • How would you see this without file access? (jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info, jstat -gcutil, or Micrometer jvm.gc.pause metrics in Grafana.)
  • What is a safepoint and why do pauses sometimes exceed the GC time? (All threads must reach a safepoint before the pause starts; a long counted loop or JNI call delays "time to safepoint". -Xlog:safepoint shows it.)

Every OutOfMemoryError and What It Actually Means

Why interviewers ask: the message after OutOfMemoryError: names the memory area that ran out, and each area has a different cause and a different tool. Candidates who answer every OOM with "increase -Xmx" fail this one.

The JVM has several independent pools: the heap, Metaspace, direct (off-heap) buffers, per-thread stacks, the code cache, and the GC's own structures. An OutOfMemoryError is raised by the JVM when one of them is exhausted. A container OOMKilled is different: the kernel killed the process because total RSS exceeded the cgroup limit, and the JVM never got to throw anything. Analogy: running out of shelf space (heap) vs running out of filing cabinets for the catalogue (Metaspace) vs the landlord evicting you because the whole building is over its weight limit (OOMKilled).

Reading the message is a decision tree. Walk it below.

# Native Memory Tracking: the only way to see where non-heap RSS goes
java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary -jar app.jar &
jcmd $(pgrep -f app.jar) VM.native_memory summary
#  Java Heap (reserved=1048576KB, committed=1048576KB)
#  Class     (reserved=1089536KB, committed=52736KB)    ← Metaspace
#  Thread    (reserved=  412672KB, committed=  41296KB) ← 400 threads x ~1MB reserved
#  Code      (reserved=  251877KB, committed=  32909KB) ← JIT cache
#  GC        (reserved=  102400KB, committed= 102400KB) ← G1 remembered sets etc.
#  Internal / Symbol / Other                            ← direct buffers show under Other
Interview angle: "Heap is 60% used in Grafana but the pod keeps getting OOMKilled." That single sentence is a native-memory question. Answer: RSS ≠ heap; enumerate the non-heap consumers, measure with NMT, and either reserve more headroom (MaxRAMPercentage=60) or cap the culprit (thread count, MaxDirectMemorySize, MaxMetaspaceSize). Bonus: glibc malloc arenas fragment badly with many threads; MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 or jemalloc is a known fix.

Pitfalls

  • Catching OutOfMemoryError and continuing. The JVM may be in an inconsistent state (half-built objects, aborted finalizers); let it dump and die.
  • -XX:-UseGCOverheadLimit to "fix" the overhead error: you have converted a fast failure into a JVM that spends hours at 100% CPU doing nothing.
  • Assuming Java heap space always means a leak. A 2× traffic increase with per-request caching is not a leak; the dump will show it is the working set.

Likely follow-ups

  • Can an OOM happen with free heap? (Yes: a humongous allocation in G1 that needs N contiguous free regions, or an array larger than the largest free chunk.)
  • What does StackOverflowError have in common? (Also a VirtualMachineError, also per-thread stack exhaustion; but recursion depth, not memory pressure.)
  • Why does the JVM sometimes exit 137 with no OOM at all? (A SIGKILL from the kernel OOM killer; nothing in Java can observe it, so look at dmesg and pod events.)

Heap Dump Analysis with Eclipse MAT

Why interviewers ask: "how would you find the leak?" is the follow-up to every memory question, and the expected answer is a concrete workflow (dump → histogram → dominator tree → path to GC roots), not "use a profiler".

A heap dump (.hprof) is a snapshot of every object, its fields and references. Two sizes matter: shallow size (the object's own bytes) and retained size (everything that would become garbage if this object were collected). Leaks are found by retained size: the culprit is a small object holding a huge retained graph. Analogy: to find who is hoarding office space you do not count desks (shallow), you ask "if this person left, how many rooms would free up?" (retained).

The dominator tree is MAT's view of retained size: object A dominates B if every path from GC roots to B goes through A. The top of the tree, sorted by retained size, is the leak nine times out of ten. Path to GC roots then explains why it is still alive: which static field, thread, or class loader pins it.

# 1. Capture (prefer jcmd; -all includes unreachable objects, default is live only)
jcmd 4242 GC.heap_dump /dumps/order-svc.hprof
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=/dumps/order-svc.hprof 4242   # older equivalent
kubectl cp order-svc-7c9f:/dumps/order-svc.hprof ./order-svc.hprof

# 2. Open in Eclipse MAT (give it -Xmx bigger than the dump: MemoryAnalyzer.ini)
# 3. Histogram (by class, sorted by retained):
#   java.util.HashMap$Node[]     1 array    shallow 64 MB   retained 1.71 GB
#   java.util.HashMap$Node       4,811,204            154 MB           1.71 GB
#   com.acme.OrderView           4,811,204            308 MB           1.64 GB
# 4. Dominator tree (top entry):
#   com.acme.OrderCache @ 0x6c0a1f2e8       retained 1.71 GB   (89.4 % of heap)
#     └ java.util.HashMap  "views"           retained 1.71 GB
# 5. Path to GC roots (exclude weak/soft refs):
#   class com.acme.OrderCache  (static field INSTANCE)   ← GC root: system class loader
#     └ OrderCache.views (HashMap)  ← no eviction, no TTL
# 6. Leak Suspects report agrees: "One instance of OrderCache occupies 1.71 GB"
  1. Capture. jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump is the modern command; jmap -dump:live is the Java 8 muscle memory. live forces a Full GC first so the dump contains only reachable objects, which is what you want for a leak. Copy it off the pod before the pod restarts.
  2. Open in MAT. Parsing computes the dominator tree once and caches index files next to the dump, so the second open is instant. For dumps larger than your laptop, run MAT headless on a big box (ParseHeapDump.sh).
  3. The Histogram groups by class. Sort by retained size. HashMap$Node at the top is typical; the interesting row is the domain class inside the nodes: 4.8 million OrderView instances, which is far more than the number of orders a service should keep in memory.
  4. The Dominator tree answers WHO: a single OrderCache instance retains 89% of the heap through its views map. Expand it and you see the map's entries, keyed by order id. The "retained" column narrowing from the whole heap to one object is the moment of diagnosis.
  5. Path to GC roots (right-click → "with all references" or "exclude weak/soft"). The chain is short: a static INSTANCE → views → the map. A static field is a GC root forever, and the map has no eviction. This is the classic "cache without a bound" leak.
  6. MAT's automatic Leak Suspects report reaches the same conclusion; use it first when you are in a hurry, but be able to reproduce the manual path. Fix: replace HashMap with a bounded Caffeine cache (maximumSize, expireAfterWrite) and confirm in the GC log that the post-GC floor is flat over a day.
Typical culprit at top of dominator treePath to GC root looks likeFix
Static Map/List used as a cacheclass → static fieldBounded cache with eviction (Caffeine), or weak keys where identity-scoped
Listener / observer registrationsevent bus → ArrayList<Listener> → your objectsUnregister in close()/@PreDestroy; weak listeners
ThreadLocal in a thread poolThread → threadLocals → ThreadLocalMap$Entry → valueremove() in finally; pool threads never die so the value never dies
Unclosed resourcesFinalizer queue / socket impl → bufferstry-with-resources; check java.lang.ref.Finalizer count in histogram
Class loader leak (redeploy)Thread → context class loader → whole webappStop threads/timers on undeploy; MAT "Duplicate classes" query
Interview angle: "The heap dump is 12 GB, MAT dies. Now what?" Options in order: (1) jcmd GC.class_histogram on the live process, taken twice ten minutes apart, and diff the counts (no dump needed); (2) run MAT headless on a machine with enough RAM; (3) JFR's OldObjectSample event, which records allocation stacks for long-lived objects with almost no overhead.

Pitfalls

  • Dumping every instance at once: each dump pauses the JVM for seconds and can push the whole cluster over its latency SLO.
  • Heap dumps contain your data: user records, tokens, secrets. Treat the file as sensitive, and never attach it to a public ticket.
  • Trusting shallow size. byte[] always dominates shallow size; it tells you nothing about who holds the bytes.

Likely follow-ups

  • Difference between GC.heap_dump and -all? (Default dumps only live objects after a GC; -all keeps unreachable ones, useful for "what was just allocated" questions.)
  • How do soft/weak references show up? (MAT excludes them from "path to GC roots" by option; a cache that leaks through strong refs only would be fixed by WeakHashMap if keys are the right identity, otherwise not.)
  • Can you dump without stopping the world? (Not with HotSpot's built-in dumper; JFR sampling is the low-overhead alternative.)

Thread Dump Analysis

Why interviewers ask: the two commonest production outages ("everything hangs, CPU idle" and "one pod at 100% CPU") are both diagnosed with a thread dump in under a minute, if you know what to look for.

A thread dump is one stack trace per thread plus its state, the monitors it holds (- locked <0x…>) and the monitor it is waiting for (- waiting to lock for synchronized, - parking to wait for for java.util.concurrent locks). Analogy: a group photo of every employee with a caption saying what they are doing right now and which meeting room key they are holding.

The rule of three: take three dumps ten seconds apart. A thread RUNNABLE in the same frames in all three is a hot loop (or a slow native call); a thread BLOCKED/WAITING on the same lock in all three is stuck. One dump shows a moment; three show a pattern. Always use jcmd <pid> Thread.print (or jstack, or kill -3 which prints to stdout): they attach at a safepoint and are safe in production.

"http-nio-8080-exec-7" #42 daemon prio=5 os_prio=31 cpu=812.45ms elapsed=3612.11s tid=0x00007f8a1c0f6800 nid=0x9d03 waiting on condition
   java.lang.Thread.State: TIMED_WAITING (parking)
        at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(java.base@17.0.8/Native Method)
        - parking to wait for  <0x00000006c2a1e4f0> (a java.util.concurrent.SynchronousQueue$TransferQueue)
        at com.zaxxer.hikari.util.ConcurrentBag.borrow(ConcurrentBag.java:151)
        at com.zaxxer.hikari.pool.HikariPool.getConnection(HikariPool.java:180)
        at com.acme.order.OrderRepository.findById(OrderRepository.java:44)
"http-nio-8080-exec-8" ... nid=0x9e03 waiting on condition        (same stack, x 198 more threads)

"OrderWorker-1" #31 prio=5 cpu=12.10ms elapsed=3600.02s nid=0x7a03 waiting for monitor entry
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
        at com.acme.ledger.Ledger.transfer(Ledger.java:42)
        - waiting to lock <0x00000006c1234560> (a com.acme.ledger.Account)
        - locked <0x00000006c1234580> (a com.acme.ledger.Account)
"OrderWorker-2" #32 prio=5 cpu=11.80ms elapsed=3600.02s nid=0x7b03 waiting for monitor entry
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
        at com.acme.ledger.Ledger.transfer(Ledger.java:42)
        - waiting to lock <0x00000006c1234580> (a com.acme.ledger.Account)
        - locked <0x00000006c1234560> (a com.acme.ledger.Account)

Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"OrderWorker-1": waiting to lock monitor 0x…560 (object 0x00000006c1234560, a Account), which is held by "OrderWorker-2"
"OrderWorker-2": waiting to lock monitor 0x…580 (object 0x00000006c1234580, a Account), which is held by "OrderWorker-1"
  1. Read the header. The name says which pool owns the thread (Tomcat, Hikari, your executor: name your pools!). cpu= vs elapsed= says whether it is hot. nid is the OS thread id in hex; top -H -p <pid> shows the same id in decimal, which is how you map a 100%-CPU OS thread back to a Java stack.
  2. The state and the frames below it. TIMED_WAITING (parking) means a java.util.concurrent wait, not a synchronized block. Walk down the stack until you hit a class you recognise: HikariPool.getConnection. This thread is queued for a database connection.
  3. Now count, do not read. grep -c "HikariPool.getConnection" gives 199 of 200 Tomcat threads. That is pool exhaustion: every request thread is waiting for one of 10 connections, so the service accepts requests and answers none. CPU is idle because nobody is computing. Next question: what are the 10 connection holders doing? Find the threads whose stack is inside JDBC driver code (socketRead = waiting on a slow query or a dead DB).
  4. A different thread, a different state: BLOCKED (on object monitor) is a synchronized wait. Note the two addresses: it has locked …580 and is waiting to lock …560. Write those down.
  5. The next thread is the mirror image: holds …560, wants …580. That is a deadlock by inspection: two Account monitors acquired in opposite order by Ledger.transfer(from, to) called as (A,B) on one thread and (B,A) on another.
  6. You did not have to find it by hand: HotSpot's detector prints Found one Java-level deadlock at the bottom of the dump whenever it can prove a cycle among monitors and owned ReentrantLocks. It cannot see semaphores, latches, or "waiting for an HTTP response that will never come", so a missing banner does not clear the JVM. Fix: acquire locks in a global order (e.g. by ascending account id) or use tryLock with a timeout and back off.
Pattern across 3 dumpsDiagnosisNext step
All request threads WAITING in the same pool borrow/takePool exhaustion (DB, HTTP client, executor)Find what the pool's holders are doing; add timeouts; size pool; circuit breaker
Many threads BLOCKED on one monitor held by one threadLock convoy / hot lockLook at the holder's stack; shrink the critical section; use concurrent structures
"Found one Java-level deadlock"DeadlockLock ordering; single lock; tryLock
Same thread RUNNABLE in the same frames every dump, high cpu=Hot loop, catastrophic regex, huge serialization, infinite retryMap via nid to top -H; async-profiler flame graph
Threads RUNNABLE in socketRead0 / SocketInputStream.readWaiting on a remote that is slow or gone (JVM calls native IO "RUNNABLE")Timeouts on the client; check the dependency
Thread count growing dump over dumpExecutor created per request / never shut downGroup by name prefix; make the executor a singleton bean
# The 100%-CPU runbook (Linux)
top -H -p $(pgrep -f app.jar) -n 1 | head -15     # hottest OS threads, TID in decimal
printf '%x\n' 40195                                # 40195 -> 9d03 (the nid in the dump)
jcmd $(pgrep -f app.jar) Thread.print > dump1.txt; sleep 10
jcmd $(pgrep -f app.jar) Thread.print > dump2.txt
grep -A 20 'nid=0x9d03' dump1.txt dump2.txt        # same frames in both = hot loop
# Or skip the mapping: async-profiler shows the hot frames directly
./profiler.sh -d 30 -f /tmp/cpu.html $(pgrep -f app.jar)

Pitfalls

  • Reading a single dump and declaring a "hang". Threads in a pool should be WAITING when idle; only the same thread stuck on the same thing over time is a problem.
  • Default thread names (pool-3-thread-7) make dumps unreadable. Give every executor a ThreadFactory with a meaningful prefix.
  • Trusting "RUNNABLE" as "computing": native IO waits are reported RUNNABLE. Check the top frame.

Likely follow-ups

  • Difference between BLOCKED and WAITING? (BLOCKED = waiting to enter a synchronized monitor; WAITING/TIMED_WAITING = Object.wait, LockSupport.park, join, sleep.)
  • Where do virtual threads show up? (Java 21: jcmd Thread.dump_to_file -format=json includes them; classic jstack only lists carriers.)
  • How do you get a dump when the JVM will not respond to jcmd? (jstack -F forces via the serviceability agent, or kill -3 which is handled by the signal thread even under load.)

The Tooling Map: Which Tool, When

Why interviewers ask: naming the right tool for each question ("is it GC?", "who holds the memory?", "what is hot?") shows you have actually done it. The expected modern answers are jcmd for one-off commands and JFR for continuous, production-safe profiling.

jcmd is the Swiss army knife that replaces most of the older j* tools: it sends a diagnostic command to a running JVM via the attach mechanism, and jcmd <pid> help lists everything available. JFR (Java Flight Recorder) is an always-on event recorder built into the JVM, with ~1–2% overhead, whose recordings you open in JDK Mission Control.
