Analogy: jcmd is the doctor's stethoscope you use during the visit; JFR is the Holter monitor the patient wears for a week.

For CPU hot spots specifically, async-profiler produces flame graphs without the safepoint bias that makes sampling-only profilers lie about where time goes. For continuous visibility, expose JVM metrics through Micrometer (Spring Boot Actuator does this by default: jvm.memory.used, jvm.gc.pause, jvm.threads.states, hikaricp.connections.pending) so you notice the trend before the outage.

ToolCommand / entry pointUse it whenOverhead / safety
jcmdjcmd <pid> VM.flags, VM.version, VM.system_properties, GC.heap_info, GC.class_histogram, GC.heap_dump, Thread.print, JFR.start/dump/stop, VM.native_memory, Compiler.codecacheAny single question about a running JVMSafepoint pause for histogram/dump; otherwise negligible
jstatjstat -gcutil <pid> 1000Live GC view without logs: % of each generation, GC counts and total time per secondNegligible
jmapjmap -histo:live <pid>, jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=x.hprof <pid>Legacy heap histogram/dump (Java 8 boxes)Full GC + pause
jstackjstack <pid>, jstack -l (lock info), -F (force)Thread dump; deadlock bannerShort safepoint
jinfojinfo -flags <pid>, jinfo -flag +HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError <pid>See or flip manageable flags on a live JVMNegligible
JFR + JDK Mission Control-XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=120s,filename=rec.jfr,settings=profile or jcmd <pid> JFR.start; open .jfr in JMCAllocation profiling, lock contention, IO waits, GC phases, exceptions, old-object sampling (leaks) in production~1–2% with default, a bit more with profile; production safe, free since Java 11
async-profiler./profiler.sh -e cpu -d 30 -f flame.html <pid>; also -e alloc, -e lock, -e wallCPU flame graphs that include native/JIT frames without safepoint biasLow; needs perf_event access in the container
VisualVMGUI over JMX/attachLocal dev: quick heap/CPU sampling, thread timelineSampling profiler; avoid the instrumenting mode in prod
Micrometer / JMX / Actuator/actuator/metrics/jvm.gc.pause, Prometheus + Grafana dashboardsContinuous trends and alerting: heap after GC, pause p99, thread states, pool pendingNegligible; this is what pages you
Eclipse MATOpen .hprofPost-mortem heap analysis (previous card)Offline
# A one-minute triage with only jcmd and jstat
PID=$(pgrep -f app.jar)
jcmd $PID VM.flags                       # are the flags what we think they are?
jstat -gcutil $PID 1000 10               # O (old %) climbing? FGC count rising? GCT growing fast?
jcmd $PID GC.class_histogram | head -20  # top classes by instance count
jcmd $PID Thread.print | grep -c 'java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED'
jcmd $PID JFR.start duration=120s filename=/tmp/triage.jfr settings=profile
# ...open /tmp/triage.jfr in JDK Mission Control: Method Profiling, Memory, Lock Instances
Interview angle: "How would you profile in production without slowing it down?" JFR with the default settings (~1%), continuous recording into a ring buffer (-XX:StartFlightRecording=disk=true,maxsize=200m,maxage=1h), and jcmd JFR.dump when something happens. Then async-profiler for the CPU-hot cases where you need exact frames. Never an instrumenting profiler (YourKit/JProfiler in instrumentation mode) on a live instance.

Pitfalls

  • Running jmap -histo without :live and concluding "10 million garbage objects are a leak". They are just uncollected yet.
  • Attach tools need the same user and the same JDK version family as the target process; in distroless images you may have no jcmd at all: bake jdk.jcmd into the image with jlink.
  • JMX remote without authentication exposed on a pod IP. Use Actuator over HTTP with auth instead.

Likely follow-ups

  • What does jstat -gcutil's output mean? (S0/S1/E/O/M percentages, YGC/YGCT young count and time, FGC/FGCT full, GCT total; watch O and FGC.)
  • Why is safepoint bias a problem? (A sampling profiler that only samples at safepoints attributes time to the nearest safepoint poll, hiding the real hot instruction; async-profiler uses perf signals to avoid it.)
  • What JFR events find a leak? (jdk.OldObjectSample with path-to-gc-roots=true.)

Memory Leak Patterns in Java Code

Why interviewers ask: "Java has GC, how can it leak?" is a filter question. A leak in Java is a reachable object that is no longer useful; the GC cannot read intent. Knowing the ten recurring shapes lets you spot them in code review, before the heap dump.

All Java leaks are the same bug in different clothes: a long-lived object (static, singleton, pool thread, class loader) holds a reference to a short-lived one and nobody removes it. Analogy: a hotel where guests check in but the register is never updated on check-out; the rooms are "occupied" forever. The fix is always one of: bound it, evict it, unregister it, or use a weak/soft reference where identity semantics allow.

PatternWhat holds the referenceSymptomFix
Unbounded cache (HashMap used as cache)The map, typically static or in a singleton beanRising GC floor; dominator tree: one mapCaffeine/Guava with maximumSize + expiry; or a request-scoped map
Static collections that only grow (audit lists, registries, "seen" sets)Class → static fieldSlow leak over daysBound; or move to a real store (DB, Redis) with TTL
Listeners / callbacks never removedEvent bus, PropertyChangeSupport, Spring ApplicationEventMulticasterEvery UI screen / session / connection stays aliveUnregister in close(); weak listener lists
ThreadLocal on pooled threadsThread.threadLocals; pool threads live foreverPer-request context (user, tenant, big buffers) accumulates; also wrong data leaking between requestsremove() in a finally/filter; prefer passing context explicitly
Non-static inner class / anonymous class / lambda capturing thisThe inner instance's hidden this$0 fieldA tiny listener keeps a huge outer object (Activity, Controller) aliveMake it static; capture only the fields you need
Unclosed streams, connections, ResultSetsNative handles, finalizer queue, pool "leaked" slotsHikari "connection leak detected"; too many open filestry-with-resources everywhere; Hikari leakDetectionThreshold
String.intern() on unbounded inputThe JVM string table (heap since Java 7, but the table itself is native)Interning user ids / request ids grows the table foreverDo not intern dynamic strings; use -XX:+UseStringDeduplication for memory, not intern
substring sharing (historical, Java ≤ 6)Pre-7u6 substring shared the parent char[]A 3-char key kept a 10 MB document aliveFixed since 7u6: substring copies. Know it as history.
Class loader leak on redeployA thread, ThreadLocal, JDBC driver registration, or static in a JDK class referencing webapp classesMetaspace grows with every hot deployStop threads on undeploy; deregister drivers; or simply restart the JVM per deploy (containers make this moot)
finalize() and Finalizer backlogObjects with finalizers need two GC cycles and a single finalizer threadMillions of java.lang.ref.Finalizer in the histogramNever override finalize (deprecated for removal since 9); use Cleaner or try-with-resources
Queues with no consumer / unbounded executor queuesLinkedBlockingQueue in Executors.newFixedThreadPoolHeap fills with pending tasks under loadBounded queue + rejection policy; backpressure
// Three leaks in twelve lines. Can you name them?
@Component
public class SessionTracker {
    private static final Map<String, UserSession> SESSIONS = new HashMap<>();     // 1
    private static final ThreadLocal<UserSession> CURRENT = new ThreadLocal<>();  // 2

    public void onLogin(UserSession s, EventBus bus) {
        SESSIONS.put(s.id(), s);
        CURRENT.set(s);
        bus.register(new Object() {                                                 // 3
            @Subscribe public void onLogout(LogoutEvent e) { SESSIONS.remove(e.id()); }
        });
    }
}
// 1: never removed on timeout, only on explicit logout. 2: never CURRENT.remove().
// 3: anonymous subscriber captures this SessionTracker and is registered per login, never unregistered.
Interview angle: "How do you prevent leaks rather than find them?" Bounded everything (caches, queues, pools); try-with-resources; a servlet filter that clears every ThreadLocal; Hikari's leakDetectionThreshold=60000; an alert on "heap used after GC" trend slope, not on heap used.

Pitfalls

  • WeakHashMap as a cache with String keys: literals are strongly held by the pool, dynamic keys are collected immediately. It is for identity-keyed metadata, not caching.
  • Soft references as a cache policy: they are cleared only under memory pressure, so the JVM runs at 100% heap and does frequent Full GCs by design.
  • Spring singletons that hold per-request state: a singleton is by definition a static-lifetime reference.

Likely follow-ups

  • Strong vs soft vs weak vs phantom? (Strong: never collected while reachable. Soft: collected under pressure. Weak: collected at next GC. Phantom: enqueued after finalization for cleanup, get() always null.)
  • Why is ThreadLocal worse in a pool than in a plain thread? (A plain thread dies and takes its map with it; pool threads are reused, so the value survives and may be observed by the next request.)
  • Is a "leak" in a 24-hour-restart service worth fixing? (If the restart is your GC, you have a leak; it hides a class of bugs and prevents scaling down the restart cadence.)

The JVM in Containers and Kubernetes

Why interviewers ask: every service now runs in a pod with a CPU quota and a memory limit, and the JVM's defaults are derived from those two numbers. Misunderstanding the derivation produces the two classic incidents: OOMKilled pods with a half-empty heap, and thread pools sized for 64 cores on a 1-CPU quota.

Since Java 10 (backported to 8u191) -XX:+UseContainerSupport is on by default: the JVM reads the cgroup limits instead of the host's. Memory: the default max heap is 25% of the container limit (MaxRAMPercentage=25), which is wasteful; set it to ~75% and leave the rest for Metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers, code cache and GC structures. CPU: Runtime.availableProcessors() returns the CPU quota rounded up (a 1500m limit → 2), and that number sizes the common ForkJoinPool, GC threads, JIT compiler threads, and most frameworks' default pool sizes.

Analogy: a container is a flat with a fixed floor area; the heap is the living room. If you make the living room 95% of the flat, there is no room for the kitchen (metaspace), the hallway (threads) or the storage (direct buffers), and the landlord (kernel OOM killer) evicts you.

ConcernWhat the JVM doesWhat you should do
Memory limitReads cgroup limit; default heap 25% of it-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 (60 for thread-heavy/Netty apps); set requests = limits for predictable scheduling
CPU quotaavailableProcessors() = ceil(quota); sizes GC/JIT/ForkJoin threadsGive ≥ 2 CPUs to any latency-sensitive JVM (GC and JIT need a core); or set -XX:ActiveProcessorCount explicitly. Below 2 CPUs / 2 GB HotSpot silently picks Serial GC.
CPU throttlingCFS quota is enforced per 100 ms period; a burst uses the quota in 20 ms and sleeps 80 msWatch container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total; raise limit or remove CPU limits (keep requests) for JVMs
OOMKilled vs OOMKernel kill (137) vs OutOfMemoryError137: NMT and headroom. OOM: heap dump. Different problems, different tools.
Startup timeClass loading + JIT warm-up can take 10–60 s for a big Spring appClass Data Sharing: -XX:SharedArchiveFile with -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit (AppCDS, Java 13+); -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 for short-lived jobs only; Spring lazy init (spring.main.lazy-initialization) for dev; readiness probe with a realistic initialDelaySeconds
Graceful shutdownSIGTERM → shutdown hooks run → after terminationGracePeriodSeconds SIGKILLserver.shutdown=graceful + spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=20s; preStop sleep so the endpoint is removed from the Service before the JVM stops accepting
Diagnostics in the podDistroless images ship no jcmdUse a JDK base image or jlink in jdk.jcmd, jdk.jfr; mount a volume for HeapDumpPath; ephemeral debug containers share the PID namespace
# Kubernetes snippet that matches the flags above
resources:
  requests: { cpu: "2", memory: "2Gi" }
  limits:   { cpu: "2", memory: "2Gi" }      # requests == limits: Guaranteed QoS, no surprise eviction
env:
  - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
    value: "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError -Xlog:gc*:file=/logs/gc.log:time,uptime:filecount=5,filesize=20m"
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
lifecycle:
  preStop: { exec: { command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"] } }
volumeMounts:
  - { name: dumps, mountPath: /dumps }
Interview angle: "The pod has a 500m CPU limit and p99 is terrible under load." availableProcessors() is 1, so GC runs single-threaded (probably Serial), JIT compiles slowly, the common pool has one thread, and CFS throttles every burst. Answer: JVMs want at least 2 CPUs; consider dropping the CPU limit and keeping the request, and check throttling metrics before touching GC flags.

Pitfalls

  • Setting -Xmx in the Dockerfile and changing the Kubernetes limit later. Percentages follow the limit; absolute values do not.
  • Java 8 before u191 ignores cgroups entirely: it sees the node's 64 cores and 256 GB and sizes itself accordingly. Upgrade or set -Xmx and ActiveProcessorCount explicitly.
  • cgroup v2 support needs Java 15+ (backported to 11.0.16 / 8u372). On a newer kernel with older Java, the JVM again sees the host.

Likely follow-ups

  • Why is memory request ≠ limit risky for JVMs? (The heap grows to the limit; the node overcommits based on requests; the kernel evicts the Burstable pod first.)
  • What is CDS? (A pre-parsed archive of class metadata mapped at startup; the default JDK archive is on since 12, AppCDS adds your app's classes and cuts startup 20–40%.)
  • How does a shutdown hook interact with Spring? (Spring registers its own hook that closes the context; in-flight requests finish only if server.shutdown=graceful.)

Performance Methodology & JIT-Aware Benchmarking

Why interviewers ask: "how did you know your optimisation helped?" exposes whether you measured or guessed. The JIT makes naive System.nanoTime() loops meaningless, and averages hide the tail that users feel.

Method first: define the SLO (p99 latency, throughput, cost), measure in production-like conditions, profile to find the top consumer, change one thing, measure again. Most "optimisations" done in a different order are noise. Analogy: you do not tune a car by polishing whichever part is nearest; you put it on a dyno and look at the curve.

Micro-benchmarks must respect the JIT: code runs interpreted, then C1-compiled, then C2-compiled with inlining and speculation; a result computed but never used is dead-code eliminated; a constant folded at compile time measures nothing. JMH (Java Microbenchmark Harness) exists to handle these: forked JVMs, warm-up iterations, Blackhole to consume results, @State to stop constant folding. Report percentiles (p50/p99/p99.9) and error bars, never a single average.

@BenchmarkMode(Mode.SampleTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.MICROSECONDS)
@Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 2) @Fork(2)
@State(Scope.Thread)
public class JoinBench {
    @Param({"10", "1000"}) int n;
    List<String> parts;

    @Setup public void setup() {
        parts = IntStream.range(0, n).mapToObj(i -> "item" + i).toList();
    }
    @Benchmark public String concat() {           // O(n^2) copies
        String s = ""; for (String p : parts) s += p; return s;   // returned → not dead code
    }
    @Benchmark public String builder() {
        var sb = new StringBuilder(); for (String p : parts) sb.append(p); return sb.toString();
    }
    @Benchmark public void joinToBlackhole(Blackhole bh) {
        bh.consume(String.join("", parts));       // Blackhole defeats dead-code elimination
    }
}
Common winWhy it helpsCheck before doing it
Avoid autoboxing in hot loops (Map<Long,Long>, Integer counters, boxed streams)Allocation + pointer chasing + cache missesJFR allocation profile shows java.lang.Long at the top
Right collection (ArrayList vs LinkedList, HashMap initial capacity, EnumMap, primitive collections)Locality and fewer resizesProfile shows HashMap.resize or LinkedList.get
StringBuilder with capacity for loops; String.join; avoid String.format in hot paths+= in a loop is quadratic; format parses the pattern every callOnly in loops; the JIT already handles single-expression concatenation (invokedynamic since 9)
Batch IO: JDBC batch inserts, bulk HTTP, fewer round-tripsLatency per round-trip dominates CPU work by 1000×Wall-clock profile (-e wall) shows time in socketRead
Connection/thread pooling with sane sizesCreating a connection is milliseconds; a pool borrow is microsecondsPool pending metric > 0; pool size ≈ cores × 2 + spindles for DBs, not 200
Caching with a bound and a hit-rate metricSkip the work entirelyMeasure hit rate; a 30% hit-rate cache is often a net loss
Reduce allocation rateFewer young GCs, less promotion, better cache behaviourGC log: young GCs every second → find the allocator with JFR
Interview angle: "Your benchmark says ArrayList is 3× faster but production did not change." The benchmark measured a hot, inlined, cache-resident loop; production time was in the database. Always profile the real system first: the top of the flame graph is rarely where you expected.

Pitfalls

  • Measuring in a unit test with one iteration: you timed the interpreter and class loading.
  • Averages: a 5 ms average with a 2 s p99 is a broken service. Alert on percentiles.
  • "Premature optimisation" as an excuse to never measure. Design-level decisions (N+1 queries, chatty APIs, unbounded fan-out) must be right early; micro-tuning can wait.

Likely follow-ups

  • What is on-stack replacement? (The JIT swapping an interpreted loop for compiled code mid-execution; why a long first loop still speeds up.)
  • Why does JMH fork? (A fresh JVM per trial removes profile pollution: C2 specialising for the first benchmark's types and then deoptimising in the second.)
  • What is a coordinated-omission bug? (A load generator that waits for slow responses under-samples the slow periods; use HdrHistogram / wrk2 / Gatling with a constant arrival rate.)

Java 8 vs 17: What Changed in Tuning and Diagnostics

Why interviewers ask: most teams are mid-migration, and the flags and tools you learned on 8 either changed names or were deleted. Listing the differences quickly signals current experience.

The headline: G1 replaced Parallel as default (9), unified logging (-Xlog, 9) replaced the zoo of Print* flags, JFR became free and open (11), CMS was removed (14), biased locking was disabled (15) and removed (18), and ZGC went production (15). Container awareness landed in 10 and was backported to 8u191.

Java 8Java 17Note
-XX:+PrintGCDetails -XX:+PrintGCDateStamps -Xloggc:gc.log-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptimeOld flags are rejected or ignored on 17; log format is different, so update your parsers
Parallel GC defaultG1 default (since 9)Migrating a batch job may lose throughput: set -XX:+UseParallelGC explicitly
-XX:+UseConcMarkSweepGCRemoved (14). JVM fails to start with the flagReplace with G1 (or ZGC for very low pause)
JFR commercial (-XX:+UnlockCommercialFeatures)Free in OpenJDK since 11; -XX:StartFlightRecordingThe single biggest diagnostic upgrade
jmap / jstack / jinfo as separate toolsjcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump / Thread.print / VM.flagsOld tools still exist; jcmd is the maintained path and works in the same JVM process attach
Biased locking on: uncontended synchronized almost free, but revocation pausesOff by default (15), removed (18)Some legacy code with heavy uncontended locking (old Vector/StringBuffer use) gets slightly slower; fix the code, do not re-enable
PermGen gone in 8; MaxMetaspaceSize existsSame, plus better Metaspace reclamation (Elastic Metaspace, 16)Metaspace fragmentation issues of 8–15 largely disappeared
No AppCDS (commercial in 8)AppCDS free (10), dynamic archive -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit (13), default CDS archive on (12)Startup wins for free
Container blind before 8u191UseContainerSupport default; cgroup v2 since 15Verify with jcmd VM.info "container information"
String as char[]Compact Strings (byte[] + coder, 9)Latin-1 strings use half the memory; heap dumps of 8 vs 17 are not comparable size-for-size
Helpful NPE: no-XX:+ShowCodeDetailsInExceptionMessages on by default (15)NPE message names the null variable/expression

Java 21 preview

Generational ZGC (-XX:+ZGenerational) closes most of ZGC's throughput gap; virtual threads change thread-dump reading (jcmd Thread.dump_to_file -format=json); pinned virtual threads on synchronized are the new "pool exhaustion" to know about (fixed in 24).

Likely follow-ups

  • What happens if a removed flag is passed? (JVM prints "Unrecognized VM option" and exits; add -XX:+IgnoreUnrecognizedVMOptions only as a temporary migration bridge.)
  • Which Java 8 GC-tuning advice is now harmful? (Explicit -Xmn/NewRatio with G1 disables adaptive young sizing; CMSInitiatingOccupancyFraction maps to InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent conceptually but with different semantics.)

A G1 log shows young pauses of 15 ms every 400 ms, and the heap after each pause reads 118M, 190M, 260M, 340M … over six hours with steady traffic. What is the most likely diagnosis?

c. The "after" value is the live set. A rising floor under steady load means references are being retained. b would show more frequent pauses, not a rising floor. d would show the total in parentheses growing, not the post-GC value; with -Xms = -Xmx it does not grow at all.

In a G1 log, what does Pause Young (Mixed) mean?

b. Mixed pauses are how G1 reclaims old gen incrementally after a marking cycle. a is Pause Full. c appears as the cause in parentheses (G1 Humongous Allocation), not as the pause type. d contradicts "pause".

Grafana shows heap at 55% of a 1.5 GB -Xmx, yet the pod is repeatedly restarted with exit code 137 and OOMKilled. Best first step?

d. Exit 137 is the kernel, not the JVM; the heap was fine, so total RSS (metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers, code cache, GC structures) crossed the cgroup limit. a makes it worse. b analyses the heap, which is not the problem. c increases footprint.

Which OutOfMemoryError message is usually not a memory problem at all?

a. It usually means the OS refused a thread: ulimit -u, the container's pids.max, or a thread pool leak, and the fix is a thread dump grouped by name. b is heap exhaustion, c class-metadata exhaustion, d off-heap buffer exhaustion.

In Eclipse MAT, which view most directly answers "which single object, if collected, would free the most memory?"

c. Retained size is exactly "memory freed if this object goes"; the dominator tree lists objects by it. a shallow size tells you byte[] is big, not who holds it. d also lands on arrays, the symptom rather than the owner.

A heap dump's path-to-GC-roots for a 1.7 GB HashMap ends at Thread[http-nio-8080-exec-3] → threadLocals → ThreadLocalMap$Entry. What is the bug?

b. Pool threads never die, so anything left in a ThreadLocal survives indefinitely (and may leak into the next request). c is thread-safety, unrelated. d cannot be: objects reachable from a live thread are not garbage regardless of dump mode.

Requests time out, CPU is near 0%, and a thread dump shows 199 of 200 http-nio-* threads in TIMED_WAITING inside HikariPool.getConnection. No deadlock banner. What happened, and what do you look at next?

d. Everyone is queued for a connection, so the holders are the story: they are usually blocked in JDBC IO on a slow query or an unreachable database. b adds more waiters. c would show high CPU during pauses and no such stack pattern. a is possible in theory but the evidence points elsewhere.

One instance sits at 100% CPU. top -H shows OS thread 40195 consuming it. How do you find the Java code responsible?

a. nid is the OS thread id in hex, which is the bridge from top -H to jstack. d is a valid candidate (GC threads would show as GC Thread#n at the top of top -H), but not "always". b and c are unrelated to CPU.

Practice

Scenario: latency spikes every few minutes, CPU is low

An order service (Java 17, Spring Boot, 4 GB container, -Xmx3g, G1 default) has a p99 of 40 ms most of the time, but every 3–5 minutes a burst of requests takes 1.5–2.5 s. Average CPU is 20%. The database team says query times are flat. Walk through how you diagnose and fix it, and what you would say to the interviewer at each step.

Tests: GC log reading, G1 tuning, distinguishing GC from lock/IO waitsFormat: scenario, model answer
Hint 1
Low CPU plus periodic multi-second stalls is "waiting", not "computing". The two waits that stop every request at once are a stop-the-world GC pause and a global lock. Which evidence separates them in ten seconds?
Hint 2
Correlate spike timestamps with -Xlog:gc lines. If you see Pause Full or to-space exhausted at those times, ask: why is G1 unable to keep up: undersized heap, humongous allocations, or marking starting too late?
Reveal model answer & runbook

Step 1: confirm it is a JVM-wide stall. Do all endpoints spike together, on one instance at a time? Yes → something stops the whole JVM. Candidates: GC pause, safepoint stall, a global lock. Check Micrometer jvm.gc.pause max in Grafana against the spike timestamps: if they line up, it is GC.

Step 2: read the GC log (-Xlog:gc* should already be on; if not, jcmd <pid> VM.log output=file=/logs/gc.log what=gc* enables it live). Expected findings at spike times, one of:

  • Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 2980M→2700M(3072M) 1800ms: the heap is nearly all live; G1 fell back to a Full GC. Note the "after" value: 2.7 GB live in a 3 GB heap.
  • Pause Young (Concurrent Start) (G1 Humongous Allocation) lines followed by to-space exhausted: big arrays fragment the heap.
  • Young pauses of 300–800 ms with Evacuation Failure: too many survivors being copied because the young gen is oversized or objects live just long enough to be promoted repeatedly.

Step 3: decide between "too small" and "leak". Take jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000 for a few minutes and look at the trend of O (old %) after each collection. Flat at ~85–90% → the working set is simply 2.7 GB and the heap is too tight for G1 (it needs ~20–30% headroom to avoid Full GCs). Rising steadily since restart → leak, go to the heap-dump runbook instead.

Step 4: fix for "too small" (the common case here). In order of preference:

  1. Reduce the live set: a look-up cache with no bound, a response cache holding whole entity graphs, per-request buffers retained by a static. Found via jcmd GC.class_histogram or JFR OldObjectSample.
  2. Give G1 headroom: raise the container to 6 GB and MaxRAMPercentage=70 (≈4.2 GB heap) rather than -Xmx3g in a 4 GB box, which also risks OOMKilled.
  3. Start marking earlier so mixed collections reclaim old gen before it fills: -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=35 (default 45; G1 adapts it in 17 via G1UseAdaptiveIHOP, so verify with the log whether it is actually the problem).
  4. If humongous allocations appear: raise -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=8m (or 16m) so those 3 MB byte arrays are no longer humongous; better, stop materialising 3 MB arrays (stream the response).
  5. Only if pauses are young-gen copying cost: tighten -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 and let G1 shrink the young gen; accept a few % throughput loss.

Step 5: prove it. Deploy to one instance, compare jvm.gc.pause p99 and the post-GC floor over 24 h, then roll out. Say out loud: "I would not switch to ZGC first: at 3 GB with a 40 ms p99 SLO, G1 with headroom is sufficient, and ZGC costs CPU we would rather spend on requests. ZGC becomes the answer if the SLO tightens to single-digit ms or the heap grows past ~30 GB."

If the GC log is clean at spike times: check -Xlog:safepoint for long "time to safepoint" (a huge counted loop or a JNI call), and take three thread dumps during a spike to look for a monitor everyone is BLOCKED on (a synchronized logger appender, a Random shared across threads, a lazy singleton init).

Scenario: OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space after 3 days of uptime

A notification service runs fine for about 72 hours, then dies with java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. Restarting fixes it for another three days. The team's workaround is a nightly restart. Traffic is flat. Give a complete runbook to find and fix the root cause, including the exact tools, what you expect to see, and the three most likely code-level culprits.

Tests: heap dump capture, MAT workflow, leak patterns, verificationFormat: scenario, model answer
Hint 1
Constant traffic + heap that fills over days = the live set grows with time, not load. What single graph proves that, and what flag makes sure you get evidence when it dies?
Hint 2
You do not have to wait 72 hours: a histogram diff (jcmd GC.class_histogram at hour 1 vs hour 6) shows which class count is growing. Then a dump at hour 24 is already enough for MAT to name the owner.
Reveal model answer & runbook

Step 1: confirm the shape. Plot "heap used after GC" (Micrometer jvm.memory.used sampled right after jvm.gc.pause, or the after-values from -Xlog:gc). A leak is a monotonically rising floor from restart to death, independent of request rate. If the floor tracks traffic instead, it is a sizing problem, not a leak.

Step 2: make sure the next death leaves evidence. Add -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps (persistent volume) and -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError. Both can be flipped on a live JVM: jcmd <pid> VM.set_flag HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError true.

Step 3: do not wait; find the growing class now.

jcmd $PID GC.class_histogram > h1.txt          # at t = 1 h
sleep 18000; jcmd $PID GC.class_histogram > h2.txt   # at t = 6 h
# compare instance counts for the top 30 classes; the leak grows linearly
join -j 4 <(sort -k4 h1.txt) <(sort -k4 h2.txt) | awk '{print $1, $2, $5, $5-$2}' | sort -k4 -n -r | head

Expect a domain class (say NotificationEvent) and its container (HashMap$Node, ArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap$Node, or ThreadLocalMap$Entry) growing by the same count.

Step 4: heap dump on a drained instance at ~24 h, when the leak is big enough to dominate but the dump is still small enough to analyse: jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /dumps/notif.hprof, then kubectl cp. Open in MAT (raise MAT's own -Xmx in MemoryAnalyzer.ini above the dump size).

Step 5: MAT in four clicks. (1) Leak Suspects report: usually "one instance of X occupies N% of heap". (2) Dominator tree sorted by retained size: the top entry is the owner. (3) Expand it to see the collection and a sample of its entries: are these events from three days ago? Then nothing is evicting. (4) Path to GC roots, excluding weak/soft references: the chain tells you which pattern you are looking at:

Path ends atCulpritFix
class X → static fieldStatic map/list used as cache or registry with no eviction (e.g. a de-duplication set of event ids)Caffeine with maximumSize and expireAfterWrite; or a TTL in Redis
Thread[pool-…] → threadLocalsThreadLocal per message on an executor thread, never removedremove() in finally; pass context as a parameter
EventBus / Multicaster → listeners listListener registered per subscription/websocket/scheduled job and never unregisteredUnregister on close; weak listeners
ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor → DelayedWorkQueueScheduled tasks created per request and never cancelled (retry timers, futures with timeouts that completed)setRemoveOnCancelPolicy(true); cancel on completion
Finalizer → ReferenceQueueUnclosed resources with finalizers (sockets, streams, drivers) faster than the finalizer thread drainstry-with-resources; remove finalize

Step 6: fix, then prove it with the same graph. After the fix, the after-GC floor must be flat over at least one full leak period (3 days). Remove the nightly restart only after that; the restart was hiding this and will hide the next one.

What the interviewer is probing: whether you reach for evidence (histogram diff, dump) before theories; whether you know retained vs shallow; and whether you treat the nightly restart as a smell rather than a solution.

Scenario: all requests time out, CPU idle, the process is alive

At 02:10 the payment API stops answering: every request hits the 30 s gateway timeout. The pod is running, health check /actuator/health still returns 200, CPU is 2%, heap is 40%. No deploy happened. Describe how you diagnose it in the first five minutes, the two root causes you would expect to find, and the fix for each.

Tests: thread-dump analysis, deadlock vs pool exhaustion, timeouts and bulkheadsFormat: scenario, model answer
Hint 1
Alive + idle + unresponsive = threads are waiting on something that never arrives. Take three thread dumps ten seconds apart and count states before reading stacks.
Hint 2
Two shapes: (a) the dump ends with Found one Java-level deadlock; (b) no banner, but every request thread is parked in the same borrow/take/await. Shape (b) needs a second question: what are the holders doing?
Reveal model answer & runbook

Minute 0–1: capture before you touch anything. The restart reflex destroys the evidence.

PID=$(pgrep -f payment)
for i in 1 2 3; do jcmd $PID Thread.print -l > /tmp/td$i.txt; sleep 10; done
grep -c 'State: BLOCKED' /tmp/td1.txt; grep -c 'State: WAITING\|TIMED_WAITING' /tmp/td1.txt
grep -A3 'Found one Java-level deadlock' /tmp/td1.txt
grep -B2 -A12 '"http-nio' /tmp/td1.txt | grep -m1 -A12 'State:'   # what is a typical request thread doing?

Minute 1–3: classify.

Root cause A: deadlock. The dump's last section reads Found one Java-level deadlock listing two (or more) threads each holding a monitor the other wants, e.g. Ledger.transfer locking from then to, called concurrently as (A,B) and (B,A). Only those threads are BLOCKED, but if they hold a shared resource (a DB connection, a cache lock) everyone else queues behind them, hence the total outage. The health check passes because it touches none of it. Fix: a global lock order (sort the two accounts by id and lock in that order), or one coarse lock, or tryLock(timeout) with backoff; long-term, do the transfer in a single DB transaction with row locks and no JVM-level locking.

Root cause B: pool exhaustion on a downstream (the more common one). No banner. 199 of 200 http-nio-* threads are TIMED_WAITING in HikariPool.getConnection (or PoolingHttpClientConnectionManager.leaseConnection, or Semaphore.acquire in a bulkhead). Now look at the threads that hold the 10 connections: they are RUNNABLE in SocketInputStream.socketRead0 inside the JDBC driver, i.e. waiting on the database or on a network path that silently dropped packets at 02:10 (a firewall idle timeout, a failover). With no socket read timeout, they wait forever; every new request queues behind them. Fix, layered:

  1. Immediate: restart the DB connections (kill -3 does not help; Hikari's softEvictConnections via JMX, or a rolling restart once dumps are saved).
  2. Timeouts everywhere: JDBC socketTimeout in the URL, Hikari connectionTimeout=3000, validationTimeout, maxLifetime below the firewall idle timeout; for HTTP clients, connect + read + pool-lease timeouts. A timeout converts a hang into a fast failure.
  3. Bulkheads: the health endpoint and non-DB endpoints on a separate executor, so a stuck DB does not take the whole Tomcat pool.
  4. Circuit breaker (Resilience4j) on the downstream so a dead dependency fails fast and recovers automatically.
  5. A readiness probe that exercises the DB pool (e.g. db health indicator) so Kubernetes stops sending traffic to a stuck instance, while liveness stays cheap so it does not restart-loop.

Minute 3–5: confirm across dumps. The same threads waiting on the same objects in td1, td2 and td3 confirm a hang rather than a transient burst. Also check hikaricp.connections.pending and hikaricp.connections.timeout metrics for the moment it started; it will be 02:10 and will match a DB-side or network event.

What the interviewer is probing: that you know the health check lying is expected (it does not touch the pool), that RUNNABLE in socketRead is a wait, and that the durable fix is timeouts and isolation, not a bigger pool.

Scenario: CPU at 100% on one instance out of six

Five instances of a catalogue service idle at 15% CPU; the sixth has been pinned at 100% for twenty minutes and its latency is 10× the others. Traffic is evenly balanced. Show exactly how you identify the code responsible, what the three most likely findings are, and how you would fix each.

Tests: top -H to nid mapping, flame graphs, hot-loop patternsFormat: scenario, model answer
Hint 1
Is it GC or application code? The names of the hot OS threads in top -H answer that immediately (GC Thread#, C2 CompilerThre, vs http-nio-…).
Hint 2
Once you have an OS thread id, it is printf '%x' away from the nid= field in a thread dump. Two dumps with identical RUNNABLE frames on that thread is your answer; async-profiler gives it with less ceremony.
Reveal model answer & runbook

Step 1: is the CPU in GC, JIT, or your code?

PID=$(pgrep -f catalogue)
top -H -p $PID -n 1 -b | head -20
#   PID  USER  %CPU  COMMAND
# 40195  app   99.3  http-nio-8080-e     ← application thread (Tomcat worker)
# 40011  app    1.0  GC Thread#0          ← would be the story if these were on top
# 40020  app    0.4  C2 CompilerThre

If the top entries are GC Thread#n: it is a GC death spiral (heap almost full, back-to-back collections); confirm with jstat -gcutil showing FGC climbing every second, and switch to the OOM/leak runbook. If it is C2 CompilerThre for minutes: pathological JIT (huge generated methods, thousands of lambdas); rare but real. Otherwise, it is application code on a specific thread.

Step 2: map the OS thread to a Java stack.

printf '0x%x\n' 40195            # → 0x9d03
jcmd $PID Thread.print > td1.txt; sleep 10; jcmd $PID Thread.print > td2.txt
grep -A 25 'nid=0x9d03' td1.txt td2.txt

The thread is RUNNABLE with the same top frames in both dumps and a cpu= value that grew by ~10 s between them. That frame is the culprit. For a cleaner picture, one command: ./profiler.sh -e cpu -d 30 -f /tmp/cpu.html $PID and read the widest tower in the flame graph. JFR works too: jcmd $PID JFR.start duration=60s filename=/tmp/hot.jfr, then Method Profiling in JMC.

Step 3: the three usual findings.

Top framesDiagnosisFix
java.util.regex.Matcher.match / Pattern$Loop / $GroupCurly under String.matches or a validatorCatastrophic backtracking on one unusual input (nested quantifiers like (a+)+$, or .* before an alternation) explains "one instance only": that instance received the poison requestRewrite with possessive/atomic groups or a hand parser; bound input length; pre-compile the Pattern (compiling per call is the second regex sin)
Your own code in a loop: while (!done) over a ConcurrentModificationException retry, HashMap.get in an infinite loop (a HashMap corrupted by concurrent writes, Java 7 legacy), a retry-without-backoff on a failing callHot loop / spin. A non-thread-safe HashMap written concurrently can create a cycle in a bucket that spins get forever (8+ tree bins make it rarer, not impossible in principle for other structures)ConcurrentHashMap; retry with exponential backoff and a cap; fix the termination condition
ObjectMapper.writeValueAsString / BeanSerializer, Hibernate lazy-load / toString on an entity graph, deep equals/hashCodeSerialisation of a huge or cyclic object graph (an entity with bidirectional relations, a 50 MB response) on that instance's requests@JsonIgnore/DTO projections; page the response; break cycles; log at debug, not toString of entities

Step 4: contain, then fix. Remove the instance from the load balancer (readiness probe or manual) so the other five carry traffic; save the dumps and profile; only then restart it. Add a per-request CPU/time budget where possible (request timeouts at the gateway will not stop a CPU-bound thread, so a Future.get(timeout) with cancellation, or input validation up front, is the durable defence). Add an alert on per-instance CPU deviation from the fleet median: this class of bug always hits one node first.

What the interviewer is probing: the top -H → hex → nid bridge (a canonical senior trick), knowing that one-of-N points at input-dependent bugs, and reaching for a profiler rather than guessing.

1️⃣3️⃣ Predict the Output — 24 Classic Traps

Interviewers love "what does this print?" because it tests whether you know the language spec or just the happy path. Every trap below has been run on a real JVM (Java 17 semantics); learn the rule behind each one, not the answer. Work top to bottom: the first nine are warm-ups, the middle nine are what a 45-minute screen usually asks, and the last six (Tough) are the ones that separate senior candidates.

How to attack predict-the-output questions

Why interviewers ask: a 12-line snippet can probe six language rules at once, and the way you reason aloud tells them whether you would spot the same bug in a code review.

Do not "run" the code in your head from line 1. First classify the trap: almost every snippet is built around one of about ten rules. Analogy: a radiologist does not read an X-ray pixel by pixel; they look for the handful of patterns they know are there. Say the rule out loud, then trace. If the trap is nondeterministic (threads, identity hash codes), say so explicitly and give the range of outcomes; guessing a single value is the wrong answer.

The checklist (run it in this order)

  • Static and instance initialization first. Find every static block/field and instance initializer; class init happens once, parent before child, in textual order, and a superclass constructor can call an overridden method before the subclass fields are assigned (prints 0/null/false).
  • Hunt for == on references. String literals and compile-time constants are pooled; new String is not. Integer is cached only for -128..127. equals across wrapper types (Long.equals(Integer)) is false.
  • Trace exceptions with finally. A return in finally overrides both the try's return value and any pending exception; System.exit skips finally; try-with-resources closes in reverse order and attaches close-exceptions as suppressed.
  • Overloading resolves at compile time on static types. Three phases: widening (no boxing) → boxing → varargs. null picks the most specific overload, and two unrelated candidates (String/Integer) fail to compile. Overriding is dynamic, but static methods and fields are hidden, not overridden.
  • Integer arithmetic is modular and evaluation is left-to-right. MAX_VALUE + 1 wraps, Math.abs(MIN_VALUE) is negative, casts truncate, i = i++ leaves i unchanged, and compound assignment saves the left operand before evaluating the right side.
  • Strings are immutable and + is left-associative. s.toUpperCase() without assignment does nothing; 1 + 2 + "3" is "33"; 'a' + 1 is an int.
  • Short-circuit vs eager operators. &&/|| skip the right side; &/| evaluate it always (side effects and NPEs happen). The ternary applies binary numeric promotion: true ? 1 : 2.0 is 1.0, and true ? nullInteger : 0 throws NPE.
  • Floating point and collections quirks. 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3, NaN != NaN, -0.0 == 0.0 but Double.compare disagrees; List<Integer>.remove(1) is by index; iterating while removing throws CME except when you remove the second-to-last element; streams are lazy and sorted() is a barrier.
Interview angle: when you see the trap, name it: "this is the integer-cache trap, so the first prints true and the second false, and I would never compare wrappers with == in production." Naming the rule and the fix earns more than the bare output.

Likely follow-ups

  • Which of these are compile errors rather than runtime surprises? (Ambiguous overloads with null, unreachable catch order, short s = s + 1, duplicate switch labels.)
  • How would you make this code not surprising? (Use equals/compareTo, volatile/AtomicInteger, removeIf, never call overridable methods from constructors.)
  • Which of these does a static analyser catch? (SpotBugs/ErrorProne flag == on boxed types, finally returns, self-assignment i = i++, and overridable calls in constructors.)

Practice — warm-ups

1. String pool: literals, new String, intern, final concat

String a = "java";
String b = "ja" + "va";              // two literals
String c = new String("java");
final String f = "ja";
String nf = "ja";
String d = f + "va";                 // f is final
String e = nf + "va";                // nf is not
System.out.println(a == b);
System.out.println(a == c);
System.out.println(a == c.intern());
System.out.println(a == d);
System.out.println(a == e);
System.out.println(a.equals(e));
Trap: string pool and compile-time constant folding
Hint
Ask of every expression: can javac compute it at compile time? If yes it becomes a pooled literal. A final local initialised with a literal is a constant variable; a non-final one is not.
Reveal solution

Output:

true
false
true
true
false
true

"ja" + "va" and f + "va" are constant expressions (JLS 15.29), folded by javac into the literal "java", so they share the pooled instance with a. new String("java") always allocates a fresh heap object; intern() returns the pooled one, so a == c.intern() is true. nf + "va" is computed at runtime (via invokedynamic/StringConcatFactory in Java 9+), producing a new object, so == is false while equals is true. Production rule: never compare strings with ==.

2. Integer cache and cross-type equals

Integer a = 127, b = 127;
Integer c = 128, d = 128;
System.out.println(a == b);
System.out.println(c == d);
System.out.println(c.equals(d));
Long l = 127L;
System.out.println(l.equals(127));
System.out.println(l == 127);
int x = 128; Integer y = 128;
System.out.println(x == y);
Trap: autoboxing, Integer.valueOf cache, wrapper equals
Hint
Autoboxing calls Integer.valueOf, which caches -128..127. Long.equals starts with instanceof Long. When one side of == is a primitive, the wrapper is unboxed.
Reveal solution

Output:

true
false
true
false
true
true

a == b compares two references to the same cached Integer(127); 128 is outside the cache so c and d are distinct objects (the upper bound can be raised with -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax, which is why relying on it is a bug). l.equals(127) boxes 127 to an Integer, and Long.equals returns false for anything that is not a Long. l == 127 and x == y have a primitive on one side, so the wrapper is unboxed and the numeric comparison is true.

3. i = i++ and compound assignment order

int i = 5;
i = i++;
System.out.println(i);
int x = 3;
x += x++ + ++x;
System.out.println(x);
int j = 1;
j = j++ + ++j;
System.out.println(j);
int k = 2;
int r = k++ * k++;
System.out.println(r + " " + k);
Trap: left-to-right evaluation, post/pre increment, compound assignment saving the left operand
Hint
x += expr means x = (int)(x + expr) where the old value of x is read first. i++ yields the old value and then writes i; the outer assignment writes afterwards.
Reveal solution

Output:

5
11
4
6 4

i = i++: the right side yields 5, then i becomes 6 as a side effect, then the assignment stores 5 back, so i is 5. x += x++ + ++x: the left operand is saved first (3), then x++ yields 3 (x=4), ++x yields 5, so x = 3 + (3 + 5) = 11. j++ + ++j is 1 + 3 = 4. k++ * k++ is 2 * 3 = 6 and k ends at 4. Java guarantees left-to-right operand evaluation (unlike C), so these are well defined, just unreadable.

4. Integer overflow, narrowing casts, promotion

System.out.println(Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1);
System.out.println(Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE));
System.out.println((byte) 200);
System.out.println((int) -3.99);
System.out.println('a' + 1);
System.out.println(-7 % 3);
System.out.println(1_000_000 * 1_000_000);
System.out.println(1_000_000L * 1_000_000);
byte bb = 10; bb += 5;      // compiles; bb = bb + 5 would not
System.out.println(bb);
Trap: two's-complement wraparound, narrowing, binary numeric promotion
Hint
int arithmetic is silently modulo 232; the type of a * b is decided by the operand types, not by where the result is stored. Casting to byte keeps the low 8 bits.
Reveal solution

Output:

-2147483648
-2147483648
-56
-3
98
-1
-727379968
1000000000000
15

MAX_VALUE + 1 wraps to MIN_VALUE, and Math.abs(MIN_VALUE) is still MIN_VALUE because +2147483648 does not fit (use Math.absExact or addExact to throw instead). (byte) 200 keeps the low byte: 200 − 256 = −56. Casting a double to int truncates toward zero (−3), % keeps the sign of the dividend (−1). 1_000_000 * 1_000_000 is computed in int before anything sees it, giving 1012 mod 232 interpreted as signed = −727379968; making one operand long fixes it. 'a' + 1 promotes the char to int (98). Compound operators carry an implicit cast, which is why bb += 5 compiles but bb = bb + 5 does not.

5. Floating point: equality, NaN, signed zero, division by zero

System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3);
System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2);
System.out.println(0.1f + 0.2f == 0.3f);
System.out.println(1.0 / 0);
System.out.println(Double.NaN == Double.NaN);
System.out.println(-0.0 == 0.0);
System.out.println(Double.compare(-0.0, 0.0));
System.out.println(Double.valueOf(0.0).equals(-0.0));
System.out.println((int) Double.NaN);
try { System.out.println(1 / 0); }
catch (ArithmeticException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); }
Trap: IEEE-754 rounding, == vs compare/equals, integer vs floating division by zero
Hint
Primitive == follows IEEE-754 (NaN is unequal to everything, −0.0 equals 0.0). Double.compare and Double.equals use doubleToLongBits, a total order where −0.0 < 0.0 and NaN == NaN. Only integer division by zero throws.
Reveal solution

Output:

false
0.30000000000000004
true
Infinity
false
true
-1
false
0
/ by zero

0.1 and 0.2 are not exactly representable, and their double sum rounds to a value one ulp above 0.3; in float the coarser rounding happens to land exactly on 0.3f, which is why the third line is true (never rely on that). Floating division by zero yields Infinity/NaN; integer division throws ArithmeticException: / by zero. NaN == NaN is false (use Double.isNaN), -0.0 == 0.0 is true, but Double.compare/equals distinguish them, which matters for sorting and for using doubles as HashMap keys. Casting NaN to int gives 0. Money: use BigDecimal or long cents.

6. Short-circuit &&/|| vs eager &/|

static int calls = 0;
static boolean t() { calls++; return true; }
static boolean f() { calls++; return false; }

public static void main(String[] args) {
    boolean a = f() && t();  System.out.println(a + " " + calls);
    calls = 0;
    boolean b = f() & t();   System.out.println(b + " " + calls);
    calls = 0;
    boolean c = t() || f();  System.out.println(c + " " + calls);
    int x = 5;
    if (x > 10 && x++ > 0) { }
    System.out.println(x);
    if (x > 10 & x++ > 0) { }
    System.out.println(x);
    String s = null;
    System.out.println(s != null && s.isEmpty());
    try { System.out.println(s != null & s.isEmpty()); }
    catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("NPE"); }
}
Trap: conditional vs non-short-circuit boolean operators with side effects
Hint
&& stops as soon as the result is known; & on booleans always evaluates both operands, then ANDs them.
Reveal solution

Output:

false 1
false 2
true 1
5
6
false
NPE

f() && t() never calls t() (1 call); f() & t() calls both (2). t() || f() short-circuits after the first true. The x++ after && is skipped so x stays 5; after & it runs, giving 6. The null guard s != null && s.isEmpty() is the idiom precisely because it short-circuits; with & the right side dereferences null. Note & and | on integers are bitwise operators, on booleans they are logical-but-eager.

7. char arithmetic, string concatenation order, immutability

System.out.println(1 + 2 + "3" + 4 + 5);
System.out.println("" + 1 + 2);
System.out.println('a' + 'b');
System.out.println("" + 'a' + 'b');
System.out.println('a' + 1);
System.out.println((char) ('a' + 1));
char c = 'a'; c++;
System.out.println(c);
char d = 'x'; d += 1;
System.out.println(d);
switch (c) { case 'b' -> System.out.println("bee " + (int) c); default -> System.out.println("other"); }
String s = "hi"; s.concat("!"); s.toUpperCase();
System.out.println(s);
System.out.println("hi" + null);
Trap: + is left-associative and only concatenates once a String is involved; char promotes to int; strings are immutable
Hint
Evaluate 1 + 2 + "3" + 4 + 5 strictly left to right: the first + is numeric, every later one is string concatenation. 'a' + 'b' has no String in it at all.
Reveal solution

Output:

3345
12
195
ab
98
b
b
y
bee 98
hi
hinull

1 + 2 is 3, then 3 + "3" becomes "33", and the rest appends: "3345". 'a' + 'b' is 97 + 98 = 195 because both promote to int; prefixing "" forces concatenation. 'a' + 1 is the int 98; the explicit cast (or c++/c += 1, which carry an implicit narrowing cast) gives back a char. concat and toUpperCase return new strings that are thrown away, so s is still "hi". Concatenating null prints the literal text null rather than throwing.

8. Ternary numeric promotion and unboxing NPE

System.out.println(true ? 1 : 2.0);
Object o = true ? 1 : "s";
System.out.println(o);
System.out.println(true ? 'a' : 0);
int i = 0;
System.out.println(true ? 'a' : i);
char x = 'x';
System.out.println(false ? 1 : x);
System.out.println(true ? null : 0);
Integer n = null;
try { Integer v = true ? n : 0; System.out.println(v); }
catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("NPE"); }
Trap: the type of ?: is computed from both branches before either is evaluated (JLS 15.25)
Hint
If both operands are numeric (including wrappers), binary numeric promotion applies to the whole expression, so a wrapper branch is unboxed even when it is not the branch chosen. A char paired with a constant int that fits in a char stays char; paired with an int variable it becomes int.
Reveal solution

Output:

1.0
1
a
97
x
null
NPE

true ? 1 : 2.0 has type double, so it prints 1.0. With 1 and "s" there is no numeric promotion; the type is lub(Integer, String) and the boxed 1 prints as 1. true ? 'a' : 0 is a char because 0 is a constant representable as char; with the variable i the result is promoted to int (97). false ? 1 : x is likewise char, printing x. true ? null : 0 has type Integer and prints null without unboxing. But true ? n : 0 mixes Integer and int, so the expression type is int: n is unboxed and throws even though we then assign to an Integer. This exact NPE is a classic production bug in map.get(k) != null ? map.get(k) : 0-style code.

9. Labeled break/continue and switch fallthrough vs arrow

outer:
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        if (j == 1) continue outer;
        if (i == 2) break outer;
        System.out.print(i + "" + j + " ");
    }
}
System.out.println();
int k = 2;
switch (k) {
    case 1: System.out.print("one ");
    case 2: System.out.print("two ");
    case 3: System.out.print("three "); break;
    default: System.out.print("dflt ");
}
switch (k) {
    case 1 -> System.out.print("ONE ");
    case 2 -> System.out.print("TWO ");
    default -> System.out.print("DFLT ");
}
String r = switch (k) { case 1, 2 -> "low"; default -> { yield "high"; } };
System.out.println(r);
Trap: labels target the loop, not the block; old-style case: falls through until break; arrow case -> never falls through
Hint
continue outer jumps to the next iteration of the outer loop, skipping the rest of the inner loop. In the colon-form switch, execution enters at the matching label and keeps going.
Reveal solution

Output:

00 10
two three TWO low

For i = 0 and i = 1 only j = 0 prints before continue outer; at i = 2, j = 0 reaches break outer before printing. The colon switch enters at case 2 and falls into case 3 until the break, so two three. The arrow switch executes exactly one branch (TWO). The switch expression must be exhaustive (hence default) and uses yield inside a block. In Java 17 a missing break in colon-form is still legal and silent; javac -Xlint:fallthrough warns.

Practice — the usual screen questions

10. finally overriding return, swallowing exceptions, and System.exit

static int f() { try { return 1; } finally { return 2; } }
static int g() { int x = 1; try { return x; } finally { x = 99; } }
static int h() { try { throw new RuntimeException("boom"); } finally { return 3; } }
static StringBuilder sb() {
    StringBuilder s = new StringBuilder("a");
    try { return s; } finally { s.append("b"); }
}
static void e() {
    try { System.out.print("try "); System.exit(0); }
    finally { System.out.print("finally "); }
}
public static void main(String[] args) {
    System.out.println(f());
    System.out.println(g());
    System.out.println(h());
    System.out.println(sb());
    e();
    System.out.println("unreachable?");
}
Trap: abrupt completion of finally discards the try's result; the return value is captured before finally runs
Hint
When try hits return x, the value of x is copied into the frame's return slot, then finally runs. If finally itself returns or throws, that wins and any pending exception is lost. System.exit halts the JVM; nothing else runs.
Reveal solution

Output:

2
1
3
ab
try

f(): the return 2 in finally replaces the pending return 1. g(): the value 1 was already captured, so reassigning the local afterwards changes nothing. h(): the RuntimeException is silently discarded because finally completes abruptly with a return, which is why javac -Xlint:finally warns "finally clause cannot complete normally". sb() returns a reference that was captured; the object it points to is mutated before the caller sees it, so ab. e() prints try and the JVM halts inside exit: finally does not run, no newline is printed, and "unreachable?" never appears. Only shutdown hooks run on exit.

11. try-with-resources close order, suppressed exceptions, exception thrown from finally

static class Res implements AutoCloseable {
    final String n;
    Res(String n) { this.n = n; System.out.print("open" + n + " "); }
    public void close() {
        System.out.print("close" + n + " ");
        throw new IllegalStateException("close" + n);
    }
}
public static void main(String[] args) {
    try (Res a = new Res("A"); Res b = new Res("B")) {
        throw new RuntimeException("body");
    } catch (Exception e) {
        System.out.println();
        System.out.println(e.getMessage());
        for (Throwable s : e.getSuppressed())
            System.out.println("suppressed: " + s.getMessage());
    }
    try {
        try { throw new RuntimeException("inner"); }
        finally { throw new IllegalArgumentException("from finally"); }
    } catch (RuntimeException e) {
        System.out.println(e.getMessage() + " " + e.getSuppressed().length);
    }
}
Trap: resources close in reverse declaration order; close failures are added as suppressed to the body exception; a plain finally that throws loses the original
Hint
Think of try-with-resources as: run body → close B (catch and attach) → close A (catch and attach) → rethrow the primary exception. Old-style finally has no such bookkeeping.
Reveal solution

Output:

openA openB closeB closeA
body
suppressed: closeB
suppressed: closeA
from finally 0

Both resources open in order, the body throws body, and the compiler-generated code closes b then a. Each close() throws, but because the body's exception is primary, the close exceptions are attached via addSuppressed in the order they occurred. If the body had not thrown, closeB would become the primary and closeA its suppressed exception. In the second block the old-style finally throws and the original inner is simply gone (suppressed count 0): one of the strongest arguments for try-with-resources. Related compile-time trap: catch (Exception e) before catch (IOException e) is an error ("exception has already been caught").

12. Overloading with null: most specific wins, ambiguity fails

static void m(Object o)       { System.out.println("Object"); }
static void m(CharSequence c) { System.out.println("CharSequence"); }
static void m(String s)       { System.out.println("String"); }

public static void main(String[] args) {
    m(null);
    m((Object) null);
    m("x");
    Object o = "x"; m(o);
    m(new StringBuilder());
    CharSequence cs = "x"; m(cs);
}
// What changes if we add: static void m(Integer i) { ... } ?
Trap: overload resolution happens at compile time using the static type of the argument; null is assignable to every reference type
Hint
Among applicable overloads, the compiler picks the one whose parameter type is a subtype of all the others. String ⊂ CharSequence ⊂ Object forms a chain, so there is a unique winner. String and Integer do not form a chain.
Reveal solution

Output:

String
Object
String
Object
CharSequence
CharSequence

m(null) is applicable to all three; String is the most specific. Casting to (Object) null narrows the candidate set to one. m(o) prints Object even though o holds a String, because overloading is resolved from the declared type, not the runtime type (that is the difference from overriding). StringBuilder implements CharSequence, so it picks that overload. Adding m(Integer) makes m(null) a compile error: "reference to m is ambiguous", since neither String nor Integer is more specific than the other; the other calls are unaffected.

13. Overriding vs hiding: static methods, fields, super.field

class A {
    String name = "A";
    static String who() { return "A.who"; }
    String me()   { return "A.me"; }
    String show() { return name; }
}
class B extends A {
    String name = "B";
    static String who() { return "B.who"; }
    String me()   { return "B.me"; }
    String show() { return name + "/" + super.name; }
}
A ab = new B();
System.out.println(ab.name);
System.out.println(ab.who());
System.out.println(ab.me());
System.out.println(ab.show());
System.out.println(((B) ab).name);
Trap: only instance methods dispatch on the runtime type; fields and static methods bind to the reference type
Hint
Ask for each line: is this a virtual call? Field access is never virtual. A static call through an instance expression is just A.who() with a misleading spelling. Object B physically contains two name fields.
Reveal solution

Output:

A
A.who
B.me
B/A
B

ab.name is resolved against the static type A, so it reads A's field. ab.who() compiles to A.who() (static methods are hidden, not overridden; many IDEs warn about calling them via an instance). ab.me() is a virtual call and runs B.me. Inside B.show(), unqualified name is B's field and super.name reaches the hidden A field, so both values are alive in the same object. Casting to (B) just changes which field the compiler picks. This is why Effective Java says never hide fields, and why @Override on a static method is a compile error.

14. equals without hashCode, and mutating a HashMap key

class P {                       // equals only
    int x; P(int x) { this.x = x; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof P p && p.x == x; }
}
class K {                       // equals + hashCode, but mutable
    int x; K(int x) { this.x = x; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof K k && k.x == x; }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Integer.hashCode(x); }
}
Set<P> s = new HashSet<>();
s.add(new P(1)); s.add(new P(1));
System.out.println(s.size());
System.out.println(new ArrayList<>(s).contains(new P(1)));
Map<K, String> m = new HashMap<>();
K k = new K(1); m.put(k, "v");
k.x = 2;
System.out.println(m.get(k));
System.out.println(m.get(new K(1)));
System.out.println(m.size() + " " + m.containsValue("v"));
Trap: hash-based collections locate the bucket by hashCode first, then call equals only within that bucket
Hint
Two P(1) objects are equals but have different identity hash codes, so they land in different buckets. After k.x = 2 the entry still sits in the bucket computed from hash(1), but the stored key now says 2.
Reveal solution

Output:

2
true
null
null
1 true

HashSet keeps both P(1)s because their default identity hash codes differ (technically they could collide, in which case equals would dedupe; do not rely on it). ArrayList.contains uses only equals, so it finds the match. For the map: m.get(k) hashes the mutated key to bucket for 2, which is empty; m.get(new K(1)) looks in the right bucket but the stored key's equals now compares 2 against 1 and fails. The entry is stranded: unreachable by key, yet still counted and still found by containsValue. Rules: always override hashCode with equals (records and Objects.hash make it trivial) and keep map keys immutable.

15. List<Integer>.remove(int) vs remove(Object)

List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5));
list.remove(1);
list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1));
list.remove((Integer) 4);
System.out.println(list);
System.out.println(list.remove(Integer.valueOf(9)));
System.out.println(list.indexOf(5));
try { list.remove(7); }
catch (IndexOutOfBoundsException e) { System.out.println("IOOBE"); }
Set<Integer> set = new HashSet<>(List.of(1, 2, 3));
set.remove(1);
System.out.println(set);
Trap: overload resolution prefers the exact primitive match remove(int index) over boxing to remove(Object)
Hint
Phase 1 of overload resolution (no boxing) already finds remove(int) applicable for an int literal, so boxing is never considered. Set has only remove(Object).
Reveal solution

Output:

[3, 5]
false
1
IOOBE
[2, 3]

list.remove(1) removes index 1 (the value 2), leaving [1, 3, 4, 5]; the boxed calls remove the values 1 and 4, leaving [3, 5]. remove(Object) returns boolean (false for absent 9) while remove(int) returns the removed element and throws IndexOutOfBoundsException for a bad index. Set.remove(1) has no index overload, so 1 boxes and the value is removed. In production write list.remove(Integer.valueOf(v)) or removeIf to make intent explicit.

16. Arrays.asList is a fixed-size view; List.of is fully immutable and null-hostile

String[] arr = {"a", "b", "c"};
List<String> view = Arrays.asList(arr);
view.set(0, "z");
System.out.println(arr[0]);
arr[1] = "y";
System.out.println(view);
try { view.add("d"); }
catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("UOE add"); }
List<String> imm = List.of("a", "b");
try { imm.set(0, "z"); }
catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("UOE set"); }
try { imm.contains(null); }
catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("NPE contains"); }
int[] ints = {1, 2, 3};
System.out.println(Arrays.asList(ints).size());
List<Integer> mod = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(1, 2));
mod.add(3);
System.out.println(mod);
Trap: Arrays.asList returns java.util.Arrays$ArrayList, not java.util.ArrayList; generics do not apply to primitive arrays
Hint
The asList view writes straight through to the backing array, supports set, but has no way to grow. List.of rejects nulls even in queries. int[] is not T[], so asList(ints) is a one-element List<int[]>.
Reveal solution

Output:

z
[z, y, c]
UOE add
UOE set
NPE contains
1
[1, 2, 3]

view.set mutates arr[0], and writing arr[1] is visible through the view: they share storage. add/remove throw because the size cannot change. List.of throws on every mutator and, less known, on contains(null) and indexOf(null). Arrays.asList(ints) with a primitive array infers T = int[], giving size 1. Copying into new ArrayList<>(...) is the standard way to get a growable list. Interview follow-up: Collections.unmodifiableList is a live read-only view of a mutable list, whereas List.copyOf snapshots.

17. Optional.orElse is eager, orElseGet is lazy

static String load(String tag) { System.out.print("load(" + tag + ") "); return "db"; }

public static void main(String[] args) {
    Optional<String> present = Optional.of("cache");
    Optional<String> empty = Optional.empty();
    System.out.println(present.orElse(load("A")));
    System.out.println(present.orElseGet(() -> load("B")));
    System.out.println(empty.orElse(load("C")));
    System.out.println(empty.orElseGet(() -> load("D")));
    System.out.println(present.map(s -> null).isPresent());
    System.out.println(Optional.ofNullable(null).or(() -> Optional.of("x")).get());
    empty.ifPresentOrElse(v -> System.out.println("v"), () -> System.out.println("none"));
    try { Optional.of(null); }
    catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("NPE"); }
}
Trap: method arguments are evaluated before the call; a Supplier defers that evaluation
Hint
orElse(load("A")) must compute load("A") to have something to pass, whether or not the Optional is present. map wraps a null result with ofNullable.
Reveal solution

Output:

load(A) cache
cache
load(C) db
load(D) db
false
x
none
NPE

Line 1 runs load("A") (printing its tag) and then discards the result because the value is present. Line 2 never invokes the supplier. When the Optional is empty both variants call load. map(s -> null) yields an empty Optional rather than an Optional containing null; or (Java 9) supplies an alternative Optional; ifPresentOrElse (Java 9) runs the second action. Optional.of(null) throws immediately; use ofNullable. Production consequence: orElse(repository.findDefault()) issues a query on every call, a real and common performance bug.

18. Records: compact constructor normalisation, array components, sealed + pattern matching (17-safe)

record Range(int lo, int hi) {
    Range { if (lo > hi) { int t = lo; lo = hi; hi = t; } }   // compact ctor
}
record Tag(int[] vals) {}
sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Sq {}
record Circle(double r) implements Shape {}
record Sq(double s) implements Shape {}

static String describe(Shape s) {
    if (s instanceof Circle c && c.r() > 10) return "big circle";
    if (s instanceof Circle c) return "circle r=" + c.r();
    return "square " + ((Sq) s).s();
}
public static void main(String[] args) {
    Range r = new Range(9, 3);
    System.out.println(r);
    System.out.println(r.equals(new Range(3, 9)) + " " + (r.hashCode() == new Range(3, 9).hashCode()));
    System.out.println(new Tag(new int[]{1}).equals(new Tag(new int[]{1})));
    int[] a = {1};
    System.out.println(new Tag(a).equals(new Tag(a)));
    System.out.println(describe(new Circle(12)));
    System.out.println(describe(new Circle(2)));
    System.out.println(describe(new Sq(4)));
    Object o = 42;
    if (o instanceof Integer i && i > 40) System.out.println("big " + i);
    if (!(o instanceof String str)) System.out.println("not string"); else System.out.println(str.length());
}
Trap: generated equals/hashCode use ==-style comparison per component for arrays; compact constructors assign the (possibly rewritten) parameters at the end
Hint
Record equals compares components with Objects.equals for references, which for arrays is identity. Pattern variables introduced by instanceof are in scope where the match is definitely true, including the else of a negated test.
Reveal solution

Output:

Range[lo=3, hi=9]
true true
false
true
big circle
circle r=2.0
square 4.0
big 42
not string

The compact constructor swaps the parameters; the implicit field assignment happens afterwards, so the record is stored normalised and equals a directly built Range(3, 9) with the same hash. Tag with two distinct int[] instances is not equal even though the contents match (override equals/hashCode with Arrays.equals/Arrays.hashCode, or use a List); the same array instance is equal. describe uses the Java 16 instanceof pattern with a guard expressed as &&, which is the 17-safe form; the pattern-matching switch with case Circle c when c.r() > 10 only became standard in Java 21 (preview in 17). Flow scoping puts str in scope in the else branch of the negated test.

Practice — Tough

19. Overloading phases: widening beats boxing beats varargs

static void m(long x)    { System.out.println("long"); }
static void m(Integer x) { System.out.println("Integer"); }
static void m(int... xs) { System.out.println("varargs"); }
static void m(Object o)  { System.out.println("Object"); }
static void n(Integer x) { System.out.println("n:Integer"); }
static void n(Object o)  { System.out.println("n:Object"); }
static void o(Long x)    { System.out.println("o:Long"); }
static void o(Object x)  { System.out.println("o:Object"); }
static void v(int... xs) { System.out.println("v:varargs"); }

public static void main(String[] args) {
    int i = 7;
    m(i);
    m((Integer) i);
    byte b = 1;  m(b);
    char c = 'c'; m(c);
    n(5);
    o(5);
    short s = 1; n(s);
    v();
}
Trap: JLS 15.12.2 resolves in three strict phases: (1) subtyping/primitive widening only, (2) allow boxing/unboxing, (3) allow varargs; a later phase is consulted only if the earlier one found nothing
Hint
Boxing converts int to Integer only, never to Long; short boxes to Short. After boxing, ordinary subtyping applies (Integer is an Object). Among phase-1 candidates, the most specific primitive wins.
Reveal solution

Output:

long
Integer
long
long
n:Integer
o:Object
n:Object
v:varargs

m(i): phase 1 finds m(long) applicable via widening, so m(Integer) (boxing) and m(int...) (varargs) are never considered. The explicit cast makes m(Integer) an exact match. byte and char both widen to long in phase 1. n(5) has no phase-1 candidate (Object is not a supertype of a primitive), so phase 2 boxes to Integer, and Integer is more specific than Object. o(5) boxes to Integer, which is not a Long, so Object wins. n(s): a short boxes to Short, not Integer, so again Object. v() with no arguments is legal and receives an empty array. If you delete m(long) the first call prints Integer; delete that too and it prints varargs.

20. Initialization order across classes, plus an overridable call from the parent constructor

class Config {
    static String NAME = init("Config.NAME");
    static String init(String s) { System.out.println("init " + s); return s; }
}
class Base {
    static String B = Config.NAME + " via Base";     // touches another class
    static { System.out.println("Base static"); }
    Base() { System.out.println("Base ctor"); describe(); }
    void describe() { System.out.println("Base.describe"); }
}
class Derived extends Base {
    static { System.out.println("Derived static"); }
    int size = 42;
    String label = "L";
    Derived() { System.out.println("Derived ctor size=" + size); }
    @Override void describe() { System.out.println("Derived.describe size=" + size + " label=" + label); }
}
class Lazy { static { System.out.println("Lazy static"); } static final int K = 7; static int v = 1; }

public static void main(String[] args) {
    System.out.println("main start");
    System.out.println(Lazy.K);
    Lazy l = null;
    System.out.println("still no Lazy init");
    new Derived();
    System.out.println(Lazy.v);
}
Trap: class initialization is lazy and recursive (JLS 12.4); object construction runs the superclass constructor before subclass field initializers
Hint
Reading a compile-time constant (static final primitive/String with a constant initializer) is inlined and does not initialize the class; declaring a variable of the type does nothing either. When Derived.describe runs from Base(), Derived's field initializers have not executed yet.
Reveal solution

Output:

main start
7
still no Lazy init
init Config.NAME
Base static
Derived static
Base ctor
Derived.describe size=0 label=null
Derived ctor size=42
Lazy static
1

Lazy.K is a constant variable, so javac inlines 7 into main and Lazy is untouched; Lazy l = null is not an active use either. new Derived() triggers initialization of Derived, which first initializes its superclass Base; Base's static field initializer reads Config.NAME (a non-constant static), so Config initializes right there, printing init Config.NAME before Base static. Then Derived static. Construction: Base() runs, calls the virtual describe(), which dispatches to Derived.describe while size and label still hold the JVM defaults 0 and null; only after Base() returns do Derived's initializers run, so its own constructor sees 42. Finally reading the non-constant Lazy.v initializes Lazy. Rule: constructors must not call overridable methods (make them final/private, or use a factory).

21. ConcurrentModificationException: when it fires, and the second-to-last quirk

List<String> a = new ArrayList<>(List.of("x", "y", "z"));
try { for (String s : a) if (s.equals("x")) a.remove(s); }
catch (ConcurrentModificationException e) { System.out.println("CME " + a); }

List<String> b = new ArrayList<>(List.of("x", "y", "z"));
for (String s : b) if (s.equals("y")) b.remove(s);
System.out.println(b);

List<String> c = new ArrayList<>(List.of("x", "y", "z"));
try { for (String s : c) if (s.equals("z")) c.remove(s); }
catch (ConcurrentModificationException e) { System.out.println("CME " + c); }

List<String> d = new ArrayList<>(List.of("x", "y", "z"));
d.removeIf(s -> s.equals("z"));
System.out.println(d);

List<String> e = new ArrayList<>(List.of("x", "y", "z"));
for (Iterator<String> it = e.iterator(); it.hasNext(); )
    if (it.next().equals("x")) it.remove();
System.out.println(e);
Trap: ArrayList.Itr.hasNext() is cursor != size and only next() checks modCount
Hint
Track two numbers after each removal: the iterator's cursor (index of the next element) and the list's size. If they happen to be equal, hasNext() returns false and the loop ends without ever calling next(), so no check runs.
Reveal solution

Output:

CME [y, z]
[x, z]
CME [x, y]
[x, y]
[y, z]

Case a: after removing x, cursor = 1 and size = 2, so hasNext() is true and the next next() sees modCount != expectedModCount and throws; the removal itself already happened, hence [y, z]. Case b: removing the second-to-last element leaves cursor = 2 = size, hasNext() returns false, and the loop exits silently: no exception, and z was never visited. Case c: removing the last element gives cursor = 3, size = 2; they differ, so next() runs and throws. removeIf and Iterator.remove keep expectedModCount in sync and are the correct tools. The check is best-effort (fail-fast), which is exactly why "it worked in my test" is not evidence; CopyOnWriteArrayList iterates a snapshot and never throws.

22. Stream laziness, vertical execution, sorted barrier, and the Java 9+ count() shortcut

Stream.of("c", "a", "b").peek(s -> System.out.print("peek " + s + " ")).map(String::toUpperCase);
System.out.println("no terminal");

Stream.of("c", "a", "b").peek(s -> System.out.print("p1:" + s + " ")).map(String::toUpperCase)
      .peek(s -> System.out.print("p2:" + s + " ")).forEach(s -> System.out.print("out:" + s + " "));
System.out.println();

Stream.of("c", "a", "b").peek(s -> System.out.print("p:" + s + " ")).sorted()
      .forEach(s -> System.out.print("out:" + s + " "));
System.out.println();

List<Integer> r = Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5).peek(i -> System.out.print(i + " "))
      .filter(i -> i % 2 == 1).limit(2).collect(Collectors.toList());
System.out.println(r);

long n = IntStream.range(0, 3).map(i -> { System.out.print("m" + i + " "); return i; }).count();
System.out.println(n);

Stream<String> s = Stream.of("x"); s.forEach(v -> {});
try { s.forEach(v -> {}); } catch (IllegalStateException ex) { System.out.println("ISE"); }
Trap: intermediate ops build a pipeline; nothing runs until a terminal op, elements flow one at a time, stateful ops buffer everything, and short-circuits stop early
Hint
Picture each element travelling the whole pipeline before the next starts (vertical), except where a stateful op like sorted() must see all elements first (horizontal barrier). Since Java 9, count() may skip the pipeline entirely if the size is known from the source and no op changes it.
Reveal solution

Output:

no terminal
p1:c p2:C out:C p1:a p2:A out:A p1:b p2:B out:B
