p:c p:a p:b out:a out:b out:c
1 2 3 [1, 3]
3
ISE

First pipeline: no terminal operation, so peek never executes. Second: elements are processed vertically, so the p1/p2/out messages interleave per element rather than "all p1 then all p2". Third: sorted() must consume everything before emitting anything, so all p: prints precede all out: prints. Fourth: limit(2) short-circuits after the second odd number, so 4 and 5 are never pulled from the source. Fifth: IntStream.range is SIZED and map preserves size, so Java 9+ count() returns 3 without executing map; nothing is printed before 3 (Java 8 would print m0 m1 m2). Last: a stream is single-use; the second terminal op throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. Never rely on peek for side effects.

23. this escapes the parent constructor: toString before the subclass exists

class Account {
    private final String id;
    Account(String id) {
        this.id = id;
        System.out.println("created " + this);          // virtual toString()
    }
    @Override public String toString() { return "Account[" + id + "]"; }
}
class Savings extends Account {
    private double rate = 2.5;
    private final String tier;
    private final String kind = "SAV";                   // compile-time constant
    Savings(String id) {
        super(id);
        this.tier = "gold";
        System.out.println("after super " + this);
    }
    @Override public String toString() {
        return super.toString() + " rate=" + rate + " tier=" + tier + " kind=" + kind;
    }
}
new Savings("S1");
Trap: string concatenation calls the runtime type's toString; subclass field initializers run only after super(...) returns; constant fields are inlined
Hint
Inside Account(String), this is already a Savings. Which of rate, tier, kind have been assigned at that moment? One of them is not a field read at all.
Reveal solution

Output:

created Account[S1] rate=0.0 tier=null kind=SAV
after super Account[S1] rate=2.5 tier=gold kind=SAV

"created " + this invokes Savings.toString() (dynamic dispatch) while the object is still in the middle of Account's constructor: rate shows the default 0.0 (its initializer = 2.5 runs after super()), and tier is null even though it is final. kind prints SAV in both lines because a final String initialised with a literal is a constant variable and javac inlines it at every use site; it is never actually read from the object. The same "partially constructed object" leak happens when a constructor registers this as a listener or publishes it to another thread. Fixes: keep constructors free of overridable calls and this-publication; log after construction or in a static factory.

24. Threads: run() vs start(), a racy counter, and the non-volatile flag that never stops

static boolean running = true;     // NOT volatile
static int counter = 0;            // NOT atomic

public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
    Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println("in " + Thread.currentThread().getName()), "worker");
    t.run();
    t.start();
    t.join();

    Thread[] ts = new Thread[4];
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
        ts[i] = new Thread(() -> { for (int j = 0; j < 100_000; j++) counter++; });
        ts[i].start();
    }
    for (Thread th : ts) th.join();
    System.out.println(counter);

    Thread spinner = new Thread(() -> { while (running) { } System.out.println("stopped"); });
    spinner.setDaemon(true);
    spinner.start();
    Thread.sleep(200);
    running = false;
    spinner.join(1000);
    System.out.println(spinner.isAlive() ? "still spinning" : "done");
}
Trap: run() is an ordinary call; counter++ is read-modify-write; without volatile the JIT may hoist the flag read out of the loop (no happens-before edge)
Hint
Three separate facts: which thread executes a plain method call; what a lost update looks like; and what the Java Memory Model does not promise about a plain field read in a loop.
Reveal solution

Output (nondeterministic; one representative run):

in main
in worker
158173
still spinning

Lines 1 and 2 are deterministic: t.run() executes the lambda synchronously on the calling thread, so it prints in main; t.start() creates the OS thread and prints in worker. Line 3 is any value from well under 400 000 up to exactly 400 000: counter++ is three bytecodes (load, add, store), and interleavings lose updates; 400 000 appears only if the threads happen not to overlap (small loops often finish before the next thread starts, which fools people into thinking it is safe). Line 4 is either stopped then done, or just still spinning: after the C2 JIT compiles the hot loop it is entitled to read running once and spin on a register forever, because no synchronization action links the write in main to the read. On a typical HotSpot run it prints still spinning; with -Xint or a debugger attached it usually prints stopped. The daemon flag is what lets the JVM exit anyway. Fixes: volatile boolean running (or AtomicBoolean/interrupts) and AtomicInteger/LongAdder or synchronized for the counter. In the interview, say explicitly "this is nondeterministic" and give the range; do not commit to one number.

What does this print?
String s = "a"; s += "b"; String t = "ab"; System.out.println(s == t);

b. s += "b" is evaluated at runtime (s is not a constant variable), producing a new heap string that is not interned, so it is a different object from the literal "ab". a would be correct only for "a" + "b" written as literals, which javac folds; c is not an error, just a bug.

What does this print?
Integer a = 100, b = 100, c = 1000, d = 1000;
System.out.println((a == b) + " " + (c == d) + " " + c.equals(d));

c. 100 is inside the Integer.valueOf cache (-128..127), so a and b are the same object; 1000 is not, so c == d compares two distinct objects. equals compares values. a is what you get only if -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax is raised, which is why d's equals result can never be false here.

What does System.out.println(f()); print?
static int f() { try { throw new RuntimeException(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { return 1; } finally { System.out.print("F"); } }

b. The catch block's return 1 captures the value, then finally runs and prints F, and only then does f() return so println prints 1. a reverses the order (println cannot print until f() has returned); c would need a return in finally that overrides the value; d ignores the catch.

What does this print?
List<Integer> l = new ArrayList<>(List.of(10, 20, 30));
l.remove(1); l.remove(Integer.valueOf(10)); System.out.println(l);

d. remove(1) binds to remove(int index) (exact primitive match, phase 1) and removes 20, leaving [10, 30]; remove(Integer.valueOf(10)) binds to remove(Object) and removes the value 10. b stops after the first call; a assumes the first call removed the value 1 (which is absent and would simply return false).

What does this print?
Stream.of(3, 1, 2).sorted().peek(x -> System.out.print(x)).findFirst();

c. findFirst() is a short-circuiting terminal operation, so the pipeline does run (d is wrong). sorted() buffers all three elements, sorts them, then starts pushing downstream in order; after 1 reaches findFirst the downstream signals cancellation, so peek never sees 2 or 3. a would be the output if peek came before sorted; b if the terminal op were forEach.

What does new C(); print?
class P { P() { hello(); } void hello() { System.out.print("P"); } }
class C extends P { String n = "C"; @Override void hello() { System.out.print(n); } }

b. C's implicit constructor calls super() first; inside P() the virtual call dispatches to C.hello(), but n = "C" has not run yet, so the field holds its default null. c ignores dynamic dispatch, a ignores construction order, and d is only a static-analysis warning, not a compile error. If n were final String n = "C", the constant would be inlined and it would print C.
